The attainment of the Path-knowledge that realizes the Four Noble Truths is known to depend on practice (paṭipatti). That practice, indeed, has its foundation in learning (pariyatti). For those who strive diligently in learning, because they know the rules, commentaries, and examples (sadda-lakkhana) that mark the grammar, there is no intense confusion regarding letters and words. Because of the absence of confusion regarding letters and words, the wise in the Teacher's Dispensation understand the meaning of the Pali. Through understanding the meaning of the Pali, the wise in the Teacher's Dispensation, free from laziness, rightly practice the path beginning with the purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi). Having practiced rightly, through the pure practice of virtue and so forth, they reach the noble Supramundane Dhamma. Since one can reach the Supramundane Dhamma by striving in learning, let those who desire that benefit (from knowing grammar to reaching the Supramundane) well-receive and learn this Saddanīti treatise which I shall speak, relying on the pure methods of the wise. In this Saddanīti treatise, I shall clearly explain roots (dhātu), forms derived from roots, euphony (sandhi) along with the rules, various types of nouns (nāma) and so forth, the inflection of words (vibhatti), and the methods of the Pali, in various ways for the benefit of the Dispensation.

## 1. Analysis of Verbs with Conjugational Signs

Among those (topics like roots and forms), in what sense is it called a 'dhātu' (root)? It is called 'dhātu' because it bears its own inherent meaning (the meaning of existence). It is also called 'dhātu' because, through connection with an excellence of meaning, it bears a meaning other than its inherent one. It is also called 'dhātu' because it bears a special meaning when connected with any of the twenty prefixes (upasaggas) that cause a distinction in meaning. It is also called 'dhātu' because it is borne (noted) by the wise in various ways, such as "This is the meaning of this root; this is the suffix that follows it." The wise effect the accomplishment of words by means of this root.
3:
Just as an object made of iron, bronze, etc., is fashioned by the elements (dhātu) of iron, bronze, etc., the wise who are skilled in the accomplishment of words fashion the accomplishment of words by means of this primary element (pakati) such as 'bhū'; therefore, it is called 'dhātu'. Thus, the meaning of the word 'dhātu' should first be understood. 

The word 'dhātu' is recognized as feminine (itthiliṅga) in the Buddha's view, as masculine (pulliṅga) in the view of the grammarians, and as both genders in the view of Kaccāyana. 

Or rather, in the Buddha's view, in the phrase 'tato gotami dhātūni', the word 'dhātu' exists with a change of gender (as neuter), like the word 'pabbata' in the phrase 'pabbatāni vanāni ca'. However, one should not say here that it is a neuter designation because it refers to bones; for even when referring to bones, it is seen in the feminine gender as 'dhātuyo'. 

Words such as 'bhū' are roots (dhātavo). They are, for example: bhū, i, ku, ke, takka, taka, taki, suka, and so forth. By group (gaṇa), they are of eight kinds: Bhūvādi-gaṇa, Rudhādi-gaṇa, Divādi-gaṇa, Svādi-gaṇa, Kiyādi-gaṇa, Gahādi-gaṇa, Tanādi-gaṇa, and Curādi-gaṇa. 

Now, I shall show the suffixes called 'vikaraṇa' for those roots. Suffixes are of many varieties because they occur in nouns (nāma), primary derivatives (kita), compounds (samāsa), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and verbs (ākhyāta). Briefly, however, there are only two types: nominal suffixes (nāma-paccaya) and verbal suffixes (ākhyāta-paccaya). 

Verbal suffixes are again of two types: vikaraṇa suffixes and no-vikaraṇa suffixes. Among them, the vikaraṇa suffixes are of seventeen kinds starting with 'a', and if excluding those already counted, they are of fifteen kinds. No-vikaraṇa suffixes are of many kinds, such as kha, cha, sa, etc. 

Those words which assist in the formation of a word, or which clarify or do not clarify a specific meaning, or which are to be elided or not elided, are called suffixes (paccaya). They are called 'paccaya' because they arise depending on various causes. Or, they are called 'paccaya' because the accomplishment of a word arises depending on them, or because the accomplishment of a word arises from this word.
4:
The analysis of the suffixes associated with nouns will be clearly explained in the section on nouns (Nāmakappa). Therefore, that analysis of noun suffixes will not be detailed here in this section on verbs (Ākhyātakappa). However, the analysis of the suffixes known as vikaraṇa will be detailed in the section on verbs.

Among these many suffixes, it should be noted that "these are the vikaraṇa suffixes." How so? After roots of the bhūvādi group, the suffix -a occurs in the sense of the agent (kattar). After roots of the rudhādi group, the suffixes -a, -i, -ī, -e, and -o occur in the sense of the agent, and there is also the insertion of the niggahīta (nasal) in the initial and middle positions. From the divādi group, the suffix -ya; from the svādi group, the suffixes -ṇu, -ṇā, and -uṇā; from the kiyādi group, the suffix -nā; from the gahādi group, the suffixes -ppa and -ṇhā; from the tanādi group, the suffixes -o and -yira; and from the curādi group, the suffixes -ṇe and -ṇaya occur in the sense of the agent.

The suffixes -a, -i, -e, -o, -ya, as well as -ṇu, -ṇā, -uṇā, -nā, -ppa, -ṇhā, -yira, -ṇe, and -ṇaya, are said to be fifteen in number, including those not previously mentioned in earlier rules (suttas). These suffixes should be known as those named vikaraṇa.

The eight groups of roots associated with these stated vikaraṇa suffixes and other suffixes are of great benefit in the suttas. Among those groups of roots, this bhūvādi group is one. The root bhū occurs in the sense of existence (satta). Between transitive roots (sakammika) and intransitive roots (akammika), this root bhū is an intransitive (akammika) root. It is not a transitive root like the other root bhū which expresses the sense of reaching (patti) in such terms as "dhammabhūto." This root bhū becomes a transitive (sakammika) root only when associated with prefixes (upasagga) such as pari- and abhi-. Even when associated with prefixes and particles (nipāta) such as upa-, parā-, and pātu-, it does not become a transitive root. Therefore, the forms derived from this root bhū should be known in two ways: as intransitive words (akammaka) and transitive words (sakammaka).

## Description of Verb Phrases of the Simple Agent

Among the transitive and intransitive words derived from the root 'bhū', whether connected with prefixes and particles or not, these 13 words—bhavati, ubbhavati, samubbhavati, pabhavati, parābhavati, sambhavati, vibhavati, bhoti, sambhoti, vibhoti, pātubhavati, pātubbhavati, pātubhoti—are intransitive words (akammaka). Among these intransitive words, 'pātu' is a particle (nipāta). Just as the particles 'āvi' and 'tiro' in words like 'āvibhavati' (becomes manifest) and 'tirobhavati' (disappears) create a distinction in meaning for the verbal word derived from the root 'bhū', so too does 'pātu' create a distinction in meaning for verbal words like 'pātubhavati', but it does not establish transitivity (sakammaka-bhāva). Words like 'u' and so forth are prefixes (upasaggas). These prefixes create a distinction in meaning, but they do not establish transitivity. Those words whose meaning is not to be connected with an object (kamma) are called intransitive (akammaka). The meaning of intransitive words should be explained according to their transitive or intransitive nature as appropriate.

These 14 words—paribhoti, paribhavati, abhibhoti, abhibhavati, adhibhoti, adhibhavati, atibhoti, atibhavati, anubhoti, anubhavati, samanubhoti, samanubhavati, abhisambhoti, abhisambhavati—are transitive words (sakammaka). In these words, 'pari' and so forth are prefixes. These prefixes, such as 'pari', create distinctions like 'oppressing' for the verbal words derived from the root 'bhū' (e.g., paribhoti) and also establish transitivity towards an object such as 'another person'. Those words whose meaning is to be connected with an object are called transitive (sakammaka). The meaning of transitive words should be explained according to their transitive nature, and in some places, also according to an intransitive nature. Thus are the verb phrases of the simple agent. This is the brief exposition (uddesa).

In that brief exposition, the word 'bhavati' has the meanings: occurs, exists, is manifest, or acquires its own form. The word 'ubbhavati' means: arises or acquires its own form. The word 'samubbhavati' means: well-arises or acquires its own form. The word 'pabhavati' means: occurs or originates. Alternatively, 'pabhavati' means: flows from somewhere, occurs without interruption, or spreads to various places. 'Parābhavati' means: reaches ruin, encounters misfortune, or reaches non-prosperity. 'Sambhavati' means: occurs well, or reaches growth, development, and abundance. 'Vibhavati' means: is cut off, perishes, or is distorted; or, it means occurs specifically or is fulfilled. These words 'bhoti, sambhoti, vibhoti'...
6:
These words 'bhavati', 'sambhavati', and 'vibhavati' have identical detailed explanations in their respective order. 'Pātubhavati' means it becomes manifest, it is seen, it is known, it appears clearly. These words 'pātubbhavati' and 'pātubhoti' have the same detailed explanation as 'pātubhavati'. Thus, in explaining the meaning of intransitive (akammaka) words, one should understand the method of defining them through transitive (sakammaka) or intransitive (akammaka) functions as appropriate. The same applies to other intransitive words that will follow.

In the seven pairs (duka) starting with 'paribhoti', the two words in each pair have identical meanings in their respective order; therefore, I shall explain them by taking them in pairs. Among those pairs, 'paribhoti' and 'paribhavati' mean one harms another, oppresses, or else despises and looks down upon. 'Abhibhoti' and 'abhibhavati' mean one overcomes another, crushes. 'Adhibhoti' and 'adhibhavati' mean one exists by trampling over another, bringing them under one's control. 'Atibhoti' and 'atibhavati' mean one exists by surpassing another. 'Anubhoti' and 'anubhavati' mean one experiences pleasure and pain, partakes of them, or is one who habitually experiences pleasure and pain. 'Samanubhoti' and 'samanubhavati' mean one experiences pleasure and pain well, partakes of them well, or is one who habitually experiences pleasure and pain well. 'Abhisambhoti' and 'abhisambhavati' mean one overcomes another, crushes. Thus, one should understand the method of defining the meaning of transitive (sakammaka) words through transitive functions. In some places, however, they are defined through intransitive functions, such as defining 'gacchati' as 'pavattati'. The same applies to other transitive words that will follow.

In expressing the verb of a pure agent (suddhakattu) based on all roots, the suffix 'a' occurs after the Bhūvādi group.

## This is the explanation of pure agent verb forms (suddhakattu-kriyāpada).

## Explanation of causative agent verb forms (hetukattu-kriyāpada)

'Bhāveti', 'vibhāveti', 'sambhāveti', 'paribhāveti'—thus are the causative agent verb forms. The meaning of these words should be taken through the single-object (ekakammaka) function.
7:
should be taken. However, the meaning of the latter word (paribhāveti) should also be taken through the double-object (dvikammaka) function. 'Paribhāvāpeti', 'abhibhāvāpeti', and 'anubhāvāpeti' are also causative agent verb forms. The meaning of these words should be taken through the double-object function. Thus, causative agent verb forms should be known in two ways, and other words should also be noted.

Among those words, 'bhāveti' means a person develops some dhamma that should be developed, associates with it, and practices it frequently. Or else, 'bhāveti' means one causes to increase. 'Vibhāveti' means one specifically develops something that should be developed, or develops it in various ways, causes it to increase. Or else, 'vibhāveti' means one makes it non-existent, causes it to disappear. 'Sambhāveti' means one praises the virtue of someone, makes it well-known, or extols it. 'Paribhāveti' means one causes something that should be developed to increase all around. Thus, the meaning should be taken through the single-object function. Or else, 'paribhāveti' means one perfumes an object that should be perfumed, causes it to take the scent. Thus, the meaning should also be taken through the double-object function. 'Paribhāvāpeti' means a person causes another person to harm an enemy. Or else, 'paribhāvāpeti' means one causes shame, or causes one to be known as inferior. 'Abhibhāvāpeti' means a person causes another person to overcome or oppress an enemy. 'Anubhāvāpeti' means a person causes another person to experience or partake of prosperity.

When associated with a causative agent, while remaining in a non-principal state,
The word that accomplishes the action of this (the one being caused) and indicates (that person) in the Teaching,
Usually appears in the form of the instrumental case (karaṇavacana).
This statement is said with reference to the place where the causative suffix (kārita) is associated in the verb (ākhyāta).
8:
A wise person skilled in usage should demonstrate by bringing forth causative instances in nouns such as 'bodhetā' and words such as 'they even cause [them] to be eaten by dogs'.

In that (causative context), this instrumental case (tatiyā-vibhatti) indicates the sense of the object (kamma). The accusative case (dutiyā-vibhatti) and genitive case (chaṭṭhī-vibhatti), which also indicate the sense of the object, should also be applied. How? In saying 'paribhāvāpeti', it should be applied as 'a person causes the person who is the enemy to be ashamed' or 'a person causes the enemy of the person to be ashamed'. The remaining words should also be shown according to the method. Thus, all these instrumental, accusative, and genitive cases only indicate the sense of the object. Therefore, the meaning should be taken through the double-object function.

## This is the explanation of causative agent (hetukattu) verb forms.

## Explanation of passive verb forms (kamma-kriyāpada)

'Bhaviyate', 'vibhaviyate', 'paribhaviyate', 'abhibhaviyate', 'anubhaviyate', 'paribhūyate', 'abhibhūyate', 'anubhūyate'—thus are the passive verb forms. Alternatively, they occur as 'bhaviyyate', 'vibhaviyyate', 'paribhaviyyate', 'abhibhaviyyate', 'anubhaviyyate', 'paribhuyyate', 'abhibhuyyate', 'anubhuyyate'. In this context, only the passive verb forms (kamma-kriyāpada) should be applied as reflexive-passive (kammakattu) verb forms. In truth, reflexive-passive verb forms cannot be obtained separately.

Among those (passive verb forms), 'bhaviyate' means that something which should be developed is developed, associated with, or practiced frequently by a person. Or else, 'bhaviyate' means it is caused to increase. 'Vibhaviyate' means that something which should be specifically developed is specifically developed or specifically brought into being by a person.
9:
Or it is increased or made to grow in various ways. Or 'vibhaviyate' means it is not increased; it is made to disappear. 'Paribhaviyate' means the enemy is oppressed or harmed by a person. Or 'paribhaviyate' means it is despised or disregarded. 'Abhibhaviyate' means the enemy is overcome or crushed by a person. 'Anubhaviyate' means prosperity is experienced or enjoyed by a person. The three terms beginning with 'paribhūyate' have the same descriptive meaning as the three terms beginning with 'paribhaviyate'.

The remaining terms are similar to those already mentioned. A word that is presented by taking the object (kamma) as primary is called a word expressing the sense of the object (kammattha). Therefore, even if the agent (kattā) is shown in the singular, if the object is spoken of in the plural, the verb of the object is seen to have a plural ending. If it is spoken of in the singular, it has a singular ending. Similarly, even if the agent is shown in the plural, if the object is spoken of in the singular, the verb of the object is seen to have a singular ending. If it is spoken of in the plural, it has a plural ending. How? It is as follows: "The Dhamma is developed by the monk," "The Dhammas are developed by the monk," "The Dhamma is developed by the monks," "The Dhammas are developed by the monks." In this way, the usage should be applied to all passive verbs.

In a passive verb expressing the sense of the object, where the object itself is conceived as the agent, that word is called a word expressing the sense of the reflexive passive (kammakattu). That word cannot be obtained separately from the passive verb. The following is the construction of the usage to clarify the meaning in this context of the reflexive passive: A fool who speaks ill, although he is oppressed by others because of that, he himself oppresses (himself). An evildoer, although he is oppressed by the hell-wardens in hell, because he himself did such a deed, he himself overcomes and oppresses (himself). In this matter, in such cases as "Water is drunk by itself," "The mat is made by itself"...

## This is the explanation of passive verbs.

## Explanation of impersonal verbs (bhāva)

Bhūyate, bhaviyate, ubbhawiyate—thus are the impersonal verbs of bhāva. Alternatively, they are bhuyyate, bhaviyyate, ubbhawiyyate. Just as in those impersonal verbs, the meaning of the word ṭhīyate is desired to be stated as ṭhānaṃ (standing) by the power of bhāva, so too the meaning of words like bhūyate should be desired to be stated as bhavanaṃ (becoming) by the power of bhāva.

Just as one desires the application of the genitive case (chaṭṭhī) when connecting with nouns ending in primary suffixes (kitanta) that express bhāva, such as ṭhānaṃ, ṭhiti, and bhavanaṃ, one should not desire the application of the genitive case when connecting with finite verbs (ākhyāta) that express bhāva, such as ṭhīyate and bhūyate. This is because finite verbs cannot be connected with words ending in the genitive case that occur in the sense of a relation (sambandha).

In a usage where a verb is made to have the same nature as a passive verb and is presented without an object, and the word expressing the agent is presented in either the nominative case (paccatta) or the instrumental case (karaṇa), that verb in that usage expresses the sense of bhāva. It is true that bhāva (state/action) does not occur without depending on an agent in every way. Even though it occurs depending on an agent, what is called bhāva is merely the meaning of the root, such as becoming, cutting, or cooking, without the admixture of the agent.

Grammarians, however, in the domain of bhāva such as ṭhīyate and bhūyate, use only the instrumental case (karaṇa), as in the passage: "Should it not be that by one who has gone forth, there should be proper dressing, proper robing, and being endowed with proper conduct?" Therefore, in their view, it should be connected with the instrumental case as: "tena ubbhawiyate" (it is become by him).

According to the Buddha's intention, however, it should be connected only with the nominative case (paccatta), as in "so bhūyate" and so on. This is because the teacher Venerable Dhammapāla in the Saccasaṅkhepa, the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) in the Niddesa Pāḷi, and the Blessed One in the Dhajagga Sutta uttered the bhāva word in dependence on the nominative case.
11:
In the Saccasaṅkhepa, it is explicitly stated in the nominative case that the connection of the word "bhūyate" expresses bhāva (becoming).

Because it is found in the Niddesa Pāḷi as "rūpaṃ vibhoti vibhaviyyati" (matter is free, matter would be free), the nominative case is more stable (than the instrumental or genitive).

Similarly, because it is found in the Pāḷi of the Dhajagga Sutta spoken by the Sage himself as "so pahīyissati" (that fear will disappear), the nominative case is stable.

Due to the power of the perfections (pāramī) from the bodies of the Great Sages (Buddhas), the teachings that emerge are not without benefit like Sanskrit and other languages, but they accomplish the benefit up to Nibbāna.

It is our desire that, upon seeing the nominative case, one should apply the three persons (purisa) and the singular and plural numbers (vacana) in the active voice (parassapada) and so on.

Therefore, it should be connected in accordance with the Buddha's word as: "rūpaṃ vibhaviyyati, rūpāni vibhaviyyanti, tvaṃ vibhaviyyasi, tumhe vibhaviyyatha, ahaṃ vibhaviyyāmi, mayaṃ vibhaviyyāma, rūpaṃ vibhaviyyate, rūpāni vibhaviyyante," and so on. Here is the clarification of the term:

The term "vibhaviyyati" is similar to a passive term, but it is not a passive term, nor is it a reflexive passive (kammakattu) term, etc.

If this term were a passive term, the nominative case would indicate the object, and the instrumental case indicating the agent would have to be mentioned.

If it were a reflexive passive term like the word "pīyate", it would be a transitive verb. However, this is not so; it only shows the meaning "becomes".

If it were an active term like the word "vibhavati", it would stand without the "ya" suffix. However, this term does not stand without the "ya" suffix.

In the group of roots beginning with bhū (bhūvādi-gaṇa), the "ya" suffix is not prescribed in the active sense (kattar). Only in the group of roots beginning with div (divādi-gaṇa) is the "ya" suffix spoken of in the active sense.
12:
The root *bhū* is not found among the group of roots belonging to the *Divādi* class. It is found only in the *Bhūvādi* and *Curādi* classes. Therefore, in words such as "*vibhaviyyati*," wise ones who understand the natural linguistics (*nirutti*) should know that the suffix '*ya*' occurs only in the sense of *bhāva* (state/action).

Having clearly defined the characteristics of the *bhāva-kāraka* (impersonal/stative voice) here, I shall now demonstrate it; listen to my words with respect.

In the example "*Tisso gacchati*" (Tissa goes), the verbal form of the agent (*gacchati*) expresses the agent Tissa in its own form. In the example "*Dhammo desiyati*" (The Dhamma is taught), the verbal form of the object (*desiyati*) expresses the object *Dhamma* in its own form. Both the agent and the object are manifest because they are expressed in their own forms.

Similarly, the *bhāva* term such as "*vibhaviyyati*" does not express the *kāraka* named *bhāva* in its own form. It only expresses the agent, which is a substance (*dabba*), in its own form. Although it expresses the agent, that *bhāva* term expresses that *bhāva* (the state/manner) which is dependent on the agent. That excellent state is made manifest by the suffix '*ya*'.

Because that which is called *bhāva* does not exist as the state of being an agent, therefore only the agent stands in the place of *bhāva* as the state of being an agent.

If this is so, how can *bhāva* be designated as an 'agent' in such cases as "*Sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi*" (There was a gathering of disciples)? If this is asked—it is because the occurrence of the dependent *bhāva* is by the power of the *kārakas* which are its support; thus, the designation of *bhāva* as 'agent' is established even in the place of the agent.

Just as in the *kārakas* called agent and object, which are the supports of an action, the 'seat' (*āsana*) and the 'pot' (*thālī*) that carry (the action) are conceived as the "basis of the action (*kriyādhāra*)"; in the same way, the wise, although showing the agent which is the support of the *bhāva*, designate the *bhāva* term as "the term that expresses *bhāva*."
13:
Some teachers say that because bhāva (state/action), which is not a substance (adabba), is a single entity, only the singular of the third person (pathamapurisa) occurs in bhāva. Their words are not authoritative when compared to the Pali scriptures. This is because the text "Those defiling states will be abandoned" (te saṅkilesikā dhammā pahīyissanti) is found in the Pali scriptures. Therefore, we shall say this: We prefer that it should be desired to be associated with all three persons and both numbers, just by seeing the nominative case (paṭhamāvibhatti). A verb in bhāva is very difficult to see in the Pali scriptures. Therefore, I have spoken this much about the means of grasping the verb in that bhāva.

## This is the explanation of the verbs of bhāva.

Thus, verbs arising from the root bhū have been explained in various ways in four types: suddhakattu (pure agent), hetukattu (causal agent), kamma (patient/object), and bhāva (state/action); or five types including kammakattu (reflexive/middle). These are mentioned separately to show the variety of usage according to the variety of bhāva for worldly people. In terms of meaning, there are only three types according to the three kārakas: kamma, kattu, and bhāva. Because the causal agent (hetukattā) is included as a part of the kāraka called pure agent (suddhakattā). Similarly, the kammakattā is included in the kammakāraka. But bhāva (state/action) is distinct. Although that bhāva is manifold as going, cooking, cutting, etc., by its nature as an action, it is a different kāraka without division. Even so, because it depends on substance (dabba), it is divided according to the division of substance. Therefore, in the Pali scriptures, a word expressing bhāva is also seen ending in the plural. In the verbal form (ākhyāta), the usage of bhāvakāraka follows the method of linguistics (nirutti), but in terms of meaning, the status of bhāva as a kāraka is not possible. That bhāva...
14:
(That verbal *bhāva*) does not produce any object, nor is it the cause of the action. In truth, only being the cause of an action is the characteristic of a *kāraka*. Thus, the status of *bhāva* as a *kāraka* is not obtained either in the primary sense or in a figurative sense. Even though it is not obtained (in those senses), that *bhāva* is called a *kāraka* because it is merely the act of doing (*karaṇa*). Indeed, *karaṇa* is called *kāra* (doing), that *kāra* itself is the action (*kriyā*), and that action itself is the *kāraka*; thus should the status of *bhāva* as a *kāraka* be understood.

However, because only being the cause of an action is the characteristic of a *kāraka*, grammarians, setting aside the designation "*bhāva-kāraka*" for nouns that have *kāraka* characteristics, use designations such as "*kattu-kāraka*" and "*kamma-kāraka*" for the six entities: agent (*kattu*), object (*kamma*), instrument (*karaṇa*), recipient (*sampadāna*), ablative (*apādāna*), and locative (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus, there are three *kārakas*: the *bhāva-kāraka* mentioned according to the method of grammar, and the two *kārakas* of *kamma* and *kattu*. The verbal form (*ākhyāta*) that expresses them also has three *kārakas*.

Intending this very meaning, the great grammarians who see the method of natural linguistics have said:
"That which has three times, three persons, expresses an action, has three *kārakas*, lacks gender, and has two numbers—that is called an *ākhyāta* (verb)."

In this matter of the verb, some grammarians definitely desire the occurrence of the *attano-pada* endings in the *bhāva* and *kamma* senses; therefore, to demonstrate the view of those teachers, we have shown the verbal forms of *bhāva* and *kamma* both in brief and in detail by way of the *attano-pada*. However, all these verbal forms with three *kārakas* should be applied by one who desires the full range of verbal forms by way of both *parassa-pada* and *attano-pada*. Indeed, in the Pali scriptures and so forth, verbal forms with three *kārakas* exist in two ways: by way of *parassa-pada* and *attano-pada*.

What are those two? For example: The Blessed One was staying (*viharati*) at Sāvatthī. Those skilled in concentration and jhāna pay homage (*vandanti*) to the Leader of the World. Wisdom is called (*vuccati*) '*mona*'. Because of the realization of the goal, the steadfast one is called (*pavuccati*) a wise man. For a person practicing in what way does form disappear (*vibhoti*) or is it made to disappear (*vibhaviyyati*)?
15:
That (fear, etc.) will disappear. Gold placed on a crimson blanket shines and glows. The worshiper receives honor. Women desiring sons receive such a son as they prayed for. One who is unattached and endowed with the quality of tādi is called a brahma. Fire and so forth should arise only in the past. That (fear, etc.) might disappear or might not disappear; thus it stands in two ways. Here, this is the classification of the Pāḷi text:

All verbal words with three kārakas are mostly seen in the three Piṭakas in connection with Parassapada.
Words connected with Attanopada are very few in prose (cuṇṇiya), but very many in verses (gāthā).
Others (Parassapada) are seen to be very numerous in both verses and prose; thus it should be shown.

The description (niddesa) of those various words like ti, anti, etc., should be joined according to their respective numbers (vacana). Thus, verbal words with three kārakas should be known by their form, classification, and description.

## Now, I shall state the decision on the root bhū by way of those without prefixes and intransitive, etc.:

The root bhū is explained as: without prefix and intransitive, with prefix and intransitive, and with prefix and transitive.
I say this excluding the sense of 'attaining' and 'experiencing' in such phrases as "dhamma-bhūto bhutvā".
In this sense, taking it as without prefix and transitive, it is known specifically as fourfold.
The root bhū which is without prefix and intransitive, or with prefix and intransitive, becomes mono-transitive (ekakamma) when the causative (kārita) suffix is present.
16:
"He cultivates wholesome Dhamma, he specially cultivates"—these examples in this Dispensation should be shown by the wise who know the Dispensation.

How should a wise man know that a root with both a prefix and an object becomes bi-transitive (dvikamma) when the causative suffix is present?

Men cause men to oppress living beings. A man causes a man to experience prosperity—thus it should be known.

"This word is called transitive, this word is called intransitive"—how should we know this [distinction] in detail? Please tell us more.

How could I speak in full detail? I will speak well in part; listen well to my words as I speak.

The word called 'verb' (ākhyāta) is said to have two divisions: transitive and intransitive. Thus the wise should explain.

Among those two, in the usage of a word, if the action accomplished by the agent cannot exist without an object, that word is called transitive.

Indeed, when someone says "cooks" (pacati), it is understood as (cooking) rice or some other thing.

But in the usage of a word where the action is understood as devoid of an object, that word is determined as intransitive.

When someone says "Devadatta stands" (tiṭṭhati), only the standing is the object of knowledge; nothing that is an object (kamma) is the object of knowledge.

In that usage, the wise explain that the transitive word shows both the agent and the object appropriately.

Examples such as "The man cooks rice", "The rice is cooked by itself" (or "The rice cooks itself") should be understood appropriately; this method applies even where not explicitly stated.
17:
The word called intransitive (akammaka) shows the agent and the state (bhāva) appropriately; thus the wise should observe.

In this word "stands" (tiṭṭhati), it indicates the agent named 'state' (bhāva). In the word "stands near" (upaṭṭhīyati), this same method applies even if not explicitly stated.

Knowing transitive and intransitive thus, the wise should apply them. One should also know the tri-transitive (tikammaka) when the causative suffix is present in roots like kar (to do).

"The man causes the person to make a gold bracelet" and "The man causes the men to carry the chariot to the village."

In this root bhū, this method (tri-transitive) is not obtained. Therefore, in this root bhū, only the bi-transitive (dvikamma) word is explained.

Such a method is not evident in the Pāḷi (canonical texts). I have explained it thus only according to the opinion of some teachers.

And here, the text "The king causes that person to undergo various punishments" exists; that text should be well-explained in the description (niddesa).

By bringing in the remaining object "by men", the wise should explain well because of seeing the text "they cause [them] to be bitten even by dogs."

One who knows this method should apply it according to the Pāḷi: "The man causes the gold bracelet to be made by the person."

Here, only the conjugational signs (vikkaraṇa-paccaya) are mentioned in their own form. This is to show the occurrence of those conjugational signs in their respective groups (gaṇa), and to let the wise know "this root occurs in this group" through those conjugational signs, not to let them know through other suffixes.

The reason is that the suffix prescribed for the state (bhāva) and the object (kamma) occurs fully in all eight groups of roots.
18:
In order to prevent confusion for students regarding the forms (rūpa) arising from the root bhū, I have explained various methods in this section.

In the world, those students who lack effort and are not skilled in verbal words with various vikaraṇa suffixes,
Even if they are wise, they have lingering doubts when they encounter verbal words.
Therefore, a wise person who delights in the welfare of oneself and others and has firm love for the Dispensation (Sāsana),
Should make an effort, desiring to become exceptionally sharp in the usage of those verbal words.

## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the proficiency of the wise in the sequences of words of the Three Pitakas along with the Commentaries having nine factors,
## The first chapter, named the Analysis of Verbs with Vikaraṇa Suffixes (Savikaraṇākhyātavibhāga), is finished.

## 2. Bhavatikriyāpadamālāvibhāga

After this first chapter, I shall continue to speak of the sequence of verbs (kriyāpadakkama) which increases the wisdom of students and explains the suffixes (vibhatti), etc.

In that sequence of verbs, there are suffixes such as ti, etc., which indicate the verbal characteristics of an ākhyāta word. Those suffixes are of eight types according to the times: vattamānā (present), pañcamī (imperative/optative), sattamī (potential), parokkhā (perfect), hiyattanī (imperfect), ajjatanī (aorist), bhavissantī (future), and kālātipatti (conditional).

Among those eight, these suffixes—ti, anti, si, tha, mi, ma, te, ante, se, vhe, e, mhe—are called vattamānā suffixes.

These suffixes—tu, antu, hi, tha, mi, ma, taṃ, antaṃ, su, vho, e, āmase—are called pañcamī suffixes.
19:
eyya, eyyuṃ, eyyāsi, eyyātha, eyyāmi, eyyāma, etha, eraṃ, etho, eyyāvho, eyyaṃ, eyyāmhe—these suffixes are called Sattamī suffixes.

a, u, e, ttha, aṃ, ma, ttha, re, ttho, vho, iṃ, mhe—these suffixes are called Parokkhā suffixes.

ā, ū, o, ttha, aṃ, mā, ttha, tthuṃ, se, vhaṃ, iṃ, mhase—these suffixes are called Hiyyattanī suffixes.

ī, uṃ, o, ttha, iṃ, mā, ā, ū, se, vhaṃ, aṃ, mhe—these suffixes are called Ajjattanī suffixes.

ssati, ssanti, ssasi, ssatha, ssāmi, ssāma, ssate, ssante, ssase, ssavhe, ssaṃ, ssāmhe—these suffixes are called Bhavissantī suffixes.

ssā, ssaṃsu, sse, ssatha, ssaṃ, ssāmā, ssatha, ssisu, ssase, ssavhe, ssiṃ, ssāmhase—these suffixes are called Kālātipatti suffixes.

Among all these suffixes, the first six words in each set are called Parassapada. The latter six words in each set are called Attanopada. In this regard, Parassapada consists of six for Vattamānā, six for Pañcamī, six for Sattamī, six for Parokkhā, six for Hiyyattanī, six for Ajjattanī, six for Bhavissantī, and six for Kālātipatti, making forty-eight varieties. Similarly, the other Attanopada also consist of forty-eight varieties. When all these suffixes are combined, there are ninety-six varieties.

The pairs of words in Parassapada and Attanopada are called Paṭhamapurisa, Majjhimapurisa, and Uttamapurisa. These persons occur as four each in Vattamānā and other suffixes; by the power of the eight groups of suffixes, they total thirty-two in measure.
20:
Among the pairs of words, the first word is called Ekavacana (singular), and the second word is called Bahuvacana (plural). Among those suffixes, the words ti, anti, si, tha, mi, ma of the Vattamānā suffixes are called Parassapada. The words te, ante, se, vhe, e, mhe are called Attanopada. Also, within Parassapada and Attanopada, ti and anti are Paṭhamapurisa; si and tha are Majjhimapurisa; mi and ma are Uttamapurisa. te and ante are Paṭhamapurisa; se and vhe are Majjhimapurisa; e and mhe are Uttamapurisa.

Among the Paṭhamapurisa, Majjhimapurisa, and Uttamapurisa, 'ti' is Ekavacana and 'anti' is Bahuvacana; thus, Ekavacana and Bahuvacana should be understood in order. Just as in these Vattamānā suffixes, the Parassapada, Attanopada, Paṭhamapurisa, Majjhimapurisa, Uttamapurisa, Ekavacana, and Bahuvacana should also be understood in the remaining suffixes.

Among those suffixes, for what reason is it called 'Vibhatti'? It is called Vibhatti because it divides (vibhajati) the meaning of the root by the power of time, etc. Or, by the power of encompassing all suffixes along with the nominal suffixes such as 'si', it is called Vibhatti because it divides meanings such as self-interest (sakattha) and other-interest (parattha). Or, it is called Vibhatti because it divides the cases (kāraka) such as Kamma by the power of Ekavacana and Bahuvacana. It is also called Vibhatti because it is to be divided by wisdom. It is also called Vibhatti because meanings are divided by this suffix. Or else, although there are expressions without suffixes in the Buddha's Dispensation, since the meaning of all words cannot be shown without suffixes, it is called Vibhatti because the wise approach and serve (bhajanti) that word in a distinctive or various manner. We shall explain the characteristics of such expressions without suffixes along with examples and illustrations.

An expression without suffix is found in nouns.
It should be understood that it is not found in verbs—this is the example here:
Nigrodhova mahārukkho, (The banyan tree is like a great tree),
Thera vādānamuttamo. (The doctrine of the Elders is the best among doctrines).
Anūnaṃ anadhikañca, (Neither deficient nor excessive),
Kevalaṃ jinasāsanaṃ. (The pure Dispensation of the Victor [is thus shown]).
21:
In that verse, the word 'Thera' is an expression without suffix (avibhattika-niddesa). It is called 'Thera' because it belongs to the Elders such as the Venerable Mahākassapa. What is that which belongs to the Elders? It is the doctrine (vāda). It should be understood that Theravāda is superior to other doctrines such as the Mahāsaṅghika.

'Your whole body is of golden hue,' in such nouns also,
An expression without suffix should be accepted by those skilled in the method.

Does an expression without suffix not also appear in verbs?
If some objector were to say so in the example, 'O friend, eat, drink' (Bho khāda piva).

If it were so, according to that objector's view,
Words such as 'Bhikkhu' and 'Bho purisa' would also be without suffixes; but they are not so.

Words such as 'Bhikkhu' and 'Bho purisa' are expressed by the elision of the 'si' suffix, which is named 'ga'.
Similarly, words such as 'khāda' are expressed by the elision of the 'hi' suffix.

Thus, an expression without suffix is not found in verbs; it is found only in nouns. Even in nouns, in the passage 'Aṭṭha ca puggala dhammadasā te,' the shortening of 'puggala' should be understood as being for the sake of the metre (chanda). It should not be regarded as an expression without suffix, like the expression 'Kakusandha' in the passage 'Kakusandho koṇāgamano ca kassapo.' However, in the passage 'Bhikkhu nisinne mātugāmo upanisinno vā hoti upanipanno vā,' the word 'Bhikkhu' has the meaning of 'Bhikkhumhi' (in the monk); therefore, it is appropriate to call it a Nominative (Paṭhamā) in the place of a Locative (Sattamī), or an expression with an unseen suffix. As for the word 'puggala,' because it has a shortening made for the sake of the metre, it is not appropriate to say that such words belong to the category of expressions without suffixes.

Among those words, 'Parassapadāni' means words that represent the meaning of another (parassa). Here, although there is the meaning of oneself in the Uttamapurisa, the term 'Attanopada' is not applied.
22:
Although the persons called Uttama (First Person) have their own meaning, because other words that do not have their own meaning are numerous, ancient teachers applied the term Parassapada to these Uttama-purisa by the power of those numerous words. Words that represent one's own meaning are called Attanopada. In these Attanopada, although the Paṭhamapurisa (Third Person) and Majjhimapurisa (Second Person) have the meaning of others, the term Parassapada is not applied to them.

Even if these Paṭhamapurisa and Majjhimapurisa have the meaning of others, the name Attanopada for other words that have their own meaning is correctly and clearly established; also, because the term Attanopada for these Uttamapurisa, Paṭhamapurisa, and Majjhimapurisa is an ancient designation; and furthermore, to eliminate the fault of mixing Parassapada and Attanopada, this term Attanopada is always applied. Since ancient teachers created many names such as Parassapada in this context of verbal suffixes (ākhyāta-vibhatti), those names should be known as ancient names. Therefore, in this context, we do not search for the derivative meaning (vigraha) of the three persons such as Paṭhamapurisa. This is because ancient teachers established the name 'Purisa' for suffixes such as 'ti' by tradition (rūḷhī).

Between the Singular (ekavacana) and the Plural (bahuvacana), a word that expresses a single meaning is called Singular. A word that expresses many meanings is called Plural. Alternatively, even if there are many meanings, expressing them as one, as if they were a single meaning unified by the mind through the power of a collective (samudāya) or through the power of a genus (jāti), is also called Singular. Expressing an object, which is designated by the name of its locus but depends on many things, as one by the power of its locus is also called Singular. Expressing many meanings as Singular through a single characteristic is also called Singular. Even when there are not many meanings, expressing a single meaning as many through self-respect, non-delimitation, the method of the matrix (mātikā) and its connection, questioning and similarity, association with many thoughts, or the power of many objects, is called Plural. Furthermore, expressing a single meaning, such as the residence or the son of many princes or citizens, as many through tradition (rūḷhī) is also called Plural. Expressing a single meaning as many by the power of designating it together with another meaning...
23:
...because it expresses many meanings, it is also called Plural (bahuvacana). Even if there is a single meaning, expressing it as one through the power of a collective (samudāya) or through the power of a genus (jāti) is also called Singular (ekavacana). Expressing an object, which is designated by the name of its locus but depends on many meanings, as one by the power of its locus is also called Singular. Even if it is a single meaning, expressing it as many through the power of specific objects or specific functions is also called Plural.

Thus, by these reasons, the Singular occurs for a single meaning or for that which is like a single meaning. The Plural occurs for many meanings or for that which is like many meanings. Puthuvacana and Anekavacana are also names for this Plural.

One who seeks the meaning of the Dispensation (Sāsana) should understand this meaning of the numbers (vacana) through the power of noun suffixes and verbal suffixes.

Therefore, to make that meaning known, I shall here present verbal examples together with nominal examples. "The king comes, my friend comes, one mind," etc., are Singular usages for a single meaning. "The kings come, my friends come, I do not hate both sons, two, three," etc., are Plural usages for many meanings.

"That army is large, many people are confident, let all people not despise you, she is superior to the group of women, I gave a pair of cloths to the Buddha, Monks, I will preach the two dhammas to you, a person should certainly have great love and confidence in the Triple Gem, the community of monks (bhikkhu-saṅgha), the body of troops, the assembly of devas, the group of noble ones," etc., and "a group of two, a group of three," etc., are Singular usages for many meanings by the power of a collective (samudāya).

In some places, even in such cases, Plural usages are seen. For instance: "Honored by the groups of relatives, the assemblies of devas have gathered, all those assemblies of devas, two communities of devas," etc.
24:
"Three pairs, four nines," and such usages are also evident. These usages should be understood as Plural usages by the power of many collectives, even though the collective itself is usually expressed in the Singular. When grouped together, they are included in the Plural of many meanings, or they are included separately. Therefore, the name of these usages should be known as "Plural considering many collectives" (bahusamudāyāpekkha-bahuvacana).

"One should not kill a living being, the crop is abundant," etc., are usages of the Singular for many meanings by the power of genus (jāti). It can also be said to be the use of the Singular for many meanings by the power of the common nature of those beings.

"The white elephant honored by the country, the city of Sāvatthī was faithful and confident," etc., are Singular usages for many meanings occurring by the power of the locus and expressed by the name of the locus.

"The three characteristics, the wholesome and the unwholesome, mind-and-matter arises because of consciousness, the six sense bases arise because of mind-and-matter, the Dhamma-Vinaya, the Gandhabba deities named Cittasena and Sena, when there is no inclination there is no coming and going, when there is no coming and going there is no passing away and rebirth," etc., are usages of the Singular for many meanings by the characteristic of unity (ekattalakkhaṇa).

"Thus we understand, it is our nature, what should we say to Meghiya who is saying 'I wish to practice meditation'?" etc., are usages of the Plural for a single meaning by the power of self-reference (atta).

"Those people said to that monk, 'Venerable sir, please eat (plural form),' I, being a human among humans, gave seats to the visiting monks," etc., are usages of the Plural for a single meaning by the power of showing respect (garukāra).
25:
“Appaccayā dhammā, Asaṅkhatā dhammā” and such expressions are usages of the plural number (bahuvacana) for a single meaning (Nibbāna), either by way of not delimiting [the extent] or by way of an indefinite number.

Some teachers also say, “The plural is used by way of falling into the flow of the teaching (desanāsota)”; that statement should not be accepted. This is because the Tathāgata does not teach the Dhamma while lacking mindfulness and clear comprehension. Furthermore, the reasoning is not evident: to say that “the Teacher, while teaching the unconditioned (appaccaya) and other states in these three instances—the Mātikā, the question, and the answer—repeatedly falls into the flow of the teaching by way of the plural.”

“Katame dhammā appaccayā” and such expressions are usages of the plural for a single meaning by way of the method of connecting the Mātikā with the question.

“Ime dhammā appaccayā” and such expressions are usages of the plural for a single meaning by way of the method of connecting the question with the answer.

“Katame dhammā no parāmāsā, [excluding those states, what are the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states?]” and such expressions are usages of the plural for a single meaning by way of similarity with the question.

“Monks, there are other states, deep, difficult to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of reasoning, subtle, to be experienced by the wise, which the Tathāgata, having realized for himself with direct knowledge, makes known.” This expression is the usage of the plural for a single meaning by way of association with many consciousnesses and having many objects.

On one occasion, the Blessed One was staying in the Sakyan country, at Kapilavatthu, in the Great Wood (Mahāvana)...
26:
“O Pajāpati (Sīvalidevī), there are sons of the Videhans, named Dīghāvu, who increase the country. They will rule in Mithilā.” Such words are usages of the plural for a single meaning—namely, the residence of many Sakyan princes or being the sons of many Videhans—by way of conventional usage (rūḷhī).

“He addressed Sāriputta and Moggallāna: ‘Go, Sāriputta [and Moggallāna], go to Kīṭāgiri and perform the act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma) from Kīṭāgiri for the monks named Assaji and Punabbhasuka; these are your co-residents (saddhivihārika).’” The sentence, “O sons of good family... you are tigers (vyagghā); go, return to your usual place,” and so on, are usages of the plural for a single meaning by way of expressing one meaning together with another.

“The couches (mañca) make a clamor” and so on, are usages of the plural for a single meaning by way of the plurality of those who depend on it (i.e., the people on the couches).

“The four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)”—this example is the usage of the plural for a single meaning by way of the distinction of objects, namely: body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena.

“The four right efforts (sammappadhāna)”—this example is the usage of the plural for a single meaning by way of the distinction of functions, such as preventing the arising of unarisen unwholesome states.

In the aforementioned discourse, there are five kinds of singular number (ekavacana): singular in a single meaning, singular in reference to a collective, singular in reference to a genus (jāti), singular in reference to what depends on that genus, and singular as a characteristic of unity. Among these five, the singular in reference to a genus should be understood as the singular in reference to a general (sāmañña) meaning.

There are fifteen kinds of plural number (bahuvacana): plural in many meanings, plural in reference to many collectives, plural in reference to oneself, plural in reference to an object of respect, plural without delimitation, plural by way of connecting the Mātikā with the question, plural by way of connecting the question with the answer, plural similar to the question, plural by way of association with the four great functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge and having many objects, plural based on residence, plural based on being a son, plural by way of expressing [meanings] together...
27:
...plural in reference to what depends on it, plural by way of distinction of objects, and plural by way of distinction of functions. Thus, all singular and plural numbers are summarized in twenty ways. Herein is the determination of the Pali:

The singular occurs in a single meaning, and the other (plural) occurs in the other (many meanings).
There are also the singular of collective, genus, and the characteristic of unity.
These are mostly seen in the Pali of the Piṭakas along with the Commentaries.

As for the plural used for a person of respect or for oneself,
It is rare in the Pali, but frequent in the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries.
Therefore, the singular alone is frequent in the Pali.
The following is an example here for [the singular used for] a person of respect or for oneself:

“Homage to you, O hero among men! Homage to you, O supreme man!
Having come to your teaching, I have reached the deathless state (Nibbāna).”

The wise one who contemplates syllables should know that such Pali passages are numerous in the Dispensation of the Conqueror (Jina-sāsana).

Since the description of the Great Sage (Mahesī), who is worthy of the highest respect, is clearly seen in connection with the singular,
Therefore, the wise one skilled in usage should use either the singular or the other (plural) according to the meaning.

The plural mostly stands in the case of residence (tannivāsa).
The singular is rare in the case of being a son (tamputta) and in the case of dependence (tannissaya).
The plural should be shown as rare in cases such as association with many consciousnesses, lack of delimitation, and connecting the Mātikā with the question.
The plural by way of expressing together, by way of function, and likewise by way of object, as well as the plural in reference to what depends on it, are also rare.
28:
Thus, having understood the combination of the two usages (vaca) along with examples, a wise person should employ the conventional usage without deviating from the Pali.

Now, I shall explain the occurrence of the ākhyāta (verb) by way of time (kāla) and so forth. A word that indicates time such as the present (vattamāna), kāraka such as the object (kamma), and person (purisa) such as the first (pathama), and which is characterized by action, is called ākhyātika (ākhyāta). Among these, time (kāla) is threefold: past, future, and present. However, by way of past, future, present, command (āṇatti), hypothesis (parikappa), and conditional (kālātipatti), it is sixfold. Each of these six times has three persons.

In the aforementioned various times, because a certain verbal inflection (ākhyāta-vibhatti) occurs, it is understood as indicating the time of that ākhyāta.

Kāraka refers to the object (kamma), the agent (kattā), and the state (bhāva). These are called 'kāraka' because they perform (karonti) or are the act of performing (karaṇa) by way of metaphorical, primary, or natural sense. These very things—kamma, kattā, and bhāva—should be understood respectively as the cause of the completion of the action, the one who completes the action, and the nature of the action.

Kamma, kattā, and bhāva—thus there are three kārakas. In these three kārakas, the inflections (vibhatti) and suffixes (paccaya) are stated. Apart from these three kārakas, they are not truly stated in other relations like the instrument (karaṇa), etc.

“Paribhaviyyati” and so forth are accomplished in the kamma-kāraka (passive).
“Sambhavati” and so forth are accomplished in the kattu-kāraka (active).
“Vibhaviyyati” and so forth are accomplished in the bhāva-kāraka (impersonal).

Thus, in these three types of kāraka, the inflections and suffixes are to be understood.

There is no ākhyāta at all that is free from the group of these three kārakas. Therefore, the ākhyāta is also said to indicate the group of those three kārakas.

As for the status of bhāva as a kāraka, even if it is not mentioned in the definition of kāraka, by that bhāva which is distinct from a substance (dabba)...
29:
On the grounds that there is no completion of action, and also by logical reasoning, that bhāva-kāraka does not exist. Nevertheless, considering that the conventional use of 'kāraka' for that bhāva in the ākhyāta is an established method in the science of Nirutti, we have stated it.

Person (purisa) consists of the first person (pathama-purisa), the middle person (majjhima-purisa), and the highest person (uttama-purisa), which are singular and plural. Among these three, the first person (pathama-purisa) follows all roots, whether it is used in a noun in the nominative case (paṭhamā-vibhatti) that has the same referent (tulyādhikaraṇa) as the ākhyāta word—whether expressing the agent or the object—excluding the words 'tumha' and 'amha', as in 'abhinīhāro samijjhāti' (the aspiration is fulfilled), 'bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ' (the knowledge in the four paths is called Bodhi), etc.; or whether it is not explicitly used but stands in the place of that noun, as in 'bhāsati vā karoti vā' (he speaks or he acts), 'pīḷiyakkho ti maṃ vidū' (they know me as Pīḷiyakkha), 'vuccatī ti vacanaံ' (it is called 'vacana' because it is spoken), etc. In some Pali passages, because the noun is not used, the meaning of the usage of the first person is very difficult to understand. For example: 'dukkhaṃ te vedayissāmi, tattha assāsayantu maṃ' (I shall announce the painful news to you, O King; in that matter, let your feet comfort me). For in this Pali, the remaining word 'pādā' (feet) is to be brought forward. The meaning is: 'Let the two feet of the King comfort me, who am weary because of not daring to speak when announcing that painful news; tell me to speak freely.'

Because there are intentions in the Pali that are very difficult to understand, a wise person should approach a teacher and accept the views of the teachers.

In this context, since it is the domain of the root bhū, the example words by way of the root bhū are: he oppresses, they oppress, oppresses, oppress. The enemy is oppressed, all wealth is enjoyed, is oppressed, is enjoyed. In a usage where, even though the noun expresses the agent, the status of having the same referent as the ākhyāta word is not obtained because it is not in the nominative case, then, depending on a co-referential word in the nominative case expressing the object, all three persons—first person and so forth—can be obtained.
30:
The way they can be obtained is: the man is oppressed by Devadatta, you are oppressed by Devadatta, we are oppressed by unwholesome states. In this regard, one should not say: 'In "nindanti tuṇhimāsinaံ" (they blame the one who sits silent) and so forth, even though the noun expresses the object, the status of having the same referent as the ākhyāta word is not obtained because it is not in the nominative case; therefore, the occurrence of the first person (pathama-purisa) should not be.' Why? Because in 'nindanti tuṇhimāsinaံ' and so forth, the status of having the same referent as the ākhyāta word is desired with the noun expressing the agent, such as 'janā' (people), which is to be supplied. The same method should be understood in subsequent cases.

Majjhima-purisa (the middle person) follows all roots, whether the word 'tumha' in the nominative case, which has the same referent as the ākhyāta word—whether expressing the agent or the object—is used, or whether it is not used but stands in the place of that word 'tumha'. You excel, you all excel, excel, excel. You are oppressed by Devadatta, you all are oppressed by Devadatta. In a usage where, even though the word 'tumha' expresses the agent, the status of having the same referent as the ākhyāta word is not obtained because it is not in the nominative case, the majjhima-purisa does not occur there. Only the other two—the pathama-purisa and uttama-purisa—occur, depending on a co-referential word in the nominative case expressing the object. For example: the enemy is oppressed by you, I am oppressed by you.

Uttama-purisa (the highest person) follows all roots, whether the word 'amha' in the nominative case, which has the same referent as the ākhyāta word—whether expressing the agent or the object—is used, or whether it is not used but stands in the place of that word 'amha'. I oppress, we oppress, oppress, oppress. I am oppressed by unwholesome states, we are oppressed by unwholesome states, is oppressed, are oppressed. In a usage where, even though the word 'amha' expresses the agent, the status of having the same referent as the ākhyāta word is not obtained because it is not in the nominative case, the...
31:
In that context (associated with the word *amha*), it is the *Uttamapurisa* (First Person). The other two persons (the *Paṭhamapurisa* and *Majjhimapurisa*) occur based on the co-referential (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) word which is in the nominative case (*paccattavacana*) and is in the passive voice (*kammavācaka*). How is this so? For example: "Prosperity is experienced by me" (*Mayā anubhaviyate sampatti*), "You are oppressed by me" (*Mayā abhibhaviyase tvaṃ*). Thus, in whatever examples nouns and such in the nominative case—whether expressing the agent or the patient—attain co-referentiality with the verbal forms, the *Paṭhamapurisa* etc. are obtained in those respective places. Therefore, the co-referentiality of nouns etc. in the nominative case is the very cause for the arising of the *Paṭhamapurisa* and others.

When two or three persons are expressed together (*ekābhidhāna*), the subsequent person (*paro puriso*) should be taken. Here, "expressed together" (*ekābhidhāna*) means being expressed as one and being expressed at the same time. Furthermore, taking the subsequent person occurs only when the word '*ca*' (and) is used. This is because the subsequent person is not taken in examples where the word '*ca*' is not used or where they are expressed at different times. Examples of such usage include: "You are skilled in the goal; we are skilled in the goal," etc.

Among those examples, in the expression "You are skilled in the goal" (*Tumhe atthakusalā bhavatha*): "He is skilled in the goal, and you are skilled in the goal; therefore, you (plural) are skilled in the goal." In this way, when two persons are expressed together, the subsequent (*Majjhima*) person is taken. In the expression "We are skilled in the goal" (*Mayam atthakusalā bhavāma*): "He is skilled in the goal, and I am skilled in the goal; therefore, we are skilled in the goal," or "You are skilled in the goal, and I am skilled in the goal; therefore, we are skilled in the goal." In this way, when two persons are expressed together, the subsequent (*Uttama*) person is taken. "He is skilled in the goal, and you are skilled in the goal, and I am skilled in the goal; therefore, we are skilled in the goal," or "He is skilled in the goal, and they are skilled in the goal, and you are skilled in the goal, and you (plural) are skilled in the goal, and I am skilled in the goal; therefore, we are skilled in the goal." In this way, when three persons are expressed together, the subsequent (*Uttama*) person is taken.
32:
Another way of explanation is also stated: "You are skilled in the goal, and he is skilled in the goal; may you (plural) be skilled in the goal," or "I am skilled in the goal, and he is skilled in the goal; we are skilled in the goal." In this manner, there are various ways of explanation. Thus, in the remaining inflections, such as the *Pañcamī* and *Sattamī*, the subsequent person (*paro puriso*) should be taken. This applies to all verbal forms ending in the plural which express multiple meanings. However, even if they end in the plural, the subsequent person is not taken in verbal forms that refer to oneself alone or to a single person who is to be respected.

In this regard, these verses illustrating the objection are stated:

"When speaking such as 'You are [so], and he also is [so],' with the subsequent person placed first,
How can the subsequent person such as 'You (plural) are' occur?"

"When speaking such as 'I am [so], and he also is [so],'
How can the noble person (*Uttamapurisa*) such as 'We are' occur?"

In this regard, it is said:

The person mentioned later according to the order of names is called "Para" (the subsequent).
In this way, the person named *Paropurisa* should be taken.
Compared to the *Paṭhamapurisa*, the *Majjhimapurisa* and *Uttamapurisa* are called "Para" (subsequent).
Compared to the *Majjhimapurisa*, the *Uttamapurisa* is called the "Para" person.
Taking it in this way alone is in accordance with usage here.
There is no fault in taking it in accordance with that usage.
"O lady, may you be happy, and may this great deer also (be happy)."
Since such a Pali passage is seen, we speak thus.
In that Pali, the meaning "May you two be happy" is evident.
Thus, this method is stated by my own judgment.
33:
Although one's own opinion (*attanomati*) is said to be the weakest (compared to *Sutta*, *Suttānuloma*, etc.), it should not be discarded (it should be established) because it is stated by adopting the method of the Pali Canon.

"My father the King has banished me from the kingdom—me, who was ruling with righteousness—along with the country-folk and the town-folk who have come together."

"I, Queen Maddī, and both Prince Jālī and Princess Kaṇhājinā, dispelling each other's sorrow, lived in the hermitage at that time."

These verses also certainly establish this meaning (of the *Paropurisa*). By the method already stated in those verses, the meaning should be very clear.

Thus should the wise understand. What is the use of many words? In speaking by any means that gladdens the heart, if the meaning is not contradictory, the wise should take that non-contradiction as the standard.

This so-called *Paropurisa* is not obtained separately from the three persons; it is obtained only because it is included within those three persons. Although it is not obtained separately, it is extracted and shown as if it were obtained, for the sake of the listeners' proficiency in the meanings of usage.

In brief, the occurrence of the person in this context should be noted thus: "In the sense of 'I', it is *Uttamapurisa*; in the sense of 'you', it is *Majjhimapurisa*; in the sense of others, it is *Paṭhamapurisa*."

Since the name "person" (*purisa*) is given to the inflections such as *ti*, it should be known that the verb ending in those inflections indicates the person. Thus, in every way, the fact that the verb indicates the tense (*kāla*), the role (*kāraka*), and the person (*purisa*) has been stated.

In this regard, how is the fact that the verb has the characteristic of action (*kriyālakkhaṇa*) to be known?
34:
This word is to be characterized by action, or it has a characteristic called action. Thus, the state of having the characteristic of action should be understood; and because it is so—

Upon hearing a word that expresses an action such as 'gacchati' (he goes), the wise who are proficient in verbs designate it as 'ākhyāta' (a verb). Just as the characteristic of a noun is the expression of a being (substance), so too the characteristic of a verb is solely the expression of an action.

In this context, the state of expressing an action by way of meaning should be understood as the characteristic of this ākhyāta, as marked by the wise who know the characteristics. When a person is asked, 'What are you doing?' and gives an answer such as 'I am cooking' (pacāmi), the state of expressing an action is understood through that reply. Thus, the state of the verb having the characteristic of action should be understood.

Now, the occurrence of inflections (vibhatti) in the various tenses should be understood as follows—
In the present tense (paccuppanna-kāla), the Vattamānā inflection occurs.
In the senses of wishing and commanding within the present tense, the Pañcamī inflection occurs.
In the senses of reflecting and permitting within the present tense, the Sattamī inflection occurs.
In the past tense (atīta-kāla) that is out of sight (not witnessed), the Parokkhā inflection occurs.
In the past tense starting from yesterday, whether witnessed or not witnessed, the Hiyattanī inflection is described.
In the past tense starting from today, whether witnessed or not witnessed, in the recent past, it is called the Ajjatanī inflection.
In the future tense (anāgata-kāla) that is yet to come, the Bhavissantī inflection occurs.
In the past where an action has just failed to be realized, or even in the future, the Kālātipatti inflection occurs; so it is said by those proficient in linguistics.

Having thus understood the occurrence of inflections in the tenses, those who desire proficiency in the various usages (payoga) seen in the Suttantas—which are the domain of very pure, extensive, and sharp wisdom—should follow the sequence of inflections starting with 'ti'...
35:
The verbal paradigms (kriyā-padamālā) should be noted: bhavati, bhavanti; bhavasi, bhavatha; bhavāmi, bhavāma; bhavate, bhavante; bhavase, bhavavhe; bhave, bhavāmhe. This is the verbal paradigm devoid of conjunction with a noun (añña-yoga), etc.

In the Suttantas, verbal forms are also seen that are devoid of conjunction with a noun, etc., even though a nominal meaning is appropriate. How so? "When one sees with wisdom: 'All conditioned things are impermanent' (sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā ti)." "O charioteer, what you say to me." "I shall go to another Seppaṇṇi tree." Such words are verbal paradigms in expressing this meaning devoid of nominal conjunction.

In this context, conjunction (yoga) in verbal forms is of three kinds: conjunction with 'you' (tumha-yoga/ta-yoga), conjunction with 'I' (amha-yoga/ma-yoga), and conjunction with another (añña-yoga/nāma-yoga). Among these three, the middle person (majjhima-purisa) should be taken by way of conjunction with 'you'; the highest person (uttama-purisa) by way of conjunction with 'I'; and the first person (paṭhama-purisa) by way of conjunction with another (noun). The following summary verse (anugīti) describes the sequence of 'ti' and other inflections here:

The first person (paṭhama) occurs by conjunction with another (noun),
The middle person (majjhima) occurs by conjunction with 'you',
The highest person (uttama) occurs by conjunction with 'I';
Thus should the wise understand.

For the sake of the listeners' proficiency in usage, we shall state another verbal paradigm together with conjunction with a noun, etc.: so bhavati, te bhavanti; tvaṃ bhavasi, tumhe bhavatha; ahaṃ bhavāmi, mayaṃ bhavāma; so bhavate, te bhavante; tvaṃ bhavase, tumhe bhavavhe; ahaṃ bhave, mayaṃ bhavāmhe. This is the verbal paradigm together with conjunction with a noun, etc.

In the Suttantas, verbal forms together with conjunction with a noun, etc., are also seen. How so? "Great King, this young prince is well-established in his feet; this also is a mark of a Great Man (mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa) for this Great Man; he will have these seven treasures. He who, in a time of slowness..."
36:
"...is swift when he should be slow, and slow when he should be swift. You are my teacher. I also wish to see my father who has come to this place." Such words are verbal paradigms in expressing that meaning (conjunction with a noun, etc.).

If a word falls into the meaning that should be expressed by the word 'tumha' (you), but is not itself a word expressing the meaning of 'you', that word does not establish the state of the verbal form being accompanied by conjunction with 'you' (tumha-yoga); rather, it establishes only the state of being accompanied by conjunction with another (añña-yoga). Likewise, if a word falls into the meaning that should be expressed by the word 'amha' (I), but is not itself a word expressing the meaning of 'I', that word also does not establish the state of the verbal form being accompanied by conjunction with 'I' (amha-yoga); rather, it establishes only the state of being accompanied by conjunction with another (añña-yoga).

Among those two, first, regarding the meaning to be expressed by the word 'tumha': "You, Brahmin Jūjaka, did not come thinking that seeing King Vessantara would be meritorious. May the venerable one not strive for the schism of the united Saṅgha. Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One wash the rag-robe in this pond." Such are the usages.

Regarding the meaning to be expressed by the word 'amha': "O Great Hero, I, Upāli, worship the feet of the Teacher. O Great Hero, I, Saraṇa, a disciple of yours, worship the Teacher." Such are the usages. Here, this conclusion should be noted: usage that expresses another meaning, other than the conjunction with 'you' or 'I' which express the meanings of 'tvaṃ, tumhe, ahaṃ, mayaṃ', is called 'añña-yoga' (conjunction with another); in that añña-yoga, the first person (paṭhama-purisa) 'bhavati' occurs.

If it is so, how is it in cases such as: "Lifting a sledgehammer made entirely of iron and of immense size, you, that one, stand in the sky. O best of sages, having heard your words, I am pleased"? For here, only the occurrence of the middle and highest persons is seen, but the occurrence of the first person is not seen—thus it is objected.

It is replied: In cases such as "Lifting a sledgehammer made entirely of iron and of immense size, you, that one, stand in the sky," because the noun 'so' (that one/he) is seen with words expressing the meaning of 'tumha' and 'amha' alongside words ending in 'syādi' inflections such as 'tiṭṭhasi'...
37:
The occurrence of the second person (majjhima purisa) and the first person (uttama purisa) should be understood because they share the same referent as the words 'tvaṃ' and 'ahaṃ', which are constantly implied, and because they function as modifiers of those words 'tvaṃ' and 'ahaṃ'. In such usages, even if the words 'tvaṃ', 'ahaṃ', and so forth are not explicitly present, they are to be brought in (implied) by seeing the verbal forms ending in inflections such as 'si'. However, in some instances, they are seen fully expressed, such as in: 'Sā tvaṃ vaṅkamanuppattā, kathaṃ maddi karissasi. So ahaṃ vicarissāmi, gāmā gāmaṃ purā puraṃ.'

Because the verb (ākhyāta) has action as its characteristic and because there is no distinction in form based on gender, we shall state another series of verbal forms to demonstrate their commonality across the three genders:

The man is, the woman is, the mind is; the men are, the women are, the minds are. O man, you are; O woman, you are; O mind, you are; O men, you are; O women, you are; O minds, you are. I, the man, am; I, the woman, am; I, the mind, am; we, the men, are; we, the women, are; we, the minds are.

This same method applies to the Atmanopada forms and to all forms of the remaining inflections. This is indeed the series of verbal forms demonstrating the commonality of the verb across the three genders.

For it has been stated in the Niruttipiṭaka: 'The verb has action as its characteristic and has no distinction in gender.' In that context, what is the meaning of 'no distinction in gender' (aliṅgabheda)? The meaning of having no difference among the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders is called 'aliṅgabheda'. For example: 'The man goes, the woman goes, the mind goes.' Just as in the verbal forms shown in four ways, taking the form ending in the 'ti' inflection after the 'a' suffix such as 'bhavati', the series of verbal forms is made in every way as 'bhavati, bhavanti, bhavasi', and so forth; likewise, taking the forms ending in the 'ti' inflection after the 'a' suffix such as 'ubbhavati', one should form 'ubbhavati, ubbhavanti'...
38:
...the series of verbal forms such as 'ubbhavati' should be formed in every way. However, taking the forms ending in the 'ti' inflection after the 'o' substitution such as 'bhoti, sambhoti', and the forms ending in the 'ti' inflection after the 'e' substitution such as 'bhāveti, vibhāveti', the series of forms should be made only according to the Pali method, and not according to the method stated in this text. The reason is that in such instances, the manner of the verb's occurrence is difficult to understand. Therefore, the series of verbal forms should be made to the extent possible. In the world, worldly teachers do not speak by joining every single root with all ninety-six verbal forms individually; even if they do not speak thus, their speech is not called incomplete. Therefore, excluding what should be excluded, the series of forms should be made as they occur. This same rule applies to the Pañcamī and other inflections. This is the demonstration of the series of verbal forms by means of the Vattamāna (present) inflection.

From here onwards, the very forms already shown are to be transformed and taken as the matrix (mātikā) for the Pañcamī and other inflections. Now, we shall show the two types of verbal series according to their association or non-association with the three persons (purisa). We shall also show the distinct forms that arise in some verbs by way of command (ādesa) so that listeners may easily memorize them and avoid confusion in the usage of the three persons.

Bhavatu, bhavantu. Bhavāhi, bhava, bhavatha. Bhavāmi, bhavāma. Bhavataṃ, bhavantaṃ. Bhavassu, bhavavho. Bhave, bhavāmase. Let him be, let them be. May you be, may you all be. I shall be, we shall be. Let him be, let them be. May you be, may you all be. I shall be, we shall be. This is the demonstration of the series of verbal forms by means of the Pañcamī inflection.

Bhaveyya, bhave, bhaveyyuṃ. Bhaveyyāsi, bhaveyyātha. Bhaveyyāmi, bhaveyyāma, bhavemu. Bhavetha, bhaveraṃ. Bhavetho, bhaveyyāvho. Bhaveyyaṃ, bhaveyyāmhe—thus it also is. He...
39:
...bhaveyya, bhave; te bhaveyyuṃ. Tvaṃ bhaveyyāsi, tumhe bhaveyyātha. Ahaṃ bhaveyyāmi, mayaṃ bhaveyyāma, bhavemu. So bhavetha, te bhaveraṃ. Tvaṃ bhavetho, tumhe bhaveyyāvho. Ahaṃ bhaveyyaṃ, mayaṃ bhaveyyāmhe—thus it also is. This is the demonstration of the series of verbal forms by means of the Sattamī (potential) inflection.

Babhūva, babhūvu. Babhūve, babhūvittha. Babhūvaṃ, babhūvimha. Babhūvittha, babhūvire. Babhūvittho, babhūvivho. Babhūviṃ, babhūvimhe—thus it also is. He has been, they have been. You have been, you all have been. I have been, we have been. He has been, they have been. You have been, you all have been. I have been, we have been—thus it also is. This is the demonstration of the series of verbal forms by means of the Parokkhā (perfect) inflection.

Abhavā, abhavū. Abhavo, abhavattha. Abhavaṃ, abhavamhā. Abhavattha, abhavatthuṃ. Abhavase, abhavavhaṃ. Abhaviṃ, abhavamhase—thus it also is. He was, they were. You were, you all were. I was, we were. He was, they were. You were, you all were. I was, we were—thus it also is. This is the demonstration of the series of verbal forms by means of the Hiyattanī (imperfect) inflection.

Abhavi, abhavuṃ. Abhavo, abhavittha. Abhaviṃ, abhavimhā. Abhavā, abhavū. Abhavase, abhavivhaṃ. Abhavhaṃ, abhavimhe—thus it also is. He was, they were. You were, you all were. I was, we were. He was, they were. You were, you all were. I was, we were—thus it also is. This is the demonstration of the series of verbal forms by means of the Ajjatanī (aorist) inflection.

In this Ajjatanī inflection, the distinct forms of the root 'bhū' should also be known by way of substituting the 'uṃ' inflection with 'iṃsu'. What are they? They were, they were well-formed, they arose, they perished, they came into existence, they became manifest...
40:
These words such as 'pātubbhaviṃsu' are intransitive (akammaka) words. (There are also words such as) paribhaviṃsu, abhibhaviṃsu, adhibhaviṃsu, atibhaviṃsu, anubhaviṃsu, samanubhaviṃsu, and abhisambhaviṃsu.

Since the form 'adhibhosuṃ' is also found in the Pāḷi Canon, the forms such as 'paribhosuṃ' should also be understood by the same method.

In this regard, this is the Pāḷi: 'O monks, visible objects overwhelm (adhibhosuṃ) a monk living in such a way (being lustful), but the monk does not overwhelm (adhibhosī) the visible objects' (as stated in the Saḷāyatana Saṃyutta Pāḷi). These words such as 'paribhaviṃsu' are transitive (sakammaka) words. Thus, in the Aorist (ajjatanī) inflection, by substituting the suffix 'ū' with 'iṃsu', these various forms of the root 'bhū' occur. Furthermore—

The verbal form 'anvabhi' is also evident in the Aorist. Therefore, forms such as 'ajjhabhi' should also be understood by the same method.
