In this regard, this is the Pāḷi: 'Due to that deed, he went to the celestial realm and continuously experienced (anvabhi) celestial bliss and delights' (as stated in the Lakkhaṇa Sutta Pāḷi). In that Pāḷi, the word 'anvabhi' should be analyzed as 'anu' and 'abhi'. It should be understood that 'anu' is a prefix (upasagga) and 'abhi' is a verbal word (ākhyāta).

Bhavissati, bhavissanti. Bhavissasi, bhavissatha. Bhavissāmi, bhavissāma. Bhavissate, bhavissante. Bhavissase, bhavissavhe. Bhavissaṃ, bhavissāmhe. (In sentences:) He will be, they will be. You will be, you (plural) will be. I will be, we will be. He will be, they will be. You will be, you (plural) will be. I will be, we will be. This is the paradigm of verbal forms (kriyāpadamālā) shown by the power of the Future (bhavissantī) inflection.

Abhavissā, abhavissaṃsu. Abhavisse, abhavissatha. Abhavissaṃ, abhavissāmhā. Abhavissatha, abhavissisu. Abhavissase, abhavissavhe. Abhavissiṃ, abhavissāmhase. (In sentences:) He would have been, they would have been. You would have been,
41:
You would have been. I would have been, we would have been. He would have been, they would have been. You would have been, you (pl.) would have been. I would have been, we would have been. This is the explanation of the paradigm of verbs (kriyāpadamālā) shown by the power of the kālātipatti suffix.

The teacher Kaccāyana, who was skilled in the distinctions of usage and possessed excellent wisdom, explained the sequence of ākhyāta suffixes starting with ti for the benefit of the Buddha's Dispensation. Following the sequence of that Kaccāyana treatise, I have spoken the sequence of verbs by the power of the root bhū.

## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the proficiency of the wise in the linguistic paths of the Three Pitakas along with the Commentaries having nine factors,
## The second chapter, named the Analysis of the Paradigm of the Verb 'Bhavati' (Bhavatino Kriyāpadamālāvibhāga), is finished.

## 3. Pakiṇṇakavinicchaya

After this chapter, I shall speak of the miscellaneous decisions (pakiṇṇakavinicchaya) for the proficiency of the wise in the meanings associated with usage.

In those miscellaneous decisions, nine types of decisions should be known: (1) Extracting the meaning, (2) Considering the meaning and the word, (3) Association with excessive meaning, (4) Grouping similar suffixes by the power of similarity and dissimilarity, (5) Counting suffixes and numbers by the power of the characteristics of augments (āgama), (6) Counting suffixes and numbers by the power of time, (7) Counting time, (8) Comparing the scriptures, and (9) Explaining the meaning of the terms of suffixes such as vattamānā, etc.

In extracting the meaning, I will first extract the meaning of words that sound the same but have different meanings. In this extraction of meaning, the meanings of the words "bhoti" and "bhave", which are called verbal (ākhyāta) words, should be extracted. In doing so, although these (verbal) words sound the same as other words "bhoti" and "bhave" which are called nominal (nāmika) words, they have different meanings and different suffixes.
42:
Indeed, in the Dispensation, some words, although having the same sound as one another, have different meanings, different bases of application (pavatti-nimitta), different genders (liṅga), different inflections (vibhatti), different numbers (vacana), different endings (anta), different times (kāla), and different word-classes (padajāta).

Regarding the difference in meaning, examples are: 'All that is dependent on the body decays (jīrati). This man of little learning grows (jīrati) like an ox. Being exhausted (santo), he is thirsty. Though being (santo) capable, he does not support. The calmed (santo) Sage praises. The virtuous (santo) are good people in the world. They are present (santo) in the world.' In these, the two 'jīrati' words, as appropriate, signify the loss of newness (decaying) and increasing. The five 'santo' words, as appropriate, should be understood to signify reaching exhaustion, being, being calmed, and existing.

Regarding the difference in the basis of application: 'The ungrateful (akataññū) person betrays a friend; he is also one without faith and ungrateful (akataññū - knower of the unmade/Nibbāna).' In this, the two 'akataññū' words should be understood as words with different bases of application because they arise based on the application of not knowing a favor done and knowing Nibbāna which is free from conditioning.

Regarding the difference in gender: 'May Pañcasikha, the Sakka, lord of devas, be happy (sukhī). And you, dear one, be happy (sukhī). Wherever that (sā - dog) stands facing. I have a mother, that (sā) mother should be supported by me.' In this, the two 'sukhī' words and the two 'sā' words should be understood as words with different genders by way of masculine and feminine genders.

Regarding the difference in inflection: 'Because of (yato) restraint in food and stomach; since (yato) he understands the Dhamma together with its cause.' In this,
43:
The two words "yato" should be understood as words with different case endings because they are associated with the nominative case (paṭhamā-vibhatti) and the ablative case (pañcamī-vibhatti).

In the state of having different numbers (vacana), these examples exist:
In examples such as "The being nourished by which mother beholds this world. The ignorant worldling, being angry, kills even that mother who gives life and peace," the word "hanti" is singular.

However, in examples such as "These hunters, having surrounded the herds of deer in the forest with snares and having cast them into a pit, at that very moment, shouting and reviling, kill the best of them with sharp spears," the word "hanti" is plural. In examples such as "He is virtuous and endowed with duties. Come here, venerable ones, be virtuous. He is peaceful, disciplined, firm, and leads the holy life. The peaceful ones indeed make it known together with the virtuous. That great king is illustrious. They are the four great kings," words such as "sīlavā" have singular and plural meanings.

In the state of having different endings, where despite having the same sound, a difference in case or a difference in number is found, those very examples apply. How is that? "To the mindful one, to the wise one; the Dhamma of the peaceful ones; he is peaceful, he is disciplined; the peaceful ones are good men," and so forth.

In the state of having different times (tenses), [examples are] such as "O Brahmin, have you not heard it being said that the gods do not envy the effort of a man? Those people will transcend the realm of death, which is very difficult to cross, and reach Nibbāna." Here, the two words "issanti" should be understood as having different times by way of the present and the future. By way of the present and future inflections, they should also be understood as having different case endings.
44:
## Asamānapadajātika (Difference in Parts of Speech)

In phrases such as "The elephant is self-composed; having known for myself, whom should I point out? The husband of her who runs on the path; having made the deerskin [draped] over one shoulder; he fell at the feet with his head. Towards the mountain Caṇḍoraṇa."
In this context, the two words "sayaṃ" should be understood as different parts of speech by way of being a noun and an indeclinable; and the three words "pati" by way of being a noun, a verb, and a prefix.

In this manner, it should be understood extensively in all places. Thus, in the Dispensation (Sāsana), some words, although having the same sound as each other, have different meanings, different origins (nimittha), different genders, different case endings, different numbers, different final consonants, different times (tenses), and different parts of speech. Among such words, that which expresses the state of a verb does not express the state of a noun. And that which expresses the state of a noun does not express the state of a verb. Even though this is so, because of the similarity in sound, they are taken as one and the meaning is extracted. Therefore, I shall describe the method of extracting the meanings of the words "bhoti" and "bhave," which are verbs having the same sound as the aforementioned nouns.

How? The word "bhoti" is a verb when connected with a subject (kattā), and it is a noun when connected with a verb. Therefore, it exists in two meanings: the meaning of a verb and the meaning of a noun. Between those two, in the meaning of a verb, it exists by way of the present tense; in the meaning of a noun, however, it exists by way of the vocative. In the meaning of a verb, there is "One person exists" (eko bhoti); in the meaning of a noun, there is "Lady, do not weep" (mā bhoti paridevesi). In this regard, it is said:

The word "bhoti" occurs in these two meanings:
In the sense of an inflected verb,
And in the sense of a noun distinguished by the vocative.
45:
The word "bhave" also occurs in the sense of the word "bhavāmi" associated with the present tense inflection. It also occurs in the senses of commanding and wishing of the word "bhavāmi" associated with the pañcamī inflection (imperative mood). It also occurs in the senses of permission and reflection of the word "bhaveyyāmi" associated with the sattamī inflection (optative mood). Among those meanings, the canonical Pali text that establishes the first meaning is:

"I am superior to the gods, I am the lord of men.
Endowed with physical marks, I am peerless in wisdom."

This, however, is our composition of verses that establishes all those meanings:

"This person is happy, and I too am happy.
May this person be happy, and may I too be happy.
By this worship of the Buddha, may all beings reach happiness.
May I too, together with my relatives and attendants, reach happiness.
This person should be happy, and I too should be happy.
If this person were happy, I too should be happy."

Thus:

The word "bhave" occurs in these three places:
In the present tense, in the pañcamī, and in the sattamī inflections.

One should illustrate the meaning of this word "bhave" as fivefold:
Once in the present tense,
And twice each in the pañcamī and sattamī.

Or, the meaning "bhoti" (he/she/it is),
Which expresses the third person in the present tense,
Is also suitable for this word "bhave".

Now, however, to establish the aforementioned meaning,
I shall bring forth a portion of the Pali text here; listen to me.
46: "Who is this person who, in the middle of the ocean, is exerting effort without seeing the shore? Having known what special benefit do you strive so greatly?" "O deity, I have reflected upon the conduct of the world and the special benefit of effort. Therefore, even though I do not see the shore in the middle of the ocean, I am exerting effort (in this way)." In that former verse, the meaning of the word "āyuhe" should be understood by the wise as "āyūhati" (he exerts). This meaning is stated by way of changing the locative case (sattamī vibhatti) to the present tense (vattamāna) in the present time, or by way of changing the "ti" suffix to "e". In the latter verse, however, the wise person who knows the word and its meaning should clarify that the meaning of the word "āyuhe" is "āyūhāmi" (I exert). Similarly, for the word "bhave" in the present tense, the meaning should be clarified in two ways: as "bhavati" (it is/becomes) and "bhavāmi" (I am/become). In other such passages as well, the wise person skilled in methods should apply this method in the Dispensation, which is like an ocean of methods. Thus, this word "bhave" occurs in five or six verbal meanings. Similarly, it also occurs in the meanings of growth (vuddhi), saṃsāra, kamma-bhava, and upapatti-bhava of a noun ending in the locative case. Indeed, in such passages as "tassa abhave nandati, tassa bhave na nandati" (he rejoices in his non-growth, he does not rejoice in his growth), it occurs in the sense of growth (vuddhi). In "bhave vicaranto" (wandering in saṃsāra), it occurs in the sense of saṃsāra. In "bhave kho sati jāti hoti, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ" (when kamma-bhava exists, birth occurs; with birth as condition, aging and death occur), it occurs in the sense of kamma-bhava. In "evaṃ bhave vijjamāne" (thus, when the upapatti-bhava of the five aggregates is manifest), it should be noted that it occurs in the sense of upapatti-bhava. By this method, the meanings of other verbs derived from the root bhū should also be extracted as appropriate.
47: The meanings such as the vocative of these words like 'bhoti' should never be taken in the sense of a verb (ākhyāta). This is because these meanings are extracted from nouns through the power of extracting meaning (atthuddhāra). What has been said is a brief demonstration of the method of extracting meaning in this Miscellaneous Decision (Pakiṇṇaka-vinicchaya). In the contemplation of meaning and words (atthasadda-cintā), it should be noted thus: "bhavante, parābhavante, parābhave" etc., are specific words (visesa-sadda) like the words "gacchati, gacchaṃ, gacchato". They are not general words (sāmañña-sadda) like the word "nāthati" which expresses meanings such as requesting or tormenting, nor like the word "deva" which expresses meanings such as king or deity. In this context, words that are specific words are always specific words. Words that are general words are also always general words. Among those words, the nature of "gacchati" etc., as specific words should be understood thus: "gacchati" is one noun and one verb. Similarly, "gacchanti" is one noun and one verb. "Gacchato" is one derivative (kitanta) and the other is a conventional term (rūḷhī-sadda). Although they are specific words, because they sound the same, they cannot produce the knowledge that understands that specific word without the connection of context or other words. Indeed, through connection with other words, when "gacchati patiṭṭhitaṃ" is said, it is known as a noun ending in the locative case. When "gacchati tisso" is said, it is known as a verb. Similarly, when "sa gacchaṃ na nivattati" is said, it is known as a noun in the nominative case. When "gacchaṃ puttanivedako" is said, it is known as a verb. When "gacchato hayato patito" is said, it is known as a derivative (kitanta). When "gacchato paṇṇapupphāni patanti" is said, it is known as a conventional term (rūḷhī-sadda) meaning a tree. Thus, in the connection of meanings of verbs and nouns that are specific words and sound the same as nouns and verbs, some connection that makes the specific meaning known must certainly be desired. Thus, the nature of "gacchati" etc., as specific words that exist separately as verbs or nouns and express individual meanings should be understood.
48: Verbs and nouns such as "nāthati" and "devo" should be known only as general words (sāmañña-sadda) because they do not sound the same as nouns and verbs but express various meanings. In the connection of meanings, if "nāthati" is said without any connection, various meanings may appear, such as "he requests," "he torments," "he exercises sovereignty," or "he desires." Similarly, if "devo" is said, meanings such as "cloud," "sky," "king," "deity," or "visuddhi-deva" (a purified being) appear. However, when there is a connection with other words, if "nāthati suppaṭipattiṃ" is said, the meaning of the verb "nāthati" is known as "he requests." If "nāthati sabbakilese" is said, the meaning is known as "he torments." If "nāthati sakacitte" is said, the meaning is known as "he exercises sovereignty." If "nāthati lokassa hitaṃ" is said, the meaning is known as "he desires." Similarly, if "devo gajjati" is said, the meaning of the noun "devo" is known as "cloud." If "viddhā vigatavalāhako devo" is said, the meaning is known as "sky." If "pivatu devo pānīyaṃ" is said, the meaning is known as "king." If "devo devakāyā cavati āyusaṅkhayā" is said, the meaning is known as "deity." If "devātidevo satapuññalakkhaṇo" is said, the meaning is known as "visuddhi-deva." In this way, other general words should also be known. Knowing all this, one should contemplate those meanings and words so that the meaning does not conflict with the word, and the word does not conflict with the meaning. In such contemplation, this is a mere indication of the manner of contemplation as an example: if "atthakusalā bhavante" or "kiccāni bhavante" is said, one should contemplate the meaning and the word thus: "this word 'bhavante' is a verb having the same meaning as 'bhavanti'." If "bhavante passāmi" or "icchāmi" is said, one should contemplate that it is a noun with the accusative meaning. If "bhavaṃ te jane pasaṃsati" or "kāmeti" is said, one should contemplate that they are two nouns with nominative and accusative meanings. If "corā parābhavante" is said, one should contemplate that this word "parābhavante" is a verb having the same meaning as "parābhavanti." If "amittānaṃ parābhavaṃ te janā icchanti" is said, one should contemplate that these words "parābhavanto" are two nouns with accusative and nominative meanings. If "eso parābhave" is said, one should contemplate that this word "parābhave" is a verb having the same meaning as "parābhaveyya." If "loke ete parābhave paṇḍito samavekkhiya" is said, one should contemplate that this word "parābhave" is a plural noun with the accusative meaning. If "parābhave sati" is said, one should contemplate that it is a singular noun in the locative case indicating a condition (bhāva-lakkhaṇa).
49:
One should contemplate both the meaning and the word, considering it a noun with an accusative sense. When it is said, 'The master praises those people' or 'He desires [them]', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying them as two nouns having nominative and accusative senses. When it is said, 'The thieves perish (parābhavante)', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying this term 'parābhavante' as a verb (ākhyāta) having the same meaning as 'parābhavanti'. When it is said, 'They desire the ruin (parābhavante) of their enemies', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying these terms 'parābhavante' as two nouns having accusative and nominative senses. When it is said, 'This person might perish (parābhave)', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying this term 'parābhave' as a verb having the same meaning as 'parābhaveyya'. When it is said, 'A wise man, having well-considered those causes of ruin (parābhave) in the world', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying this term 'parābhave' as a plural noun with an accusative sense. When it is said, 'There being ruin (parābhave)', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying it as a singular noun in the locative case (sattamī) indicating a state (bhāvalakkhaṇa). When it is said, 'May you all cause devotion (sambhave) in me', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying this term 'sambhave' as a verb having the same meaning as 'sambhavatha'. When it is said, 'O sister named Sambhavā, come here', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying this term 'sambhavavhe' as a noun in the vocative case, feminine gender, denoting a woman named Sambhavā. When it is said, 'Come here, you who are established in the man named Sambhava', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying it as a masculine gender in the locative case, denoting a man named Sambhava.

Elder Varuṇa and Elder Brahmadatta were the chief disciples.
The attendant of the Great Sage Revata Buddha was named Sambhava.
Such is the Pali text (as evidence). When it is said, 'The phenomena appear (pātubhavante)', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying this term 'pātubhavante' as a verb accompanied by an indeclinable (nipāta), having the same meaning as 'pātubhavanti'. When it is said, 'May the master protect those people (pātu bhavante)', [one should contemplate] the words expressing the meaning, 'May the master protect those people'...
50:
...identifying them as verbal, participial (kita), and pronominal (sabbanāma) terms; thus one should contemplate both the meaning and the word. When it is said, 'You appear (pātubhavase) through virtues', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying this term 'pātubhavase' as a verb having the same meaning as 'pātubhavasi'. When it is said, 'You who appear (pātubhavase) because of virtue', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying them as verbal and nominal terms joined with an indeclinable, expressing the meaning, 'Because of your own virtue, may you appear'. When it is said, 'I appear (pātubhave) through my own virtues', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying this term 'pātubhave' as a verb accompanied by an indeclinable, having the same meaning as 'pātubhavāmi'. When it is said, 'May this meritorious deed protect (pātu) me (bhave) in saṃsāra', one should contemplate both the meaning and the word, identifying them as verbal and nominal terms expressing the meaning, 'May [this] protect me in saṃsāra'.

In this manner, one should contemplate the meaning and the word appropriately in all instances. In such contemplation, among certain words that sound the same, such as in the following: 'They do not store [wealth] in a granary (koṭṭhe). One should not go between (antarā) them. O Licchavis, I shall preach to you (vo) the seven principles of non-decline. Great King, these are your enemies (sattavo). And you are the highest of beings (uttamasattavo),' a distinction in pronunciation is desired.

When there is a distinction in pronunciation, the words become clear. When the words are clear, the meaning becomes clear. For those who grasp the meaning, the attainment of the meaning becomes effortless, like seeing a reflection on a perfectly pure mirror surface. Such effortless understanding occurs only for one who has previously grasped the conventions and knows at least one of the connections of meaning, etc.; otherwise, it does not. Regarding this, the ancient teachers said:

'Words that have not come within the range [of the senses] do not make the meaning known.
Those unknown words do not reveal meanings through the mere word.'

As we have stated here, 'a distinction in pronunciation is desired,' this is the verse that illustrates that distinction in pronunciation and provides the method along with the meaning.
51:
In the passage “Na te saṃ koṭṭhe openti,” the wise one should split the words as “na te” and certainly recite “saṃ koṭṭhe.” The meaning should be stated as: “Those monks do not put wealth into granaries.” This same method applies to other such passages as well.

Furthermore, for what purpose is it stated “according to the view of some teachers”? It is to show that in passages such as “Gacchati patiṭṭhitaṃ, gacchati tisso, bhavante passāmi, atthakusalā bhavante, vadantaṃ ekapokkharā, vadantaṃ paṭivadati,” a distinction in the pronunciation of homonymous words (samānasutika) is not obtained. Therefore, this should be noted here: where a distinction in the pronunciation of homonymous words is possible, and a distinction in meaning is also obtained through the division (vibhāga) or non-division (avibhāga) of words, then in such usage, certain homonymous words should be recited by splitting them. For example: “Hetu hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo. So tena saddhiṃ bhāsati, sotena vuyhati. Bhavante jane pasaṃsati, bhavante passāmi,” and so forth. Here, one should recite “hetu” with a slight split before “hetusampayuttānaṃ.” Likewise, one should split “so” before reciting “tena saddhiṃ.” One should split “bhava” before reciting “te jane.”

As for the remaining homonymous words, they should not be recited with a split. If one recites with a split in a place where it should not be split, the meaning is ruined. Thus, the distinction in meaning and pronunciation of homonymous words should be understood through the power of word division and non-division. Here, in “so tena” and so forth, taking the meaning of two words is called division (vibhāga), while taking the meaning of a single word is intended as non-division (avibhāga). Here, the conceptualization of homonymy by combining words that exist separately and sound different is only for the purpose of conveying a specific meaning and showing the distinction in pronunciation. Because...
52:
These words are not homonymous in a single meaning, as in “Sappo sappo” (Snake! Snake!) and the like. Even so, by taking a trace of homonymy obtained through combination, they are called “samānasutika” (homonymous words) for the purpose of conveying a specific meaning and showing the distinction in pronunciation. This method applies to other such instances as well. This should be noted here:

In a usage where a distinction in meaning is obtained through any one of the eighteen modes of homonymous words, but if splitting the pronunciation results in a lack of linguistic elegance (saddavilāsa) or the meaning is ruined, then in such usages, the homonymous words should not be recited with a split. In that regard, through which modes is the distinction in meaning obtained? It occurs through these eighteen modes: by word division (vibhāga), by non-division (avibhāga), by proximity of letters (akkharasannidhāna), by proximity of words (padasannidhāna), by proximity of words and letters (padakkharasannidhāna), by distributive repetition (vicchā), by the power of a governing particle (kammapavaccanīya), by the power of reiterated utterance (āmeḍita) spoken when fear, anger, etc., arise, by the power of repeating an adjective (guṇavācaka), by the power of repeating a verb (kriyāpada), by the power of splitting a euphonic combination (saṃhitāpudaccheda), by the power of showing disrespect (agāravattha), by the power of showing continuous meaning (nirantarattha), by the power of showing non-continuous meaning (nanirantarattha), by the power of showing the meaning “again and again” (punappunaṃ), by the power of the word “iva” in a simile (upamāna), by the power of showing the meaning of a word or term based on the word “iti,” or by the power of showing the state of mind (cittaparidīpana) occurring in such a way. In detail, however, a distinction in meaning is obtained through twenty-six modes or even more.

Here, regarding the attainment of a distinction in meaning of homonymous words through word division or non-division, there are such usages as: “Sā naṃ saṅgati pāleti (Association with that virtuous person protects him), abhikkamo sānaṃ paññāyati (The increase of those feelings is evident). Mā no deva avadhi (O Great King, do not kill us), māno mayhaṃ na vijjati (Conceit does not exist in me),” and so forth.
53:
In obtaining a special meaning through the combination of letters (akkharasannidhāna), there are usages such as: "Santēhi mahitō hitō" (The Buddha, who is honored by the virtuous and is the bringer of welfare); "Saṅgā saṅgāmajiṃ muttaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ" (Him I call a Brahmin, who is released from the five attachments and has conquered the battlefield); "Dāṭhī dāṭhīsu pakkhandi, manyamānō yathā purē" (The tusked tiger, thinking as before, rushes at the tusked boars); "Sabbābhibhuṃva sirasāsirasā namāmi" (I bow with my bowed head to the Buddha who overcomes all things); "Bhūmitō uṭṭhitā yāva, brahmalōkā vidhāvati. Acci accimatō lōkē, ḍayhamānamhi tējasā" (When the world is consumed by the heat of the world-destroying fire, the flame rising from the earth runs up to the Brahma realm).

In obtaining a special meaning through the combination of words (padasannidhāna), there are usages such as: "Āpō āpōgataṃ" (Water that has reached the state of water); "Rājarājamahāmattādayō" (The great ministers of kings, etc.); "Sukhō lōkassa lōkassa, kārakō ñāṇacakkhudō" (The Buddha, who brings light to the world and gives the eye of wisdom, brings happiness to the world); "Nirāpadē padē ninnō" (He is inclined towards the state of Nibbāna, which is free from danger); "Anantañāṇaṃ karuṇālayaṃ layaṃ, malassa buddhaṃ susamāhitaṃ hitaṃ" (To the Buddha who possesses infinite wisdom, who is the abode of great compassion, who is not the abode of impurity, who is well-composed in concentration, and who brings welfare to those to be tamed); "Namāmi dhammaṃ bhavasaṃvaraṃ varaṃ, guṇākarañcēva niraṅgaṇaṃ gaṇaṃ" (I bow to the noble Dhamma that protects from the dangers of saṃsāra, and to the Saṅgha which is the source of virtues and free from defilements).

In obtaining a special meaning through the combination of both words and letters (padakkharasannidhāna), there are usages such as: "Pamāṇarahitaṃ hitaṃ" (Immeasurable welfare); "Siddhatthō sabbasiddhatthō, tilōkamahitō hitō" (The Lord Siddhattha, who is honored by the three worlds, who brings welfare to the three worlds, and who fulfills all benefits); "Upagantvāna sambuddhā, idaṃ vacanamabravī" (Approaching the Buddha, he spoke these words).

Regarding these combinations of letters and so forth, there are verses to clarify the meaning:

If the letter 'Ma' is removed from the word 'Mahitō', the word becomes meaningless in this context. Therefore, the wise call the letter 'Ma', which makes the special meaning known here, an 'akkhara' (letter).

In phrases such as 'Santēhi mahitō hitō', the distinction in meaning of words with similar forms is known through their association with letters.

Prefixes (upasagga), particles (nipāta), and other words that clarify meaning, even if they consist of only a single letter, are called 'pada' (word) by the wise.
54:
I have spoken with the intention that the coexistence of words and the coexistence of words and letters can be obtained in a compound (samāsa).

In obtaining a special meaning through the power of vīcchā (repetition for pervasiveness), there are usages such as: "In every village (gāmē gāmē), there are a hundred pots; every village (gāmō gāmō) is delightful." Here, by the power of vīcchā, all villages are included.

The desire to pervade various objects existing in different locations at a single moment is called vīcchā.

In obtaining a special meaning through the power of kammapavacanīya (prepositional particles), there are usages such as: "The moon shines over every single tree (rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pati); the moon shines around every single tree (rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pari)." This means it shines above and over the trees.

In obtaining a special meaning through the power of āmeḍita (emphatic repetition) spoken when fear, anger, and so forth arise, there are these usages: In fear, "Thief! Thief!", "Snake! Snake!", etc. In anger, "Vile man! Vile man!", "Outcaste! Outcaste!", "Strike! Strike!", "Hit! Hit!", etc. In praise, "Sāriputta, well said! Well said!", "It is very pleasing, Bhante! It is very pleasing!", etc. In haste, "Vāseṭṭha, come forward! Come forward!", "Go! Go!", "Reap! Reap!", etc. In curiosity, "Come! Come!", etc. In wonder, "How amazing are the Buddhas! How amazing are the Buddhas!", etc. In joy, "How happy! How happy!", "How pleasant! How pleasant!", etc. In grief, "Where has my only son gone? Where has my only son gone?", etc. In devotion, "The Vajjians will prosper! The Vajjians will prosper!", etc. Thus, a special meaning is obtained through the power of āmeḍita speech when fear, anger, and so forth arise. In this case, even if there is no other distinct meaning, the clarification of the meaning of the words through the power of strengthening (daḷhīkamma) is itself the attainment of a special meaning.
55:
The wise should employ āmeḍita (repetition of a word) in cases of fear, anger, praise, haste, curiosity, wonder, joy, grief, and devotion.

The word 'ca' (and) has the sense of including what has not yet been mentioned. By that word 'ca', it should be understood that contempt, lack of respect, and so forth are also included. Thus, āmeḍita should be understood in the sense of contempt in "Evil one! Evil one!", in the sense of lack of respect in "O beautiful one! O beautiful one!", and in the sense of excess in "Who is this monk? He is like one who is extremely silent (or extremely confused)."

In obtaining a special meaning by doubling an adjective, there are usages such as: "It is very black (kaṇhō kaṇhō) and it is terrifying." "Kaṇhō kaṇhō" means extremely black.

In obtaining a special meaning by doubling a verb, there are usages such as: "Blow, blow (dhamē dhamē), but do not blow excessively." There, "blow, blow" means one should blow moderately and should not remain without blowing. "Do not blow excessively" means one should not blow beyond the proper measure.

In obtaining a special meaning through word junction and word separation, there are usages such as: "Humans and non-humans (narānara), devas and non-devas (surāsura); kukkucca is the repeated worry occurring in the form of dissatisfaction, focusing on the unwholesome deeds that have been done and the wholesome deeds that have not been done."

Here, I shall compose a verse for the sake of producing supreme skill in the wise:

## O Victorious Lord, by Your power, having reached the most noble supramundane Dhamma—which is a welfare exceeding mundane welfare—and having abandoned unwholesome states, may we be those who are free from disease and the ailments of defilements.

In illustrating a lack of respect, there are usages such as: "While saying 'You, you' (tuvaṃ tuvaṃ), slandering, quarreling, strife, and disputes occur." In illustrating continuity (without interval), there are usages such as: "He consumes it day after day (divasē divasē)."
56:
In obtaining a special significance, there are usages such as 'pīti uppajjati khane khane' (joy arises moment by moment). In obtaining a special significance by way of illustrating the meaning of repetition, there are usages such as 'muhuṃ muhuṃ bhāyayate kumāre' (he frightens the children again and again). In obtaining a special significance in the context of a simile by the power of the word 'iva', there are usages such as 'Rājā rakkhatu dhammena, attano va pajaṃ pajaṃ' (May the king protect the beings with righteousness, just as he protects his own children).

In obtaining a special significance by way of illustrating the meaning of a word depending on the word 'iti', there are usages such as 'Buddhā Buddhā ti kathayanto, somanassaṃ pavedayi' (Saying 'Buddha, Buddha', he expressed his joy). In obtaining a special significance by way of illustrating the state of mind that has arisen in such a way, there are usages such as 'Buddhā Buddhā ti cintento, maggaṃ sodhemahaṃ tadā' (Thinking 'Buddha, Buddha', I cleared the path at that time).

In such usages, words that sound identical should not be recited with a break. If they are recited with a break, the elegance of the sound does not occur. In some places, such as 'katākata-kusala-akusala-visayaṃ', the meaning of the words becomes corrupted if recited with a break. Therefore, they should not be recited with a break, but should be recited as a single continuous unit. Thus, the decision regarding identical-sounding words has been shown, adorned with twenty-six modes and even more.

Since the decision regarding identical-sounding words has been shown, the decision regarding non-identical sounding words should also be shown. Therefore, I shall show that as well—wherever a reading is known where the following character is elided after a niggahīta, or where a conjunct consonant becomes simplified. In those usages, the word with the niggahīta should be recited as a single continuous unit together with the following word. What are those? Usages such as 'Sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ-sā’jīvo garahito mama' (If I were to have eaten, my livelihood would be blameworthy), 'Pupphaṃ’sā uppajji' (A flower arose for her), and 'Khayamattaṃ na nibbānaṃ’sa gambhīrādivācato' (Nibbāna is not merely cessation, because of the expression of its depth, etc.). Here, with 'Sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ' and so forth...
57:
Without making a break, one should recite as a single continuous unit together with the subsequent words, just as one recites two identical-sounding words that occur in the middle of two adjacent verse feet as one, in the manner of 'Sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ-sā’jīvo garahito mama'. Indeed, this specific manner of recitation is desired by all ancient wise ones and has been recited by them. This is because it is consistent with conveying the meanings such as 'My livelihood would be blameworthy', 'It arose for her', and 'Because of the expression of depth, etc.'

However, in usages where the meaning becomes particularly clear when a certain recitation is performed, a word should be recited with a slight break in places associated with particles such as 'ca' and 'pana'. For example: 'Vālā ca lapasakkharā', 'Accantasantā pana yā, ayaṃ nibbānasampadā'. Also, 'To one who speaks the words "Idaṃ dukkhaṃ" (This is suffering), does the knowledge "Idaṃ dukkhaṃ" arise? Yes, it does. Does the knowledge arise as "i", as "daṃ", as "du", or as "khaṃ"? It should not be said so.' Such are the usages.

Among these, in the first usage, one should recite 'lapasakkharā' after a slight break from 'Vālā ca'. In that context, 'lapasakkharā' means those who have sweet speech like sugar-gravel (jaggery). In the Jātaka Commentary, however, it is said, 'They are sweet like sugar-gravel due to their useless words.' Therefore, in this context, the compound should be understood in two ways, by the power of Bahubbīhi and Tappurisa compounds: 'Lapasakkharā' means those whose words (lapā) are like sugar-gravel (sakkharā), or 'Lapasakkharā' means those who are like sugar-gravel by their talking (lapehi).

In the second usage, one should recite 'yā' after a slight break from 'Accantasantā pana'. The meaning is: 'That which is the attainment of Nibbāna is indeed utterly peaceful.'
58:
In the third usage, in these four instances—'iti ca', 'danti ca', 'duti ca', and 'khanti ca'—one should recite the words 'ti ca' immediately after a slight break from the characters 'i', 'daṃ', 'du', and 'khaṃ'.

In this usage, if recited without a break, the meaning is corrupted because it would be understood in another way (different from what is intended). How does the meaning get corrupted? If recited without a break in these instances, the word 'iti' would be a particle (nipāta) expressing the meaning 'evaṃ' (thus); it would not be the conventional word (rūḷhī-sadda) expressing the meaning of the letter 'i' by way of euphonic combination (sandhi). The word 'danti' would have the meaning of 'taming' (damana); it would not be the conventional word expressing the letter 'daṃ'. The word 'duti' would be meaningless; it would not be the conventional word expressing the letter 'du'. The word 'khanti' would have the meaning of 'patience' (khamana); it would not be the conventional word expressing the letter 'khaṃ'. Therefore, one should recite with a slight break after the characters 'i', 'daṃ', 'du', and 'khaṃ'.

In this usage, the word-splitting (saṃhitā-padaccheda) should be understood as 'i iti', 'daṃ iti', 'du iti', 'khaṃ iti', and so forth, and the subsequent letter 'i' should be elided. It should not be said here that 'In the case of vowels of the same form, the subsequent vowel of the same form is not elided, only the preceding vowel is elided, as in the example "tatrāyaṃ"'. This is because in the Pali 'Akilāsuno vaṇṇapathe khaṇantā, udaṅgaṇe tattha papaṃ avindu', the elision of the subsequent vowel of the same form is seen. Indeed, the commentators have explained the meaning of the word 'papaṃ' as 'great water' (pavaddhaṃ āpaṃ). Therefore, in this instance of 'iti ca' as well, having split the words as 'i iti ca', the subsequent 'i' of the two 'i' characters should be elided, not the preceding one.

This is because if the preceding 'i' character, which expresses the letter 'i', were lost, the meaning designated as the letter 'i' could not be known through the particle 'iti'. However, even if the 'i' of the particle 'iti' is lost, that meaning is still understood, as in the example 'Devadattoti me sutaṃ' (Thus I have heard, Devadatta).
59:
In this context, it is like the meaning of the word 'Devadatta'. Therefore, only the vowel 'i' of the subsequent word 'iti' should be elided, not the preceding vowel 'i' which denotes the letter 'i'. In the Kaccāyana grammar, however, with a view to general usage, it is stated that a dissimilar vowel following another dissimilar vowel is elided, but it does not mention the elision of a similar vowel following a similar vowel. Alternatively, it should be understood that the elision of a similar subsequent vowel is stated by the Mahāpadesa Suttas.

In phrases such as "Antarā ca Rājagahaṃ antarā ca Nāḷandaṃ," even when there is a connection with the word 'ca' and so on, the words should not be recited by breaking them apart. In usages where augment letters (āgama) and the like are seen, the preceding words should not be recited separately; they must be recited together with the subsequent words that contain the augment letters. For example: "Nakkhattarājāriva tārakānaṃ," "Bhagavā etadavoca," and such usages. Where a separate connection of words is seen and the meaning is appropriate, those words should be recited by breaking them according to the meaning. For example: "Nahāne ussukkaṃ akāsi, ussukkampi akāsi yāguyā khādanīye bhattasmiṃ," and such usages. Here, one should recite by pausing at "Nahāne ussukkaṃ akāsi" and then reciting "ussukkampi akāsi yāguyā khādanīye bhattasmiṃ." When recited in this way, it is capable of showing the meaning that the monk was not only concerned with bathing, but indeed was also concerned with the rice gruel, the hard food, and the meal; thus, the word 'api', which expresses a conjunctive meaning (samuccaya), is no longer applied in an inappropriate place.

In usages where a connection is seen between certain words and either one other word or both words together, along with logical consistency of meaning, those words should be recited by pausing as appropriate. For example: "He, the Blessed One, teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and with the phrasing, completely fulfilled and pure..."
60:
...proclaims the holy life. "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Law of Dependent Origination; listen to it, attend well to it." "Serenity within, and singleness of mind"—such are the usages. In this regard, there are these verses that make the intention known:

The wise one should recite this phrase "sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ" (with meaning and phrasing) by connecting it either with the word "dhamma" or with the word "brahmacariya" (holy life).

The wise one should recite the word "sādhukaṃ" (well) by connecting it with the word "suṇātha" (listen), or likewise with the stated word "manasikarotha" (attend to), or by connecting it with both words.

One should understand that a connection is seen with each one individually or a connection with both, together with the logical consistency of the meaning.

This meaning stated by me here is not stated by my own wish (intellect); it is stated by me relying on the method of the noble former teachers (pubbācariya).

In other such Pali texts as well, this method should be applied by the wise one who is skilled in methods and who seeks the meaning of the Dispensation.

Having reflected on the word according to the meaning, and the meaning according to the word, the wise one should speak; he should not speak randomly (without reflection).

This is the investigation of meaning and word in this context.

Regarding the application of intensified meaning (atthātishaya-yoga), it should be noted thus: the root 'bhū' is found in the sense of 'increase' (vaḍḍhana) due to its connection with intensified meaning. For example: "The Licchavi Mahānāma, sitting at one side, uttered an inspired exclamation: 'The Vajjis will prosper, the Vajjis will prosper!'" Or: "I alone have committed the fault of destroying the prosperity of the great King Mahāpatāpa." Or: "The Vedas are no protection for that man who betrays a friend and destroys prosperity (bhūnahu)." Or: "I have committed the destruction of prosperity (bhūnahacca)." Thus, it is found in the sense of increase.
61:
Regarding the grouping of similar inflections (vacanasaṅgaha), it should be noted thus: The second person plural of the Parassapada in the Vattamānā (present tense) inflection is similar to the second person plural of the Parassapada in the Pañcamī (imperative) inflection. (Example:) Tumhe bhavatha.

In the group of four Uttamapurisa (first person) forms of the Parassapada in the Vattamānā and Pañcamī inflections, the singular is similar to the singular, and the plural is also similar to the plural. (Example:) Ahaṃ bhavāmi, mayaṃ bhavāma.

The second person singular of the Attanopada in the Vattamānā inflection is similar to the two second person singular forms of the Attanopada in the Hiyyattanī (imperfect) and Ajjatanī (aorist) inflections in certain usages, excluding the slight difference of the augment 'a' due to the combination of letters. This method should also be applied hereafter. Tvaṃ bhavase; this is the form of the Vattamānā. Tvaṃ abhavase; this is the form of the Hiyyattanī and Ajjatanī.

The first person singular of the Attanopada in the Vattamānā inflection is similar to these two forms: the first person singular of the Attanopada in the Pañcamī inflection, and the second person singular of the Parassapada in the Parokkhā (perfect) inflection. Ahaṃ bhave; this is the form of the Vattamānā and Pañcamī. Tvaṃ babhūve; this is the form of the Parokkhā.

The first person plural of the Attanopada in the Vattamānā inflection is similar to the two first person plural forms of the Attanopada in the Parokkhā and Ajjatanī inflections. Mayaṃ bhavāmhe; this is the form of the Vattamānā. Mayaṃ babhūvimhe; this is the form of the Parokkhā. Mayaṃ abhavimhe; this is the form of the Ajjatanī.

The second person plural of the Attanopada in the Pañcamī inflection is similar to the second person plural of the Attanopada in the Parokkhā inflection. Tumhe bhavavho; this is the form of the Pañcamī. Tumhe babhūvivho; this is the form of the Parokkhā.

The third person plural of the Parassapada in the Parokkhā inflection is similar to these two forms: the third person plural of the Parassapada in the Hiyyattanī inflection, and the third person plural of the Attanopada in the Ajjatanī inflection. Te babhūvu; this is the form of the Parokkhā. Te abhavu; this is the form of the Hiyyattanī and Ajjatanī.
62:
The second person plural active ending (Parassapada) of the Parokkhā tense is identical to four other endings: the third person singular middle ending (Attanopada) of the same tense, the second person plural active ending of the Hiyyattanī tense, the third person singular middle ending of the Hiyyattanī tense, and the second person plural active ending of the Ajjatanī tense. *Tumhe babhūvittha, so babhūvittha*; these are the forms of the Parokkhā tense. *Tumhe abhavattha, so abhavattha*; these are the forms of the Hiyyattanī tense. *Tumhe abhavittha*; this is the form of the Ajjatanī tense.

The first person singular active ending of the Parokkhā tense is identical to two other endings: the first person singular active ending of the Hiyyattanī tense and the first person singular middle ending of the Ajjatanī tense. *Ahaṃ babhūvaṃ*; this is the form of the Parokkhā tense. *Ahaṃ abhavaṃ*; this is the form of both the Hiyyattanī and Ajjatanī tenses.

The first person plural active ending of the Parokkhā tense is identical to the first person plural active ending of the Hiyyattanī tense. *Mayaṃ babhūvimha*; this is the form of the Parokkhā tense. *Mayaṃ abhavimha*; this is the form of the Hiyyattanī tense.

The first person singular middle ending of the Parokkhā tense is identical to two other endings: the first person singular middle ending of the Hiyyattanī tense and the first person singular active ending of the Ajjatanī tense. *Ahaṃ babhūviṃ*; this is the form of the Parokkhā tense. *Ahaṃ abhaviṃ*; this is the form of both the Hiyyattanī and Ajjatanī tenses.

The third person singular active ending of the Hiyyattanī tense is identical to the third person singular middle ending of the Ajjatanī tense. *So abhavā.*

The second person singular active ending of the Hiyyattanī tense is identical to the second person singular active ending of the Ajjatanī tense. *Tvaṃ abhavo.*

The second person plural active ending of the Bhavissantī tense is identical to two other endings: the second person plural active ending of the Kālātipatti mood and the third person singular middle ending of the Kālātipatti mood.
63:
*Tumhe bhavissatha*; this is the form of the Bhavissantī tense. *Tumhe abhavissatha, so abhavissatha*; these are the forms of the Kālātipatti mood.

The second person singular middle ending of the Bhavissantī tense is identical to the second person singular middle ending of the Kālātipatti mood. *Tvaṃ bhavissase*; this is the form of the Bhavissantī tense. *Tvaṃ abhavissase*; this is the form of the Kālātipatti mood.

The second person plural middle ending of the Bhavissantī tense is identical to the second person plural middle ending of the Kālātipatti mood. *Tumhe bhavissavhe*; this is the form of the Bhavissantī tense. *Tumhe abhavissavhe*; this is the form of the Kālātipatti mood.

The first person singular middle ending of the Bhavissantī tense is identical to the first person singular active ending of the Kālātipatti mood. *Ahaṃ bhavissaṃ*; this is the form of the Bhavissantī tense. *Ahaṃ abhavissaṃ*; this is the form of the Kālātipatti mood. It should be noted that the endings of the remaining eight tenses/moods are mutually distinct. Here are the verses:

In the Vattamānā and Pañcamī, the two *tha* endings are said to be identical.
In the case of "*Tumhe bhavatha*", the example is shown in two ways.

In those same tenses/moods, the two *mi* endings and the two *ma* endings are each said to be of two kinds.
Here, one should point out the forms as "*Bhavāmi*" and "*Bhavāmā*".

In the Vattamānā, Hiyyattanī, and Ajjatanī tenses,
there are three *se* endings: from the Vattamānā tense as "*Tvaṃ bhavase*",
and from the Hiyyattanī and Ajjatanī tenses as "*Abhavase*".

In the Vattamānā, Pañcamī, and Parokkhā tenses/moods,
three *e* endings are mentioned here; among those three, by virtue of the first two [Vattamānā and Pañcamī],
one should know them as "*Ahaṃ bhave*", and from the Parokkhā as "*Tvaṃ babhūve*".

In the three [tenses]—Vattamānā, Parokkhā, and Ajjatanī—[the three *mhe* endings] are mentioned.
64: In the Vattamānā, Parokkhā, and Ajjatanī tenses, three *mhe* endings are mentioned. One should point out the forms in order as *sambhavāmhe*, *babhūvimhe*, and *abhavimhe*, which are distinguished by the word '*mayaṃ*'. In the Pañcamī and Parokkhā, there are two *vhe* endings. Here, one should point out the forms *bhavavho* and *babhūvivho*, which are distinguished by the word '*tumhe*'. In the Parokkhā, Hiyyattanī, and Ajjatanī tenses, there are three *u* endings. One should know the form *te babhūvū* as arising from the Parokkhā tense. One should know the form *te abhavū* as arising from the Hiyyattanī and Ajjatanī tenses. In the Parokkhā, Hiyyattanī, and Ajjatanī tenses, the group of five *ttha* endings, which are *tatha*-conjuncts, should be pointed out thus: Among those endings, the two forms of *babhūvittha* arising from the Parokkhā tense should be known as the second person and third person, by way of plural and singular respectively. The two forms of *abhavattha* arising from the Hiyyattanī tense should also be known as the second person and third person, by way of plural and singular respectively. This form *abhavitthā* arises from the Ajjatanī tense. That form, in the plural, should be joined with the word '*tumhe*'. In the Parokkhā, Hiyyattanī, and Ajjatanī tenses, three *aṃ* endings are mentioned. Among those three, the form *babhūvaṃ* is mentioned for the first, the Parokkhā tense. The form *abhavaṃ* of the remaining two tenses should be joined with the word '*ahaṃ*'. By virtue of the Parokkhā and Hiyyattanī tenses, two *mha* endings are mentioned. One should know the two forms *mayaṃ babhūvimha* and *abhavimha* in order. In the Parokkhā, Hiyyattanī, and Ajjatanī tenses, there are three *iṃ* endings. Among those three, the form *babhūviṃ* arises from the Parokkhā tense. All the forms *abhaviṃ* of the remaining tenses are joined with the word '*ahaṃ*'.
65:
In the Hiyattanī and Ajjatanī suffixes, two 'ā' characters should be known. The form 'abhavā' occurs in the singular third person (paṭhamapurisa).

In the Hiyattanī and Ajjatanī suffixes, two 'o' characters are mentioned. The form 'abhavō' occurs in the singular second person (majjhimapurisa).

In the two types of suffixes, Bhavissantī and Kālātipatti, three 'ssatha' forms with the 's-saṃyoga' (double 's') are mentioned in the plural and singular. The form 'tumhe bhavissatha' is known to be from the Bhavissantī suffix. The two forms 'abhavissatha tumhe' and 'abhavissatha so' are mentioned as being from the Kālātipatti suffix.

In the second person (majjhimapurisa) position of the Bhavissantī and Kālātipatti suffixes, a pair of 'ssase' with the 's-saṃyoga' is mentioned. The wise should demonstrate these applications as 'bhavissase tvaṃ' and 'tvaṃ abhavissase' in those suffixes.

A group of four—two 'ssavhe' and two 'ssaṃ' conjoined with the 's-saṃyoga'—is also mentioned in the two types of suffixes previously stated. The form 'bhavissavhe' is the plural second person of the Bhavissantī. The form 'abhavissavhe' in the plural is the second person of the Kālātipatti.

The form 'bhavissaṃ' is the singular first person (uttamapurisa) of the Bhavissantī. The form 'abhavissaṃ' in the singular is the first person of the Kālātipatti.

In this manner, all those suffixes that reach similarity with certain other suffixes according to the method already mentioned, stand in 41 varieties. The remaining 55 suffixes are entirely dissimilar. Taking this method, it is stated according to what is possible in all instances.

## This is the summary of suffixes (vibhatti) shown by grouping them according to their similarity and dissimilarity in this treatise.
66:
## In the summary of suffixes and numbers (vacana) by the power of the characteristics of augments (āgama), it should be noted as follows:

In the Bhavissantī, Parokkhā, Ajjatanī, and Kālātipatti suffixes, the occurrence of the 'i' augment is constant in some places and not constant in others. That occurrence of the 'i' augment in the Parokkhā suffix happens in the plural second person (ttha) position and also in the plural first person (mha) position.

This statement is made with reference to the Parassapada. It should be noted that in the singular first person of the Attanopada of that Parokkhā, the 'i' augment does not occur. In the Bhavissantī suffix, the 'i' augment occurs in all twelve forms.

In the Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, and Kālātipatti suffixes, however, it should be noted that the 'a' augment occurs in all suffixes. In the Ajjatanī suffix, the 'i' augment occurs along with the 'a' augment in the plural second person and plural first person.

In the Kālātipatti suffix, the occurrence of the 'i' augment is constant. However, the occurrence of the 'a' augment in that Kālātipatti is said to be not constant.

In the Hiyattanī suffix, only the occurrence of the 'a' augment is evident. In the Parokkhā and Bhavissantī suffixes, only the occurrence of the 'i' augment is evident. In the Ajjatanī and Kālātipatti suffixes, however, both the occurrence of the 'a' augment and the 'i' augment are found.

In the three remaining suffixes—Vattamānā, Pañcamī, and Sattamī—the three modes (the occurrence of 'a', the occurrence of 'i', and the occurrence of both) are not mentioned.

The two suffixes, Parokkhā and Bhavissantī, are associated only with the 'i' augment. Among those suffixes, it should be noted that 7 forms in the Parokkhā and 12 forms in the Bhavissantī are associated with the 'i' augment. Only the Hiyattanī suffix is associated with the 'a' augment. It should be noted that in that Hiyattanī, 12 forms are associated with the 'a' augment.
67:
The suffixes associated with both 'a' and 'i' augments are only two (Ajjatanī and Kālātipatti). In this context, four forms (of the Ajjatanī suffix) and twelve forms (of the Kālātipatti suffix) occur with both 'a' and 'i' augments. The suffixes that are free from the three modes such as the 'a' augment are only three (Vattamānā, Pañcamī, and Sattamī). It should be demonstrated that there are thirty-six forms in these suffixes. In the Parokkhā and Ajjatanī suffixes, five and eight forms respectively are free from the 'i' augment. Thus, in this context, the summary of the ninety-six varieties of forms of the suffixes should be understood by the wise.

This is the summary of suffixes and numbers (vibhatti-vacana-saṅgaha) presented here by the power of the characteristics of augments (āgama).

In the summary of suffixes and numbers by the power of time (kāla), there are two types: summary by the power of the three times (kālattaya) and summary by the power of the six times (kālachakka). Among those suffixes, the Vattamānā, Pañcamī, and Sattamī suffixes occur in the present time; words ending in Vattamānā, Pañcamī, and Sattamī suffixes are present-tense words. The Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, and Ajjatanī suffixes occur in the past time; words ending in Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, and Ajjatanī suffixes are past-tense words. The Bhavissantī suffix occurs in the future time; words ending in the Bhavissantī suffix are future-tense words. The Kālātipatti suffix, however, occurs in the past time in some applications and in the future time in others; therefore, words ending in that suffix are both past-tense words and future-tense words. This is the summary of suffixes and numbers by the power of the three times.

This is the summary of suffixes and numbers by the power of the six times: The Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, and Ajjatanī suffixes occur in the past time; words ending in Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, and Ajjatanī suffixes are past-tense words. The Bhavissantī suffix occurs in the future time; words ending in the Bhavissantī suffix are future-tense words. The Vattamānā suffix occurs in the present time; words ending in the Vattamānā suffix are present-tense words. The Pañcamī suffix...
68:
Words ending in the Pañcamī suffix are called āṇatti-vacana because they express the imperative time (āṇatti-kāla). Words ending in the Sattamī suffix are called parikappa-vacana because they express the time of reflection (parikappa-kāla). In this context, the terms "āṇatti-vacana" and "parikappa-vacana" are used primarily as principal designations, as Pañcamī and other suffixes are also seen in senses such as āsiṭṭha (aspiration) and anumati (consent). Words ending in the kālātipatti suffix are called kālātipatti-vacana because they express the time of conditional occurrence (kālātipatti-kāla). Thus, the compendium of verbal terminations (vibhatti-vacana-saṅgaha) should be understood by way of the six times.

## Kāla-saṅgaha (Compendium of Time)
In the compendium of time, there are three types: the compendium of three times, the compendium of four times, and the compendium of six times.

The Vattamāna, Pañcamī, and Sattamī suffixes occur in the present time.
The Parokkhā and other suffixes, together with the Kālātipatti suffix, occur in the past time.
The Bhavissantī suffix and also the Kālātipatti suffix occur in the future time.
In this way, the three times and the verbs (ākhyāta) that express those three times should be understood.

Is it not stated in the Kaccāyana treatise that time is of four kinds: present (paccuppanna), anuttakāla, past (atīta), and future (anāgata)?
It is true that it is so stated; however, anuttakāla is intended as the present. 
Because the meaning is possible, it is intended as "anu samīpe vuttakālo anuttakālo" (the time proximate to the stated time is anuttakāla).
For that reason, the teachers also say, "whichever three times."
No verb (ākhyāta) is ever seen to be exempt from time.

In that word "anuttakāla," is the meaning "avuttakāla" (unspoken time) not also appropriate?
For that reason, the six times are shown in the Nirutti treatise.
There are six: past, future, present, āṇatti (imperative), parikappa (reflection), and the surpassing of time (atipatti).
Among those six, the two suffixes āṇatti and parikappa are spoken of by those learned in grammar without specifically referring to a time.
69:
When words such as "gacchatu" or "gaccheyya" are spoken, it is true that the action (of going) is not completed, nor is it not yet completed, nor is it future, nor is it a past that has been surpassed.

Just as grammarians definitely state in grammatical treatises that Kālātipatti suffixes occur in the past and the future, they do not state in those treatises that the āṇatti and parikappa suffixes, known as Pañcamī and Sattamī, occur in the present.

Therefore, whatever word is stated as "anuttakāle" in the Kaccāyana treatise, the meaning of that word should be understood simply as "avuttakāle" (in the unspoken time).

Even though this is true, a wise person who knows the method should regard the āṇatti and parikappa suffixes as also existing in the present. Why? Because ordering (āṇāpana) and conjecture (parikappa) are evident as meanings that are actually accomplished in the present.

The word "anuttakāle" illuminates that (present) meaning. Or, it is because it shows the meaning as "proximate to the stated time" (samīpe vuttakāle).

Since the completion of meanings such as going is not seen in the time stated by "gacchatu" or "gaccheyya," the suffixes expressing those meanings are pointed out as being in the unspoken time (avuttakāla). Alternatively, in this context, avuttakāla is taken as time itself. It is like in the Dakkhiṇāvisuddhi-pāṭha, where the third kind of offering is designated as "purity" (visuddhi) (even though it is not pure).

The expression of the time of those suffixes is appropriate in this way, and not otherwise. To show the two kinds of meanings, the Elder Kaccāyana spoke the word "anuttakāle" in the treatise named Kaccāyana.

Thus, the compendium of times has been stated by way of three and four. Now, the compendium of times will be presented by way of the sixfold division.
70:
These three types of suffixes—Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, and Ajjatanī—are shown to be in the past time. The Bhavissantī suffix is said to occur in the future time. The Vattamāna suffix occurs in the present time. Thus, the suffixes are established in five ways across the three times (as Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, Bhavissantī, and Vattamāna).

The suffixes called Pañcamī and Sattamī occur in the senses of command (āṇatti) and reflection (parikappa). When taken inclusively, they are included within the present time.

Because it is equal in position to the Vattamāna suffix, which is the fifth (after Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, and Bhavissantī), that suffix is designated as Pañcamī.

As for the Sattamī suffix, although it is the seventh from those suffixes, it is our opinion that it is called "Sattamī" simply because it is the seventh.

If it were so (in sequential order), since the Kālātipatti suffix expresses the past time, the Vattamāna suffix should be the sixth (chaṭṭhī). Since the Pañcamī suffix is equal in position to that sixth Vattamāna, should it not also be the sixth? And because of those seven types of suffixes, should the Sattamī suffix not be the eighth (aṭṭhamī)?

If someone should speak thus, one should refute it, saying, "It is not so." This is because the Kālātipatti suffix can occur not only in the past time but also in the future time.

Therefore, this Kālātipatti suffix is shown separately in the Cūḷanirutti treatise. It should be shown that the Kālātipatti suffix can occur in both the past and the future.

If it is asked why it is said only in the past time as "kriyātipannetīte" in the Kaccāyana treatise, one should answer in this matter, "mostly" (yebhuyyena) (because it is commonly used in the past).

It should be noted that in common usage, the expression associated with the Kālātipatti suffix usually occurs in the past time.

In this context, an example of the Kālātipatti suffix expressing the past time is: "Monks, if this King Ajātasattu had not deprived his father, the righteous king who ruled by Dhamma, of life, then in this very seat, there would have arisen for him the dustless, stainless..."
71:
The Eye of Dhamma (the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry) would have arisen."

"Look, Ānanda, at this son of the merchant Mahādhana, who, having squandered one hundred and sixty crores of wealth in this very city of Vārāṇasī, now wanders for alms with his wife. If this merchant's son had applied himself to business in the first stage of life without squandering his wealth, he would have become the foremost merchant in this very city. If he had left the household life and ordained, he would have attained Arahantship, and his wife would have been established in the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala). If he had applied himself to business in the middle stage of life without squandering his wealth, he would have become the second-ranking merchant. If he had left the household life and ordained, he would have become a Non-returner (Anāgāmī), and his wife would have been established in the Fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmiphala). If he had applied himself to business in the last stage of life without squandering his wealth, he would have become the third-ranking merchant. If he had left the household life and ordained, he would have become a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī), and his wife would have been established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala)."

Or: "If the Blessed One had remained in the household life, he would have become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). The novice Rāhula would have been the Treasurer-jewel, the Therī (Yasodharā) would have been the Woman-jewel, and the sovereignty of the entire universe would have belonged to them alone." In this way, the past tense is expressed using the Kālātipatti mood.

How is the future tense expressed using the Kālātipatti mood? "If we had not quarreled, there would have been food for a long time. But now, the fox has carried away the rohita-fish, which has neither head nor tail." Or: "Ānanda, if women had not received the going forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, then, Ānanda, the holy life (the Dispensation) would have endured for a long time." Or: "This mother of Aṅgulimāla is going, thinking, 'I will bring Aṅgulimāla back.' If they meet, Aṅgulimāla, thinking, 'I will complete the thousand fingers,' would kill his mother. If I (the Buddha) did not go, there would be a great loss." In this way, the future tense is expressed using the Kālātipatti mood.
72:
In this way, the past tense is expressed using the Kālātipatti mood. In the Kaccāyana grammar, however, it should be understood that the past-time nature of the Kālātipatti mood is stated mostly with reference to occurrences in the past.

Alternatively, even in the Kaccāyana grammar, this Kālātipatti mood is also used for the future; this meaning is also evident.

In the characteristic of the sutta "Appaccakkhe parokkhātīte," although the word 'atīta' (past) is present, disregarding that word 'atīta,' because the Kālātipatti mood is mentioned immediately after the sutta "Anāgate bhavisanti," it draws in the sense of the future.

Therefore, excluding the Kālātipatti mood which has an indefinite time, when counting by the moods that occur in the past, future, and present, the Sattamī mood is only the seventh; it is not the eighth.

In order to include the Pañcamī and Sattamī moods within the present tense, the Chaṭṭhī (sixth) mood is not mentioned between them.

Likewise, when counting starting from the five moods, although the Pañcamī mood should be the sixth, that Pañcamī mood is not called "Chaṭṭhī."

Even though it exists as the sixth, the name "Pañcamī" is stated, as the wise should understand, for the purpose of including the Pañcamī mood within the present tense.

When counting starting from the Pañcamī, although the Sattamī mood should be the sixth, it is not called "Chaṭṭhī"; it is called only "Sattamī" starting from the Pañcamī which is the sixth.

This manner of speaking without showing the Chaṭṭhī mood in the middle should be understood as being stated for the purpose of including the Sattamī mood within the present tense.

For it is the nature of those who explain deep meanings to make their intention known by whatever means possible.
73:
(Continued from the previous page) ...it is called only Sattamī based on the Chaṭṭhī mood. This manner of mentioning only Pañcamī and Sattamī without showing the Chaṭṭhī mood in between should be understood as being stated for the purpose of including the Sattamī mood within the present tense. Indeed, it should be known that it is the nature of speakers to make their desire known by some means regarding deep meanings.

If that is the case, one should first state the moods that occur in the past and future, and then state the moods that occur in the present. Why is it not taught this way in the text named Kaccāyana? Why are only the present tense moods taught at the beginning?

Because those present tense moods are mostly spoken in worldly usage. Therefore, those moods are of frequent use. According to the principle that only the frequently used mood should be stated at the beginning, it should be noted that only the moods occurring in the present are taught at the beginning.

When the past and future are stated and then the present is stated, there is euphony (smoothness of speech) in the world. Therefore, in euphonic speech, with regard to the past etc., these Pañcamī and Sattamī are taught immediately after the Vattamāna (present) mood for the purpose of including them among the present tense moods.

In this matter, for example, when one says "Mātāpitaro" (mother and father), there is euphony. In that same expression, if one reverses the order and says "Pitāmātaro" by way of a compound (samāsa), there is no euphony. Therefore, such an arrangement of words is not to be used. The text "Pitā mātā ca me dajjuṃ," however, is acceptable because it is used as desired by way of analysis (vigraha). Similarly, when one says "Atītānāgatapaccuppanna" (past, future, present), there is euphony. When one says "Atītapaccuppannānāgata" etc., there is no euphony. Therefore, such an arrangement of words would be unacceptable. The expression "Atītārammaṇā paccuppannānāgatagocarā," however, is acceptable because it is used as desired for the sake of ease in composing verses. In this matter, the following Pali should be known:

"Whatever form, whether past, future, or present..."
"The only path... the flood..."
"Those who... the nature..."

The Blessed One, who has seen Nibbāna, the end of the suffering of the round of rebirths, and who has compassion for the welfare of beings, knows the Ariyan Path, which is the one-way journey. By this path, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Ariyan disciples of the past have crossed over the four floods.
74:
“The Buddha, who sees Nibbāna which is the end of birth, and who is compassionate for the welfare of beings, knows the Noble Path which is the sole way. By this path, those in the past have crossed the four floods, those in the present are crossing, and those in the future will cross.”

“Those Buddhas of the past, those Buddhas of the future, and those Buddhas of the present who destroy the sorrow of many beings—all of those Buddhas dwelt, dwell, and will dwell respecting the True Dhamma. This dwelling in respect of the Dhamma is the nature of the Buddhas.”

In many such linguistic usages, among the eight terminations (vibhatti) occurring in the three times of past, future, and present, the three terminations of the present—Vattamānā, Pañcamī, and Sattami—are mentioned at the beginning. This initial mention is for the purpose of making known their frequent usage, as they mostly occur in the course of speech. Among these three, the names ‘Pañcamī’ and ‘Sattami’ for the two terminations are stated in order for the sake of smooth expression, and are made in consideration of the terminations occurring in the past and future.

Thus, with the usage as desired, the present terminations were divided into three and spoken of at the beginning by the teacher Kaccāyana.

That mention at the beginning should be indicated as being for the purpose of making known their frequent usage, as they mostly occur in speech.

In the smooth expression made in consideration of the past etc., the names of the two terminations were certainly made as ‘Pañcamī’ and ‘Sattami’.

This statement is made excluding the Kālātipatti termination.

If one says so, this following fault will occur, there should be no doubt.

Thus a person unskilled in the meaning might speak.
75:
If it is said that the Kālātipatti termination is not included in the verbal forms occurring in the three times, one should forbid it saying, “Do not say so.” It is not desired that Kālātipatti be excluded from verbal forms of the three times; it is desired only that it be included. Our view is that the names Pañcamī and Sattami were made without considering the Kālātipatti termination.

Taking various methods, it should be believed according to the essence. By whichever specific method this meaning is stated, therefore that view is not weak. Wherever and in whatever manner a praiseworthy meaning is obtained, there and in that manner it should be taken by the wise.

For it is said in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā: “Wherever and in whatever manner the meaning is obtained, there and in that manner it should be taken.”

Some say that the names Pañcamī and Sattami are conventional names (rūḷhī). That should not be taken so; they speak without knowing. This name is not spoken by way of convention like Purisasaññā or Jhalasaññā; it is spoken according to the actual meaning. Since this designation is established by comparison with Parokkhā etc., it should be noted that the ancient teachers established it as a meaningful name (anvatthasaññā).

Thus, the six times are briefly considered as three. Intending this meaning, the ancient teachers said, “Yaṃ tikālaṃ” (That which is of the three times).

## This is the Summary of the Six Times (Kālasakkhasangaha) in this text.
76:
Thus, a person of good wisdom should analyze the divisions of time shown by those wise in time, whether by three, four, or six ways. By taking the past, future, and the Kālātipatti termination separately, there are also five ways; thus also should it be analyzed.

In this matter, the method is just as the terminations of the past and future times are spoken of in the Pāli text, “Whether internal or external” (ajjhatta-bahiddhā vā). Thus, in every way, the Summary of Time (Kālasangaha) is completed.

Now, for the purpose of generating skill in grasping the meaning for the wise, I shall speak of the comparison of texts in the sequential arrangement of the two terminations known as “Pañcamī” and “Sattami,” which occur in the times of command (āṇatti) and reflection (parikappa), and are mentioned immediately after the Vattamānā in this text, also by way of other treatises.

In the Katantra (Kalāpa) treatise, ten verbal terminations are established in accordance with the Sanskrit language. In the Kaccāyana treatise, however, eight are established in accordance with the Māgadha language. And in the Nirutti treatise, six are established by way of past, future, present, command, reflection, and Kālātipatti, also in accordance with the Māgadha language.

Among those, in the Katantra, they are divided into ten: Vattamānā, Sattami, Pañcamī, Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, Parokkhā, Svātanī, Āsī, Bhavissantī, and Kriyātipatti. In the Kaccāyana, however, they are divided into eight: Vattamānā, Pañcamī, Sattami, Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, Bhavissantī, and Kālātipatti. Thus, in these two treatises of Katantra and Kaccāyana, the terminations are established in a dissimilar order. Although the sequential arrangement here is dissimilar, those terminations, by way of the division of time such as the past mentioned in the Nirutti treatise, coincide and agree as one, setting aside some specific differences.
77:
How is it consistent? In the Kātantra (Kalāp) treatise, first of all, these three verbal terminations—Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, and Parokkhā—occur strictly in the past tense. These three—Svātanī, Āsī, and Bhavissantī—occur strictly in the future tense. Vattamānā alone occurs in the present tense. However, Sattamī and Pañcamī occur in two times by virtue of both the present and future. This is because they are suitable for such usage as: "One should perform merit today; one should also perform it tomorrow" (Sattamī), and "Go today, or go tomorrow" (Pañcamī). The Kriyātipatti termination has an indefinite time. This is because it is suitable for such usage as: "If he had obtained a vehicle yesterday, he would have gone," "If he were to obtain a vehicle today before sunset, he would go," and "If he were to obtain a vehicle tomorrow, he would go." Thus, they should be defined without confusion.

Having thus defined them, this method which we are about to state should be carefully noted. How should it be noted? There are six terminations that are strictly past or future by virtue of Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, Parokkhā, Svātanī, Āsī, and Bhavissantī. There is only one termination that is strictly present by virtue of Vattamānā; when counted in order, it occupies the seventh position. Thus, in order to include it in this seventh position known as Vattamānā, one termination—which is known as "Parikappakālika" (time of reflection) by the method of Nirutti treatises and called "Paccuppannānāgatakālika" (present-future time) by the method of grammar treatises—was designated as "Sattamī" (the seventh) because it shares the same position as the Vattamānā termination which is the seventh. Furthermore, after counting the three terminations that are strictly future by virtue of Svātanī, Āsī, and Bhavissantī, that termination which occurs in the present and future and has received the name "Sattamī" was made the fourth because it shares the same position as those three terminations in being of the future. Then, one termination—which is known as "Āṇattikālika" (time of command) by the method of Nirutti treatises and called "Paccuppannānāgatakālika" by the method of grammar treatises—was designated as "Pañcamī" (the fifth) by completing the count of five.
78:
Since the Kriyātipatti termination has an indefinite time, this decision was made by excluding that Kriyātipatti, and that decision is indeed based solely on the Nirutti method. This is the preference of us who desire a significant designation (anvatthasaññā) for the Sattamī and Pañcamī terminations mentioned immediately after the Vattamānā termination in the Kātantra. This preference has been approved, consented to, and accepted by the elder teachers who know the True Dhamma, saying, "It is just so, friend; it is just so, friend." It has also been approved, consented to, and accepted by the grammarians, saying, "It is just so, venerable sir; it is just so, venerable sir." Thus, it has been rejoiced in and not rejected by all those former teachers.
