In the Kaccāyana treatise, however, because the terminations are stated in eight ways in accordance with the Buddha's words (Buddhavacana), the Vattamānā termination stands in the fifth position. How? There are four terminations that are strictly past or future by virtue of Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, and Bhavissantī. There is only one termination that is strictly present by virtue of Vattamānā; when counted in order, it enters the fifth position. Thus, in order to include it in this fifth position known as Vattamānā, the termination known as "Āṇattikālika" by the Nirutti method and called "Anuttakālika" was designated as "Pañcamī" because it shares the same position as the Vattamānā termination which is the fifth. Beyond that, by placing that fifth (Vattamānā) in the sixth position and taking the six terminations by virtue of counting as Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, Bhavissantī, Vattamānā, and Pañcamī, the termination known as "Parikappakālika" by the Nirutti method and called "Anuttakālika" was designated as "Sattamī" by completing the count of seven.

Since the Kālātipatti termination occurs in the past and future, this decision was made by excluding that Kālātipatti, and that decision is indeed based solely on the Nirutti method. This decision is the preference of us who desire a significant designation for the Pañcamī and Sattamī terminations mentioned immediately after the Vattamānā termination in the Kaccāyana. This preference has also been approved without rejection by the elder teachers who know the True Dhamma...
79:
"It is just so, friend; it is just so, friend," they acknowledged and accepted. The grammarians also, without raising any objection, agreed, acknowledged, and accepted, saying, "It is just so, venerable sir; it is just so, venerable sir." In this way, all those former teachers also joyfully accepted it and did not object.

For although the Kātantra and Kaccāyana treatises differ from each other in the order of their case-endings, they harmonize and agree as one according to the divisions of time, such as the past, as stated in the Nirutti treatise. Therefore, taking only the method of Nirutti as the essence, our preference in devising and designating the significant names (anvatthasaññā) for the Pañcamī and Sattami endings was joyfully accepted by the former teachers, and they did not object. For this very reason, it is impossible for anyone to suppress this doctrine and establish another. This method is extremely subtle and difficult to see, like an atom (paramāṇu); it is difficult to penetrate, like a great forest; and it is very deep, like the great ocean. Therefore, in this Saddanīti treatise, noble sons endowed with faith should make a great effort for the benefit of the Dispensation (Sāsana). Indeed, those who make an effort in this treatise become victors over opponents who raise arguments regarding the four types of words, such as nouns (nāma) and verbs (ākhyāta).

Just as the Sage, the Bull among Sages,
Conquered the wicked monks, Pūraṇa and others,
Who were filled with false doctrine;
So too, those who make an effort in this Saddanīti,
Which follows the view of the Tathāgata,
Conquer their opponents.

This is the harmonization of the treatises regarding the sequential placement of the Pañcamī and Sattami endings.

## Now we shall explain the meaning of the terms Vattamānā, etc. —
Among those endings, why is Vattamānā so called? It is because it expresses the present time (vattamānakāla). It is called Vattamāna because it occurs in the state of being present; it is the time known as the present action. By virtue of expressing that time, the present time belongs to this ending; therefore, this ending, such as ti and anti, is called Vattamānā.
80: Indeed, in this sentence "Gacchati Devadatto" (Devadatta goes), only the word 'ti', which is the ending, expresses the present action of going by Devadatta. Therefore, because of the meaning that the present time belongs to this ending by virtue of expressing that present action, it is called Vattamānā. Why is Pañcamī so called? It is called Pañcamī because of the sense of reaching the fifth place, which is the present (vattamāna), and because of the sense of completing the number five. For indeed, among the five endings known as Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, Bhavissantī, and Vattamānā, which occur in the permanent times of past, future, and present, it is called Pañcamī because it goes to the fifth place of the present, having a common basis with the Vattamānā by virtue of being of the present time itself. It is like how a river is called 'nadī' because it goes along sounding (or flowing). Furthermore, in relation to the four endings known as Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, and Bhavissantī, which occur in the permanent past and future times, it is called Pañcamī because it itself, like the Vattamānā ending, completes the number five. Why is Sattami so called? It is called Sattami because of the sense of completing the number seven. For indeed, in relation to the six endings known as Parokkhā, Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, Bhavissantī, Vattamānā, and Pañcamī, which occur in the past, future, and present times, it is called Sattami because it itself, being of the present time, completes the number seven. Why is Parokkhā so called? It is called Parokkhā because of the sense of occurring out of sight. For indeed, that which is beyond (paro) the eye (akkha), known as the sense faculty of the eye, etc., is parokkha (out of sight). It is called Parokkhā because it occurs out of sight by virtue of expressing that which is out of sight. Why is Hiyattanī so called? It is called Hiyattanī because of the sense of occurring in the past time starting from yesterday (hiyyo), and by virtue of expressing that past time. Why is Ajjatanī so called? It is called Ajjatanī because of the sense of occurring in the past time starting from today (ajja), and by virtue of expressing that past time. Why is Bhavissantī so called? It is called Bhavissantī because it manifests the meaning "it will be thus in the future," and because of the sense of going (occurring). Why is Kālātipatti so called? It is called Kālātipatti because of the sense of speaking of the passing of time. For indeed, the passing of time, the occurrence beyond or exceeding time, is called Kālātipatti; it is devoid of the accomplishment of the benefit that should be obtained...
81:
Transgression of action (kriyātikkamana) refers to the transgression of an action that is devoid of the occurrence of the desired result. In this context, the word 'kāla' is intended to mean action. Doing is called 'kāra'; in that very word 'kāra', by changing the letter 'r' to 'l' for the sake of pronunciation, it becomes 'kāla'. This inflection is called 'kālātipatti' because it expresses that transgression of action. This is the explanation of the derivative meanings of the inflections such as the present tense (vattamānā).

In the noble Dispensation of the Buddha, which is filled with various diverse methods and bears complex characteristics, the Miscellaneous Decisions (Pakiṇṇakavinicchaya) have been stated for the purpose of increasing the wisdom of the wise.

## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the proficiency of the wise in the linguistic paths of the Three Piṭakas along with the Commentaries consisting of the nine limbs,
## the Third Chapter,
## called the Miscellaneous Decisions (Pakiṇṇakavinicchaya), is finished.
## 4. Analysis of Nominal Forms derived from the root Bhū (Bhūdhātumayanāmikarūpavibhāga)

The morphology known as 'ākhyāta' (verb) of the root 'bhū sattāyaṃ', ending in 'ti' etc., has been stated in various ways without confusion.

Now, I shall speak of the morphology of that same root known as 'nāmika' (nominal), ending in 'si' etc., for the proficiency of the listeners in the meanings of the Pāḷi texts.

Wise men call a word 'nāma' (name) because it inclines other meanings towards itself, or it itself inclines towards meanings (or ultimate meanings).

In this context, 'nāma' and 'nāmika' are identical in meaning. This 'nāmika' should be understood as having gender (liṅga) and being accompanied by case endings (vibhatti).

Gender (liṅga), which expresses a substance, consists of the feminine (itthiliṅga), masculine (pulliṅga), and neuter (napuṃsakaliṅga). In the context of nouns, there are only seven case endings; however, in verbs, they say there are eight.

There are seven case endings: Paṭhamā, Dutiyā, Tatiyā, Catutthī, Pañcamī, Chaṭṭhī, and Sattamī.

Among them, the first case (Paṭhamā) occurs in the sense of the gender-meaning (liṅgattha); that Paṭhamā is divided into two: si and yo. The second case (Dutiyā) occurs in the sense of the object (kammattha); that Dutiyā is also divided into two: aṃ and yo.
82:
The third case (Tatiyā) occurs in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa); that Tatiyā is also divided into two: nā and hi.
The fourth case (Catutthī) occurs in the sense of the recipient (sampadāna); that Catutthī is divided into two: sa and naṃ.
The fifth case (Pañcamī) occurs in the sense of the ablative (apādāna); that Pañcamī is divided into two: smā and hi.
The sixth case (Chaṭṭhī) occurs in the sense of the owner (sāmi); that Chaṭṭhī is also divided into two: sa and naṃ.
The seventh case (Sattamī) occurs in the sense of the location (okāsa); that Sattamī is also divided into two: smiṃ and su.
The eighth case (Aṭṭhamī) occurs in the sense of addressing (āmantana); those vocative endings are only si and yo, making a total of fourteen case endings.
Each of these case endings is associated with two numbers (singular and plural).
In this treatise, the meaning known as 'satta' (being/entity) is also to be understood by the name 'dabba' (substance).
He who performs is called the agent (kattar). That which is performed is called the object (kamma).
That by which it is performed is called the instrument (karaṇa).
He to whom one gives or he who is pleased is known as the recipient (sampadāna).
That from which one departs or from which fear arises is celebrated as the ablative (apādāna).
That to which there is a connection or a group is indeed taught as the owner (sāmi).
That in which an action is performed is called the location (okāsa).
That which is addressed is called the vocative (āmantana).
Alternatively, making a manifest object face towards oneself by means of sound is called āmantana.

It should be understood that, excluding the vocative sense, the occurrence of the first case etc. in the sense of gender etc. is stated by way of implication (upalakkhaṇa).

In this context, this philological characteristic (niruttilakkhaṇa) should be noted: the first case (Paṭhamā) occurs in the sense of the nominative (paccatta); the second case (Dutiyā) occurs in the sense of the accusative (upayoga); the third case (Tatiyā) occurs in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa); the fourth case (Catutthī) occurs in the sense of the dative (sampadāna); the fifth case (Pañcamī) occurs in the sense of the ablative (nissakka); the sixth case (Chaṭṭhī) occurs in the sense of the genitive (sāmi); the seventh case (Sattamī) occurs in the sense of the locative (bhumma); the eighth case (Aṭṭhamī) occurs in the sense of the vocative (āmantana). The summary of these meanings is:

The nominative (paccatta), the accusative (upayoga), the instrumental (karaṇa), the dative (sampadāna), the ablative (nissakka), the genitive (sāmivacana), the locative (bhumma), and the eighth, the vocative (ālapana).
83:
Among those case endings, the Nominative case (Paccattavacana) has the meaning of expressing the respective nature of the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders, which are distinguished by the three genders. The Accusative case (Upayogavacana) has the meaning of indicating the connection between the doer and the action performed. The Instrumental case (Karaṇavacana) has the meaning of indicating the appropriate performance or accomplishment of that action. The Dative case (Sampadānavacana) has the meaning of indicating the act of giving to that person. The Ablative case (Nissakkavacana) has the meaning of indicating freedom from or separation from that. The Genitive case (Sāmivacana) has the meaning of indicating ownership of that object. The Locative case (Bhummavacana) has the meaning of indicating the state of being the location of that. The Vocative case (Āmantanavacana) has the meaning of indicating such a calling. Knowing this, one should apply the sentence usages without confusion.

Bhūto (creature), bhāvako (one who develops), bhavo (development), abhavo (decline), bhāvo (desire), abhāvo (absence), sabhāvo (nature), sabbhāvo (presence), sambhavo (arising), pabhavo (constant arising or origin), pabhāvo (power/influence), anubhavo (experience), ānubhāvo (majesty/power), parābhavo (ruin), vibhavo (absence/separation), pātubhāvo (manifestation), āvibhāvo (becoming visible), tirobhāvo (disappearance), vinābhāvo (separation), sotthibhāvo (purity or well-being), atthibhāvo (existence), natthibhāvo (non-existence)—these are masculine nouns ending in -o.

Abhibhavitā (conqueror), paribhavitā (conqueror/scorner), anubhavitā (experiencer), samanubhavitā (experiencer), bhāvitā (developer), paccanubhavitā (experiencer)—these are masculine nouns ending in -ā.

Bhavaṃ (development), parābhavaṃ (ruin), paribhavaṃ (oppression), abhibhavaṃ (oppression), anubhavaṃ (experience), samanubhavaṃ (experience), paccanubhavaṃ (experience), pabhavaṃ (ability), appabhavaṃ (inability)—these are masculine nouns ending in -ṃ (niggahīta).

Dhanabhūti (attainment of wealth), siribhūti (attainment of glory), sotthibhūti (attainment of purity), suvatthibhūti (attainment of well-being)—these are masculine nouns ending in -i.

Bhāvī (one who usually becomes), vibhāvī (one who especially becomes), sambhāvī (one who well becomes), paribhāvī (one who becomes all around)—these are masculine nouns ending in -ī.

Sayambhū (self-become/self-enlightened), pabhū (lord/master), abhibhū (conqueror), vibhū (one who especially becomes), adhibhū (superior/chief), patibhū (lord/master), gotrabhū (one who overcomes the lineage), vatrabhū (Sakka, king of gods), parābhibhū (one who conquers others), rūpābhibhū (conqueror of forms), saddābhibhū (conqueror of sounds), gandhābhibhū (conqueror of smells), rasābhibhū (conqueror of tastes), phoṭṭhabbābhibhū (conqueror of touches), dhammābhibhū (conqueror of mental objects), sabbābhibhū (conqueror of all)—these are masculine nouns ending in -ū.

In this context, these six types of masculine genders derived from the root bhū have been briefly pointed out.
84:
Masculine nouns ending in -u derived from the root bhū are not common; however, masculine nouns ending in -u derived from roots other than bhū, such as "bhikkhu" and "hetu", are well-known. Together with those (masculine nouns ending in -u derived from other roots), there are seven types of masculine genders; all of these should be understood as masculine by nature. In this context, the word "bhūta" which expresses the meaning of "creature" (sattavā) should also be understood as always masculine. However, other words such as bhūta, parābhūta, sambhūta, etc., which are suitable for use in all three genders—as in "yo dhammo bhūto, yā dhammajāti bhūtā, yaṃ dhammajātaṃ bhūtaṃ"—and thus have variable genders, are also evident in the noble Pali Canon. To generate proficiency in wise people regarding the composition of words through the power of connecting with various prefixes (upasagga) and particles (nipāta), and in grasping subtle meanings, I shall present them by including them among the fixed masculine genders. They are:

Bhūto, parābhūto, sambhūto, vibhūto, pātubhūto, āvibhūto, tirobhūto, vinābhūto, bhabbo, paribhūto, abhibhūto, adhibhūto, addhabhūto, anubhūto, samanubhūto, paccanubhūto, bhāvito, sambhāvito, vibhāvito, paribhāvito, anuparibhūto, paribhavitabbo, paribhotabbo, paribhavanīyo, abhibhavitabbo, abhibhotabbo, abhibhavanīyo, adhibhavitabbo, adhibhotabbo, adhibhavanīyo, anubhavitabbo, anubhotabbo, anubhavanīyo, samanubhavitabbo, samanubhotabbo, samanubhavanīyo, paccanubhavitabbo, paccanubhotabbo, paccanubhavanīyo, bhāvetabbo, bhāvanīyo, sambhāvetabbo, sambhāvanīyo, vibhāvetabbo, vibhāvanīyo, paribhāvetabbo, paribhāvanīyo, bhavamāno, vibhavamāno, paribhavamāno, abhibhavamāno, anubhavamāno, samanubhavamāno, paccanubhavamāno, anubhonto, samanubhonto, paccanubhonto, sambhonto, abhisambhonto, bhāvento, and sambhāvento.
85:
Vibhāvento, paribhāvento, paribhaviyamāno, paribhuyyamāno, abhibhaviyamāno, abhibhūyamāno, anubhaviyamāno, anubhuyyamāno, samanubhaviyamāno, samanubhuyyamāno, paccanubhaviyamāno, and paccanubhuyyamāno—these terms are genders included within the fixed masculine genders (niyata-pulliṅga). Thus, the six types of masculine genders derived from the root bhū, by way of endings such as okāranta (ending in -o), have been shown. This is the brief presentation of examples by way of the masculine gender.

Bhāvikā, bhāvanā, vibhāvanā, sambhāvanā, and paribhāvanā are feminine genders ending in -ā (ākāranta-itthiliṅga).

Bhūmi, bhūti, and vibhūti are feminine genders ending in -i (ikāranta-itthiliṅga).

Bhūrī, bhūtī, bhotī, vibhāvinī, parivibhāvinī, sambhāvinī, pātubhavantī, pātubhontī, paribhavantī, paribhontī, abhibhavantī, abhibhontī, adhibhavantī, adhibhontī, anubhavantī, anubhontī, samanubhavantī, samanubhontī, paccanubhavantī, paccanubhontī, abhisambhavantī, and abhisambhontī—these terms are feminine genders ending in -ī (īkāranta-itthiliṅga).

Bhū and abhū are feminine genders ending in -ū (ūkāranta-itthiliṅga).

In this context, the four types of feminine genders derived from the root bhū have been briefly presented.

The feminine gender ending in -u (ukāranta-itthiliṅga) derived from the root bhū is not well-known; however, feminine genders ending in -u derived from other roots, such as "dhātu" and "dhenu," are well-known. Including those, there are five types of feminine genders; or, if the word "go" in its feminine form as an okāranta is included, there are six types. All of these should be understood as feminine genders by their very nature. Here also, terms with variable genders (aniyata-liṅga) such as bhūta, parābhūta, and sambhūta are employed according to the feminine gender.

How? They should be taken in detail as bhūtā, parābhūtā, and sambhūtā. The nine terms beginning with "anubhonto samanubhonto"...
86:
(Excluding the nine terms such as anubhontī shown on the previous page), those terms are joined by way of the ending -ī (īkāranta). These terms (such as bhūtā) are genders included within the fixed genders (niyata-liṅga). Thus, the four types of feminine genders derived from the root bhū, by way of endings such as ākāranta, have been shown. This is the presentation of examples (udāharaṇuddesa) by way of the feminine gender.

Bhūtaṃ (materiality), mahābhūtaṃ (great element), bhavittaṃ (prosperity), bhūnaṃ (growth), bhavanaṃ (becoming), parābhavanaṃ (ruin), sambhavanaṃ (arising), vibhavanaṃ (absence), pātubhavanaṃ (manifestation), āvibhavanaṃ (manifestation), tirobhavanaṃ (disappearance), vinābhavanaṃ (becoming without), sotthibhavanaṃ (well-being), paribhavanaṃ (contempt), abhibhavanaṃ (conquering), adhibhavanaṃ (overpowering), anubhavanaṃ (experiencing), samanubhavanaṃ (fully experiencing), and paccanubhavanaṃ (repeatedly experiencing)—these are neuter genders ending in niggahīta (-ṃ).

Atthavibhāvi (the wisdom that clarifies the meaning) and dhammavibhāvi (the mind that clarifies the Dhamma) are neuter genders ending in -i (ikāranta-napuṃsakaliṅga).

Gotrabhū (change-of-lineage consciousness), cittasahabhū (matter arising with consciousness), and nacittasahabhū (matter not arising with consciousness) are neuter genders ending in -u (ukāranta-napuṃsakaliṅga).

All these terms should be understood as neuter genders by their very nature. In this regard, it should also be noted that the word bhūta, when expressing a being or a great element, is always neuter. Here also, terms with variable genders such as bhūta, parābhūta, and sambhūta are employed according to the neuter gender.

How? Bhūtaṃ, parābhūtaṃ, sambhūtaṃ, vibhūtaṃ, and so on. [Pe]. Samanubhavamānaṃ, paccanubhavamānaṃ, anubhontံ, anubhavantံ, samanubhontံ, samanubhavantံ, paccanubhontံ, paccanubhavantံ, sambhontံ, sambhavantံ, abhisambhontံ, abhisambhavantံ, pātubhontံ, pātubhavantံ, paribhontံ, parubhavantံ, abhibhontံ, abhibhavantံ, adhibhontံ, adhibhavantံ, bhāventံ, sambhāventံ, vibhāventံ, paribhāventံ, paribhāviyamānaṃ, paribhuyyamānaṃ, and so on, along with paccanubhaviyamānaṃ and paccanubhuyyamānaṃ—these terms are genders included within the fixed neuter genders. Thus, the three types of neuter genders ending in niggahīta derived from the root bhū...
87:
...have been shown. This is the presentation of examples by way of the neuter gender. Thus, the three genders derived from the root bhū have been presented by way of the masculine gender and so forth.

In this regard, whatever terms I have declared as not well-known, those terms should be searched for in various Pali passages by the wise.

The varieties of masculine gender established in the seven types of endings: -o, -ā, bindu (niggahīta), -i, -ī, -u, and -ū, are stated by those skilled in philology (Nirutti).

The five types of endings: -ā, the i-vanna (-i, -ī), and the u-vanna (-u, -ū), should be known as varieties of feminine gender; or six types including the ending -o.

The three endings: bindu (niggahīta), -i, and -u, should be known by the wise as varieties of neuter gender, as stated by those skilled in philology.

There are only seven endings in the masculine, five or six in the feminine, and three in the neuter; thus, there are fifteen or sixteen types in total.

Indeed, in this presentation, when terms such as 'bhūto' are spoken by way of definition (nibbacana), explanation of the denoted meaning (abhidheyyakathana), supporting evidence (sādhakavacana), synonymous terms (pariyāyavacana), and extraction of meaning (atthuddhāra), they become clear and easy to understand. Therefore, for the sake of generating joy in the wise and for the listeners to attain a sharper intellect regarding the meanings, I shall state the definitions and so forth of those terms as appropriate.

Among those terms, it is called 'bhūto' because it 'becomes' (exists) through the manifestation of the aggregates (khandha); this is first the definition (nibbacana). By the term 'bhūto', a 'being' (satta) is expressed by way of encompassing all; this is the explanation of the denoted meaning (abhidheyyakathana).

'Yo ca kālaghaso bhūto' and so forth, and 'Sabbeva nikkhipissanti, bhūtā loke samussayaṃ'—these statements are the supporting evidence (sādhakavacana) for this meaning.

Alternatively, 'bhūto' refers to a specific type of non-human being (amanussa) with this name; this is the abhidheyyakathana. 'Bhūtavijjā, bhūtavejjo, bhūtaviggahito'—these statements are the supporting evidence for this meaning. The words found in various places such as 'satto, macco, pajā' are the synonymous terms (pariyāyavacana) for this meaning.
88:
## 
'Satto' is a synonym for the word 'bhūta', which expresses a specific meaning. The statement in the Niddesa Pali, 'Macco means a being (satta), a man (nara), a youth (mānava), a person (posa), an individual (puggala), a life (jīva), a jagu, a being (jantu), a hindagu, a human (manuja),' is also a synonymous expression. To summarize all of them:

Satta, macca, jana, bhūta, pāṇa, hindagu, puggala,
Jantu, jīva, jagu, yakkha, pāṇī, dehī, tathāgata,
Sattava, mātiya, loka, manuja, mānava, nara,
Posa, and sarīrī—these words are masculine.
The word 'bhūtaṃ' is neuter.
The word 'pajā' is said to be feminine by gender, but not by meaning.
Thus, the words expressing 'being' exist in all three genders.
That being which moves by means of its legs (jaṅghā) is called 'jaṅghala' in this context.
The names of beings have been expanded upon with terms such as pāṇa and deha.

In this treatise, the terms 'pariyāyavacana' (synonym), 'abhidhāna' (appellation), and 'saṅkhā' (designation), etc., are intended to have the same meaning. However, by way of extracting specific meanings, the word 'bhūta' is found to refer to the five aggregates, a human, an element, eternity, that which is manifest, an Arahant, a being, a tree, and so on. These usages will be made clear later in the analysis of the triad of meanings.

'Bhāvaka' is so called because it causes development (bhāveti); this is the etymological definition (nibbacana). One who performs cultivation (bhāvanā) is called a 'bhāvaka'; this is the statement of the denotation (abhidheyya). The phrase 'Bhāvako nipako dhīro' is the supporting evidence that establishes this meaning. 'Bhāvaka, one intent on cultivation, one engaged in cultivation, one endowed with cultivation'—these are synonyms. These two words, 'bhūta' and 'bhāvaka', are spoken in terms of the simple agent (suddhakattu) and the causative agent (hetukattu). From here onwards, because it is easy to understand according to the established method, I shall not begin with 'this is the etymological definition' and so forth.
89:
From here onwards, following the method already stated, because it is easy to understand, I will no longer explicitly state 'this is the etymological definition' and so forth. Instead, I will show only the supporting evidence for the meaning, synonyms, and the extraction of meanings in certain places as appropriate. If all these were shown for every single word, the treatise would be excessively long. Therefore, for words whose meanings are obvious and clear, I will not state the denotation but only their etymological definition. For words with profound meanings, however, I will state the denotation.

Growth is called 'bhava'; 'bhava' refers to increase (vuddhi). Since the word 'bhū' is associated with the excellence of meaning, it is also found in the sense of increase; thus, increase is considered to be 'bhava'. The statement, 'The king's prosperity (bhava) and the king's non-prosperity (abhava),' is the supporting evidence for the meaning of increase. Alternatively, 'bhava' refers to eternity (sassata). The view that exists in the form of eternity, such as 'The self and the world are eternal,' is called 'sassatadiṭṭhi' (eternalist view). Therefore, the term 'bhavadiṭṭhi' is the supporting evidence for this meaning. Likewise, 'bhava' means 'bhavadiṭṭhi'. Because it exists in the manner of standing eternally, the eternalist view is called 'bhavadiṭṭhi'. In the compound 'bhavadiṭṭhi', the latter member 'diṭṭhi' is dropped, and it is simply called 'bhava'. The statement, 'They spoke of liberation from existence (bhava) through the eternalist view (bhava),' is the supporting evidence for this meaning. Here, the meaning of the Pali is: some recluses or brahmins spoke of the purity of the round of rebirths, which is liberation from all existence, either through the eternalist view (bhavadiṭṭhi) or through the existence of sensual desire (kāmabhava), etc. Alternatively, because beings grow by means of this merit, success (sampatti) and merit (puñña) are also called 'bhava'. The statement, 'One who has thus transcended both prosperity (bhava) and adversity (abhava),' is the supporting evidence for this meaning. In this context, the meaning of the Pali is: 'bhava' is success (sampatti), and 'abhava' is failure (vipatti). Likewise, 'bhava' is growth, and 'abhava' is decline. 'Bhava' is the eternalist view, and 'abhava' is the annihilationist view. 'Bhava' is merit, and 'abhava' is demerit. It refers to one who has transcended all of those.
90:
The aggregates together with their location (okāsa) are also called 'bhava'. Phrases such as 'sensual existence' (kāmabhava) and 'fine-material existence' (rūpabhava) are supporting evidence for this meaning. Among these, the aggregates are called 'bhava' because they have a manifest nature and arise continuously due to causes such as ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā). The location (okāsa) is called 'bhava' because beings and mental-material phenomena (nāmarūpa) arise there. Furthermore, action-existence (kammabhava) is also 'bhava', and rebirth-existence (upapattibhava) is also 'bhava'. The statement, 'With clinging as condition, existence is of two kinds: there is action-existence and there is rebirth-existence,' is the supporting evidence for this meaning. Between those two, kamma itself being existence is 'kammabhava'. Likewise, rebirth itself being existence is 'upapattibhava'. Here, rebirth is called 'bhava' because it 'becomes' (arises). Kamma, however, is to be understood as 'bhava' by the name of its fruit, because it is the cause of existence, just as the arising of the Buddhas is said to be 'happiness' because it is the cause of happiness. Alternatively, because it has the characteristic of causing to become, it is called 'bhava' in the sense of 'causing to become' (bhāveti). What does it cause to become? It causes rebirth (upapatti). Thus, because it causes rebirth to become, it is called 'bhava'. The meaning of the word 'bhāveti' is 'causes to arise' in the sense of the causative agent (hetukattu). Alternatively, according to the statement 'With existence as condition, birth arises,' action-existence (kammabhava) is called 'bhava' because birth arises by means of this kamma.

'The uninterrupted succession of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases is called saṃsāra.' Saṃsāra, which has this defined characteristic, is also called 'bhava'. The statements 'Suffering in existence is bhava-dukkha' and 'Wandering in existence' are supporting evidence for this meaning. In that context, for what reason is saṃsāra called 'bhava'? Because the conventional designation 'being' occurs in this collection of phenomena known as the succession of aggregates...
91:
...due to the meaning (the round of rebirths is called bhava). This is an explanation of the meaning of the word bhava by way of the sādhana (grammatical derivations) of bhāva (state), kattu (agent), karaṇa (instrument), and adhikaraṇa (location).

Herein, I shall set forth the various meanings of the word bhava—

Growth, attainment, merit, the aggregates together with the physical world (okāsa), the round of rebirths (saṃsāra), and the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi)—all these are expressed by the word bhava.

Craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), the view of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi), and likewise rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava) and kamma-existence (kamma-bhava)—all these are also expressed by the word bhava.

In some Pāli texts, the two—craving for existence and the view of existence—are expressed by the word bhava alone, with the latter part of the compound elided.

Abhava means that which is not bhava. In the Dispensation, four meanings are expressed by the word abhava: ruin, decline, the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi), and evil.

Bhāva means intention (ajjhāsaya), which is also called 'adhippāya'. 'The intention of women is difficult to know. A wise minister should show affection toward the queens. He reveals the intention within his heart'—such passages are evidence for this meaning. Furthermore, an objective reality (vatthu-dhamma) is also called bhāva. 'The accomplishment of the signs of reality (bhāva-saṅketa)'—this phrase is evidence for this meaning. Mind (citta) is also called bhāva. 'You perform a very cruel deed; there is not even a little merit in your mind (bhāva)'—this phrase is evidence for this meaning. Action (kriyā) is also called bhāva. 'The characteristic of action (bhāva-lakkhaṇa), the locative absolute (bhāva-sattamī)'—this phrase is evidence for this meaning. Furthermore, some say that bhāva is a synonym for a being (satta), or it is a designation for a root (dhātu). In that context, intention, objective reality, mind, and being are called bhāva because they 'become' (bhavanti). Likewise, it is called bhāva because it 'causes to become' (bhāveti).
92:
In the case of action (kriyā), the occurrence (bhavana) is called 'bhāva'. That occurrence is of various kinds by way of becoming, going, cooking, and so forth. Furthermore, sex-materiality (bhāva-rūpa) is also called 'bhāva', which is referred to as femininity (itthibhāva), masculinity (pumbhāva), and the female faculty (itthin-driya). The etymological definition (vacanattha) regarding that sex-materiality is: 'Because of this bhāva-rūpa, the mind and the designation arise as either "woman" or "man"'; thus it is called 'bhāva'. This derivation is not produced by my own wisdom alone. It is brought forth by relying on the views of the former teachers who were like lion-kings. For it was said by the ancient teachers: 'The state of a woman is femininity (itthibhāva); because of this bhāva-rūpa, the mind and the designation arise as "woman", therefore it is called itthibhāva.' Therefore, in the word masculinity (pumbhāva) as well, the derivation should be understood thus: the state of a man is pumbhāva; because of this bhāva-rūpa, the mind and the designation arise as "man", therefore it is called pumbhāva. This is the explanation of the meaning of the word bhāva by way of the sādhanas of kattu, bhāva, and karaṇa.

Abhava means non-becoming. What is that abhava? It is emptiness (suññatā) and non-existence (natthitā). Sabhāva means one's own state (attano bhāva); the meaning is one's own nature (pakati). Alternatively, sabhāva means that when there is the possibility of the existence of the essence of phenomena (dhamma), they obtain a certain form; the meaning is the mode such as bending, changing, hardness, or touching, which is known as the 'characteristic' (lakkhaṇa) that is the state of that phenomenon. 'The characteristic of phenomena is known as either the general nature (sāmaṇya-sabhāva) or the specific nature (visesa-sabhāva)'—this statement is evidence for this meaning. Furthermore, sabhāva means an ultimate reality (paramattha-dhamma) possessing its own characteristic. In what sense? In the sense of being 'with a state' (saha bhāvena). Sabbhāva means the state of the virtuous; the meaning is the Dhamma of the virtuous (sappurisa-dhamma). Alternatively, one's own state is sabbhāva. 'They cause one to take up the sabbhāva'—this statement is evidence for this meaning. Or, an existing state is sabbhāva. 'Thus, the existing state of grasping'—this statement is evidence for this...
93:
(This statement) is evidence. The preceding explanation is the meaning of the words sabhāva and sabbhāva by way of the bhāva-sādhana.

Sambhava means arising (sambhavana), the action of arising, or suitability (yutti). For suitability is called 'sambhava' in such passages as 'Sambhava is the cause of grasping.' Alternatively, it is called 'sambhava' because it arises from this (cause). For that from which anything arises is called sambhava. Pabhava means continuous arising (pabhavana) or the state of being uninterrupted (acchinnatā). Alternatively, it is called 'pabhava' because it flows continuously from this (such as the Anavatatta lake). That place where something, such as water, first arises is called pabhava.

These words sambhava and pabhava should be understood as having the same meaning in some places and different meanings in others. How? The word sambhava expresses the action of arising, suitability (yutti), designation (paññatti), reproductive matter (sambhava-rūpa), and the sense of condition (paccaya). The word pabhava expresses the action of arising, the source of a river, and the sense of condition. Therefore, excluding the sense of condition, they should be taken as having different meanings. However, in the sense of condition, they should be taken as having the same meaning. For it has been said: 'Paccaya, hetu, nidāna, kāraṇa, sambhava, pabhava, etc., are one in meaning but different in phrasing.'

'Mūla, hetu, nidāna, sambhava, pabhava,
samuṭṭhāna, āhāra, ārammaṇa, paccaya, and samudaya.'
This verse also serves as evidence for this meaning. The preceding explanation is the meaning of the words sambhava and pabhava by way of the bhāva-sādhana and apādāna-sādhana.

Thus, in this context, the six sādhanas have been revealed by way of bhāva, kattu, kamma, karaṇa, apādāna, and adhikaraṇa. When combined with the sampadāna-sādhana, they are of seven kinds. That sampadāna-sādhana will be made clear further on with such examples as 'Dhanamassa bhavatūti dhanabhūti' (May wealth be for him, thus it is wealth-becoming). Thus, by way of the kitaka (derivative suffixes), the sādhanas are of seven kinds in every way. These sādhanas are also called 'kārakas'. There is no other sādhana apart from these seven sādhanas. In the usages and meanings derived from this root bhū...
94:
For the wise, the term 'sādhana' is presented (to facilitate proficiency in Pali). This is true: linguistic expressions associated with words having poorly established derivations (sādhana) have meanings that are difficult to understand, whereas linguistic expressions associated with words having well-established derivations have meanings that are easy to understand. Therefore, expressions are rooted in derivation (sādhana), and meaning is rooted in expression. It should be understood that only those wise persons with particularly sharp intellect in meanings derived through the power of sādhana—such as in the passage, 'Being requested, he uses much robes; unrequested, he uses little'—and in other meanings, who can explain the meaning accurately and consistently with the linguistic expression, are truly the bearers of the Buddha's Pariyatti Sāsana.

Henceforth, because it is easily understood through the method, I shall no longer say, 'This is such-and-such a sādhana.' In this work, for the purpose of generating great appreciation among the wise for the linguistic expressions shown here, and to expand the wisdom of listeners regarding the words of the Great Conqueror (Jina) which have various and wonderful Pali styles and various sublime meanings, I shall extract and present only the words that accomplish the meaning from the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, and so on, from various Pali passages as appropriate.

'Pabhāva' is so called because it arises in a special way (pakarato bhavati); it is indeed the same as majesty (ānubhāva). The statement, 'I do not see your power (pabhāva) by which you would go to Mithilā,' is the evidence for this meaning. 'Anubhava' means the act of experiencing (anubhavanaṃ). What is that? It is enjoyment (paribhuñjanaṃ). 'Ānubhāva' refers to power (teja), effort (ussāha), counsel (manta), mastery (pabhū), and ability (satti). The designation 'Mahānubhāva' (of great majesty), as in 'This king has great majesty consisting of power, or consisting of effort, counsel, mastery, and ability,' is the evidence for this meaning.

Power, effort, counsel,
Mastery, and ability—these five
Are called 'ānubhāva';
One may also call them 'pabhāva'.

When the word 'ānubhāva'
Is used to denote power and so on,
The wise should provide the grammatical derivation
According to the context.
95:
Alternatively, 'ānubhāva' refers to the fruit to be experienced. The statement, 'He has great majesty (mahānubhāva) because of the greatness of the fruit to be experienced,' is the evidence for this meaning. 'Parābhava' means ruin; or it is called 'parābhava' because it tends toward ruin. The statement, 'Ruin (parābhava) is easily known,' is the evidence for this meaning. Furthermore, in accordance with the text, 'He who does not love the Dhamma will suffer ruin,' the derivation should also be understood by way of the future tense as 'that which will ruin.' Alternatively, it is called 'parābhava' because one is ruined by these things, such as hating the Dhamma. What is the cause of that ruin? It is hating the Dhamma and so on. The statement, 'That (hating the Dhamma, etc.) is the first cause of ruin,' is the evidence for this meaning.

'Vibhava' refers to Nibbāna. Because it is departed from existence (bhava), it is called 'vibhava' (departed from existence). Because the causes of existence (ignorance and craving) are absent, existence is departed from this Nibbāna; therefore, it is called 'vibhava'. It is also called 'vibhava' because the great thieves of defilements, which are the opposite of noble wealth such as faith, are absent, cut off, and destroyed from this Nibbāna. In the sense of the word 'vibhava' denoting Nibbāna, the statement, 'Even though existence exists thus, Nibbāna (vibhava) should be desired,' is the evidence in this context. These are the synonyms for Nibbāna:

Nibbāna, Vibhava, Mokkha (Release),
Nirodha (Cessation), Amata (Deathless), Sama (Peace).
Saṅkhārūpasama (Quieting of formations), Dukkha-nirodha (Cessation of suffering),
Accuta (Deathless/Infallible), Akkhaya (Imperishable).
Vivaṭṭa (Absence of the round), Akata (Unconditioned), Attha (Cessation),
Santipada (State of peace), Asaṅkhata (Unconditioned).
Pāra (The further shore), Taṇhākkhaya (Destruction of craving), Dukkha-kkhaya (Destruction of suffering),
Saṃyojanakkhaya (Destruction of fetters).
Yogakkhema (Security from the four bonds), Virāga (Dispassion),
Lokanta (End of the world), Bhavakkhaya (Destruction of existence).
Apavagga (Departure from the round), Visaṅkhāra (Non-formation),
Sabbhi (The true state), Suddhi (Purity), Visuddhi (Supreme purity).
Vimutti (Liberation), Apacaya (Diminution of the round), Mutti (Release),
Nibbuti (Peaceful coolness), Upadhikkhaya (Destruction of acquisitions).
Santi (Peace), Asaṅkhata-dhātu (Unconditioned element),
Disā (The direction/goal to be seen), Sabbato-pabha (The harbor accessible from all sides).
96:
In stating these synonyms of Nibbāna, the wise person should note that these names denote Nibbāna without needing additional qualifying words. Indeed, in this context, names such as 'tāṇa' and 'leṇa' are shown to be dependent on qualifying words.

Tāṇa (Protection), Leṇa (Shelter), Arūpa (Formless),
Santa (Tranquil), Sacca (Truth), Anālaya (Without attachment),
Sududdasa (Very difficult to see), Saraṇa (Refuge),
Parāyaṇa (Final resort), Anītika (Free from affliction),
Anāsava (Free from taints), Dhuva (Stable), Nicca (Permanent),
Viññāṇa (To be known by special knowledge), Anidassana (Invisible to eye-consciousness),
Abyāpajja (Free from ill-will), Siva (Auspicious), Khema (Secure),
Nipuṇa (Subtle), Apalokika (Indestructible),
Ananta (Infinite, without arising, presence, or dissolution), Akkhara (Imperishable),
Dīpa (Island/Support), Accanta (Absolute end),
Kevala (Unmixed with the round), Pada (Objective of the path and fruit),
Paṇīta (Sublime), Accuta (Deathless)—thus it should be understood in many ways.

Teachers who explain the meaning of the term 'gotrabhū' state that Nibbāna is called 'gotta'; thus they declare the meaning of the word 'gotta' to be Nibbāna.

Alternatively, the word 'vibhava' also refers to destruction, prosperity, wealth, and the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). Among these four, in the sense of destruction, it is called 'vibhava' because of the meanings of departing, cutting off, and perishing. The statements, 'The destruction (vibhava) of all phenomena,' and 'Some people designate the cutting off, the destruction, the vibhava of an existing being,' are the evidence for this meaning. In the sense of prosperity, it is called 'vibhava' because it arises in a special way. The statement, 'They wish to see the king's glorious prosperity (vibhava),' is the evidence for this meaning. In the sense of wealth, it is called 'vibhava' because by means of this wealth, beings prosper, increase, grow, and reach abundance. The statement, 'He was reborn as the son of a brahmin possessing eighty crores of wealth (vibhava),' is the evidence for this meaning. These are the synonyms for wealth:

Dhana, Saṃ, Vibhava, Dabba, Sāpateyya, Pariggaha,
Oḍḍa, Bhaṇḍa, Saka, Attha—
These words denote the meaning of wealth.

In the sense of the annihilationist view, it is called 'vibhava' because of the grasp that 'the self and the world do not arise again after death'; it is called 'vibhava' because of the sense of being cut off.
97:
“Vibhavataṇhā”—this word is the evidence for this meaning. Indeed, vibhavataṇhā is the name for craving accompanied by the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi). Here, the extraction of meaning is stated—

Wealth, Nibbāna, prosperity, destruction, and the annihilationist view are expressed by the word “vibhava”; thus should the wise understand.

Pātubhāva means manifestation. Āvibhāva means appearance. Both of these have the meaning of becoming evident. Tirobhāva means concealment, the state of being hidden. Vinābhāva means absence, separation. Sotthibhāva means the absence of danger, happiness, the state of having well-being. In terms of meaning, it is simply the state of being fearless and free from affliction. Atthibhāva means the state of existence, being present, non-emptiness. Natthibhāva means the state of non-existence, being absent, emptiness, hollowness, vanity, voidness. These are the indications for masculine nouns ending in o.

One is called “abhibhavitā” because of subduing; it refers to anyone who oppresses others. Likewise, there is paribhavitā. One is called “anubhavitā” because of experiencing; it refers to anyone who experiences pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure. Likewise, there are samanubhavitā and paccanubhavitā. Here, just as in phrases like “amatassa dātā (giver of the Deathless)” and “anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā (producer of the unarisen path),” where the agent nouns (kattuvācaka) like dātā are seen in conjunction with words in the genitive case (chaṭṭhī) like amatassa, so too should these words be construed, such as “paccāmittassa abhibhavitā (conqueror of the enemy).” Other words of this nature should be construed in the same way. This is the indication for masculine nouns ending in ā.

One is called “bhavaṃ” because of becoming. Or, one is called “bhavaṃ” because of being about to become; it refers to a person who prospers. There is evidence such as: “The one who prospers is easy to know, the one who declines is easy to know.”
98:
“The one who loves the Dhamma prospers; the one who hates the Dhamma declines”—this word is the evidence for this meaning. Alternatively, the person with whom one speaks should be addressed as “bhavaṃ (Sir/Venerable),” as in: “Venerable Kaccāyana,” “Venerable Ānanda,” “I think the Venerable (Jūjaka) desires the King's wife (Queen Maddī), who is devoted to her husband,” and so on. In such speech, one should not focus on the root meaning of the verb, but rather on the conventional meaning (sammuti), because of the saying: “Conventional speech is true, for it is based on worldly convention.” For in the sphere of usage, worldly convention alone is primary and should not be overstepped.

One is called parābhavaṃ because of declining or being ruined. In the same way, there are paribhavaṃ, abhibhavaṃ, and anubhavaṃ. One is called pabhavaṃ because of being able, sufficient, or capable; it refers to anyone who is capable. One who is incapable is called appabhavaṃ. This word “appabhavaṃ” is found in the Jātaka—

“Like a cloud severed by the wind, I approached the tree with a roaring sound.
I, being unable to reach [the trunk] there, grasped the branch with my hands.”

This is the evidence for the word appabhavaṃ. This is the indication for masculine nouns ending in niggahīta.

One is called dhanabhūti because of the meaning “May wealth be to this person.” Siribhūti is a name for beauty, wisdom, and merit. One is called siribhūti because of the meaning “May that glory, wisdom, and beauty be to this person.” In the same way, there are sotthibhūti and suvatthibhūti. This is the indication for masculine nouns ending in i.

Bhāvī refers to one who habitually becomes, one whose nature is to become, or one who excels in becoming. In the same way, there are vibhāvī, sambhāvī, and paribhavī. Among these, such as bhāvī, a wise person who is capable of making the meaning clear is called vibhāvī. In this word vibhāvī, synonyms such as vidvā, vijjāgato, and ñāṇī should be understood. These synonyms are as follows—

Vidvā, vijjāgato, ñāṇī,
Vibhāvī, paṇḍito, sudhī,
Budho, visārado, viññū,
Dosaññū, viddasu, vidူ.
99:
Vipassī (one who sees clearly), paṭibhāṇī (one who has ready wit), medhāvī (a quick and sharp-witted sage), nipako (a mature sage), kavi (one who speaks pleasantly).

Kusalo (the skillful), viduro (the wise), dhīမာ (the wise), gatimā (the wise), mutimā (the wise); this wise person.

Cakkhumā (one with the eye of wisdom), kaṇṇavā (one with the ear of wisdom), dabbo (the wise), dhīro (the wise), bhūri (the wise), vicakkhaṇo (the wise).

Sappañño (the wise), buddhimā (the wise), pañño (the wise); those with such names are called vibhāvī (the wise).

## Indication for Masculine Nouns Ending in Ī.

Sayambhū is so called because he becomes (enlightened) by himself. Who is he? He is the Blessed Sakyamuni Buddha, who, without following the instructions of others, personally penetrated all things that should be known and attained omniscience (sabbaññuta). For this was said by the Blessed One—

“I have no teacher; no one like me exists.
In the world including the devas, I have no equal.
For I am the Worthy One (Arahaṃ) in the world; I am the unsurpassed Teacher.
I alone am the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha); I am cooled and extinguished.”

In terms of meaning, however, the continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna) is called Sayambhū—that which is permeated by the perfections, which has completely removed and destroyed all defilements along with their residual traces (vāsanā) through self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhūñāṇa), and which is the locus of immeasurable groups of qualities such as Great Compassion and Omniscience. Such a continuum of aggregates is called the Supreme Person in the world. For this was said by the Blessed One: “Monks, there is one person appearing in the world who is an extraordinary human being. Who is that one person? Monks, it is the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.” That one person is now famous by names acquired through true qualities such as “Sabbaññū” and “Sugata”; by lineage as “Gotama” and “Ādiccabandhu”; and by clan as “Sakyaputta,” “Sakka,” “Sakyamuni,” “Sakyasīha,” and “Sakyapungava.”
100:
He is known as Suddhodanī and Māyādevīsuta because of his parents, and he is also well-known by the name Siddhattha, which was given to him. In this regard, there are the following verses:

That Blessed One, who was the unique and peerless individual, superior to those who preach the Four Noble Truths, is known by the lineage as Gotama, and likewise as Ādiccabandhu.

Because he was born in the Sakyan clan, he is famous as Sakyaputta. He is also called Sakka, and likewise Sakyamuni.

Because of his excellence in the entire world and his excellence within the Sakyan clan, that Blessed One is designated as Sakyasīha and Sakyapungava.

By his father's name, he is famous as Suddhodanī, like the moon in the sky. By his mother's name, he is also famous as Māyādevīsuta.

He is Sabbaññū (All-knowing), Sugata (Well-gone) who speaks good words, Buddha (Enlightened One) who knows the Four Noble Truths, Dhammarājā (King of Dhamma), and Tathāgata (Thus-gone).

He is Samantabhadra (Wholly Auspicious), Bhagavā (Blessed One), Jina (Conqueror) who has conquered the five Maras, Dasabala (Ten-powered), and Muni (Sage) who knows the two worlds.

He is Satthā (Teacher) who disciplines, Vināyaka (Leader) who leads to Nibbāna, Nātha (Protector) who is the refuge, Muninda (Lord of Sages) who is the master of monks, and Lokanāyaka (Guide of the World) who leads the world to Nibbāna.

He is Narāsabha (Bull among men), Lokajina (Conqueror of the World), Sambuddha (Self-Enlightened), and Dvipaduttama (Supreme among bipeds).

He is Devadeva (God of gods), Lokagaru (Teacher of the World), Dhammassāmī (Lord of Dhamma), and Mahāmuni (Great Sage).

He is Samantacakkhu (All-seeing), Purisadammasārathi (Charioteer of men to be tamed), and Māraji (Conqueror of Mara).

He is Dhammissara (Lord of Dhamma), Advejjhavacana (One whose words are not double), and Satthavāhaka (Caravan Leader).

He is Visuddhideva (Deity by purity), Devātideva (God above gods/Brahmas), and Samaṇissara (Lord of Monks).

He is Bhūripañña (One with wisdom as vast as the earth), Anadhivara (One who has no superior), Narasīha (Lion among men), and Cakkhumā (The One with Vision).

He is Munimuni (Sage of sages), Naravara (Excellent among men), Chaḷabhiñña (Possessor of the six higher powers), and Suta (The Renowned One).

He is Aṅgīrasa (The Radiant One), Yatirājā (King of Ascetics), Lokabandhu (Kinsman of the World), and Amatandada (Giver of the Deathless Nibbāna).

He is Vattā (The Speaker of Truth), Pavattā (The Proclaimer), Saddhammacakkavattī (The Turner of the Wheel of True Dhamma), and Yatissara (Lord of Ascetics).
101:
The Blessed One is the lighthouse and refuge of the world. He is the accumulation of all glory. He is the Lord of monks. He is supreme among humans. He knows the three worlds. He shines with the light of wisdom in the world. He is the Great Man.

He sees the Four Noble Truths. He is endowed with the major and minor marks resulting from countless meritorious deeds. He has a true name. He is a kinsman of the Sun. He is equal only to the peerless Buddhas of the past. He possesses the five types of eyes. He is the most supreme individual.

He overcomes all things of the three planes of existence. He knows all things of the four planes. He possesses a true name. He has reached the further shore through the six methods. He is the extraordinary man. He sees everything. He is the one who disciplines people.

That Blessed One is known as 'Sammāsambuddha' and 'Sattuttama'. He is endowed with the quality of 'Tādī', being unshakeable by the worldly winds. He is 'Vibhajjavādī', one who teaches analytically. He is 'Mahākāruṇika', the one with great compassion.

He is praised as being like the eye, like the Dhamma, and like knowledge. He is praised as being like the noble practice and as the noble hero among men. He is greater than the world. He is 'Sayambhū', the self-enlightened one. He is 'Mahesi', the great seeker who sought the special virtues such as the aggregate of virtue. He crushes and destroys the five Maras.

He does not speak vain words. He has the Dhamma-body. He overcomes the five Maras. For the Buddha, the Great Seeker, there are innumerable names due to his own virtues. What wise person could fully state the names that are based on his virtues?

Among those names, names such as 'Sabbaññū' are common (sādhāraṇa) to all Buddhas. However, names such as 'Gotama' do not apply to all Buddhas. In the Dispensation, both Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas are called 'Sayambhū'. Some say that 'Brahma is Sayambhū', but that statement does not pertain to the Dispensation.

Terms such as 'Buddha, Tathāgata, Satthā, Bhagavā' occur repeatedly in more than a thousand places. Among these, the courageous wise person should understand that the first term 'Buddha' and the last term 'Bhagavā' also occur together. Terms are of two kinds: 'Apekkhakapada', which depend on qualifying terms, and 'Anapekkhapada', which do not.
102:
Indeed, names such as Satthavāha, Naravara, and Chaḷabhiñña are dependent on qualifying terms (apekkhakapada). How so? "Disciples who have attained the three knowledges and abandoned death attend upon that peerless Caravan Leader (Satthavāha) who has thus conquered the battle. Wise men should know this noble dispensation of that Naravara (Excellent among men), who is worshipped by the world and always saluted by the world along with its guardians," and "The dispensation of the Chaḷabhiñña (One with six higher powers)." Thus, they depend on qualifying terms. On the other hand, names such as Buddha, Jina, and Bhagavā should be understood as not depending on qualifying terms.

In this matter, some might say, "Names mentioned here such as Muninda, Samaṇinda, Samaṇissara, Yatissara, Ādiccabandhu, and Ravibandhu have the fault of redundancy (punaruttidosa) because they do not have distinct meanings." That should not be said, because names are seen to be of two kinds: elaborated names (abhisankhata) and unelaborated names (anabhisankhata). Indeed, in some places, some people, based on the name "Sakyasīha," elaborate various names such as "Sakyakesarī" and "Sakyamigādhipa." In the Pāḷi scriptures as well, there is the passage received by Venerable Ānanda: "He obtained the mark of having a jaw like that of a lion-king, the best of four-footed animals." Similarly, some people, based on the name "Dhammarājā," elaborate names such as "Dhammadisampatī." Based on the name "Sabbaññū," they elaborate "Sabbadassāvī" and "Sabbadassī." Based on the name "Sahassakkha," they elaborate "Dasasatalocana." Based on the name "Ādiccabandhu," they elaborate "Aravindasahāyabandhu." Based on the name "Ambuja," they elaborate "Nīraja" and "Kuñca." In the Pāḷi scriptures also:
103:
Indeed, considering that a lotus is called "jalaja" (water-born), the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who have attained the Analytical Insights (Paṭisambhidā), by the power of the elegance of teaching, used the text "Jalajuṭṭara-nāmino" in the place where "Padumuttara-nāmino" should be said. Thus, such prepared names (abhisaṅkhata-abhidhāna) are found.

However, the names "Buddha" and "Bhagavā" are unconditioned names (anabhisaṅkhata-abhidhāna). This was stated by the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta: "The name 'Buddha' was not made by his mother, not made by his father, not made by his sister, not made by his relatives and kinsmen, not made by the deities. This name 'Buddha' is a realized designation (sacchikā paññatti) of the Blessed Buddhas, occurring at the end of their liberation at the foot of the Bodhi tree, together with the attainment of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)." Likewise, he said: "The name 'Bhagavā' was not made by his mother... it is a realized designation, namely 'Bhagavā'."

Thus, the names "Buddha" and "Bhagavā" are unconditioned names. These names, along with "Satthā" (Teacher), "Sugata" (Well-gone), "Jina" (Conqueror), and so on, are not prepared based on any other name; nor are other names found to be prepared based on these names. Indeed, names such as "Bujjhita," "Bodhetā," and "Bodhaka" are not prepared based on the name "Buddha." Similarly, names such as "Sampannabhaga," "Anusāsaka," and "Sundaravacana" are not prepared based on names like "Bhagavā," "Satthā," and "Sugata."

It should be understood that we have used repetition in this manner—"Muninda, Samaṇinda, Samaṇissara, Yatissara, Ādiccabandhu, Ravibandhu," etc.—to demonstrate this distinction. This method should be applied in other places as well. In this regard, it is said:

"There are prepared names and unconditioned names.
'Dviduggamavara' is a prepared name, while 'Buddha' is an unconditioned name;
thus, a name may be of two kinds."

"Prabhū" means one who exists having overcome others; a Lord (Issara). The statement "This hunter is the lord (prabhū) of the forest" is a sentence that proves this meaning.
104:
"Abhibhū" is so called because he overcomes; it refers to the non-percipient being (asaññasatta). What does he overcome? He overcomes the four formless aggregates (nāma-khandha). Because he has thus overcome the four formless aggregates, he is called "Abhibhū." Although that non-percipient being lacks the action of overcoming due to being unconscious, previously, at the time of being a jhana-attainer before arising in the non-percipient realm, he developed the fifth jhana he had attained by way of detachment from perception (saññā-virāga). He thus endeavored to overcome the four formless aggregates by making them non-existent in the non-percipient realm. Since that task of overcoming is now accomplished in the non-percipient realm, he is called "Abhibhū" in the sense that "he has overcome."

Furthermore, even though there is no activity (byāpāra) of overcoming due to being unconscious, because there was activity previously when he was conscious, it is appropriate to speak of him as having activity by way of metaphor (upacāra), just as one would for a conscious being. Indeed, in the world and in the Dispensation (Sāsana), it is common to metaphorically attribute activity to inanimate things as if they were conscious. How is this seen? In the world, it is said, "The bank wishes to fall." In the Dispensation, however:

"Seeing the children weeping,
the great trees, being agitated,
bent down of their own accord
and approached the children."

And: "Venerable Sir, the trees are now like glowing embers, seeking fruit, having cast off their covering (of old leaves)." And: "The fruit pleases the farmer," and so on. Regarding the fact that the word "Abhibhū" designates a non-percipient being, the text "He perceives the Abhibhū as Abhibhū" is the evidence here. Alternatively, "Abhibhū" is anyone who overcomes others. Specifically, only the Tathāgata is the "Abhibhū." For it was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is the Overcomer (Abhibhū), the Unconquered, the Seer of all, the Wielder of Power." Some teachers, however, say: "Abhibhū is the Brahma of a thousand worlds (Sahassa-Brahmā)."

"Vibhū" is so called because he is distinguished. The text "If the Buddha has crossed the stream of existence, reached the end of the world, and is the Vibhū..." is for this meaning...
105:
...the evidence. Here, "Vibhū" means one who is distinguished by the perfection of the form-body (rūpa-kāya) and the Dhamma-body (dhamma-kāya). It is said:

"If even his visible form-body
is first of all inconceivable,
what can be said of the Dhamma-body,
which is the ground of uncommon knowledge?"

"Adhibhū" is so called because he overcomes transcendently; it refers to a Lord (Issara).

"Then the Overlord of the Heavens (Tidivādhibhū), distressed by the power of my austerity, assuming the form of a brahmin, approached me for alms."

This statement is the evidence for this meaning. "Patibhū" is so called because he exists as a master. The phrase "The guarantor (or owner) of the ox" is the evidence for this meaning. "Gotrabhū" (Change-of-lineage) is so called because he exists having made the deathless Great Nibbāna, known as the lineage (gotta), his object. It refers to a person endowed with powerful insight-consciousness (vipassanā-citta) that has reached its peak as the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya) for the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). For it was said by the Blessed One: "Which person is a Gotrabhū? The person endowed with those states immediately following which the descent into the Noble State (ariya-dhamma) occurs is a Gotrabhū." This is the evidence for the meaning here.

Furthermore, a monk who merely wears the yellow robe around his neck (kāsāvakaṇṭha) is also called a "Gotrabhū" because he experiences only the name of the lineage (gotta). He is called "Gotrabhū" because he experiences or possesses only the lineage of being a "monk," while the qualities of a monk (samaṇa-dhamma) do not exist within him. The statement "Ānanda, in the future there will be those of the lineage (gotrabhū), wearing the yellow robe around their necks, who are immoral and of evil nature" is the evidence for this meaning.

"Vatrabhū" refers to Sakka. He is called "Vatrabhū" because, having attained the status of Sakka through the seven vows (vatta) such as supporting his parents, he overcomes other deities by his vows. In the Commentaries on the Agamas, however, taking the meaning of "attainment" found in the root 'bhū', it is said: "One who has reached the lordship of the devas by overcoming others through his vows."
106:
"Vatrabhu" is mentioned. Because he overcomes the Asura named Vatra, he is called "Vatrabhu". The statement "Vatrabhu jayataṃpitā" (Vatrabhu is the father of the victors) is the evidence that establishes this meaning. Here, Vatrabhu is the overcomer of the Asura named Vatra. Jayataṃpitā is the father of those who are victorious. "Sakka, Inda, Purindada," etc., are synonymous terms. These synonyms will be explained in the section on roots (Dhātādhikāra).

Because he overcomes others (para), he is called "Parābhibhū". In the same way, "Rūpābhibhū" and others should be understood. Because he overcomes all things that should be overcome, he is called "Sabbābhibhū". This name "Sabbābhibhū" is suitable only for the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
"I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all;
In all things, I am unsullied.
Having renounced all, liberated in the destruction of craving,
Having known for myself, whom should I point to as a teacher?"

This is the explanation of the masculine gender ending in -ū. This is the presentation of fixed masculine gender terms (niyata-pulliṅga).

Now, the explanation of words with unfixed gender (aniyata-liṅga) such as bhūta, parābhūta, sambhūta, etc., which are included among the fixed genders, will be stated. Among those terms, because it has come to be through its own conditions, it is called "bhūta". Bhūta carries the meanings of arisen, manifest, produced, appeared, or come into being. Or, whatever has acquired its own form, whether conscious or unconscious, is called "bhūta". Or, because it exists in a true manner, it is called "bhūta". Bhūta refers to whatever is true, real, not false, and not perverted. Here, the word "bhūta" has the meaning of truth (sacca). For that meaning, the expression "bhūtaṭṭho" is the supporting evidence. Because of reaching defeat, it is called "parābhūta". Because of being well-arisen, it is called "sambhūta". Because of arising specially, it is called "vibhūta". Or, because of arising clearly, it is called "vibhūta". The expression "vibhūtārammaṇaṃ" is the evidence for this meaning. Or, because of being destroyed, it is called "vibhūta", meaning ruined. "When form is destroyed, they do not touch..."
107:
"...contacts" (phassā) is the evidence for this meaning. Because of being manifest, it is called "pātubhūta". Because of being clearly manifest, it is called "āvibhūta". Similarly, there are "tirobhūta" (vanished) and "vinābhūta" (separated). Because of being worthy or fit to become, it is called "bhabba". Because that person is oppressed, he is called "paribhūta". When someone is oppressed or reviled by anyone, he is called "paribhūta". The meaning understood occurs as desired. Because of being overcome, it is called "abhibhūta". Because of being oppressed, it is called "adhibhūta".

Similarly, there is "addhabhūta". Here, the word "addha" has the same meaning as "adhi". "Monks, the eye is addhabhūta (oppressed); forms are addhabhūta; eye-consciousness is addhabhūta"—this statement is the evidence for this meaning. Furthermore, "Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk does not oppress himself who is not oppressed (anaddhabhūta) by suffering"—this phrase is also evidence. In that Pali, "anaddhabhūta" means not being oppressed by suffering. That which is not oppressed by suffering is called the human state (human life). One should understand the meaning of the sutta passage as not oppressing or overcoming that human life.

Because of being experienced, it is called "anubhūta". Similarly, there are "samanubhūta", "paccanubhūta", and "bhāvita". Here, in passages such as "Kassapa, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness has been well-expounded by me and developed (bhāvita)," the principal term denoting a quality should be seen in the Dispensation. However, in the views of outsiders (tirthikas), "bhāvita" refers to the strands of sensual pleasure. Thus, it is said in the Pali: "He does not long for the developed (bhāvita) sensual pleasures." In that Pali, "bhāvita" refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure. One should understand the meaning of the sutta passage as not longing for or indulging in those sensual pleasures.

Because of being praised, it is called "sambhāvita". Similarly, there are "vibhāvita", "paribhāvita", and "anuparibhūta". "Manaṃparibhūta" means because that person is slightly oppressed, he is called "manaṃparibhūta". Here, "manaṃparibhūta" refers to reaching only a slight degree of oppression. "Manaṃ" is an indeclinable (nipāta). "Because of a very wise son, Devadatta was slightly burned by his own ignorance..."
108:
"...and because of the absence of patience, loving-kindness, etc., the Elder Kumāra Kassapa and the Theri were nearly ruined, and the Elder Mahā Kassapa was nearly swept away"—the usage of the word "manaṃ" should be understood in such places. Here, I shall state a slight justification for the word "manaṃ".

The word "manaṃ" is divided into two: as a noun and as an indeclinable.
"His mind (manaṃ) is peaceful," and "I have a slightly (manaṃ) burned body" are examples.

"Paribhavitabba" means capable of being oppressed by another; therefore, it is called "paribhavitabba". Similarly, there are "paribhotabba" and "paribhavanīya". In the context of the suffix -tabba, the application of the word "capable" (sakkuneyya) is seen: "An object not yet obtained is capable of being obtained (laddhabba, labhanīya, or laddhuṃ sakkuneyya)." Alternatively, it means worthy of being oppressed; therefore, it is called "paribhavitabba". Similarly, there are "paribhotabba" and "paribhavanīya". Thus, in the context of the suffix -tabba, the application of the word "worthy" (arahati) is seen: "He is worthy of a gain that is capable of being sought; therefore, it is called laddhabba." In this regard, the existence of the word "paribhotabba" is evidenced by the Pali: "O Great King, a noble of royal birth should not be despised or oppressed just because he is young." The root "bhū" preceded by "abhi-" and "adhi-" have the same meaning. The remaining pairs ending in the suffixes -tabba and -aniya, such as "anubhavitabba", should be understood according to the method already mentioned.

"Bhamāna" means it becomes/arises; therefore, it is called "bhamāna". It should be noted that the letter 'va' is elided in the middle. In this matter, this conclusion is stated:

"What kind of person is that Bhamāna Saccaka?"—in this Pali, however, the form of the root "bhū" as "bhamāna" is seen only through the elision of the letter 'va'.

The Pali here is: "What kind of person is that Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, who would raise a challenge against the Blessed One?" "Vibhavamāna" means it is without/vanishes; therefore, it is called "vibhavamāna". The same applies to "paribhavamāna" and others. Among those examples, the meaning of the word "abhisambhonta" is one who performs or accomplishes. "One who accomplishes all tasks should dwell in the king's residence"—this statement is the evidence for this meaning.
109:
These words such as *bhavamāno* are words ending in the nominative case occurring in the present tense, representing an action not yet completed. Therefore, one who is remembering (*saramāno*) weeps; one who is going (*gacchanto*) takes. Just as in the phrase, "That Bharadvāja, while going (*gacchanto*), saw the hermit Accuta," one should apply them by providing a complete subsequent verb, such as "Being (*bhavamāno*) a king, he enjoys prosperity."

In fact, words such as *saramāno* and *gacchanto* are not like the words *yāto* (gone), *gato* (gone), and *patto* (reached); like words ending in the *tvā* suffix, they depend on a subsequent verb.

*Paribhaviyamāno* means he is being oppressed, thus he is *paribhaviyamāno*. The same applies to words like *paribhuyyamāno*. These also are words ending in the nominative case occurring in the present tense representing an incomplete action. Therefore, by providing a complete subsequent verb, as in "The thief being led (*nīyamāno*) by the king's men thought thus," one should apply them as: "The person being oppressed (*paribhaviyamāno*) by others seeks a protector," or "The wealth being enjoyed (*anubhaviyamāno*) by the person reaches exhaustion." In this way, one should apply this to all such *vippakata-vacana* (incomplete expressions). This is the exposition (*niddesa*) of the words *bhūta*, *parabhūta*, and *sambhūta*, which are of uncertain gender but are included among those of fixed gender. Thus, the exposition of masculine words derived from the root *bhū* has been explained through their respective etymological definitions (*nibbacana*) and so forth.

Now, the exposition of the feminine gender is stated—therein, *bhāvikā* means she causes to become, thus she is *bhāvikā*. The woman who performs the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is called *bhāvikā*. *Bhāvanā* means growth (*vaḍḍhanā*), expansion (*brūhanā*), increasing (*phātikaraṇa*), cultivation (*āsevanā*), and frequent practice (*bahulīkāra*). *Vibhāvanā* means manifestation (*pakāsanā*) or clear demonstration (*sandassanā*). Alternatively, *vibhāvanā* means non-cultivation or causing to disappear. *Sambhāvanā* means uplifting or praising. *Paribhāvanā* means perfuming (*vāsanā*) or growth from all sides. This is the exposition of feminine nouns ending in 'ā'.

*Bhūmi* means that which exists by being manifest, thus it is *bhūmi*. Alternatively, it is called *bhūmi* because both the stationary (*thāvara*) such as mountains and trees (inanimate things) and the mobile (*jaṅgama*) such as humans (animate beings) are born and grow here. *Bhūmi*...
110:
The earth is called *bhūmi*. However, in phrases such as "*paṭhamāya bhūmiyā pattiyā*" (attaining the first stage), the supramundane path (*lokuttara-magga*) is called *bhūmi*. The names for the earth as known by the common foolish folk are these: *pathavī, medanī, bhūmi, bhūrī, bhū, puthuvī, mahī, chamā, vasumatī, ubbī, avanī, ku, vasundharā, jagatī, khiti, vasudhā, dharaṇī, go, dharā*.

If it is asked, "Where have the words *bhū, ku,* and *go* been seen before to mean 'earth'?" The wise should understand that in words such as *bhūpāla* (king/protector of earth), *kumuda* (lotus/delight of earth), and *gorakkha* (cowherd/protector of earth), the words *bhū, ku,* and *go* certainly refer to the earth.

*Bhūti* means becoming or existence. *Vibhūti* means destruction, or special existence; or it is called *vibhūti* because beings exist specially through this prosperity—it is indeed prosperity (*sampatti*). The phrases "the king's prosperity (*vibhūti*)" and "desirable prosperities (*vibhūtiyo*)" are statements that prove this meaning. This is the exposition of feminine nouns ending in 'i'.

*Bhūrī* means the earth. It is called *bhūrī* because beings exist (*bhavanti*) here. Or it is called *bhūrī* because it is manifest and it grows. Or it is called *bhūrī* because beings, whether divine or human, who depend on it, delight (*ramanti*) here. Indeed, beings who depend on the earth delight only in the earth; therefore, the earth is called *bhūrī* for this reason as well. In the usage of the word *bhūrī* for earth, the term *bhūripañño* (one of broad wisdom) is a statement that proves this meaning.

Alternatively, it is called *bhūrī* because it is as extensive as the earth—this refers to wisdom (*paññā*). It is a name for wisdom that is as wide as the earth. The commentary's statement on the verse, "From endeavor wisdom (*bhūrī*) arises, from lack of endeavor wisdom perishes," is the evidence for this meaning. Or it is called *bhūrī* because it delights in manifest meanings; this is a name for wisdom, as in "*bhūrī medhā pariṇāyikā*" (broad and leading wisdom).
111:
In this matter, the words of the Commentary are the evidence for this meaning. Alternatively, wisdom alone is called '*bhūrī*' because it overcomes states such as lust (*rāga*). It is also called '*bhūrī*' because it overcomes enemies such as lust. Thus, it was said by the Venerable Sāriputta in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: "It is called *bhūrī* wisdom because it overcomes lust; it overcomes hatred, delusion... Lust is an enemy (*ari*); it is called *bhūrī* wisdom because it crushes that enemy. Hatred is... delusion is... all kamma leading to rebirth are enemies; it is called *bhūrī* wisdom because it crushes those enemies."

In this context, although it should be said as '*aribhū*' like the word '*gotrabhū*', it should be understood that the word '*bhūrī*' is pronounced by placing the word '*bhū*' at the beginning and through the power of euphonic combination (*sandhi*). Furthermore, it should be noted that in such nouns, meanings like 'overcoming' can be obtained even without a prefix (*upasagga*), whereas they cannot be obtained in verbal forms.

These are the synonymous names for wisdom (*paññā*):

*Paññā, pajānanā, cintā, vicaya, upalakkhaṇā,*
*pavicaya, paṇḍicca, dhammavicaya,*
*sallakkhaṇā, kosalla, bhūrī, paccupalakkhaṇā,*
*nepuñña, vebhabyā, medhā, upaparikkha-kā,*
*sampajañña, pariṇāyikā, vipassanā,*
*paññindriya, paññābala, amoha, sammādiṭṭhi,*
*patoda*—these names I have taken from the *Abhidhamma*.

*Ñāṇa, paññāṇa, ummaṅga, sattha, sota, diṭṭhi,*
*mantā, bodha, buddhi, buddha, paṭibhāna, bodhi,*
*dhamma, vijjā, gati, mona, nepakka, go, matī, muti,*
*vīmaṃsā, yoni, dhonā, paṇḍā, paṇḍiccaya,*
*veda, paṇḍitiya, cikicchā, miriyā.*

The two names for knowledge (*ñāṇa*) called "*sota*" and "*bodhi*" are also applicable to the Buddha, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples (*sāvakas*).
112:
The two names "Abhisambodhi" and "Sambodhi" apply only to Paccekabuddhas and Omniscient Buddhas (Sabbaññu-buddhas).

The designation of the knowledge called "Abhisambodhi" with the preceding term "Parama" (Supreme) applies only to the Omniscient Buddha (Sabbaññu-sambuddha).

The designation of the knowledge called "Sammāsambodhi" with the preceding term "Anuttara" (Unsurpassed), or the name "Buddha," applies only to the Omniscient Buddha.

The knowledge called "Sabbaññutā" (Omniscience) is appropriate only for the Omniscient Buddha. However, other designations of knowledge apply to all [wise persons].

Although the Dhamma-eye (Dhammacakkhu) and others exist as forms of knowledge, I [the author] have not presented them in this treatise because they do not serve any other special purpose here.

"Bhūtī" refers to the wife of a bhūta. Just as the wife of a peta is called "Petī," so too the wife of a bhūta is called "Bhūtī." "Bhotī" is the term by which a person speaking with a woman should address her; therefore, it should be understood that a woman is referred to by this term. Just as a person speaking with a man refers to him as "Bhavaṃ," so too a person speaking with a woman refers to her as "Bhotī." Examples here are: "From where did the venerable (Bhavaṃ) Bhāradvāja bring these children?" and "I shall serve the lady (Bhotī); let the lady not be angry."

Alternatively, in this world, some beings receive a name by virtue of the feminine gender (itthi-liṅga); such a being should be addressed as "Bhotī." Therefore, it should be understood that by this term, even a non-female being who has received a name in the feminine gender is addressed. Thus, even a son of the devas (devaputta) is addressed as "Bhotī" in consideration of the word "Devatā," because he must be referred to by the feminine gender of "Devatā"; how much more so a daughter of the devas (devadhītā). For instance, in the phrase "The lady (Bhotī) now knows; being asked, please tell me that," the feminine address "Bhotī" is used in consideration of the word "Devatā."
113:
The meaning of the Sutta passage in this context is: "If that deceitful ascetic who desires wealth does not know, does the lady deity (Bhotī Devatā) know?" Furthermore—

"O Yakkha, you desire my benefit; O Devatā, you desire my welfare. I shall follow your word; you are my teacher"—

In the story of Maṭṭhakuṇḍali, the male Maṭṭhakuṇḍali deity is addressed as "Atthakāmo" in the masculine gender in consideration of the masculine word "Yakkha," and as "Hitakāmā" in the feminine gender in consideration of the feminine word "Devatā."
