By forming pairs such as “Cetā, Ceto” and “Tātā, Tāto,” one should distinguish the meanings of the words, the declension of the original forms, and the similarities and differences of the words.

Among those words, “Cetā” first stands in the original u-ending base and later becomes a masculine ā-ending word; the word “Tātā” is the same. The word “Ceto” first stands in the original a-ending base and later becomes a masculine o-ending word; the word “Tāto” is the same. Among them, “Cetā” is so called because he collects or makes a pile; it means a person who builds a wall, a bricklayer. “Ceto” refers to the mind (citta), or a hunter of that name. Here, the mind is called “Ceto” by virtue of the meaning “cetayati cinteti—it thinks”; the hunter is called “Ceto” by virtue of designation (paññatti). “Tātā” is so called because he protects. “Aghassa tātā hitassa vidhātā—Protector from danger, provider of welfare” is its usage. In the word “Tāto” as well, it is called “Tāto” because he protects; it is used by sons toward fathers, by fathers toward sons, and toward other dear persons...
190:
This is a conventional expression used in common speech. The usage of the word 'tāta' (dear/father/son) should be understood in sentences such as: "That lonely father, dear one, will surely weep for a long time in the hermitage. The wealth acquired with great difficulty (by blowing the conch), the father has destroyed by blowing (the conch). Come, dear one." 

"Ceta, cetā, cetāro; cetāraṃ, cetāro"—this is the paradigm (padamālā) according to the Satthu-naya (the method of the word 'Satthu'). "Ceto, cetā; cetaṃ, cete; cetasā, cetenā"—this should be understood according to the Manogaṇa-naya (the method of the 'Mano' group). This is the nominal paradigm of the word 'ceta' when it signifies the mind (citta). "Ceto, cetā; cetaṃ, cete; cetenā"—this should be understood according to the Purisa-naya (the method of the word 'Purisa'). This is the nominal paradigm of the word 'ceta' when it signifies a designation (paññatti). 

"Tātā, tātā, tātāro; tātāraṃ"—this should be understood by the Satthu-naya. "Tāto, tātā, tātaṃ"—this should be understood by the Purisa-naya. In this way, in these nominal paradigms, the similarity and dissimilarity of the words should be determined. Likewise, by making a group of four based on gender and ending (anta) as "ñātā, ñāto, ñātaṃ, ñātā," one should determine the meaning of the words, the nominal paradigm of the original form, and the similarity and dissimilarity of the words.

Among those words, "ñātā" is a masculine form that first exists in the original u-kāranta (ending in u) and later becomes ā-kāranta (ending in ā). "Ñāto" and "ñātaṃ" are respectively masculine and neuter forms in the expressed genders, which first exist in the original a-kāranta and later become forms ending in 'o' and the niggahīta (ṃ). Indeed, their usages are seen as: "ñāto attho sukhāvaho" (a known meaning brings happiness) and "ñātametaṃ kuraṅgassa" (this is known by the deer). However, this word "ñātā" is a feminine form in the expressed genders, which first exists in the original ā-kāranta and remains ā-kāranta afterwards. Thus, there is the usage: "esā itthimayā ñātā" (this woman is known by me). Among those, on the masculine side, the meaning should be taken by the power of the active voice (kattukāraka) in the present tense as: "one knows, therefore he is a ñātā (knower)." On the side of the feminine and others, "it was known, therefore ñātā..."
191:
In the words "ñāto" and "ñātaṃ," the meaning should be taken by the power of the passive voice (kammakāraka) in the past tense. This method should be observed in other places as well, as applicable. The words "ñātā, ñātā, ñātāro, ñātāraṃ" should be understood by the method of the word 'Satthu'. The words "ñāto, ñātā, ñātaṃ" should be understood by the method of the word 'Purisa'. The words "ñātaṃ, ñātāni, ñātā, ñātaṃ, ñātāni, ñāte" should be understood by the method of the word 'Citta', which will be mentioned later. The words "ñātā, ñātā, ñātāyo, ñātaṃ, ñātā, ñātāyo" should be understood by the method of the word 'Kaññā', which will be mentioned later. In this way, in these nominal paradigms, the similarity and dissimilarity of the words should be determined. In other places too, similarity and dissimilarity should be investigated by this method as appropriate. The etymologies (nibbacana) of words such as vattā, dhātā, gantā, etc., should be understood as applicable, such as: "one who speaks is called vattā," "one who bears is called dhātā," "one who goes is called gantā."

Regarding the miscellaneous remarks we have made here, it should not be said that "this was spoken in an inappropriate place." Because this treatise called Saddanīti is undertaken for the purpose of manifesting the suitability and unsuitability of words and meanings; therefore, it is only beautiful when it is spoken by thoroughly stirring up the entire Māgadha language (Pali) in various ways, and not otherwise. Thus, because the desire to speak in various ways is possible, it should not be said that "this was spoken in an inappropriate place." Furthermore, because it is undertaken for the purpose of informing the wise through various means, the fault of repetition (punaruttidosa) should not be considered here. On the contrary, this Saddanīti should be respectfully learned by sons of good family endowed with faith for the sake of assisting the three Pitakas.

Thus, the words such as vattā, dhātā, gantā, which are similar to the word 'abhibhavitā', have been shown. Now, we shall show those that are dissimilar to that word. They are as follows:

Guṇavā gaṇavā ceva, balavā yasavā tathā.
Dhanavā sutavā vidvā, dhutavā katavāpi ca.
192:
The Blessed One (Bhagavā) is one who has welfare, one who has glory, one who has steadfastness, and one who has strength. Likewise, words such as one who has effort (yatavā), one who has generosity (cāgavā), and one who has snow (himavā) should be understood. After masculine and neuter words ending in 'a' (a-kāranta), the suffix 'vantu' usually follows. Those words ending in the vantu-suffix are guṇavā and so on. Because of seeing such forms as one who has perception (saññāvā), one who has rays (rassmivā), one who has a beard (massuvā), and one who has attendants (yasassivā), it should be shown that this vantu-suffix occurs in some places after words ending in 'ā', 'i', and 'u' in the feminine gender and so forth.

One who has mindfulness (satimā), one who has wisdom (gatimā), one who habitually sees the meaning (atthadassimā), one who has steadfastness (dhitimā), one who has wisdom (mutimā), one who has wisdom (matimā), one who has radiance (jutimā), one who has shame (hirimā), one who has praise (thutimā), one who has delight (ratimā), one who has restraint or a monk or effort (yatimā), one who has strength (balimā); likewise, one who has scratching or writing (kasimā), one who has a needle or purity (sucimā), one who has wisdom (dhīmā), one who has beauty (rucimā), one who has eyes (cakkhumā), one who has relatives (bandhumā), one who has a cause (hetumā), the venerable one (āyasmā), one who has a banner (ketumā), one who has Rahu (rāhumā); likewise, one who has a stump (khāṇumā), one who has radiance (bhāṇumā), one who has cattle (gomā), one who has lightning (vijjumā), one who has wealth (vasumā), and so on. Also, the Evil One who has demerit (pāpimā), one who has a son (puttimā), and the moon-god who has a moon-mansion (candimā) occur. These should be understood by the wise as words dissimilar to 'abhibhavitā'. After the letters 'i', 'u', and 'o', the suffix 'mantu' should follow. After words ending in 'ā' and 'i', it should be understood that the suffix 'imantu' occurs.

Guṇavā, guṇavā, guṇavanto. Guṇavantaṃ, guṇavante. Guṇavatā, guṇavantena, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Guṇavatā, guṇavantā, guṇavantasmā, guṇavantamhā, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Guṇavati, guṇavante, guṇavantasmiṃ, guṇavantamhi, guṇavantesu. O virtuous one! O virtuous ones! O virtuous ones!
193:
In this context, because the nominative plural forms "sīlavā" and "cakkhumā" are found in the Pāḷi texts, such as: "Come, friends, be virtuous (sīlavā)," and "Those who have gone under the influence of women, though strong, become weak; though powerful, they decline; though possessing vision (cakkhumā), they become blind," the plural form is used for "guṇavā" in the nominative and vocative positions. The same method applies to "guṇavā," "satimā," and so on.

In the Cūḷanirutti, the nominative plural and vocative plural forms appear as "guṇavā." However, in the Niruttipiṭaka, it appears only as the nominative singular. In both the Cūḷanirutti and the Niruttipiṭaka, the vocative singular appears as "bho guṇava" with a short vowel (rassa).

We, however, observe the long vowel (dīgha) form of the vocative singular "bhagavā" in hundreds of passages such as: "Indeed, O Blessed One (bhagavā), the factors of enlightenment (are good)," and "O Blessed One (bhagavā), how is it that a disciple is delighted in your teaching?" Therefore, in the case of the -vantu suffix, we consider it more appropriate to use the long vowel form, such as "bho guṇavā."

In the case of the -mantu and -imantu suffixes, because the short vowel (rassa) form of the vocative singular is seen in Pāḷi passages such as "cakkhuma" in "O you who have transcended all enmity and fear, I pay homage to your feet, O Visionary (cakkhuma)" and "Know thus, O Evil One (pāpima)," we consider it more appropriate to use the short vowel form, such as "bho satima" and "bho gatima."

Alternatively, since the vocative singular is stated with a long vowel as "āyasmā tissa" in the Commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, one should apply the -mantu suffix method to the -vantu suffix and vice versa, except for the specific words stated with long vowels like "bhagavā" and "āyasmā." Thus, in texts like Kaccāyana, three types of vocative singular are stated—using the niggahīta, the short vowel, and the long vowel—as "bho guṇavaṃ, bho guṇava, bho guṇavā." By this method, forms such as "bho satimaṃ, bho satima, bho satimā" should also be understood.
194:
In the nominative plural position, three forms are stated: "guṇavanto, guṇavantā, guṇavanti." By these forms, the method for "satimanto, satimantā, satimanti," etc., is also shown. Among those forms, "bho guṇavaṃ, bho satimaṃ, guṇavantā, guṇavanti" and other such words are not well-known in the Pāḷi texts, unlike the well-known word "āyasmantā." Therefore, whatever is stated in the Cūḷanirutti, the Niruttipiṭaka, and texts like Kaccāyana should be accepted in a way that does not contradict the Pāḷi and the Commentaries, just as the waters of the Ganges and the Yamuna truly blend and harmonize.

Indeed, in this matter, this distinction should also be noted. What is that distinction? It is because the vocative singular "paññavanta" is found in the Pāḷi as: "O Great Hero, wise one (paññavanta), bearer of the light of wisdom, your daughter..."

And because the vocative singular "paññavanta" is found in the Commentary on this Jātaka Pāḷi: "O King, who has followers, is wise (paññavanta), and endures the unendurable... all these (virtues) are thus perfected. Having obtained great fame and wealth never before received, one should not abandon one's former appearance and strength." Therefore, forms such as "bho guṇavanta, bho guṇavantā, bho satimanta, bho satimantā" must certainly be desired as vocative singulars. Indeed, in that Pāḷi, the commentators desire the vocative expression "yasassi paññavanta." The word "naṃ" is merely an expletive particle (nipāta) used to complete the verse. The word "paññavantaṃ" is stated by adding the niggahīta (anusāra) to protect the meter. Thus, the occurrence of the vocative for words associated with the -vantu suffix, etc., in the Pāḷi should be understood by the method shown as "bhagavā, āyasmā, paññavanta, cakkhuma, pāpima."

In this context, because it is seen in the Pāḷi as: "The river Ganges, named Bhāgīrathī, originates from the Himālaya (himavantā)," and "'From where have you come, Bhante?' 'From the Himālaya (himavantā), O King,'"...
195:
...the word "guṇavantā" is stated as the ablative singular (pañcamī vibhatti). Just as the declension (padamālā) of the word "guṇavantu" is arranged, so should the declensions of "dhanavantu," "balavantu," etc., and "satimantu," "gatimantu," etc., be arranged.

Now, although words like "vidvā" follow the same pattern as the word "guṇavā," the declension of the original form "vidvantu," etc., will be stated along with the definitions (nibbacana), etc., in part, to remove confusion for listeners regarding their usage: Knowledge is called "veda"; he who has it is "vidvā" (the wise). The evidence for the existence of the word "vidvā" is the direct Pāḷi passage: "Knowing thus, the wise man (vidvā) should live equanimously." The declension of this word is: vidvā, vidvā, vidvanto (nominative); vidvantaṃ, vidvante (accusative); vidvatā, vidvantena (instrumental). All remaining cases should be understood accordingly.

Vedanāvā, vedanāvā, vedanāvanto. Vedanāvantaṃ, vedanāvante. Vedanāvatā, vedanāvantena. All remaining cases should be understood accordingly. The same applies to "saññāvā, cetanāvā, saddhāvā, paññavā, sabbāvā," etc. In this context, the example phrases are: "the self possessing sensation (vedanāvantaṃ)" or "the world possessing all (sabbāvantaṃ) beings." Here, "sabbāvantaṃ" means possessing all beings or joined with all beings. This word has a long vowel (dīgha) in the middle. Generally, however, words like "paññavā, paññavanto" also have short vowels (rassa) in the middle.

He who has famous people as his followers is "yasassivā." Alternatively, because he is both famous (yasassī) and possesses famous people (yasassivā), he is called "yasassivā." This is a compound where one of two similar parts is retained (ekadesa-sarūpekesa). The evidence for the existence of the word "yasassivā" is this verse:
"A Khattiya of noble birth, well-born and famous (yasassivā), a righteous king of the Videhans, a son shall be born to you."
196:
This is an illustration. The forms should be derived as "yasassivā, yasassivā, yasassivanto; yasassivantaṃ," and so on. The nature of habitually seeing the meaning or benefit is called 'atthadassī'. What is that dhamma? It is indeed wisdom (ñāṇa). One who possesses that 'atthadassī' (wisdom) is called 'atthadassimā'. In this context also:

"In that assembly, the wise Vidhura, who is possessed of wisdom, effort, and intelligence, who sees the meaning and the cause, and who explains all dhammas, spoke this word."

This statement serves as proof for this meaning. The forms should be derived as "atthadassimā, atthadassimā, atthadassimanto; atthadassimantaṃ," and so on. One who has evil is called 'pāpimā', which refers to Māra who is possessed of a mass of unwholesome states. One who has sons is called 'puttimā', meaning one with many children. In the passage, "One with children sorrows because of children," the term 'puttimā' refers to one with many children. One who has the moon is called 'candimā'. Here, 'canda' refers to the moon mansion (candavimāna), while the deity dwelling in the moon mansion is called 'candimā'. This is because in passages such as, "The moon has arisen; in dimension, the moon is forty-nine yojanas in length, breadth, and height, and one hundred and fifty yojanas minus three (147) in circumference," the moon mansion is called 'canda'. However, in passages such as, "The moon deity (candimā) has gone for refuge to the Tathāgata, the Arahant," the moon deity is called 'candimā'. Another method: One who has the moon is called 'candimā'. Here, 'canda' refers to the moon deity, while his residence, the moon mansion, is called 'candimā'. This is because in passages such as, "Rāhu, lord of asuras, release the moon (canda); the moon dwells in a mansion made of jewels," the moon deity is called 'canda'.

"Indeed, that young monk who strives in the Buddha's dispensation illuminates this world like the moon (candimā) freed from a cloud."

In such passages, the moon mansion, which is the residence of that deity, is called 'candimā'. Thus, both 'canda' and 'candimā' should be understood as names for the moon deity...
197:
## Paradigm of Masculine Nouns Ending in -a

...and also as names for the moon mansion. Among those terms, "pāpimā, puttimā, candimā" should be understood as being established by the power of the suffix -imantu, which occurs in the sense of "that is his" (tadassatthi) following the word 'pāpa' and others.

Venerable Sir, should they not be established by the power of the suffix -mantu alone? No, because the suffix -mantu does not occur after words ending in -a (akāranta) anywhere. Venerable Sir, even if that is so, could they not be established by first applying the i-augment (i-āgama) after the words 'pāpa', 'putta', and 'canda', and then applying the suffix -mantu? Although it could be established in terms of mere form, that method is not elegant. This is because if the suffix -mantu were prescribed with an i-augment after words ending in -a like 'pāpa' and 'putta', it would lead to the undesirable consequence of having to apply the suffix -mantu with an i-augment after other words ending in -a such as 'guṇa' and 'yasa'. Indeed, in many hundreds of thousands of Pali texts, the suffix -mantu is nowhere seen with an i-augment after words ending in -a like 'guṇa' and 'yasa'. Since it is not the proper place for an i-augment, the forms "pāpimā, puttimā," etc., are established only when the suffix -imantu is applied without an i-augment after words ending in -a like 'pāpa' and 'putta'.

Venerable Sir, if that is so, why is only the suffix -mantu mentioned in the Kaccāyana grammar, and not the suffix -imantu? Both are indeed mentioned. If one asks, "How is this known?"—it is because in that Kaccāyana grammar, after stating the four sūtras: "tapādito sī, daṇḍādito ika ī, madhvādito ro, guṇādito vantū" by way of their proximity to words ending in the suffix -to, the teacher stated the sūtra "satyādīhi mantu" in the middle in a different manner, and then stated the sūtra "saddhādito ṇā" by way of proximity to the suffix -to. Therefore, it is understood that the suffix -imantu is also stated by the power of that sūtra "satyādīhi mantu," which was formulated differently from the preceding and succeeding sūtras. It is the nature of teachers to make their intention known by whatever means. In this context, the second meaning should be taken by the power of vowel sandhi (sarasandhi). This is because in that sūtra, "satyādīhi..."
198:
..."mantu" is the first meaning, and "satyādīhi imantu" is the second meaning. Thus, just as in the usage "seto dhāvati" (which can mean 'the white ox runs' or 'the dog runs from here'), in the sūtra "satyādīhi mantu," the understanding of two meanings arises through the power of the conjunction of distinct powers (bhinnasatti-samaveta). Therefore, by this sūtra which possesses an extremely subtle and profound meaning, the suffix -mantu is desired after certain words such as 'sati', 'gati', 'setu', and 'go'. It should be understood that the suffix -imantu is desired after certain words such as 'sati', 'pāpa', and 'putta'.

However, since the word 'sati' shares the same status with 'gati', 'dhī', 'setu', 'go', etc., by way of the suffix -mantu, and with 'pāpa', 'putta', etc., by way of the suffix -imantu, it is taken as a representative type (pakāra) for them. Therefore, the meaning of the sūtra is as follows: "After words of the same type as 'sati', the suffixes -mantu and -imantu occur as appropriate in the sense of 'that is his'." The intention here is this: Just as the suffix -mantu occurs after the i-ending word 'sati' in the form "satimā," so too the suffix -mantu occurs after words ending in -i, -ī, -u, and -o, such as "gatimā, dhīမာ, setumā, gomā." And just as the suffix -imantu occurs after the i-ending word 'sati' in the form "satimā," so too the suffix -imantu occurs after words ending in -i and -a, such as "gatimā, pāpimā, puttimā." Thus, the suffixes -mantu and -imantu occur as possible after words of the same type as 'sati'.

If this is so, why was it not stated as "satyādito imantu mantu," similar to the sūtra "daṇḍādito ika ī" which prescribes two suffixes? There is a reason for not stating it that way. If the sūtra had been stated as "satyādito imantu mantu" like "daṇḍādito ika ī," then by the simultaneous mention of -imantu and -mantu, one would have to expect two different forms from words like 'sati' and 'gati', just as the two forms "daṇḍiko" and "daṇḍī" arise from the word 'daṇḍa'. But such dual forms do not exist.
199:
Therefore, it should not be said: "From satyādi, imantu and mantu." Alternatively, if it were said thus, the text would become heavy due to the abundance of syllables. For a sutta should be characterized by few syllables, lack of ambiguity, essence, profound determination, comprehensiveness, and faultlessness. In the Kaccāyana treatise also, suttas such as "Upāja-dhikissara-vacane" and "Sarā sare lopaṃ" are mostly seen to possess such qualities as having few syllables, containing profound meaning, and being the domain of extremely pure knowledge. This sutta "Satyādīhi mantu" is also one among those profound suttas. Therefore, it should not be said: "From satyādi, imantu and mantu." Even if the sutta is not composed in this way, it should be understood that it is stated as "Satyādīhi mantu" by the method of bhinnasatti-samaveta (inherent distinct powers) in order to include the imantu suffix as well.

Another method—in suttas such as "Tapādito sī," the plural nature of the word ending in -to is not very clear because the -to suffix occurs in both singular and plural. However, in this sutta "Satyādīhi mantu," the plural meaning of the word ending in -hi is very clear. Therefore, it should also be noted that by taking the plural, the imantu suffix is formed.

O Venerable Sir, even without the imantu suffix, the word "pāpī" is formed as "pāpam-assatthi" (evil is his); and "pāpī" itself becomes "pāpimā." Is it not possible for words like "pāpimā" and "puttimā" to be accomplished by merely applying the suffix -ma in its own meaning, just like the word "chaṭṭhamo" with the suffix -ma in the phrase "chaṭṭhamo so parābhavo"?

You are one who is very skilled in methods; you are said to be very skilled in methods. However, you do not know the ways of words (saddagati), and the ways of words are of many varieties. For instance—chaṭṭha itself is chaṭṭhama; there is the way of words joined by the masculine method (purisanaya) in such cases as "suttameva suttantaṃ"; the way of words joined by the feminine method (kaññānaya) in such cases as "devo-yeva devatā"; and the way of words joined by the neuter method (cittanaya) in such cases as "diṭṭhi eva diṭṭhigataṃ." Among such ways of words, what kind of way of words do you call "pāpī itself is pāpimā"? "Satthā rājā brahmā sakhā attā sā..."
200:
In words such as "pumā," what kind of linguistic behavior do you speak of? In what word-category is it included? In what declension paradigm (nāmika-padamālā) do you think it should be joined? When questioned thus, that objector, seeing nothing further, will surely remain silent. Therefore, such a method should not be accepted. In such a method, forms like "pāpimatā" and "pāpimato" cannot be accomplished, but they can be accomplished by the method of the imantu suffix. Therefore, this method alone should be well-attended to by the venerable ones as the most praiseworthy method.

Here is the illustration:
"This victory belongs only to the Blessed One, the Glorious One (Sirīmanto);
And this defeat belongs to Māra, the Evil One (Pāpimato).
Then the joyful hosts of devas at the seat of enlightenment (Bodhimanda),
Proclaimed the victory of the Great Sage (Mahesino)."
And also: "Like a great tree with a trunk (khandhimā), endowed with branches, leaves, and fruits."

Pāpimā, pāpimā, pāpimanto. Pāpimantaṃ. The rest of the declension should be understood. This method also applies to words like "khandhimā" and "puttimā."

Now, I shall speak briefly on the distinctions of words such as himavantu and satimantu according to the Pali scriptures. Himavanto pabbato (the snowy mountain). Satimaṃ bhikkhuṃ (the mindful monk [acc.]). Bandhumaṃ rājānaṃ (the king who has kinsmen). Candimaṃ devaputtaṃ (the moon-deity). Satimassa bhikkhuno (to the mindful monk). Bandhumassa rañño (to King Bandhuma). The mind of one who has psychic power and the mind of another arise in a single moment. Such distinctions should be understood.

Furthermore, in this context, it should be understood that "āyasmantā" is the form used for two persons, and "āyasmanto" is the form used for many persons. Thus it is said: "When wishing to inform two persons, one should say 'āyasmantā dhārentu'; when wishing to inform three persons, one should say 'āyasmanto dhārentu'." Here, "three persons" is merely the beginning of the expression; therefore, it means that for four, five, or even more than a hundred persons, (āyasmanto should be used).
201:
This is shown. The Pali texts such as "Venerable ones (āyasmanto), the four pārājika rules have been recited" are established based on many (four, five, etc.). Between these two, the word "āyasmantā" refers only to two persons according to Vinaya usage and is not common to all usages. It does not occur in other usages apart from Vinaya usage. The word "āyasmanto," however, occurs in all usages; thus the distinction between these two should be understood.

Among those words, "himavanto" is mostly singular, but in some places, it is also plural. Therefore, the Elder (Mahākaccāyana) said in the Niruttipiṭaka: "Himavā tiṭṭhati (Mount Himavā stands), Himavanto tiṭṭhanti (The Himavā mountains stand)." This singular method of "himavanto-va pabbato" should be taken according to the Pali as it is uttered (yathāruta-pāḷi). What is called yathāruta-pāḷi is as follows:

"The virtuous shine from afar like the Himavā mountain.
The wicked are not seen here, like arrows shot in the night.
At that time, I was a Naga king of great power,
Atula by name, meritorious and possessing the glow of majesty.
That sage was one who possessed wisdom (gatimanto), mindful (satimanto), and energetic (dhitimanto);
The Elder Ānanda, the bearer of the True Dhamma, was a mine of jewels."

And so forth. In this Pali, although words like "puññavanto" are repeatedly stated as plural in many places, in some places they are singular. The singular nature of these words is seen in the context of verses (gāthā). Therefore, those words should be taken as they appear in the Pali scriptures (yathāpāvacanaṃ).

Having thus understood the distinctions of words such as himavantu and satimantu, one should further determine the meaning of words having two genders by way of their gender-endings, the declension paradigm (nāmika-padamālā) of the original form, and the similarity or dissimilarity of the words.
202:
## 
Among those words, the word "Sirimā" is twofold because it occurs in two genders based on the similarity of sound. In the sense of "Sirimā puriso" (a man possessing glory and wisdom), it is an ā-ending masculine gender; in the sense of "Sirimā nāma devī" (a queen named Sirimā), it is an ā-ending feminine gender. Both of these have an u-ending nature (stem). Alternatively, the latter feminine word has an ā-ending nature. The derivative definition (vigraha) is made by way of the masculine gender as: "He who has glory (sirī) is Sirimā." The derivative definition is made by way of the feminine gender as: "She who has glory (sirī) is Sirimā."

In this regard, although these two words are identical to each other in terms of sound and derivative meaning, they should be understood as having different meanings because they denote the meaning of a masculine word and the meaning of a feminine word respectively. This method should also be applied in other similar instances.

Sirimā, sirimā, sirimanto. Sirimantaṃ, sirimante. Sirimatā, sirimantena. The nominal declension table (nāmikapadamālā) is just like that of the word "Guṇavantu."

Sirimā, sirimā, sirimāyo. Sirimaṃ, sirimā, sirimāyo. Sirimāya. This should be understood according to the method of the word "Kanyā" which will be mentioned later.

In this way, in the nominal declension tables of words that have the same sound but are divided into two types, the similarity and dissimilarity of the words should be distinguished. Even if the derivative meaning is the same, in the nominal declension table of the word "Sirimā" which does not have the same sound, no similarity whatsoever is found with these words. In this regard, it is said:

"The word 'Sirimā' is twofold, as it occurs in both masculine and feminine. One should distinguish that it is divided; here, the masculine gender is desired."

Thus, words such as "Guṇavā" and "Satimā," which are dissimilar to the word "Abhibhavitā," have been shown along with their nominal declension tables. Now, I shall show other words that are also dissimilar to that word "Abhibhavitā" along with their nominal declension tables. What are those words? They are:

Rājā (king), Brahmā (Brahma), Sakhā (friend), Attā (self), Ātumā (self), Sā (dog), Pumā (man), Rahā (evil/secret), Daḷhadhammā (one with a firm bow), Paccakkhadhammā (one who has realized the Dhamma), and Vivaṭacchadā (one with the covering removed).
203:
## 
Vattahā, tathā, vuttasirā, yuvā, maghavā, addhā, muddhā, and so on should be known by the wise. Among these words, only the word 'Sā' is an ā-ending word with an ā-ending base. The remaining words, however, are ā-ending words with an a-ending base.

The declension of the word Rājā is as follows:
Rājā, rājā, rājāno. Rājānaṃ, rājaṃ, rājāno. Raññā, rājinā, rājūhi, rājūbi. Rañño, rājino, raññaṃ, rājūnaṃ, rājānaṃ. Raññā, rājūhi, rājūbi. Rañño, rājino, raññaṃ, rājūnaṃ, rājānaṃ. Raññe, rājini, rājūsu.
In the vocative: 'Bho rāja, bhavanto rājāno, bhavanto rājā.' This is our preference (ruci).

Although the plural form 'Rājā' does not appear in texts such as the Niruttipiṭaka, it does appear in the Cūḷanirutti. Even if it does not appear in the Niruttipiṭaka and others, because the word 'Sakhā' is seen in both plural and singular forms in the Pali verse: 'Netādisā sakhā honti, labbhā me jīvato sakhā,' the plural form 'Rājā' should also be desired. Likewise, words such as Brahmā and Attā also have plural forms without any special morphological difference because they follow the same pattern as the word Rājā.

In this context, the form 'Rājaṃ' is mentioned because it is found in the teaching: 'Gahapatiko nāma ṭhapetvā rājaṃ rājabhogaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ avaseso gahapatiko nāma.' However, this form does not appear in the Niruttipiṭaka. The form 'Rājinā' is mentioned due to the usage 'Sabbadattena rājinā.' The form 'Rājānaṃ' is mentioned as the dative and genitive due to the usage 'Ārādhayati rājānaṃ, pūjaṃ labhati bhattusu.'

In the Kaccāyana and Rūpasiddhi texts, however, the words 'Rājena, rājehi, rājebhi, rājesu' are mentioned. These words do not appear in the Cūḷanirutti and Niruttipiṭaka. Since they are not found in the Pali Canon, their absence is more appropriate. Therefore,
204:
## 
we have not mentioned those words (such as rājena, etc.) here. When investigating the method of the Pali Canon, such words are found only in compounds (samāsa) and not elsewhere. The usages found in compounds are: 'Āvutthaṃ dhammarājena,' 'Sivirājena pesito,' 'Pajāpatissa devarājassa dhajaggaṃ,' and 'Nikkhamante mahārāje, sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane.' Thus, when investigating the Pali method, words like 'Rājena' are seen only in compounds. Not only in the Pali method, but also when investigating the method of the ancient Commentaries (Porāṇaṭṭhakathā), they are seen only in compounds and not elsewhere. Even so, this matter should be investigated thoroughly. Indeed, who is able to discern all the methods in the Word of the Buddha, the Tipiṭaka along with the Commentaries, except for the Arahants who have attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā)?

In this regard, the nominal declension tables of the word 'Rāja' at the end of a compound are stated in two ways: by way of the o-ending and the ā-ending. Among them, the o-endings are 'Mahārājo, yuvarājo, sivirājo, dhammarājo,' and so on. The ā-endings are 'Mahārājā, yuvarājā, sivirājā, dhammarājā,' and so on. Here, although words like 'Mahārājo' do not exist in the Pali and the ancient Commentaries, because 'Sabbasakho' is seen in the Pali verse 'Sabbamitto sabbasakho, sabbabhūtānukampako,' words like 'Mahārājo' must also be desired. For that reason, 'Dhammarājena, dhammarājassa,' and so on are seen in compounds. These words are only o-ending forms and not ā-ending forms.

The declension of the word Mahārājo is as follows:
Mahārājo, mahārājā. Mahārājaṃ, mahārāje. Mahārājena, mahārājehi, mahārājebhi. Mahārājassa, mahārājānaṃ. Mahārājā, mahārājasmā, mahārājamhā, mahārājehi, mahārājebhi. Mahārājassa, mahārājānaṃ. Mahārāje, mahārājasmiṃ, mahārājamhi, mahārājesu.
In the vocative: 'Bho mahārāja, bhavanto.'
205:
Mahārājā.

According to the methods of the Kaccāyana and Cūḷanirutti grammars, the singular and plural forms of "Bho Mahārājā" (O Great King) should also be noted. Just as it occurs by the power of the -o ending word "Mahārājo", the declension of the original form should likewise be applied to other -o ending words such as "Sivirājo", "Dhammarājo", and "Devarājo".

This is the declension shown by the power of the -ā ending:
Mahārājā (the king), Mahārājā, Mahārājāno (the kings). Mahārājānaṃ, Mahārājaṃ (the king [acc.]), Mahārājāno (the kings [acc.]). Mahāraññā, Mahārājinā (by the king), Mahārājūhi, Mahārājūbi (by the kings). Mahārañño, Mahārājino (to/of the king), Mahāraññaṃ, Mahārājūnaṃ (to/of the kings). Mahāraññā (from the king), Mahārājūhi, Mahārājūbi (from the kings). Mahārañño, Mahārājino (of the king), Mahāraññaṃ, Mahārājūnaṃ (of the kings). Mahāraññe, Mahārājini (in the king), Mahārājūsu (in the kings). Bho Mahārāja (O king), Bhavanto Mahārājāno (O kings).

In this declension of -ā ending nouns as well, the singular and plural forms of "Bho Mahārājā" should be noted according to the methods of the two treatises. Just as it occurs by the power of the -ā ending word "Mahārājā", the declension of the original form should likewise be applied to other -ā ending words such as "Sivirājā", "Dhammarājā", and "Devarājā".

In this context, to clarify further meanings, the declension will be stated by combining with verbs, through the mixture of -ā and -o endings:
Mahārājā, Mahārājo tiṭṭhati (The great king stands); Mahārājāno, Mahārājā tiṭṭhanti (The great kings stand). Mahārājānaṃ, Mahārājaṃ passati (He sees the great king); Mahārājāno, Mahārāje passati (He sees the great kings). Mahāraññā, Mahārājinā, Mahārājena kataṃ (It was done by the great king); Mahārājūhi, Mahārājūbi, Mahārājehi, Mahārājebhi kataṃ (It was done by the great kings). Mahārañño, Mahārājino, Mahārājassa dīyate (It is given to the great king); Mahāraññā, Mahārājā, Mahārājasmā, Mahārājamhā nissaṭaṃ (It emerged from the great king); Mahārājūhi, Mahārājūbi...
206:
...emerged from the great kings. The retinue of the great king; the retinue of the great kings. Established in the great king; established in the great kings. "O great king, you stand; O great kings, you all stand" (it is said). Likewise for "Yuvarājā", "Yuvarājo", etc.

In this regard, some might say: "Why has the author of this treatise exerted such great effort and endeavor here? Among these words, some exist in the Buddha's words (Buddhavacana), while others do not, isn't that so?"

To them, the wise should reply: "The author of the treatise exerted that great effort and endeavor for the benefit of the Dispensation (Sāsana), by producing thorough proficiency in both the sounds (sadda) and meanings (attha) for the listeners of the Teacher's ninefold Dispensation together with the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). Among these words shown by the teacher, some exist in the Buddhavacana, while others do not. Among those that exist or do not exist, the words present in the Buddhavacana are taken as they are. Those not present are taken as they exist in the ancient commentaries (Porāṇaṭṭhakathā) and according to the method of the Pali language (grammatical logic)."

In this context, this is the clarification of the meaning in brief:
"King Kaṃsa, the ruler of Bārāṇasī, having spoken these words, cast aside his bow and quiver, and entered the state of a recluse."
This verse is an example of the word "Mahārāja" ending in -ā. Since the Pali "Sabbasakho" exists, the -o ending is also established as "Mahārājo" by that method, and it should be applied according to the method of the word "Purisa". For that very reason, forms such as "Tamabravi mahārājā" and "Nikkhamante mahārāje" are seen.
207:
Thus, when it is established that the word "Mahārāja" is an -o ending noun, the singular ablative (pañcamī) forms "Mahārājā", "Mahārājasmā", and "Mahārājamhā", and the singular locative (sattamī) forms "Mahārāje", "Mahārājassiṃ", and "Mahārājamhi" are indeed established, for they should be accepted by way of method (naya) even if they do not exist directly in the Pali texts. However, forms like "Rājena" and "Rājassa" should not be accepted by way of method. Why? Because words like "Rājā", "Brahmā", "Sakhā", and "Attā" are not entirely similar to each other in every way like "Puriso" and "Urago". Indeed, for those words like Rāja, Brahma, Sakha, and Atta, there are dissimilar forms such as "Raññā", "Brahmunā", "Sakhinā", "Attanā", "Attena", "Sānā", and "Pumunā"; therefore, it is not possible to know those forms merely by way of method. Because they are thus difficult to know, only the words directly present in the Pali texts and ancient commentaries should be taken.

Only when it is established that words like "Mahārāja" are -o ending nouns is the adoption of the method seen, as in "These words fall within the method of Purisa"; therefore, we have stated "Mahārājā", "Mahārājasmā", etc., by way of method. For example:

"This is difficult for you to know, you who sleep like the dead;
While I (the jackal) am pulling you,
the staff is not released from your hand."

In this (Jātaka), because the singular ablative form of an -o ending noun is seen as "hatthā", and in the verse "attadaṇḍā bhayaṃ jātaṃ" as "daṇḍā", the singular ablative forms of -o ending nouns like "uragā", "pataṅgā", and "vihagā" should also be accepted. Furthermore, because the verbal forms are seen as "maññavho" in the verse "dāṭhini mātimaññavho, siṅgālo mama pāṇado", and as "kappayavho" in the verse "suddhā suddhehi saṃvāsaṃ, kappayavho patissatā", forms like "gacchavho", "bhuñjavho", and "sayavho" should also be accepted. The wise who are very proficient in the Dispensation accept such word forms; therefore, we also, by the power of adopting the method...
208:
We have stated the forms such as "Mahārājā" and "Mahārājasmā". If one does not accept them by way of method (nayaggāha), how can the series of nominal forms (nāmikapadamālā) be complete? They become complete only when such a method is accepted.

For in the Buddhavacana, hundreds of thousands of nouns and verbs are not always found individually conjoined with the seven or eight nominal case-endings in singular and plural, nor with the ninety-six verbal terminations of the Ākhyāta. However, they do exist by way of method. Therefore, we have established forms such as "Mahārājā" and "Mahārājasmā" by way of method. As for the phrases "Mahārājā tiṭṭhanti" and "Mahārājā tumhe tiṭṭhatha", they are stated because they are found in the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta as: "Then the four Great Kings (Mahārājā), with a great army of Yakkhas and a great army of Kumbhaṇḍas..."

And because they are found in the Mahāsamaya Sutta as:
"Those four Great Kings (Mahārājā),
In the four directions all around,
Standing brilliant and radiant,
In the forest of Kapilavatthu."

Forms such as "Mahārājaṃ" are also stated only after seeing the Pali text and the method of the Pali. We do not see forms such as "Rājaṃ" or "Rājena" in non-compound (asamāsa) usage; therefore, this point should be carefully considered. This is a difficult matter to see, to be known only by the wise who possess diligence. 

If you, venerable sirs, should see forms such as "Rājaṃ" or "Rājena" in non-compound usage either in the Buddhavacana or in the ancient commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), then please bear them well in mind. For who else, other than the great Arahants (Khīṇāsava) who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), is able to know the distinctions of usage in the Buddhavacana in every aspect?

Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One:
"He who is free from craving, without grasping,
Skilled in linguistics (nirutti) and the analysis of terms,
Who knows the assembly of letters,
And their sequence of preceding and following."
209:
Brahmā, Brahmā, Brahmāno (Nominative). Brahmānaṃ, Brahmaṃ, Brahmāno (Accusative). Brahmunā, Brahmehi, Brahmebhi, Brahmūhi, Brahmūbi (Instrumental). Brahmassa, Brahmuno, Brahmānaṃ, Brahmūnaṃ (Dative). Brahmunā, Brahmehi, Brahmebhi, Brahmūhi, Brahmūbi (Ablative). Brahmassa, Brahmuno, Brahmānaṃ, Brahmūnaṃ (Genitive). Brahmani, Brahmesu (Locative). O Brahmā, O Brahmā, O Brahmās (Vocative). According to the preference of the Great Elder Yamaka, there is also the plural vocative "Bho Brahmā". Here, the forms "Brahmūhi, Brahmūbhi, Brahmūnaṃ, Brahme" are stated because of the sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) statement: "By the wise, by the devas, by the Brahmās (Brahmūhi)"; and the commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) statements: "The voice of the Brahmās (Brahmūnaṃ) occurs," and "In the mansions of the Brahmās (Brahmūnaṃ), the influx of sensual desire (kāmāsava) which is passion does not occur"; and because of the Pali verse spoken directly by Sahampati Brahmā himself: "Thinking it would be wearying, I did not speak the proficient, sublime Dhamma to men, O Brahmā (Brahme)." These forms do not appear in the Cūḷanirutti, Niruttipiṭaka, and Kaccāyana grammars.

Sakhā, Sakhā, Sakhino, Sakhāno, Sakhāyo (Nominative). Sakhaṃ, Sakhāraṃ, Sakhānaṃ, Sakhino, Sakhāno, Sakhāyo (Accusative). Sakhinā, Sakhārehi, Sakhārebhi, Sakhehi, Sakhebhi (Instrumental). Sakhissa, Sakhino, Sakhīnaṃ, Sakhārānaṃ, Sakhānaṃ (Dative). Sakhārasmā, Sakhinā, Sakhārehi, Sakhārebhi, Sakhehi, Sakhebhi (Ablative). Sakhissa, Sakhino, Sakhīnaṃ, Brahmānaṃ, Sakhānaṃ (Genitive). Sakhe, Sakhesu, Sakhāresu (Locative). O friend, O friend, O friend, O friend, O friend, O friends (Vocative). According to the view of the Great Elder Yamaka, "Bho Sakhā" is also plural. However, in the Pali of the Suvaṇṇakakkaṭa Jātaka, the word "Sakhā" spoken with a long vowel (dīgha) as in "Hey friend (Sakhā), why do you abandon me?" is a singular vocative. Therefore, one might say that the method of the Great Elder Yamaka is not appropriate.
210:
Should one say it is not appropriate? No, it is appropriate. Because in the Manoja Jātaka, the word "Sakhā" is both singular and plural, as in: "Such friends (Sakhā) do not exist; a friend (Sakhā) is to be obtained by me while I live." In that Jātaka, it is plural in the first foot of the verse and singular in the second foot. Therefore, the Great Elder Yamaka stated the word "Sakhā" in the position of the plural nominative and vocative. Also here, the declension of the word "Sakha" obtained in a compound (samāsa) according to the text "Friend of all (Sabbasakho), compassionate to all beings," follows the method of the word "Purisa" as: "Sabbasakho, Sabbasakhā, Sabbasakhaṃ, Sabbasakhe," etc. The analysis of the compound (vigga-ha) there is: He is the friend of all people (sabbesaṃ janānaṃ sakhā), or all people are friends to him (sabbe vā janā sakhino etassa), thus he is "Sabbasakho". It is like the word "Sabbaverī".

Attā, Attā, Attāno (Nominative). Attānaṃ, Attaṃ, Attāno (Accusative). Attanā, Attena, Attanehi, Attanebhi (Instrumental). Attano, Attānaṃ (Dative). Attanā, Attanehi, Attanebhi (Ablative). Attano, Attānaṃ (Genitive). Attani, Attanesu (Locative). O self, O self, O selves (Vocative).

Here, the form "Attaṃ" is stated because it is found in Pali texts such as: "Having cast aside the self (attaṃ), he pursues pleasant things," and:
"If you go to the Pañcāla kingdom,
You will quickly abandon yourself (attaṃ).
As a great danger follows a deer on the path,
So a great danger will come to you."

The form "Attena" is stated because of the Pali: "Empty of self (attena) or what belongs to self (attaniyena)." In the Cūḷanirutti, the singular dative and genitive form "Attassa" appears; this is not seen in the Kaccāyana and Niruttipiṭaka. In some places, the form "Attesu" appears. All these should be accepted after observing the method of the Buddha's Pali along with the commentaries.
211:
"Ātumā, ātumā, ātumāno. Ātumānaṃ, ātumāṃ, ātumāno. Ātumena, ātumchi, ātumebhi," etc., are spoken according to the method of purisa, and one should say, "Bho ātuma, bhavanto ātumā, ātumāno."

Among those words (atta, ātuma), in the compound of the word atta, the declension table (nāmika-padamālā) should be applied only according to the method of purisa as: "Bhāvitatto, bhāvitattā. Bhāvitattaṃ, bhāvitatte. Bhāvitattena, bhāvitattehi, bhāvitattebhi."

Sā, sā, sāno. Sānaṃ, sāne. Sānā, sānehi, sānebhi. Sāssa, sānaṃ. Sānā, sānehi, sānebhi. Sāssa, sānaṃ. Sāne, sānesu. Bho sā, bhavanto sāno. The word "sā" refers to a dog.

In this context, "Na yattha sā upaṭṭhito hoti" (Where the dog is not present), "Sāva vārenti sūkaraṃ" (Like dogs warding off a pig) are the illustrative examples. However, some [teachers of Rūpasiddhi] state forms such as "saṃ, se, sena" in the accusative, instrumental, and other cases of the word sā; this is not appropriate. This is because those forms like "saṃ, se, sena" are not found in the Buddha's words (Tipiṭaka), the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), or the Niruttipiṭaka.

In the Niruttipiṭaka, it is stated thus: "Sā tiṭṭhati (The dog stands), sāno tiṭṭhanti (The dogs stand). Sānaṃ passati, sāne passati. Sānā kataṃ, sānehi kataṃ, sānebhi kataṃ. Sāssa dīyate, sānaṃ dīyate. Sānā nissaṭaṃ, sānehi nissaṭaṃ, sānebhi nissaṭaṃ. Sāssa pariggaho, sānaṃ pariggaho. Sāne patiṭṭhitaṃ, sānesu patiṭṭhitaṃ. Bho sā, bhavanto sāno." Therefore, the declension table should be taken only according to the method stated in the Niruttipiṭaka.
212:
## In this matter, it should be stated thus:

Just as for the word "sa" which expresses the meaning of "one's own property" in the masculine gender, as in "Sehi dārehi asantuṭṭho" (Not content with one's own wives), the forms occur according to the method of purisa in the sense of "this property of one's own is sa": "So, sā. Saṃ, se. Sena, sehi, sebhi. Sassa, sānaṃ. Sā, sasmā, samhā, sehi, sebhi. Sassa, sānaṃ. Se, sasmiṃ, samhi, sesu." However, the forms of the word "sā" meaning "dog" do not occur in that way.

Or, just as for the word "sa" which expresses the meaning of "one's own property" in the neuter gender, as in "Hiṃsanti attasambhūtā, tacasāraṃva saṃ phalaṃ. Sāni kammāni tappenti, kosalaṃ sena'santuṭṭhaṃ, jီvagāhaṃ agāhayī" (Evil deeds born of oneself destroy [the person], just as its own fruit destroys the bamboo. One's own deeds cause torment; he caused the King of Kosala, who was not content with his own country, to be captured alive), the forms occur according to the method of citta: "Saṃ, sāni, sā. Saṃ, sāni, se. Sena, sehi, sebhi. Sassa, sānaṃ. Sā, sasmā, samhā, sehi, sebhi. Sassa, sānaṃ. Se, sasmiṃ, samhi, sesu." However, the forms of the word "sā" meaning "dog" do not occur in that way.

This being so, why did those teachers state "saṃ, se, sena" in the accusative and instrumental positions? And why did they state "sā, sasmā, samhā" in the ablative position, and "se, sasmiṃ, samhi" in the locative position? All of this is without reason; it is a groundless assertion taken merely by conjecture.

The reason is that the word "sā" meaning "dog" has a natural stem ending in -ā (ākāranta); it does not have a natural stem ending in -a (akāranta) like the words purisa and citta. The base (prakṛti) that would allow such forms to exist for this word does not exist. This word is not like "rājā, brahmā, sakhā, attā," etc., which first exist as ending in -a and later acquire the ending in -ā. Rather, it is a word that always has a natural stem ending in -ā, just as the word "go" always has a natural stem ending in -o. For a word that always has a natural stem ending in -ā, such forms do not occur. Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, who attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), did not teach [those forms] in the Niruttipiṭaka. If they think that because "attaṃ, attena" are seen, these forms like "saṃ, sena" should be taken [by analogy]...
213:
There is also another point to be stated here. Indeed, when it is said, "Sāhi nārīhi te yanti" (They go with their own women), for the feminine word "sā" which has the meaning of "one's own woman" and is similar to the word kaññā, the forms occur according to the method of kaññā: "Sā, sā, sāyo. Saṃ, sā, sāyo. Sāya, sāhi, sābhi. Sāya, sānaṃ. Sāya, sāhi, sābhi. Sāya, sānaṃ. Sāya, sāyaṃ, sāsu." The forms of this word "sā" meaning "dog" do not occur in that way.

This being so, why do those teachers desire the forms "sāhi, sābhi" in the instrumental plural position? And why do they desire "sāsu" in the locative plural position? This desire is also without logical reason because [the word for dog] is a masculine stem ending in -ā (ākāranta pulliṅga). Furthermore, why do they desire the form "sassa" in the dative and genitive singular positions by shortening the preceding syllable? This desire is also without logical reason because the word "sā" meaning "dog" has a natural stem ending in -ā. For the word "sā" which has a natural stem ending in -ā, such a form does not exist, unlike the dative and genitive singular form "purisassa" of the word purisa which has a natural stem ending in -a.

For that very reason, when the Venerable Kaccāyana showed the form of the word "sā" meaning "dog" in the Niruttipiṭaka, he stated the form "sāssa" in the dative and genitive singular positions by lengthening the preceding syllable. Furthermore, why do those teachers desire the form "sāya" in the dative singular position? This desire is also without logical reason. The reason is that, except for the feminine stems ending in -ā called gha, the substitution of āya for the nā etc. suffixes after an -ā ending, and from an -a ending...
214:
The substitution of *āya* for the dative singular case ending following masculine and neuter stems, as well as the substitution of *āya* for the dative singular following an *ākāranta* (stems ending in -ā) masculine stem that does not have the designation '*gha*', is not found in any usage. Such a form is also not mentioned in the *Niruttipiṭaka*. Since it does not appear in the *Buddhavacana* (the Word of the Buddha), the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentaries), and so forth, it is more appropriate not to mention it. Relying on the *Niruttipiṭaka* and the *Buddhavacana*, we have stated the declension table (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word '*sā*' which denotes a dog; only that declension table should be accepted as the essence. In this context, one should also understand the similarity and difference of the words in the declension tables of the original forms of these three words—*sā*, *so*, and *saṃ*—which occur in various meanings and are included in the three genders.

In this matter, there might be a question: 'How can one know that the word *sā*, which you intend to occur in the meanings of the word *taṃ* (that), a dog, and one's own property, denotes this specific meaning just by saying *sā*?' (The answer is:) They cannot know it [just by the word alone]. However, worldly people and the wise know it by the power of usage (*payoga*). By the power of usage, in such passages as 'That Maddī climbed the elephant, like a cow elephant not too tightly bound,' the meaning of the word *sā* as the word *taṃ* (that) is understood. Thus, the word *sā* occurs in the meaning of the word *taṃ*. In such passages as 'Where a dog (*sā*) is not present' and 'Having heard even the birth of a dog (*sā*) of the Blessed One, beings become partakers of the taste of the Deathless,' the meaning of the word *sā* as denoting a dog is understood.

'O famous Maṇḍavya, you have prepared this food.
They chew it, eat it, and drink it.
Know me as one who lives depending on what others give,
Let the dog-cooker (*sapāko*) receive the alms-food obtained while standing nearby.'

In this context, however, by making the word *sā* short (*rassa*), the Pali stands as '*sapāko*'. Without taking the meaning [as just 'dog-cooker'], one takes the meaning as '*sānam* (of dogs), this meat is *saṃ* (dog-meat)'; thus, it means '*sapāko*' because he cooks *saṃ* (dog-meat).
215:
The word '*sapāko*' should be understood as '*sapākacaṇḍāla*' (a Caṇḍāla who cooks dog meat). In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it is also stated: "*Sapāko* means *sapākacaṇḍāla*." That statement also illustrates this very meaning mentioned above. Thus, the word '*sā*' occurs in the meaning of a dog. However, in the statement "*Sā dārā jantūnaṃ piyā*" (One's own wives are dear to beings), the word '*sā*' is clearly shown to denote 'one's own' (*svaka*) by way of illustrating the meaning as "*Sakā dārā sattānaṃ piyā*" (One's own wives are dear to beings). Thus, the word '*sā*' also occurs in the meaning of 'self' or 'one's own'. In this way, the word '*sā*' is known as a word denoting such meanings by the power of usage (*payoga*). In this regard, it is said:

The word '*sā*' occurs in the meaning of the word '*taṃ*', 
in the meaning of a dog, and also in the meaning of 'one's own'. 
That word '*sā*' should indeed be known 
only by the power of usages.

In this context, the declension table (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word '*sā*' denoting a dog is taught as "*Sā, sā, sāno. Sānaṃ, sāne. Sānā*," etc., because the singular usage is seen in the Pali: "*Na yattha sā upaṭṭhito hoti*" (Where a dog is not present), and because the plural usage is seen in: "*Asantā kira maṃ jammā, tāta tātāti bhāsare. Rakkhasā puttarūpena, sāva vārenti sūkaraṃ*" (The ignoble who are not virtuous call me 'Father, Father' in the form of a son. Those who are like Rakkhasas prevent me as dogs prevent a pig), and because forms like "*sāno*" are seen in the *Niruttipiṭaka*.

Now, the declension table of the word '*puma*' (man) is stated:
*Pumā, pumā, pumāno. Pumānaṃ, pumāne. Pumānā, pumunā, pumena, pumānehi, pumānebhi. Pumassa, pumuno, pumānaṃ. Pumānā, pumunā, pumānehi, pumānebhi. Pumassa, pumuno, pumānaṃ. Pumāne, pumānesu. Bho puma, bhavanto pumā, pumāno.* The method for the plural "*Bho pumā*" should also be understood.
216:
In this regard—
"Only daughters are born to him, no men (*pumā*) are born in his family,
whoever, knowing the answer to a question asked, explains it otherwise."
This Pali passage establishes the plural status of the word '*puma*'. In the *Kaccāyana* grammar, the vocative singular '*he pumaṃ*' is found with a *niggahīta*. Since such vocative words ending in *niggahīta* are not found in many other Pali passages or in the Commentaries, I do not mention it here. If it is found appropriate upon investigation, it should be accepted. In the phrase "*yasassī naṃ paññavantaṃ visahyā*," it should be understood that the *niggahīta* occurs only by the power of augment (*āgama*) for the sake of protecting the meter (*chanda*), and not by its inherent nature. This is the declension table by way of the *ākāranta* (ending in -ā).

"Among sixteen thousand women,
no man (*pumo*) was present then.
With the passing of days and nights,
I alone was born."
And,
"Just as among the species of cranes, there is never a male (*pumo*),
when the clouds thunder, they then conceive."
Because these are seen in the Pali, the declension table should also be known by way of the *okāranta* (ending in -o).
*Pumo, pumā. Pumaṃ, pume. Pumena, pumehi, pumebhi. Pumassa, pumānaṃ. Pumā, pumas mā, pumamhā, pumehi, pumebhi. Pumassa, pumānaṃ. Pume, pumasmiṃ, pumamhi, pumesu. Bho puma, bhavanto pumā.* Or as "*Bho pumā*." Thus, the declension table of the word '*puma*' is of two kinds.

Now, the mixed method (*missakanaya*) is stated:
*Pumā, pumo. Pumā, pumāno. Pumānaṃ, pumaṃ. Pumāne, pume. Pumānā, pumunā, pumena.* The plural "*Bho pumā*" should also be known. Now, the declension table of the word '*raha*' is stated: Unwholesome states are called "*rahā*." *Rahā. Rahā, rahino. Rahānaṃ. Rahāne. Bhavanto rahā.* Now, the declension table of the word '*daḷhadhamma*' is stated: One who has a firm bow is called "*daḷhadhammā*." *Daḷhadhammā. Daḷhadhammā, daḷhadhammāno.* The plural "*Bho daḷhadhammā*" should also be known. In the same way, the declension table of the word '*paccakkhadhamma*' should be applied. In this regard also: "Bhikkhus, for example, there are four archers (*daḷhadhammā*) with firm bows..."
217:
Pumā, Pumo (a man). Pumā, Pumāno (men). Pumānaṃ, Pumaṃ (a man [acc.]). Pumāne, Pume (men [acc.]). Pumānā, Pumunā, Pumena (by/with a man). Pumānehi, Pumānebhi, Pumehi, Pumebhi (by/with men). Pumassa, Pumuno (of a man). Pumānaṃ (of men). Pumānā, Pumunā, Pumā, Pumasmā, Pumamha (from a man). Pumānehi, Pumānebhi, Pumehi, Pumebhi (from men). Pumassa, Pumuno (of a man). Pumānaṃ (of men). Pumāne, Pume, Pumasmiṃ, Pumamhi (in a man). Pumānesu, Pumesu (in men). O man! O men! There is also "O men!"

Now, the nominal declension (nāmika-padamālā) of the word Raha will be stated:

Raha refers to an unwholesome state (pāpadhamma). Rahā (an unwholesome state). Rahā, Rahino (unwholesome states). Rahānaṃ (an unwholesome state [acc.]). Rahāne (unwholesome states [acc.]). Rahinā (by/with an unwholesome state). Rahinehi, Rahinebhi (by/with unwholesome states). Rahassa (of an unwholesome state). Rahānaṃ (of unwholesome states). Rahā (from an unwholesome state). Rahānehi, Rahānebhi (from unwholesome states). Rahassa (of an unwholesome state). Rahānaṃ (of unwholesome states). Rahāne (in an unwholesome state). Rahānesu (in unwholesome states). O unwholesome state! O unwholesome states!

Now, the nominal declension of the word Daḷhadhamma will be stated:

Daḷhadhammā (one with a strong bow). Daḷhadhammā, Daḷhadhammāno (those with strong bows). Daḷhadhammānaṃ (one with a strong bow [acc.]). Daḷhadhammāne (those with strong bows [acc.]). Daḷhadhamminā (by/with one with a strong bow). Daḷhadhammehi, Daḷhadhammebi (by/with those with strong bows). Daḷhadhammassa (of one with a strong bow). Daḷhadhammānaṃ (of those with strong bows). Daḷhadhamminā (from one with a strong bow). Daḷhadhammehi, Daḷhadhammebi (from those with strong bows). Daḷhadhammassa (of one with a strong bow). Daḷhadhammānaṃ (of those with strong bows). Daḷhadhamme (in one with a strong bow). Daḷhadhammesu (in those with strong bows). O one with a strong bow! O those with strong bows! The plural form "O those with strong bows!" should also be known. In the same way, the declension of the word Paccakkhadhamma should be applied.

In this context, the Pali passage "Monks, there are four archers with strong bows..." serves as an example. However, because "Daḷhadhammā" appears in this Pali as a plural form, it is not clear whether the word Daḷhadhamma ends in -ā (ākāranta) or -o (okāranta), because the plural forms of words with those endings are identical in appearance. Nevertheless, we have arranged the declension table according to the -ā ending. In such compound cases, to say that the word Daḷhadhamma is either -ā ending or -o ending...
218:
...is appropriate because the form is indistinct. However, in other Pali passages, the word Daḷhadhamma ending in -o (okāranta) is seen very clearly in two ways: as an attributive word (guṇasadda) and as an appellative word (paṇṇattivācakasadda). Among those two, in the passage "I am skilled in archery, known as Daḷhadhamma (one with a strong bow)," the word Daḷhadhamma is an -o ending attributive word. In the passage "In the city of Bārāṇasī, a king named Daḷhadhamma ruled," it is an appellative word. Thus, the -o ending word Daḷhadhamma is seen in two ways. Its declension should be known according to the method of the word Purisa as: "Daḷhadhammo, Daḷhadhammā; Daḷhadhammaṃ, Daḷhadhamme." Also, the mixed declension (missaka-padamālā) based on both -ā and -o endings should be known. How?

Daḷhadhammā, Daḷhadhammo (one with a strong bow). Daḷhadhammāno, Daḷhadhammā (those with strong bows). Daḷhadhammānaṃ, Daḷhadhammaṃ (one with a strong bow [acc.]). Daḷhadhammāne, Daḷhadhamme (those with strong bows [acc.]). Daḷhadhamminā, Daḷhadhammena (by/with one with a strong bow). Daḷhadhammehi, Daḷhadhammebi (by/with those with strong bows). Daḷhadhammassa (of one with a strong bow). Daḷhadhammānaṃ (of those with strong bows). Daḷhadhamminā, Daḷhadhammā, Daḷhadhammasmā, Daḷhadhammamhā (from one with a strong bow). Daḷhadhammehi, Daḷhadhammebi (from those with strong bows). Daḷhadhammassa (of one with a strong bow). Daḷhadhammānaṃ (of those with strong bows). Daḷhadhamme, Daḷhadhammasmiṃ, Daḷhadhammamhi (in one with a strong bow). Daḷhadhammesu (in those with strong bows). O one with a strong bow! O those with strong bows! In the same way, the mixed declension of Paccakkhadhammā, Paccakkhadhammo should also be applied.

Now, the nominal declension of the word Vivaṭacchada will be stated:

Vivaṭacchadā (the Buddha who has opened the roof of defilements). Vivaṭacchadā, Vivaṭacchadāno (the Buddhas). Vivaṭacchadānaṃ (the Buddha [acc.]). Vivaṭacchadāne (the Buddhas [acc.]). Vivaṭacchadena (by/with the Buddha). Vivaṭacchadehi, Vivaṭacchadebi (by/with the Buddhas). Vivaṭacchadassa (of the Buddha). Vivaṭacchadānaṃ (of the Buddhas). Vivaṭacchadā (from the Buddha). Vivaṭacchadehi, Vivaṭacchadebi (from the Buddhas). Vivaṭacchadassa (of the Buddha). Vivaṭacchadānaṃ (of the Buddhas). Vivaṭacchade (in the Buddha). Vivaṭacchadesu (in the Buddhas). O Buddha! O Buddhas!

This nominal declension [is based on the passage]: "If he goes forth from home to homelessness, he will be an Arahant, a Sammasambuddha in the world, one who has opened the roof [of defilements] (vivaṭacchadā)..."
219:
The word "Vivaṭacchadā" is taught as an ākāranta (ending in -ā) as seen in the Pali texts. Based on the occurrence in the Pali text "Loke vivaṭacchado", it is also taught as an okāranta (ending in -o) as "vivaṭacchado, vivaṭacchadā, vivaṭacchadaṃ, vivaṭacchade". Furthermore, by the mixed method (missaka) of both ākāranta and okāranta, it is taught as "vivaṭacchadā, vivaṭacchado, vivaṭacchadāno, vivaṭacchadā; vivaṭacchadānaṃ, vivaṭacchadaṃ, vivaṭacchāne, vivaṭacchade".

Now, I shall present the nāmikapadamālā (declension table) of the word "Vattaha", which refers to Sakka. Vattaha means Sakka.
Vattahā (the Sakka), vattahāno (the Sakkas). Vattahānaṃ (to/for the Sakka), vattahāne (to/for the Sakkas). Vattahānā (by the Sakka), vattahānehi, vattahānebhi (by the Sakkas). Vattahino (of the Sakka), vattahānaṃ (of the Sakkas). Vattahānā (from the Sakka), vattahānehi, vattahānebhi (from the Sakkas). Vattahino (of the Sakka), vattahānaṃ (of the Sakkas). Vattahāne (in the Sakka), vattahānesu (in the Sakkas). O Vattaha, O Vattahāno. Or, it also exists as "O Vattahā, O Vattahāno".

Now, I shall present the nāmikapadamālā of the word "Vuttasira":
Vuttasirā (the one with a shaven head), vuttasirā, vuttasirāno (the ones with shaven heads). Vuttasirānaṃ (the one with a shaven head - acc.), vuttasirāne (the ones with shaven heads - acc.). Vuttasirānā (by the one with a shaven head), vuttasirānehi, vuttasirānebhi (by the ones with shaven heads). Vuttasirassa (of the one with a shaven head), vuttasirānaṃ (of the ones with shaven heads), vuttasirā (from the one with a shaven head), vuttasirehi, vuttasirebi (from the ones with shaven heads). Vuttasirassa (of the one with a shaven head), vuttasirānaṃ (of the ones with shaven heads). Vuttasire (in the one with a shaven head), vuttasiresu (in the ones with shaven heads). O Vuttasira, O Vuttasirāno. The okāranta reading "Vuttasiro" is also seen.

Now, I shall present the nāmikapadamālā of the word "Yuva":
Yuvā (the youth), yuvā, yuvāno, yuvānā (the youths). Yuvānaṃ, yuvaṃ (the youth - acc.), yuvāne, yuve (the youths - acc.). Yuvānā (by the youth), yuvena, yuvānena (by the youth), yuvānehi, yuvānebhi, yuvehi, yuvebhi (by the youths). Yuvānassa, yuvassa (of the youth), yuvānānaṃ, yuvānaṃ (of the youths).
220:
Yuvānā, yuvānasmā, yuvānamhā (from the youth), yuvānehi, yuvānebhi, yuvehi, yuvebhi (from the youths). Yuvānassa, yuvassa (of the youth), yuvānānaṃ, yuvānaṃ (of the youths). Yuvāne, yuvānasmiṃ, yuvānamhi, yuve, yuvasmiṃ, yuvamhi (in the youth), yuvānesu, yuvāsu, yuvesu (in the youths). O Yuva, O Yuvāna, O Yuvānā.

In this context, three methods are observed: partially the ākāranta method, entirely the okāranta method, and partially the okāranta method.

Teachers also form the nāmikapadamālā for the word "Maghava" like the word "Yuva", such as "maghavā, maghavā, maghavāno, maghavānā", and so on. However, in the Niruttipiṭaka, it is presented according to the method of the word "Guṇavā" (guṇavantu): "Maghavā tiṭṭhati, maghavanto tiṭṭhanti. Maghavantaṃ passati, maghavante passati. Maghavatā kataṃ, maghavantehi kataṃ, maghavantebhi kataṃ. Maghavato diyate, maghavantānaṃ diyate. Maghavatā nissaṭaṃ, maghavantehi nissaṭaṃ, maghavantebhi nissaṭaṃ. Maghavato pariggaho, maghavantānaṃ pariggaho. Maghavati patiṭṭhitaṃ, maghavantesu patiṭṭhitaṃ. O Maghavā, O Maghavanto." The Cūḷanirutti also presents it in the same way. That presentation is consistent and comparable with the Pali texts. For in the Pali texts, it is said: "Mahāli, Sakka the lord of devas, when he was a human in the past, was a youth named Magha; therefore, he is called Maghavā." By this statement, the formation of the word is shown through the power of the suffix -vantu, which expresses the sense of possession (atthiattha): "The name Magha belongs to him, therefore he is Maghavā." Therefore, the nāmikapadamālā of this word Maghavā should be formed like the word "Guṇavantu".

Now, I shall present the nāmikapadamālā of the word "Addha": For the word "Addha" which occurs in the sense of time and path, the nominative form "Addhā" is seen in places such as "Atīto addhā" (the past time), "Dīgho addhā suduggamo" (a long journey is very difficult to travel). That form in places such as "Addhā idaṃ mantapadaṃ sududdasaṃ" (Truly, this verse of the mantra is very difficult to see)...
221:
...is similar to the indeclinable (nipāta) "addhā" which occurs in the sense of "certainly". However, a declension table (padamālā) is not formed for indeclinables; it is formed only for nouns.

Addhā, addhā, addhāno. Addhānaṃ, addhāne. Addhunā, addhānehi, addhānebhi. Addhuno, addhānaṃ. Addhunā, addhānehi, addhānebhi. Addhuno, addhānaṃ. Addhani, addhāne, addhānesu. O Addha, O Addhā, O Addhāno.

Here, I shall show some examples: Three periods of time (tayo addhā). One who has transcended time or a journey (addhānaṃ vītivatto). By this long period of time (iminā dīghena addhunā). At the end of a long period of time (dīghassa addhuno accayena). Like the moon on the fifteenth day standing in the middle of the sky-path (pathaddhuno pannaraseva cando). In the past time, there was a monk who demonstrated patience (ahū atītamaddhāne, samaṇo khantidīpano). When time passes, it will be known (addhāne gacchante paññāyissati). These and others should be understood. In this matter, this method should also be known: the word "Addhānaṃ" is a form spoken as an accusative singular, and also as a dative or genitive plural. In phrases like "Addhānamaggapaṭippanno hoti", it is similar to the neuter word "Addhāna" which expresses a long path, merely by the similarity of sound.

Now, I shall state the nāmikapadamālā of the word "Muddha":

Muddhā, muddhā, muddhāno. Muddhaṃ, muddhe, muddhāne. Muddhānā, muddhehi, muddhebhi. Muddhassa, muddhānaṃ. Muddhānā, muddhehi, muddhebhi. Muddhassa, muddhānaṃ. Muddhani, muddhanesu. O Muddha, O Muddhā, O Muddhāno.

Thus, these are the words that are dissimilar to the word "Abhibhavitā". In this way, through various methods, words like "Vattā" which are similar to the word "Abhibhavitā", and ākāranta words like "Guṇavā" and "Rāja" which are dissimilar, have been shown along with their nāmikapadamālās.
222:
If a person of wise nature makes an effort in this treatise,
their supreme knowledge will flourish in the distinctions of usage (like a lion king).

## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the purpose of making the wise skillful in the linguistic usage of the Tipitaka together with its Commentaries and the ninefold Dispensation,
## the Sixth Chapter,
## known as the Classification of the Paradigms of Nouns (Nāmika-padamālā-vibhāga),
## which includes the determination of the original forms of masculine nouns ending in "ā", is finished.
## The masculine nouns ending in "ā" with the original forms of "u" and "a" endings are finished.

## 7. Paradigm of Masculine Nouns Ending in Niggahīta
Then, placing the views of former teachers at the forefront, I shall state the paradigm of nouns (nāmika-padamālā) of the original forms of masculine nouns ending in Niggahīta, such as "bhavanta," "karonta"—

Gacchaṃ, mahaṃ, caraṃ, tiṭṭhaṃ, dadaṃ, bhuñjaṃ, suṇaṃ, pacaṃ.
Jayaṃ, jaraṃ, cavaṃ, mīyaṃ, saraṃ, kubbaṃ, japaṃ, vajaṃ.

Gacchaṃ, gacchanto, gacchantā. Gacchaṃ, gacchante. Gaccatā, gacchantehi, gacchantebhi. Gaccato, gacchantassa, gacchantānaṃ, gaccataṃ. Gaccatā, gacchantehi, gacchantebhi. Gaccato, gacchantassa, gacchantānaṃ, gaccataṃ. Gacchati, gacchantesu. Bho gacchaṃ, bho gacchā, bhavanto gacchanto.

Other similar words such as "gaccha" should also be understood in this way; this is the view of the Great Elder Yamaka. In this regard, although these words "gacchantena, gacchantā, gacchantasmā, gacchantamhā, gacchantasmiṃ, gacchantamhī" do not appear (in the original text) in the third case singular and so on, they should be accepted because they are seen in various usages.

In that regard, the Great Elder Yamaka stated the plural nature of "gacchanto, mahanto, caranto" and so on only in the place of the vocative plural...
223:
The singular form is stated in the place of the nominative case. Some teachers, however, state both singular and plural forms in the place of the nominative case, and only the plural form in the place of the vocative case. For words such as "gacchaṃ", "mahaṃ", and "caraṃ", the singular form is stated in the place of the vocative.

We, however, in the Word of the Buddha and in many commentaries, do not see plural usages such as "gacchanto" and "mahanto", nor do we see vocative singular usages with the niggahīta such as "gacchaṃ" and "mahaṃ". Since we only see nominative singular usages such as "gacchanto bhāradvājo", "sa gacchaṃ na nivattati", and "mahanto lokasannivāso", we consider such forms [plural or vocative singular with niggahīta] as being unable to withstand scrutiny by wisdom.

In the Niruttipiṭaka text, only the plural form is stated for "mahanto", "bhavanto", "caranto", etc., in the nominative and vocative places; the singular form is not stated. This is because in that text, after stating the verse "mahaṃ bhavaṃ caraṃ tiṭṭhaṃ", it is said: "mahaṃ tiṭṭhati, mahanto tiṭṭhanti", "bho mahā, bhavanto mahanto", and "bhavaṃ tiṭṭhati, bhavanto tiṭṭhanti", and so on.

In this context, the words "bhavaṃ" and "bhavanto" do not express the verbal meaning of "being" or "becoming" (honti/hontā). In such usages, they occur in other meanings, as in "bhavaṃ kaccāno" and "mā bhavanto evaṃ avacuttha", and thus they have singular and plural forms. Therefore, just like the word "santo" in "santo sappurisā loke" and the word "arahanto" in "arahanto sammāsambuddhā", the plural form of the word "bhavanto" is able to withstand scrutiny by wisdom.

However, the plural form of "mahanto", "caranto", "tiṭṭhanto", etc., appears to us as unable to withstand scrutiny by wisdom. Indeed, in no Pāḷi text do we find plural-ended usages for hundreds of words like "gacchanto", "mahanto", and "caranto", excluding the words "santo", "arahanto", and "bhavanto". This is because—
224:
Just as words like "jānaṃ" are evident in the plural sense in some places, words like "gacchanto" are not thus evident in the plural sense. Just as words like "santo" are also evident in the plural sense in some places, words like "gacchanto" are not thus evident in the plural sense. The word "arahanto" is indeed certainly evident in the plural sense; words like "gacchanto" are not thus evident in the plural sense. Among hundreds of readings such as "viharanto", the occurrence of even a single word in the plural sense is not seen.

If the word "gacchanto" were taken according to the plural method, many faults would truly become evident. Just as when one house burns, the neighboring houses also burn, if the word "gacchanto" were to express the plural, then words like "viharanto" would also express the plural. And the undesirable grammatical method would have to be accepted in many ways.

Even so, because it is famous in the world that "the Niruttipiṭaka was composed by the Great Arahant Mahākaccāyana, who attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)", this matter should be investigated and reflected upon again and again. Although this is said here out of respect for the Elder, one should prioritize the method of the Pāḷi canon and discard the unseen plural method in favor of the seen singular method. In this way, the method for words ending in niggahīta becomes beautiful. This is our preference—

"bhavaṃ", "karaṃ", "arahaṃ", "saṃ", "mahaṃ"—these words should be noted as being dissimilar to one another. "gacchaṃ", "caraṃ", "dadaṃ", "tiṭṭhaṃ", "cintayaṃ", "bhāvayaṃ", "vadaṃ", "jānaṃ", "passaṃ", etc., are indeed similar. Among those, words like "jānaṃ" should be understood as changing in some places by the power of case, gender, and number.
225:
Among those words, first we shall state the declension (nāmika-padamālā) of the word "bhavanta". The word "bhavaṃ" also expresses the meanings of "increasing" and "being". This is the declension based on those meanings.

Bhavaṃ, bhavanto, bhavantā. Bhavantaṃ, bhavante. Bhavantena, bhavantehi, bhavantebhi. Bhavantassa, bhavantānaṃ. Bhavantā, bhavantasmā, bhavantamhā, bhavantehi, bhavantebhi. Bhavantassa, bhavantānaṃ. Bhavante, bhavantasmim, bhavantamhi, bhavantesu. He bhavanta, he bhavantā.

In that declension, the meanings of words like "bhavaṃ" and "bhavanto" should be understood as "increasing", "being", etc. Accordingly, there are such usages: "The one who is easy to know is one who prospers (bhavaṃ hoti). The one who loves the Dhamma is one who prospers (bhavaṃ hoti). The king rejoices (modati) with various successes. The crab-hole connected to the Ganges fills with Ganges water when the Ganges is full; when the water is low, the water descends from the hole to the Ganges." Therefore, this declension should be trusted as essential.

In this regard, excluding the word "bhavaṃ", the masculine method (purisa-naya) like "bhavanto" and "bhavantā" is obtained for the word "bhavanta", just as in the words "gacchamāna" and "caramāna". When expressed in the neuter gender, the neuter method (citta-naya) like "bhavantaṃ" and "bhavantāni" is also obtained. Thus should the declension of the word "bhavanta", which expresses the meanings of increasing and being, be understood.

The distinction is this: when the word "bhavanto" occurs in a meaning other than increasing or being, it is only plural. For example, "bhavanto āgacchanti" (The venerable ones are coming). When it occurs in the meanings of increasing or being, it is only singular. In this regard, there are such usages: "The one who prospers gradually attains wisdom. A monk should remain unconcerned with such matters; only a monk who prospers in this way would be a good monk." The word "bhavaṃ", however, is only singular in both meanings.
226:
Therefore, now, based on the observation of usages such as "Venerable Ānanda," "The venerable ones are coming," "May the venerable ones be quiet," "May the venerable ones not make a sound," etc., another nominal paradigm (nāmika-padamālā) will be stated, depending on a different meaning occurring in a specific usage:

Bhavaṃ, bhavanto, bhonto. Bhavantaṃ, bhavante. Bhavatā, bhotā, bhavantena, bhavantehi, bhavantebhi. Bhavato, bhoto, bhavantassa, bhavantānaṃ, bhavataṃ. Bhavatā, bhotā, bhavantehi, bhavantebhi. Bhavato, bhoto, bhavantassa, bhavantānaṃ, bhavataṃ. Bhavati, bhavante, bhavantasmim, bhavantamhi, bhavantesu. Bho, bhavanto, bhonto.

In this context, since the three words beginning with "bho" are vocative words (ālapana) occurring in a specific usage, they are not words having "bho" etc. as an adjunct (upapada), like the words "āvuso" and "bhante." In expressions such as "bho purisa" (O man), "bhavanto brāhmaṇā" (O brahmins), "bhonto samaṇā" (O ascetics), "bho rāja" (O king), only the words "purisa" etc. are words having "bho" etc. as an adjunct. Here, the words "bho, bhavanto, bhonto" are stated as having the same meaning as the word "bhavaṃ" in the sentence "bhavaṃ Ānando." However, they do not have the same meaning as the word "bhavaṃ" in the sentence "dhammakāmo bhavaṃ hoti" (one who loves the Dhamma is prosperous). In the first method, by virtue of the meaning of prosperity/increase, words like "bho" etc. become adjuncts to vocative words, as in "bho bhavanta, bhavanto bhavantā, bhonto bhavantā"; but this is not so in the second method. By virtue of repetition (āmeḍita), words such as "bho bho, bhavanto bhavanto, bhonto bhonto" occur, just as "bhante bhante" exists.

To show brief Pali examples by virtue of the root √bhū: "Why is one who relies on the forest prosperous?" "How, sir, shall I know that venerable Gotama?" "Thus, Ambaṭṭha..." and so on.
227:
After the young man assented to the words of the brahmin Pokkharasāti, he said: "Venerable ones, do not speak thus. Venerable ones, listen to this. O man, know thus; those of evil nature are unrestrained," and so forth. In this context, it should be understood that words such as "bhavaṃ" are nouns derived from the root √bhū.

Furthermore, among those words, "bho, bhavanto, bhonto" should be determined as being particles (nipāta) as well. Regarding expressions like "bho purisā," one should not dispute whether they are particles or not. In the Kaccāyana, it is stated: "bho ge tū." In other texts, it is said: "It is a particle in the sense of addressing (āmantana)," and so on. Likewise, in the Niruttimañjūsā, it is stated: "The word 'bho' is a particle in the sense of addressing. It is not only singular but also plural; thus, the plural usage 'bho purisā' is also accepted. However, the word 'bhavanto' is only plural, and thus 'purisā' is stated again."

In the Pāḷi and the Commentaries, the word "bho" as a particle is found in two forms, singular and plural, while the other words are found only in the plural. If these words are particles, there is no need for the process of morphological derivation (rūpa-nipphādana). Among them, because the word "bho" is a particle, it is also seen in usage when addressing inanimate objects in the feminine gender, such as: "O great stone slab, emerge! O great stone slab, float!"

Here are the verses illustrating the occurrence of the word "bho":
"O friend, go from here to a happy destination, to the companionship of human beings."
In such instances, the word "bho" should be noted as singular.
"O friends, look at this clansman."
In such instances, this word "bho" should be known as plural.
228:
