The word "bho" is found in three types: in addressing a person, in addressing a quality (dhamma), and in addressing an inanimate object.
Among these three, in addressing a quality, only the singular is obtained.
In the other cases (person and inanimate), it can be either singular or plural.
In addressing a quality, an attributive word (guṇīpada) is always required.
The phrase "O friend, how wonderful indeed!" is an example here.
In addressing a person, an attributive word is required.
The phrase "O man, know thus" is an example here.
Even if there is no attributive word, in addressing a person,
the meaning is supplied in instances such as "O friend, come," and so on.
Addressing pots and so forth is addressing inanimate objects.
In the world, people sometimes address inanimate objects as if they were living beings.
Addressing inanimate objects occurs occasionally when one wishes to convey a meaning.
The Pāḷi "O great stone slab, emerge!" is an example.
Here, some wise ones desire a change of gender.
According to their view, the gender should be changed to "bhotī."
Otherwise, since the word "bho" is a particle, it is like a sopada (particle).
Therefore, there is no contradiction in the three genders and two numbers.
Even so, since the word "bho" is mostly found in two genders,
the wise state that word in only two genders.
When it comes to the feminine gender, only "bho" should be used.
The wise say that such usage is good usage.
229:
If you should present [the word 'bho'] as an improper usage (duppayoga), as in the phrase 'O great stone slab, emerge!', even then, that usage is not improper. This is because in the Dhamma taught by the Victorious Buddha (Jina), who is skilled in conventional usage (vohāra), there is no such thing as improper usage. I have stated that the use of the word 'bhoti' in the feminine gender (itthilinga) is endearing to poets (kavi). Thus, the declension (nāmikapadamālā) of the word bhavanta is divided into two types according to the Pali method: by way of the meanings of prosperity (vaḍḍhana), becoming (bhavana), and other meanings.

The forms of the word karonta are:
Karaṃ, karonto, karontā. Karontaṃ, karonte. Karotā, karontena, karontehi, karontebi. Karoto, karontassa, karontānaṃ, karotaṃ. Karotā, karontā, karontasmā, karontamhā, karontehi, karontebi. Karoto, karontassa, karontānaṃ, karotaṃ. Karonte, karontasmiṃ, karontamhi, karontesu. Bho karonta, bhavanto karontā. These are the forms.

The example 'A person who does evil does not have evil done [to them]' (Karatā na kariyatī pāpaṃ) illustrates the existence of the word karoto here. When used in the feminine gender, it should be joined as 'karontī, karontiyo', etc. When used in the neuter gender, it should be joined as 'karontaṃ, karontāni', etc.

The forms of the word arahanta are:
Arahaṃ, arahanto. Arahantaṃ, arahante. Arahatā, arahantena, arahantehi, arahantebi. Arahato, arahantassa, arahantānaṃ, arahatṃ. Arahatā, arahantā, arahantasmā, arahantamhā, arahantehi, arahantebi. Arahato, arahantassa, arahantānaṃ, arahatṃ. Arahante,
230:
Arahantasmiṃ, arahantamhi, arahantesu. Bho arahanta, bhavanto arahanto. These are the forms.

This is the declension (nāmikapadamālā) of the word arahanta expressing an attribute (guṇa). There are also forms such as 'arahā, arahanto, arahantā'. These forms are found in the Samantapāsādikā commentary, in the explanation of the definition of a human (manussaviggaha). In the Uttirimanussadhamma Pāḷi, the phrase 'We are non-arahants' (mayañcamhā anarahanto) is found. [The forms] arahantaṃ, arahante exist, and the rest should be understood by extension. This is the declension of the word arahanta expressing a designation (paññatti).

Indeed, in phrases such as 'The Arahaṃ is the Fully Enlightened One' (Arahaṃ sammāsambuddho), 'The Arahaṃ is the Well-gone One in the world' (Arahaṃ sugato loke), and 'The Arahants are the Fully Enlightened Ones' (Arahanto sammāsambuddhā), the word arahaṃ and others express attributes. In places such as 'He became an arahant (arahā)', 'I am indeed an arahant (arahā) in the world', and 'There were one arahant, and sixty-one arahants in the world';

'Whether in a village or in a forest, in a valley or on a hill, wherever arahants dwell, that ground is delightful.'

In phrases such as 'We are non-arahants', etc., it should be understood that the word arahā and others express designations. Here, the distinct methods of expression by way of the feminine and neuter genders are not well-known. If it is asked, 'How should a woman who has reached the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya) be described? How should a mind that has reached the destruction of taints be described?'—as for a woman, according to the statement 'If a woman were an Arahaṃ Sammāsambuddha', she is called 'Arahaṃ' by way of attribute. By way of designation, however, it should be said, 'The woman became an arahant (arahā)'. As for the mind, it should be called 'Arahaṃ cittaṃ' only by way of attribute.
231:
The declensions of the word santa are:
Saṃ, santo, santo, santā (Nominative). Saṃ, santaṃ, sante (Accusative). Satā, santena, santehi, santebi, sabbhi (Instrumental). Satoto, santassa, santānaṃ, sataṃ, satānaṃ (Dative). Satā, santā, santasmā, santamhā, santehi, santebi, sabbhi (Ablative). Satoto, santassa, santānaṃ, sataṃ, satānaṃ (Genitive). Sati, sante, santasmiṃ, santamhi, santesu (Locative). Bho santa, bhavanto santo. These are the forms.

In this context, however, the word 'satānaṃ' is used as seen in the Jayaddisa Jātaka Pāḷi: 'Dear son, this is the Dhamma of the virtuous (satānesa dhammo).' There, 'satānesa' should be analyzed as 'satānaṃ esā'; the formation of the word should be understood through the methods of shortening (rassatva) and the elision of the vowel with the niggahīta. Accordingly, in the commentary to that Jātaka, the meaning is stated as: 'Dear son, this is certainly the nature (dhammo/sabhāvo) of the virtuous and wise (satānaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ).' This is the declension of the word santa expressing those who are called 'good people' (sappurisa), 'noble ones' (ariya), and 'wise ones' (paṇḍita) in the world. In the sense of its negation, there are forms such as asaṃ, asanto, and in some places asantā. Accordingly, the Pāḷi is found: 'O father, the base and wicked (asantā) call me "father, father".' It should be declined as 'asaṃ, asantaṃ, asante, asatā', etc. (similar to the word santa). In this sense, these words 'santo' and 'asanto' occur only in the plural; they never occur in the singular anywhere. Why? Because they express a designation (paññatti). In other cases such as 'santo, danto' (calm, tamed), etc., only singular forms are used; as for the word santa expressing the sense of 'existent' (vijjamāna), why [is it used in the singular]? It should be understood that it is because it does not express a designation.

Now I shall speak of some usages (payoga) of those words expressing designations:
232:
The wicked meet with the wicked. O King, whatever person one associates with—whether virtuous or wicked—one becomes like them. A place where the virtuous are not present is not called an assembly. The wicked go to hell, while the virtuous have heaven as their destination. A wise person should not associate with the wicked; one should associate only with the virtuous. One should dwell only with the virtuous. The Dhamma of the virtuous... and so forth.

Although we have applied this word "Sabbhi" in the *Padamālā* (word-paradigm) according to the Instrumental and Ablative plural, it is formed from the stem *Santa* ending in '-a'. In other contexts, however, "Sabbhi" should be applied as an '-i' ending stem. Accordingly, "Sabbhi" is a name for the virtuous and for Nibbāna, or it is a name for that which is good. All these meanings, along with the Commentary, should be illustrated by this Pali: "O Fire-god (Jātaveda), this act of worshipping with a tail is indeed an act [done] with the wicked," and by this Pali: "The virtuous indeed proclaim [the Dhamma] with the virtuous."

In the Vocative and the Nominative,
In the Instrumental and the Ablative,
And also in Compounds,
A wise person should employ the word 'Sabbhi'.

The application in this context is as follows: "O virtuous ones, stay" (Vocative); "The virtuous stay" (Nominative); "One goes with the virtuous" (Instrumental); "Depart from the virtuous" (Ablative); "A man like the wicked" (Compound). Since this usage is in accordance with the Dispensation (Sāsana), in order to demonstrate that accordance and to enable listeners to gain bold wisdom in the diverse and profound methods of the Buddha's Pali which are beyond the reach of mere reasoning, I shall show the usages from the Sāsana. They are: "O Fire-god, this act of worshipping with a tail is indeed an act [done] with the wicked." "One should make intimacy with the virtuous." "In the Sālavana forest, Senaka committed a vile deed like the wicked." "This disease is like the wicked (severe)." "One who is displeased, stubborn..."
233:
In the term "Asabbhirūpo," even if the Vocative case is seen, the Nominative case (subject) is already implicitly seen in the Pali, even if it does not appear in its own form. Similarly, if the Instrumental case is seen, the Ablative case is also implicitly seen. If the word-form is seen in a compound (*samāsa*), the word-form in the resolution (*vigga-ha*) is also implicitly seen as far as possible, except for terms such as "Hetusatthāradassanaṃ" and so forth.

If that word (Sabbhi) is a word denoting Nibbāna, it is feminine, like the words *Santi*, *Visuddhi*, and *Nibbuti*. According to the view of the Great Elder Yamaka, it should be applied according to the *Ratti* method. This is because that method is common to all feminine nouns ending in '-i'. If it is a word denoting a good meaning, it should be applied according to the *Aggi*, *Ratti*, and *Aṭṭhi* methods, as it is an adjective (*vāccalinga*). In the passage "Sabbhidhammabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ," the meaning is "Nibbāna which is the good Dhamma."

After knowing the occurrence of the word *Sabbhi* in the five places such as the Vocative according to the Pali method, its occurrence should also be known according to the method of the Commentaries. How? In the *Sagāthāvagga Aṭṭhakathā*, in the passage "Santo 'sabbhīhi saddhiṃ sataṃ dhammo na jaraṃ upetī'ti pavedayanti," the teachers of the Commentary showed a specific word arrangement by using the *hi*-suffix (plural) as "Sabbhīhi." Therefore, the word *Sabbhi* should be applied in all cases and numbers. In this regard, we shall say this:

The teachers have stated the meaning in the Pali as "Sabbhīhi saddhiṃ."
Therefore, the wise should apply the word *Sabbhi* in all places.
"Asabbhirūpo" is also heard in the context of compounds.
Therefore, the learned should apply the word *Sabbhi* in all cases.
234:
In the passage "Ovadeyyānusāseyya, asabbhā ca nivāraye," it should be understood that the word "Asabbhā" is accomplished by the power of the *ṇya*-suffix among the various *taddhita* (derivative) suffixes. How? Generally, the Dhamma that arises among the wicked (*asabbhi*) is called *asabbha*. What is that Dhamma? It is unwholesome Dhamma (*akusala-dhamma*). Therefore, the meaning is: "One should restrain [others] from unwholesome deeds (*asabbhā*) and establish them in wholesome deeds."

In the passage "Amhe asabbhāhi vācāhi vikkosamānā tibbāhi sattīhi hanissanti," the words of the wicked are called "Asabbhā," or they are called "Asabbhā" because they are not the words of the virtuous. Thus, the word formation should be understood through the etymological definition (*nibbacana*) and the power of the *ṇya*-suffix.

In this work, we have shown the *Padamālā* (paradigm) of the word *Santa* as "Saṃ, santo; saṃ, santaṃ, sante," and so forth. In that paradigm, when the word "Asaṃ" is seen in the Pali "Sameti asatā asaṃ," the word "Saṃ" is implicitly seen even if it does not directly appear in the Pali, because they naturally exist as a pair. Thus, the taking of the unseen through the seen should be understood. Alternatively, in the term "Asaṃ," since it can be understood through the analysis of the compound (*samāsa-vigga-ha*) as "na saṃ asaṃ," the word "Saṃ" is already seen. This method applies elsewhere as well.

In that context, *Santi* refers to a virtuous person, and *Asanti* refers to a wicked person. When expressed in the feminine gender, the forms become "Asatī" and "Asā." The noun paradigm should be applied according to the feminine method to be mentioned later: "Asatī, asatī, asatiyo, asā; asatiṃ, asatī, asatiyo; asāya, asatiyā, asatīhi, asatībhi; asatiyā, asatīnaṃ."

In this context, examples such as "Asā lokitthiyo nāma, velā tāsaṃ na vijjati; mā ca vasaṃ asatīnaṃ nigacche" should be shown. The words "Asā" and "Asatī" have the same meaning; their meaning is "those of a wicked nature (wicked women)." In the Jātaka Commentary, however, it is said: "Asā" refers to the low "Asatī" (wicked women); or else, "Sāta" is said to be happiness, and since that happiness does not exist in those women, and they give only unpleasantness (suffering) to those whose minds are attached to them, they are called "Asā."
235:
The word "asā" is defined as having the meaning of being unpleasant, suffering, or the basis of suffering. Therefore, it is called "asā" because there is no pleasure (assāda) in it. The declension (nāmikapadamālā) of the word "asā" should be applied according to the "citta" method as "rittassaṃ, rittassāni, rittassa," and also according to the "kaññā" method as "asā, asā, asāyo; asaṃ, asā, asāyo; asāyā."

In this context, the word "santo" which we have shown expresses the meaning of "existing" (saṃvijjamāna) in some places in both singular and plural forms. Based on that meaning, the declension table is: 
santo, santo, santā; santaṃ, sante; satā, santena, santehi, santebhi; sato, santassa, sataṃ, santānaṃ; satā, santā, santasmā, santamhā, santehi, santebhi; sato, santassa, sataṃ, santānaṃ; sati, sante, santasmiṃ, santamhi, santesu; bho santa, bhavanto santo, bhavanto santā.

Here, examples (prayogā) include: "Monks, there is an eighth auspicious thoroughbred horse existing in this world," "Monks, there are these four types of persons existing in this world," "They accuse with what is non-existent, empty, false, and untrue," "When there is becoming, birth comes to be," and so on. However, in "When there are formations, consciousness comes to be," etc., the word "sati" should be understood as standing by way of vacanavipallāsa (permutation of number).

Among the words "santo" existing in two ways as singular and plural, excluding the plural "santo," the remaining words also express the meaning of "samāna" (equal/being). Therefore, the meaning should be stated as "santo" is "samāno," "santā" is "samānā," and so on.
236:
The word "santo" is defined as "samāno" (being). This meaning of "samāno" should be understood as in the examples: "Being one who is capable and habitually contemplating many benefits, for what reason do you not cause me suffering?" etc. The usages are:

"If a person, though being capable (pahu santo), does not support his parents who are aged and past their youth, that [neglect] is a cause of ruin."

"To me, who is existing even in this world and being a deity (devabhūtassa me sato), life has been obtained once again; know thus, sirs," and so on.

Furthermore, since the word "santo" also expresses the meanings of "tired" (kilanta), "calmed" (upasanta), and "ceased" (niruddha), the declension of the word "santa" based on those meanings should be known according to the "purisa" method as "santo, santā; santaṃ, sante; santena," and so on. Here, examples are: "A tired person thirsts," "A league is long to one who is tired," "One who is calm, tamed, and certain, a practitioner of the holy life," "One who is ceased, disappeared, and completely gone," and so on.

When expressed in the neuter gender, the declension is "santaṃ, santāni" according to the "citta" method. That word should be known as a term indicating the meanings of existing, being, tired, calmed, and ceased. Alternatively, because neuter usages are found in "When there is clinging, becoming comes to be," etc., when the word "santa" expresses the meaning of existing (saṃvijjamāna), the forms "satā, sato, sataṃ, sati" should be specifically mentioned in the third, fifth, fourth, sixth, and seventh case positions. The remaining forms are to be known according to the "citta" method.

When expressed in the feminine gender, it is "santā, santā, santāyo; santaṃ, santā, santāyo; santāyā" according to the "kaññā" method, and also as "santī, santī..." and so on (should be known).
237:
...santiyo; santiṃ, santī, santiyo; santiyā. Thus, the declension should be applied according to the feminine method. Among these (santī words), the first santī word is a term indicating the meanings of 'existing, tired, calmed, ceased,' and the usages here are easy to understand. The second santī word, however, is a term indicating the meaning of 'being existing.' Therefore, in "santī āpatti āvikātabbā" (an existing offense should be revealed), the existing one is called "santī."

In this verse: "The man supported by which mother looks upon this world; even that life-giving mother who is such (a benefactor), the angry worldling kills," here, the one who is being/existing is called "santiṃ." Other declensions expressed in the feminine gender should also be known. Since the word "santī" expresses the meaning of existing, and feminine usages are seen in "jātiyā kho sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hoti" (when there is birth, aging and death come to be), etc., the forms "sati, satiyā, satiyaṃ, santiyā, santiyaṃ, santīsu" should be stated in the locative case position. The remaining forms are to be known according to the feminine method. This is the third method. Here also, the Pali "asantiyā āpattiyā tuṇhī bhavitabbaṃ" (if there is no offense, one should remain silent) is an illustration of the meaning of existence for "santiyā," etc.

Another method: Since the word "satī" is found in the Pali texts in the sense of "being" as "yā tvaṃ vasasi jiṇṇဿ, evaṃ dahariyā satī" and "ye taṃ jiṇṇassa pādaṃsu, evaṃ dahariyaṃ satiṃ," the forms "satī, satī, satiyā; satiṃ, satī, satiyā; satiyā," etc., should also be applied, or by way of eliding the 'n' in the cluster (saṃyoga).

Now, we shall explain the determination of the usage of the two words "santo" and "santā" so that listeners may not be confused in the usages. Thus, as "sappurisā" or "paṇḍitā" by way of the plural...
238:
One who wishes to express the meaning should say the plural 'santo' which is similar to the singular 'santo' in the phrase 'santo danto'. One who wishes to express the meaning in the sense of the singular 'saṃvijjamāno' (one who exists) should say the singular 'santo'. One who wishes to express the meaning in the sense of the plural 'saṃvijjamānā' (those who exist) should say the plural 'santo' or 'santā', similar to the plural used in 'santo sappurisā' or 'santo saṃvijjamānā'. One who wishes to express the meaning in the sense of the singular such as 'kilanto' (one who is weary), 'samāno' (one who is becoming), 'upasanto' (one who is peaceful), or 'niruddhā' (one who has ceased) should say the singular 'santo', similar to the plural used in 'santo sappurisā'. However, one who wishes to express those same meanings in the plural should say the plural 'santā', as in 'santā sūnehi pādehi, ko ne hatthe gahessatī'. This method should be well-borne in mind. This is a point of confusion for those of dull intellect. Here, this summary should also be understood: 'The word sati, which ends in the locative case (sattamī), is seen in the sense of the three genders, in the singular, and also in the plural. That word occurs in the plural by way of metathesis (vipallāsa).'

Now, the paradigm of nominal declension (nāmikapadamālā) for the word mahanta will be stated:

Mahaṃ, mahā, mahanto, mahantā. Mahantaṃ, mahante. Mahatā, mahantena, mahantehi, mahantebhi. Mahato, mahantassa, mahantānaṃ, mahataṃ. Mahatā, mahantā, mahantasmā, mahantamhā, mahantehi, mahantebhi. Mahato, mahantassa, mahantānaṃ, mahataṃ. Mahati, mahante, mahantasmiṃ, mahantamhi, mahantesu. Bho maha, bho mahā, bhavanto mahanto—this is our preference.

Here, the masculine method (purisanaya) such as 'mahanto, mahantā; mahantaṃ, mahante; mahantena' is also obtained; therefore, the vocative forms 'bho mahanta, bhavanto mahantā' should be applied. In the neuter gender...
239:
When the word 'mahanta' is expressed (in the neuter gender), the method of citta (cittanaya) is also obtained, such as 'mahantaṃ, mahantāni'. When expressed in the feminine gender, the feminine method (itthinaya) is also obtained, such as 'mahatī, mahatī, mahatiyo. mahatiṃ, mahatī, mahatiyo. mahatiyā, mahatīhi, mahatībhi'. Phrases such as 'mahatiyā ca yakkhasenāyā' are illustrative examples here. Alternatively, the method of kaññā (kaññānaya) is also obtained, such as 'mahantā, mahantā, mahantāyo. mahantaṃ'. Phrases such as 'mahantā nidhikumbhiyo' are illustrative examples here. In the Kaccāyana grammar, however, the form 'mahantī' is found. Since that form is not well-known in the Pali Canon, like 'guṇavantī, kulavantī', etc., it should be investigated.

Venerable Sir, since forms such as 'gacchantī, carantī' and the word 'iddhimantī' are seen in the Dispensation (Sāsana), should not 'mahantī, guṇavantī', etc., also exist? If this is asked, they should not. This is because they should not be taken by such a method, and because only the method of 'mahatī, guṇavatī', etc., is seen. This is so because in the Pali Canon and the Commentaries, usages are seen such as: 'seyyathāpi nāma mahatī naṅgalasīsā (as if it were a great plowshare), itthī siyā rūpavatī (a woman might be beautiful), sā ca sīlavatī siyā (and that woman might be virtuous). satimatī cakkhumatī. iddhimatī pattimatī'; and 'mahatiṃ senaṃ disvā (having seen the great army) mahosadhasenā mandā, ayaṃ ativiya mahatī senā dissati'. However, forms such as 'mahantī, rūpavantī' are not seen.

Some teachers say that the word 'mahā' cannot be obtained in the analysis (viggaha/vyāsa), but can only be obtained in a compound (samāsa), as in 'mahāpuriso'. That statement should not be accepted. This is because usages are seen such as: 'mahā te upါသက pariccāgo (Lay follower, your sacrifice is great). mahā vatāyaṃ bhante bhūmicālo (Venerable Sir, this earthquake is indeed great). ghoso ca vipulo mahā (The sound is also vast and great). bārāṇasirajjaṃ nāma mahā (The kingdom of Bārāṇasī is great). senā sā dissati mahā (That army appears great)'. Thus, even in the analysis (viggaha/vyāsa)...
240:
...it should be understood that it is obtained. Therefore, it should be applied completely as follows: in the masculine gender, 'mahaṃ, mahā, mahanto, mahantā; bho mahanta, bhavanto mahantā'; in the neuter gender, 'mahantaṃ, mahā, mahantāni; bho mahanta, bhavanto mahantāni'; and in the feminine gender, 'mahantā, mahā, mahantā, mahantāyo; bhoti mahante, bhotiyo mahantā, mahantāyo'. In compounds (samāsa), forms such as 'mahāsatto, mahāupါသကော, mahāupါသိကာ, mahabbalo, mahāvanaṃ, mahaggataṃ, mahapphalaṃ, mahabbhayaṃ' occur. In derivatives (taddhita), forms such as 'mahattano, mahattaṃ, mahantattaṃ, mahantatā' occur. For the word 'gacchanta', the paradigm of nominal declension (nāmikapadamālā) should be understood by stating the forms 'gacchanto, gacchantā' and expanding the remaining forms according to the method stated for the word 'mahanta'. Likewise, the masculine method (purisanaya) 'gacchanto, gacchantā', the neuter method (cittanaya) 'gacchantaṃ, gacchantāni', and the feminine method (itthinaya) 'gacchantī, gacchantī, gacchantiyo' should be taken. In this way, by means of the three genders, the paradigms of thousands of words such as 'caraṃ, caranto, carantaṃ, carantī; dadaṃ, dadanto, dadantaṃ, dadantī' should be expanded.

Certain teachers desire 'gacchanto' etc., to be the nominative (paccatta) and vocative plural, and 'gacchaṃ' etc., to be the vocative singular. We do not accept their view because such usage is not seen in the Dispensation and should not be taken by that method. Therefore, we do not mention those forms here. However, this distinction is seen. What is that distinction?

In the Dispensation of the Sage (Munisāsana), words such as 'gacchaṃ, vidhamaṃ' are in some places verbal forms (ākhyātika), and in some places nominal forms (nāmika).

'I shall go (gacchaṃ) to the presence of that [venerable] one; he will be my teacher.'
'O King, your son Vessantara is destroying (vidhamaṃ) your country.'
241:
"An unrighteous charioteer would bury you in the forest." Such usages (payoga) should be known here by the wise.

In the Dispensation of the Buddha (Jinasāsana), those who know the meanings speak of meanings according to various times and persons, such as "I shall go, I shall destroy," etc. However, in the case of pure nouns, they speak of meanings such as "one who goes, one who destroys," etc.

Now, although they have the same course, I shall speak of the distinction seen in words like jānaṃ (knowing) and passaṃ (seeing) according to the differences in gender (liṅga), case (vibhatti), and number (vacana). For instance, in contexts such as "That woman, though knowing, says 'I do not know'; though seeing, she says 'I do not see'," it should be understood that the words jānaṃ and passaṃ undergo a change of gender to jānantī and passantī. By this, the word gacchaṃ also acquires the meaning of a woman speaking as gacchantī according to usage, because it has the same course as those words. The reason is shown that the word gacchanto cannot acquire the meaning of a woman speaking as gacchantī because it does not have the same course as those words.

"O venerable ones, do you live knowing and seeing the world of absolute happiness?" In this context, it should be understood that there is a change of number to jānantā and passantā. By this, the word gacchaṃ also acquires the plural meaning gacchantā according to usage, because it has the same course as those words. The reason is shown that the word gacchante cannot acquire the plural meaning gacchantā because it does not have the same course as those words. This method applies to what follows as well.

"Parents support [their children], remembering what was done in the past." In this context, the word anussaraṃ undergoes a change of number to anussarantā. "The True Dhamma should be revered, remembering the teaching of the Buddhas." In this context, the word saraṃ undergoes a change of case to sarantena. "Touching the nature of beings with the mind..."
242:
"...like one who takes," in this context, the word phusaṃ also undergoes a change of case to phusantassa. Similarly, in the passage, "One who does not give to one who begs is unloved," the word yācaṃ also undergoes a change of case to yācantassa. Alternatively, yācaṃ refers to the wealth that should be begged; in this way, various changes should be understood.

Thus, these three modes—the dissimilar paradigms (visadisa-padamālā) of bhavaṃ, karaṃ, etc., the similar paradigms (sadisa-padamālā) of gacchaṃ, caraṃ, etc., and the change in certain places due to differences in gender, case, and number in jānaṃ, passaṃ, etc.—are taught along with the explanation of the meanings of verbal nouns in the excellent teaching of the Buddha, so that listeners may attain proficient wisdom regarding words and meanings. With reference to all this, these verses are spoken:

## “Bhavaṃ karaṃ arahaṃ saṃ, mahaṃ” iti padāni tu.
## Visadisāni sambhonti, aññamaññanti lakkhaye.
## “Gacchaṃ caraṃ dadaṃ tiဋ္ဌံ, cintayaṃ bhāvayaṃ vadaṃ.
## Jānaṃ passa” ntiādīni, samānāni bhavanti hi.
## Tatra “jāna” ntiādīnam, katthaci parivattaṃ.
## Liṅgavibhattivacana-ntarato pana dissatīti.

It should be noted that the words "bhavaṃ, karaṃ, arahaṃ, saṃ, mahaṃ" are dissimilar to one another. "Gacchaṃ, caraṃ, dadaṃ, tiဋ္ဌံ, cintayaṃ, bhāvayaṃ, vadaṃ, jānaṃ, passaṃ," etc., are similar. Although they are similar, in words like jānaṃ, etc., changes are seen in certain places due to differences in gender, case, and number.

Furthermore, this is the nature (pakati) of all masculine nouns ending in niggahīta; it is a change by virtue of one of the two genders, six cases, or thirteen numbers. Here, this system should also be understood:

## “Gacchaṃ cara” ntiādīni, vippakatavaco siyūṃ.
## “Gacchamāno caramāno”, iccādīni padāni ca.
## “Mahaṃ bhava” nti etāni, vippakatavacopi ca.
## Avippakatavaco ca, siyūṃ atthānurūpato.

Words like "gacchaṃ, caraṃ," etc., may be words of incomplete action (vippakata-vaco). Words such as "gacchamāno, caramāno," as well as the words "mahaṃ, bhavaṃ," may be words of incomplete action or words of complete action (avippakata-vaco), according to the meaning.
243:
"Arahaṃ, saṃ"—these syllables are entirely exempt from these modes. A wise person should keep these three modes in mind.

This is the analysis of the nominal paradigms (nāmika-padamālā) of the natural forms of masculine nouns ending in niggahīta, together with the decisions.

The masculine nouns ending in niggahīta with the characteristic of ending in ā (ākāranta) are finished.

Now, I shall state the analysis of the nominal paradigms of the natural form Dhanabhūti and others similar to it, giving priority to the views of former teachers.

Aggi, aggī, aggayo (Paṭhamā). Aggiṃ, aggī, aggayo (Dutiyā). Agginā, aggīhi, aggībhi (Tatiyā). Aggissa, aggino, aggīnaṃ (Catutthī). Agginā, aggīhi, aggībhi (Pañcamī). Aggissa, aggino, aggīnaṃ (Chaṭṭhī). Aggismiṃ, aggimhi, aggīsu (Sattamī). O aggi, o aggī, o aggayo (Ālapa). This is the view of the Great Elder Yamaka.

In this context, although the forms "aggismā, aggimhā" do not appear in the place of the Ablative (nissakka) case, they should be accepted because similar usages are found in various places. The sequence agginā, aggismā, aggimhā should also be understood.

Dhanabhūti, dhanabhūtī, dhanabhūtayo. Dhanabhūtiṃ, dhanabhūtī, dhanabhūtayo. Dhanabhūtinā, dhanabhūtīhi, dhanabhūtībhi. Dhanabhūtissa, dhanabhūtino, dhanabhūtīnaṃ. Dhanabhūtinā, dhanabhūtismā, dhanabhūtimhā, dhanabhūtīhi, dhanabhūtībhi. Dhanabhūtissa, dhanabhūtino, dhanabhūtīnaṃ. Dhanabhūtismiṃ, dhanabhūtimhi, dhanabhūtīsu. O Dhanabhūti, o Dhanabhūtī, o Dhanabhūtayo.

Siribhūti, Sotthibhūti, Suvatthibhūti, Aggini, Gini, Joti, Dadhi, Pāṇi, Isi, Sandhi, Muni, Maṇi.
244:
The words such as Byādhi, Gaṇṭhi, Ravi, Muṭṭhi, Kavi, Giri, Kapi, Nidhi, Kucchi, Vatthi, Vidhi, Sāli, Vīhi, Rāsi, Ahi, Masi, Sāti, Kesi, Kimi, Bondi, Bodhi, Dīpi, Pati, Hari, Ari, Dhani, Timi, Kali, Sārathyudadhi, Añjali, Adhipati, Narapati, Asi, Ñāti, Nirūpadhi, Samādhi, Jaladhi, and so forth, should be understood as being similar to the word Dhanabhūti.

Alternatively, among these words, regarding the word Adhipati, according to the occurrence in the Pali text 'Adhipatiyā sattā', the locative form 'Adhipatiyā' is also desired. Furthermore, in the Pali 'Asāre sāramatino', it is observed that the suffix -yo is substituted with -no from a compound word ending in -i. Therefore, in some compound words ending in -i such as Adhipati, the nominative and accusative plural forms like 'Adhipatino' and so forth are also desired. This is similar to the nominative, accusative, dative, and genitive forms like 'Daṇḍino' in words ending in -ī such as Daṇḍī.

However, in compound words such as Gahapati and Jānipati, such nominative and accusative plural forms are not desired. This is because their forms should be taken only as they appear in the Pali scriptures, according to the method of 'Gahapatayo, Jānipatayo', etc. Regarding the words Isi and Muni, in the vocative case, other forms like 'Ise' and 'Mune' should also be accepted. This is because of the usage found in 'Putto uppajjataṃ ise. Paṭiggaṇha mahāmune'.

In this context, regarding the words Aggini and Gini mentioned by us, some teachers say: 'The word Aggini is only available in the nominative singular, and not in the nominative plural or accusative cases, etc.' Others say: 'In the Pali scriptures, there is no such word as Aggini; only the word Gini exists.' Others say: 'There is no such word as Gini...'
245:
"...only the sound 'Aggini' exists here." All such claims are inappropriate. This is because both the sounds Aggini and Gini are found, and they are seen to be used in all cases and both numbers. For instance, in the Kokālika Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta:

'Those who speak do not speak pleasantly,
They do not run away, they do not reach a refuge.
They lie on a bed spread with glowing coals,
They enter the intensely blazing Aggini (fire).'

In this passage, the accusative form 'Agginiṃ' is found. Therefore, the commentator stated: 'Agginiṃ sampajjalitaṃ means the fire blazing intensely all around and in all directions.' In that same Kokālika Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta:

'Then they enter an iron cauldron,
Blazing with Aggini (fire).
They are cooked in those for a long time,
Floating in cauldrons that are like fire.'

In this passage, because it is a compound (samāsa), 'Agginisañjallitaṃ' carries the meaning 'blazed by fires' (Agginīhi sañjallitaṃ). Likewise, 'Agginisamāsu' carries the meaning 'similar to fires' (Agginīhi sadisāsu). Thus, through the formation of compounds, the instrumental case 'Agginīhi' is also found.

The sound 'Gini' is also found in the Pali scriptures. For instance, in the Cūḷabodhi-cariyā: 'From whichever wood that fire (Gini) is born, it burns that very wood.' Here, the sound Gini is found. Some say that in this instance, the letter 'a' is elided due to sandhi, and the 'ga' of the double consonant is elided. That claim is also inappropriate according to the commentary of that Pali text.
246:
"Yasmā means from which wood; Ginī means fire." This is because it is stated by explicitly mentioning the sound Gini. Likewise, in the commentary on the Dhaniya Sutta, 'The hut is thatched, the fire (Gini) is kindled,' it is stated: 'Āhito means brought or kindled; Ginī means fire.' Similarly, in the explanation of the Thera-gāthā, 'The great fire (Mahāgini) blazes, it is extinguished without fuel,' it is stated: 'Ginī means fire.' If the sound Gini did not exist separately, the commentators would have explained the meaning of 'Jāyate ginī' etc., by breaking the words as 'Jāyate aggini' etc. Since they did not say so, but instead said 'Ginī means fire,' it is known that 'the word Gini also exists separately.' The words of those who say 'the word Gini does not exist' should not be accepted, because the word Gini is found in the Dispensation (Sāsana). Even in the commentary on the Sutta Nipāta, while explaining the text 'The hut is thatched, the fire (Gini) is kindled,' it is mentioned as another name: 'In those places, Aggini is called Gini.' Therefore, we shall compose a verse here:

In the middle of the Videha country, there is a country famous by the name of Pabbata, which is sightly and delightful. In that place, there is a beautiful city named Dhammakoṇḍa. In the language of the people in that place, there is the collection of the word 'Gini'. The wise speak of it as 'Gini, Ginī, Ginayo', etc. A wise person should know the declension (padamālā) just like the word Aggi.

Thus, it should be understood that just like the sounds Alābu and Lābu, the sounds Aggini and Gini also exist in the Buddha's teaching. Just as the word Aggini is established as being applicable in all cases and both numbers, the word Gini is likewise established. Therefore, here:

The word 'Asabbhā' should be understood as being formed with the suffix -ṇya among the various Taddhita suffixes. How? Because it arises among the unvirtuous (Asabbhī), it is called 'Asabbhī'. The state that arises among those unvirtuous is an unwholesome state (akusala dhamma). It means 'one should restrain from those unwholesome states called Asabbhā, and establish oneself in wholesome states.' In the Vessantara Jātaka, it is stated: 'They will revile us with unvirtuous words (Asabbhāhi vācāhi) and kill us with sharp spears.' Here, it should be understood that the word is formed with the suffix -ṇya by defining it as 'words that are the property of the unvirtuous' or 'words that are not the property of the virtuous'.
247:
Aggini, agginī, agginayo. Agginiṃ, agginī, agginayo. Aggininā, agginīhi, agginībhi. Agginissa, agginīnaṃ. Aggininā, agginismā, agginimhā, agginīhi, agginībhi. Agginissa, agginīnaṃ. Agginismiṃ, agginimhi, agginīsu. O aggini, O agginī, O agginayo.

"Gini, ginī, ginayo. Giniṃ, ginī, ginayo, gininā"—all should be applied in the same way. Thus, the nominal declension (nāmikapadamālā) of the words aggini and gini has been presented according to the methods of Pali. Alternatively, just as in the Sanskrit language, words like sattva, padva, and svāminī are spoken with conjunct consonants (saṃyoga), but upon reaching the Magadhi language, they are seen in Pali pronounced without conjuncts as sattava, paduma, and suvāminī, as in "tvañca uttamassattavo" and so on. 

Similarly, the word spoken in Sanskrit as "agni" with a conjunct consonant, upon reaching the Magadhi language, is seen in Pali pronounced as "agginī" by turning the conjunct into the letter 'na', as in "agginiṃ sampajjalitaṃ pavisantī" and so on. Just as grammarians apply the Sanskrit word agni to all cases and all three numbers, the Magadhi word aggini must also be applied to all cases and both numbers. Therefore, we have presented that word aggini in this text. The word gini should also be understood to be applied in the same way because it has the same meaning as aggini and a slightly similar form.

In this context, there is a point to consider: If the word aggini is to be applied to all cases and numbers, why does the Kaccāyana grammar, with the rule "aggissinī", only show the substitution of ini at the end of the word aggi when the si case follows? It is true; just as the word dasa (ten), which is an ekasesa formed by setting aside nine instances, is substituted with nava in the yo case, and the yo case is substituted with uti, resulting in the form "navuti" (ninety), then navuti is again treated as a base (pakati) and the naṃ case is added to form the word "navutīnaṃ"...
248:
It is as if completed. In the feminine gender, however, by taking the singular cases starting with 'nā' and substituting them with 'yā', the form 'navutiyā' is completed. For this reason, usages such as 'channavutīnaṃ pāsaṇḍānaṃ dhammānaṃ pavaraṃ yadidaṃ sugatavinayaṃ, navutiyā haṃsasahassehi parivuto' and so forth are seen. Similarly, although the form 'aggini' is completed by substituting the end of the word 'aggi' with 'ini' in the 'si' case, one should conclude: 'Why would forms such as aggini, aggīnī, agginayo; agginniṃ, aggīnī, agginayo; aggininā, etc., not be completed by again taking aggini as the base and applying suffixes such as yo, aṃ, nā, etc., after it?'

## This is the analysis and decision on the declension paradigm of the basic forms of masculine nouns ending in -i.

The masculine nouns ending in -i, having the nature of ending in -i, are finished.

Now, I shall state the analysis of the declension paradigm of the basic form 'bhāvī' and other similar words, placing the views of former teachers at the forefront.

daṇḍī, daṇḍī, daṇḍino. daṇḍiṃ, daṇḍī, daṇḍino. daṇḍinā, daṇḍīhi, daṇḍībhi. daṇḍissa, daṇḍino, daṇḍīnaṃ. daṇḍinā, daṇḍīhi, daṇḍībhi. daṇḍissa, daṇḍino, daṇḍīnaṃ. daṇḍismiṃ, daṇḍimhi, daṇḍīsu. bho daṇḍi, bho daṇḍī, bhavanto daṇḍino. This is the view of Yamaka Mahāthera.

In this context, although the accusative singular 'daṇḍinaṃ', the ablative singulars 'daṇḍismā, daṇḍimhā', and the locative singular 'daṇḍinī' do not appear here, they should certainly be accepted because similar usages are seen in various places.
249:
"Speak, friend, the entire meaning and Dhamma as permitted. For there are young birds (pakkhī), wise and possessed of power."

Because the nominative plural "pakkhī" is seen in the Pali, it should be understood that the word "daṇḍī" is also used in the nominative and accusative plural.

The declension of the word bhāvī is: Bhāvī, bhāvī, bhāvino. Bhāviṃ, bhāvinaṃ, bhāvī, bhāvino. Bhāvinā, bhāvīhi, bhāvībhi. Bhāvissa, bhāvino, bhāvīnaṃ. Bhāvinā, bhāvismā, bhāvimhā, bhāvīhi, bhāvībhi. Bhāvissa, bhāvino, bhāvīnaṃ. (Bhāvini) bhāvismiṃ, bhāvimhi, bhāvīsu. O bhāvi, O bhāvī, O bhāvino.

In this way, the words vibhāvī, sambhāvī, paribhāvī, dhajī, gaṇī, sukhī, rogī, sasī, kuṭṭhī, makuṭီ, kusalī, balī, jaṭီ, yogī, karī, yānī, tomarī, musalī, phalī, dantī, mantī, sudhီ, medhီ, bhāgī, bhogī, nakhī, sikhī, dhammī, saṅghī, ñāṇī, atthī, hatthī, cakkhī, pakkhī, dāṭhī, raṭṭhī, chattī, mālī, cammī, cārī, cāgī, kāmī, sāmī, mallakārī, pāpakārī, sattughātī, dīghajီvī, dhammavādī, sīhanādī, bhūmisāyī, sīghayāyī, vajjadassī, pāṇī, and yasassī, and so on, should also be known. Some variations of these words will be briefly stated. Among the masculine nouns ending in -ī, for words like "vajjadassī, pāṇī", etc., in the positions of the accusative and locative cases, forms like "vajjadassinaṃ, pāṇine", etc., also occur. In this regard:

"One should see the person who points out faults (vajjadassinaṃ) like one who points out hidden treasure."

"Thus aging and death oppress living beings (pāṇine)."
250:
“The moon approaches the expanse of the sky.”

“The one in the middle, having placed the mind on the glorious noble elephant...”

“At that time, being destroyed along with the kingdom, it became the middle of the forest.”

“Among those with enmity, let us live very happily without enmity.”

Such expressions and others should be understood. This method can also be obtained in words such as “daṇḍī” and so on. This is because words like “daṇḍī” are similar in nature to words like “vajjadassī”. Therefore, in the place of the accusative case (upayoga), it should be declined as “daṇḍiṃ, daṇḍinaṃ, daṇḍino, daṇḍine”; and in the place of the locative case (bhumma), it should be declined as “daṇḍismiṃ, daṇḍimhi, daṇḍini, daṇḍine, daṇḍīsu, daṇḍinesu”. This method should be applied to other masculine nouns ending in -ī as appropriate, excluding words such as “gāmaṇī” and “senānī”.

This is the analysis and decision on the paradigm of noun declension (nāmikapadamālā) for the natural forms of masculine nouns ending in -ī.

## The section on masculine nouns ending in -ī is finished.

Now, since masculine nouns ending in -u formed from the root “bhū” are rarely used, we shall complete the paradigm of noun declension for the natural forms by way of other masculine nouns ending in -u. What are those words? They are “bhikkhu, hetu, setu, ketu, rāhu, bhāṇu, khāṇu, saṅku, ucchu, veḷu, maccu, jantu, sindhu, bandhu, ruru, neru, sattu, babbu, paṭu, bindu, garu” and so on.

bhikkhu, bhikkhū, bhikkhavo (Nominative). bhikkhuṃ, bhikkhū, bhikkhavo (Accusative). bhikkhunā, bhikkhūhi, bhikkhūbi (Instrumental). bhikkhussa, bhikkhuno, bhikkhūnaṃ (Dative). bhikkhunā, bhikkhusmā, bhikkhumhā, bhikkhūhi, bhikkhūbi (Ablative). bhikkhussa, bhikkhuno, bhikkhūnaṃ (Genitive). bhikkhusmiṃ, bhikkhumhi, bhikkhūsu (Locative). bho bhikkhu, bhavanto bhikkhū, bhikkhave, bhikkhavo (Vocative). Words such as “bhikkhu” and other similar words should be understood in this same manner.
251:
In this context, this distinction should also be known: hetu, hetū, hetuyo, hetavo (Nominative). hetuṃ, hetū, hetuyo, hetavo (Accusative). O hetu, O hetū, hetave, hetavo (Vocative). The remaining case inflections are similar to the word “bhikkhu”.

Alternatively, because usages such as “hetuyā” are found, the masculine form “hetuyā”, which is similar to the feminine form “dhenuyā”, is also desired (to be used) in the locative case. Indeed, some masculine forms are similar to certain feminine forms. How is that? “O worker, arise quickly. O fool, come, ask for forgiveness from the powerful King Kusa.” By showing this method, one should not entertain doubts about the gender transformation (gender irregularity) in cases like the three forms in “hetuyā”, the seven forms in “adhipatiyā”, and “uṭṭhehi katte”, etc., for the terms: brother, mother, lord, night, cause, cow, wisdom, and father.

jantu, jantū, jantuyo, jantuno, jantavo (Nominative). jantuṃ, jantū, jantuyo, jantuno, jantavo (Accusative). O jantu, O jantū, jantave, jantavo (Vocative). The remaining case inflections are similar to the word “bhikkhu”.

garu, garū, garavo, garuno (Nominative). garuṃ, garū, garavo, garuno (Accusative). O garu, O garū, garavo, garuno (Vocative). The remaining case inflections are similar to the word “bhikkhu”. In this regard, there is the Pali evidence: “The wise honor both the husband and the teacher in every way.” Therein, the vocative term “bhikkhave” is found only in prose (cuṇṇiya), not in verses (gāthā). The nominative term (paccatta) “bhikkhavo” is found only in verses, not in prose. Furthermore, the vocative term “bhikkhave” is found only in the context of sandhi in the Pali where disciples address monks, not in non-sandhi contexts. However, in the Pali where the Buddha addresses monks, it is found in both sandhi and non-sandhi contexts. The vocative term “bhikkhavo” is found in the Pali where the Buddha addresses monks in verses and...
252:
...is found; in prose, however, it is found only in the context of sandhi. This should be understood as the distinction between the two. This is indeed true: in passages such as “Monks, in this way you should recite this training rule,” the word “bhikkhave” is seen only in prose. In passages such as “These three hundred monks, requesting with joined palms...” the nominative word “bhikkhavo” is seen only in verses. In passages such as “The Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: ‘Friends, monks,’” the word “bhikkhave” is seen only in the context of sandhi in the Pali where disciples address monks. In passages such as “He addressed the monks for the sake of those desiring to listen: ‘Monks,’” and “Here, monks, a monk...” the word “bhikkhave” is seen in both sandhi and non-sandhi contexts in the Pali where the Buddha addresses monks. In passages such as “In the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty house, O monks...” and “Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Monks,’” the vocative word “bhikkhavo” is seen in the Buddha’s address to monks in verses, and in prose it is seen only in the context of sandhi. Thus:

The word “bhikkhave” is seen only in prose (cuṇṇiya) in two ways,
As it occurs in both sandhi and non-sandhi contexts.
The word “bhikkhavo” is seen in both verse (gāthā) and prose;
In prose, however, it should be pointed out that it occurs only in the context of sandhi.

This is the analysis of the paradigm of noun declension for the natural forms of masculine nouns ending in -u, together with the decision.

## The section on masculine nouns ending in -u is finished.

Now, we shall state the paradigm of noun declension for the natural form “sayambhū” and similar words:
253:
The declension of the word *Sayambhū* is as follows:
Sayambhū, Sayambhū, Sayambhūvo (Paṭhamā).
Sayambhuṃ, Sayambhū, Sayambhūvo (Dutiyā).
Sayambhunā, Sayambhūhi, Sayambhūbhi (Tatiyā).
Sayambhussa, Sayambhuno, Sayambhūnaṃ (Catutthī).
Sayambhunā, Sayambhusmā, Sayambhumhā, Sayambhūhi, Sayambhūbhi (Pañcamī).
Sayambhussa, Sayambhuno, Sayambhūnaṃ (Chaṭṭhī).
Sayambhusmiṃ, Sayambhumhi, Sayambhūsu (Sattamī).
Bho Sayambhū, Bho Sayambhū, Bhavanto Sayambhū, Sayambhūvo (Ālapana).

Words such as *Pabhū*, *Abhibhū*, and *Vibhū* are also declined in this same manner.

The declension of the word *Sabbaññū* is as follows:
Sabbaññū, Sabbaññū, Sabbaññuno (Paṭhamā).
Sabbaññuṃ, Sabbaññū, Sabbaññuno (Dutiyā).
Bho Sabbaññu, Bhavanto Sabbaññū, Sabbaññuno (Ālapana).
In the remaining cases, the forms are similar to the word *Bhikkhu*. Words such as *Vidū*, *Viññū*, *Kataññū*, *Maggaññū*, *Dhammaññū*, *Atthaññū*, *Kālaññū*, *Rattaññū*, *Mattaññū*, *Vadaññū*, and *Avadaññū* are also declined in this same manner.

Among those words, in the Pāḷi passage: "Those who have attained human status, who are *vadaññū* (understanding the words of those requesting), and are free from stinginess," the use of "Vadaññū" is seen as a Nominative plural. Therefore, the Nominative and Accusative plural forms of words like *Sayambhū* and *Sabbaññū* should also be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, in words like *Vidū* and *Viññū*, since the feminine usage is seen as "*Paracittavidunī*" (a woman who knows the minds of others), if the feminine gender is intended, the paradigm should be formed according to the method of the word *Itthī* as: "Vidunī, Vidunī, Viduniyo. Viduniṃ, Vidunī, Viduniyo. Viduniyā."

Likewise, because the feminine usage "Viññū" is found in the context of "a wise woman who can distinguish between well-spoken and ill-spoken words," and the feminine usage "Akataññū" is found in the context of "a woman who is wrathful, ungrateful, a slanderer, and a destroyer of friendship," the paradigms should be formed according to the method of the word *Jambū* as: "Viññū, Viññū, Viññuyo. Viññuṃ, Viññū, Viññuyo. Viññuyā," and "Kataññū, Kataññū, Kataññuyo. Kataññuṃ, Kataññū, Kataññuyo, Kataññuyā." The same applies to words like *Maggaññū* and *Dhammaññū*.
254:
However, because the expressions 'sayambhū-knowledge' and 'gotrabhū-consciousness' are found, if one intends the neuter gender, the method for the neuter word 'āyu' should also be taken: 'sayambhu, sayambhū, sayambhūni; sayambhuṃ, sayambhū, sayambhūnī'. This method should also be applied to the remaining words as appropriate.

This is the analysis of the declension paradigm of the basic forms of masculine nouns ending in -ū.

## The masculine nouns ending in -ū, having the nature of ending in -ū, are finished.

## Thus, in every way, the analysis of the declension paradigm

## of the basic forms of masculine nouns is completed.

Although this section is completed, if any point is found in the scriptures (Piṭaka) etc. where listeners might be confused, it should be stated again to dispel doubt through objection and clarification (codanā-sodhanā) out of compassion for the listeners. Therefore, I shall discuss a certain portion here.

If it is asked: In the Pāḷi, the forms found in 'saññate brahmacārayo, apace brahmacārayo' are like the form 'aggayo' from the word 'aggi' which ends in -i. Should it not rather be said as 'brahmacārino', like the form 'daṇḍino' from the word 'daṇḍī' which ends in -ī?

The answer is: It is true. In that context, because it is desired as an -i ending, like the word 'muni' in the sense of 'one who practices the noble practice', the form becomes 'brahmacārayo' like 'munayo' and 'aggayo'. In other places, however, if one takes the sense of 'one who habitually practices' as in 'dukkhaṭakammakārī' (one who habitually does evil deeds) and treats it as an -ī ending, the form becomes 'brahmacārino' like 'dukkhaṭakammakārino', or like 'daṇḍino' from the word 'daṇḍī' which ends in -ī in the sense of 'one who possesses a staff'. This is true because it is found as: 'These people are those who live according to the Dhamma, who live in harmony, who live the noble life (brahmacārino)', and so forth.
255:
"...who are speakers of truth, who are virtuous, and who are of good nature, they will acknowledge it." Thus, as an *i-ending* noun, the Nominative, Accusative, and Vocative plural form "*Brahmacārayo*" is appropriate. Again, as an *ī-ending* noun, the Nominative, Accusative, and Vocative plural form "*Brahmacārino*" is also appropriate. Therefore, the paradigm should be understood according to the *Aggi* method as "Brahmacāri, Brahmacārī, Brahmacārayo," and according to the *Daṇḍī* method as "Brahmacārī, Brahmacārī, Brahmacārino."

In the passage "As the ascetics (*yatino*) shine, adorned with the ornament of virtue," why does the Venerable Buddhaghosa show the form "*Yatino*" like the form "*Daṇḍino*" of the *ī-ending* word *Daṇḍī*, instead of saying "*Yatayo*" like the form "*Aggayo*" of the *i-ending* word *Yati*? Does this not appear to be a clerical error (*pamādalekhā*)? For if one examines the Pāḷi usage such as "O King, the cocks, the gems, the staffs, and the Sivis are angry with you," the form should only be "*Yatayo*" because it is an *i-ending* noun. 

This is not a clerical error. It is faultless if it is applied as an *ī-ending* noun by taking the sense of habit (*tassīla*), as in the word *Vādī* (meaning "one whose nature is to speak"). Therefore, it should be understood that the Venerable Buddhaghosa showed the Nominative plural form "*Yatino*" (which is similar to the Dative and Genitive singular) by keeping the *tassīla* sense in mind as "one whose nature is to strive (*yatanasīlo*) is a *yatī*," thus treating it as an *ī-ending* noun. The Accusative and Vocative plural forms are also the same.

However, in places where the *tassīla* sense is not taken, and the *i-ending* status is taken through the sense of the agent (*kattukāraka*) as "he strives, he exerts effort, therefore he is a *yati*," as in the passage "He who knows both worlds is called a *muni*," then the forms ending in *-yo* such as "*Yatayo*" occur, like the forms "*Munayo*", "*Maṇayo*", and "*Sivayo*."
256:
The nominative plural form and the accusative and vocative plural forms occur. Thus, it should be noted that in these three positions for masculine nouns ending in -ī, only forms ending in -yo occur.

If that is so, what about words such as sāramati, suddhadiṭṭhi, sammādiṭṭhi, micchādiṭṭhi, vajirabuddhi, etc., which end in -i? Although these words are indicated as ending in -i, because they are compound words (samāsa), they do not follow the aggi pattern but follow the daṇḍī pattern as appropriate; therefore, they only have forms ending in -no. For this reason, the nominative plural Pali ending in -no is found: "Those who perceive the essence in the essenceless." The accusative and vocative plural forms should be understood in the same way. O... in the Kaccāyana grammar, in the phrase "atthe visāradamatayo", since the nominative plural text ending in -yo is shown for a masculine compound word ending in -i, should not words like sāramati also have forms ending in -yo like the form "visāradamatayo"? They should not. This is because in the Buddha's word (the Pali canon), no form similar to "visāradamatayo" is found for masculine compound words ending in -i.

O... in the Buddha's word—
"Householders have these five benefits.
They are masters of their wives, and they speak endearing words to one another"
—forms ending in -yo similar to "visāradamatayo" are found for masculine compound words ending in -i. This being so, why is it said, "Because no form similar to visāradamatayo ending in -yo is found for masculine compound words ending in -i in the Buddha's word"? Here, it is said—on account of the difference. In words such as gahapati, the word pati is masculine by its very nature. It did not first have a feminine base before becoming masculine after compounding. Therefore, in such places, there are forms ending in -yo such as "gahapatayo, jānipatayo", and [forms like] "senāpatayo, senāpatino"...
257:
Forms ending in the letter 'no' occur in the Nominative (Paccatta), Accusative (Upayoga), and Vocative (Ālapana) plural. This is indeed true; the Commentary text is seen as "tattakā senāpatino." Because terms such as Sāramati, Suddhaditthi, Sammaditthi, Micchaditthi, and Vajirabuddhi—specifically the words 'mati' and 'ditthi'—were originally feminine in gender before forming a compound, but later attained masculine gender by virtue of being a Bahubbīhi compound, therefore, in such instances, forms like "Sāramatino, Suddhaditthino, Sammaditthino, Micchaditthino, Vajirabuddhino," etc., are only the Nominative, Accusative, and Vocative plural forms ending in the letter 'no'. It should be understood as a certainty here that they are identical to the Dative (Sampadāna) and Genitive (Sāmī) singular forms.

How is it in the case of these words: Seṭṭhi, Sārathi, Cakkavatti, and Sāmi? Here, this distinction should be understood—in some texts, the long vowel (dīgha) of the final letter is seen as "Seṭṭhī, Sārathī, Cakkavattī, Sāmī," while in others, the short vowel (rassa) of the final letter is seen as "Seṭṭhi, Sārathi, Cakkavatti, Sāmi." Although the short form of these words is seen, it is known that they are recited by making them short because usages such as "Seṭṭhino, Sārathino," etc., are found in the sense of the Nominative case and so on. Therefore, the following etymological meaning (vigga-attha) should be taken: One who possesses excellent wealth or a high status (ṭhānantara) is called a Seṭṭhī. One who has the nature of driving horses to be trained and so on is called a Sārathī. One who has the nature of turning the wheel is called a Cakkavattī. One who possesses his own property is called a Sāmī. Indeed, words expressing the sense of possession (atthi) or habitual nature (tassīla) follow the same grammatical path by virtue of the form ending in the letter 'no', such as "daṇḍino" and "bhūmisāyino."

There is also another etymological meaning by virtue of the ending in the vowel 'ī': One who trains horses to be trained and so on is called a Sārathī. This is indeed true; it is said, "Because he trains men to be trained, he is called Purisadammasārathī." Because he causes the wheel to turn, he is called a Cakkavattī. Thus, taking the ending in 'ī' by virtue of the agent (kattu-kāraka), and without regarding the ending in 'i' that is obtained in some places, in accordance with the Buddha's words (buddhavacanānurūpa)...
258:
Taking the forms ending in the letter 'no' such as "Sārathino, Cakkavattino," and excluding forms such as "daṇḍinī," they should be applied according to the method of 'daṇḍī'. Thus, it should be understood that "Seṭṭhino, Sārathino, Cakkavattino, Sāmino," etc., are only forms ending in the letter 'no'.

Here, I shall state some usages as mere examples: "Dear son, the three merchants (seṭṭhino) are of great help to us"; and, "When they had finished their meal, they said, 'We great merchants (mahāseṭṭhino) shall go'"; and, "The charioteers (sārathino) said"; and, "Two wheel-turning monarchs (cakkavattino)," and so on. In those instances, although the short vowel (rassa) text such as "Seṭṭhi, Sārathi," etc., is seen in some places, it should be understood that such a text is not naturally short, but is a text where the long vowel has been made short. The declension table (padamālā) of this word should also be understood by the method already mentioned.

How is it in the case of the word Mahesī? In this word "Mahesī," although it is indicated by virtue of ending in 'ī', it should be declined according to the method of 'aggī' because it follows the same path as the word 'isi', and because the word 'isi' has the same declension table as the word 'aggī'. O friend, is it not that the sense of habitual action (tassīla-attha) is seen here as "Because he has the nature of seeking the great aggregates of virtue and so on, he is called Mahesī"? Therefore, should the declension table not be made only according to the method of 'daṇḍī', like the word "bhūmisāyī"? It should not be made so, because the sense of habitual action is not possible. For this word, only the sense that is not habitual action (atassīla-attha) is appropriate, as in: "He sought (esi), searched for (gavesi), and having sought, he stood in the great aggregates of virtue and so on; therefore, he is called Mahesī." This is because it is merely a name occurring for the Noble Ones (ariyas) such as the Buddha who have completed what was to be done. This word is slightly similar to the word 'isi'; it is recited only with the long vowel at the end of a compound, but with the short vowel as "Mahā isi mahesī"...
259:
Distinguishing the words. Because it is appropriate to form the declension of that word by taking the short vowel (rassa), the form ending in 'i' is found as "saṅgāyiṃsu mahesayo". In the Tipiṭaka Buddha-vacana along with the Commentaries, the plural form for the nominative, accusative, and vocative is nowhere found as "mahesino", which is like the singular form of the dative and genitive. Therefore, even though it is pronounced as ending in 'ī', the declension should be made as if it were pronounced as a short vowel: "mahesi, mahesī, mahesayo. mahesiṃ, mahesī, mahesayo. mahesinā".

Alternatively, when the word 'mahesī' refers to the chief queen of a king, it is feminine. According to that feminine gender, the declension should be made according to the feminine method to be mentioned later: "mahesī, mahesī, mahesiyo. mahesiṃ, mahesī, mahesiyo. mahesiyā".

How is it for the word 'hatthī'? In the word 'hatthī', if it is taken as ending in 'ī' as in "hattho assa atthīti" (the trunk belongs to that creature), the form becomes "hatthino". Thus, the usage "vane hatthino" is found. In that same sense, if it is taken by making it short, the form becomes "hatthayo". Thus:

"Swans, cranes, and peacocks,
elephants and pasada deer,
all are afraid of the lion;
there is no equality in body.

Even so among humans,
if one is wise though young,
he is the great one among those people;
a fool with a large body is not a great one."

In this Keḷisīla Jātaka, the direct word "hatthayo" is found. Thus, the two types of declension for that word 'hatthī' should be known, by the daṇḍī method and the aggi method. In this way, also in places not yet mentioned...
260:
The declension should be applied in accordance with the Pali method and the ancient Commentary method.

By this much, the nominal declension of masculine nouns derived from the root 'bhū' has been shown in various ways along with other genders, other words, and other meanings.

This Saddanīti treatise, which has good principles and is wonderful,
should be well-preserved by the wise.
He who always reflects well and teaches it,
that man attains the excellence of extensive knowledge.

## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the proficiency of the wise in the matters of speech of the Three Piṭakas along with the Commentaries of the Ninefold Dispensation,
## the analysis of the nominal declension of the natural forms of
## masculine nouns ending in niggahīta and others, along with the decisions,
## the Seventh Chapter is concluded.
## The masculine gender is completed in every way.
## 8. Itthilinganāmikapadamālā (Feminine Nominal Declension)

Now, although the nominal declension of the word 'bhāvikā', which is a natural form derived from the root 'bhū' in the feminine gender, should be spoken, I shall first speak the nominal declension of the well-known word 'kaññā':

Kaññā, kaññā, kaññāyo. Kaññaṃ, kaññā, kaññāyo. Kaññāya, kaññāhi, kaññābhi. Kaññāya, kaññānaṃ. Kaññāya, kaññāhi, kaññābhi. Kaññāya, kaññānaṃ. Kaññāya, kaññāyaṃ, kaññāsu. Bhoti kañေ, bhotiyo kaññā, kaññāyo. This is our preference.
261:
Here, the word 'kaññā' is spoken by way of singular and plural. In the Niruttipiṭaka treatise, there is no method spoken by way of plural. Because of that, in that treatise, only this much is spoken: "saddhā tiṭṭhati (faith stands), saddhāyo tiṭṭhanti (faiths stand). saddhaṃ passati (he sees faith), saddhāyo passati". The plural form "saddhā" does not appear. Although it does not appear, according to the experience of the Pali texts such as "bāhā paggayha pakkanduṃ (raising their arms, they wept), sivikaññā samāgatā (the Sivi princesses assembled). ahetu appaccayā purisassa saññā uppajjantipī nirujjhantipī (without cause or condition, the perceptions of a man both arise and cease)", the plural status of words such as bāhā, kaññā, saññā, and saddhā should be accepted.

In the Cūḷanirutti treatise, two singular forms are spoken as "bhoti kañေ, bhoti kaññā", and one plural form is spoken as "bhotiyo kaññāyo". In the Niruttipiṭaka treatise, however, one singular form is spoken as "bhoti saddhā", and one plural form is spoken as "bhotiyo saddhāyo". We, however, according to the experience of the Pali texts such as "ehi bāle khamāpehi (come, young girl, ask for forgiveness), kusarājaṃ mahabbalaṃ (from King Kusa of great strength). phussatī varavaṇṇābhe (Phussatī of excellent complexion). ehi godhe nivattassū (come, iguana, turn back)", desire only these forms of the vocative singular and plural: "bhoti kañေ" as the vocative singular, and "bhotiyo kaññā, kaññāyo" as the vocative plural. Here, the method "bhoti kañေ" is not obtainable in words such as 'ammā' and 'mātā'.

Bhāvikā, bhāvikā, bhāvikāyo.
Bhāvikāṃ, bhāvikā, bhāvikāyo.
Bhāvikāya, bhāvikāhi, bhāvikābhi.
Bhāvikāya, bhāvikānaṃ.
Bhāvikāya, bhāvikāhi, bhāvikābhi.
Bhāvikāya, bhāvikānaṃ.
Bhāvikāya, bhāvikāyaṃ, bhāvikāsu.
Bhoti bhāvikေ, bhotiyo bhāvikā, bhāvikāyo.

In this way, the nominal declension of the 'ā'-ending words such as 'bhāvanā, vibhāvanā' derived from the root 'bhū' mentioned below, and other 'ā'-ending words, should be applied. Here, other 'ā'-ending words mean words such as 'saddhā'.
262:
Saddhā (faith), Medhā (intellect), Paññā (wisdom), Vijjā (knowledge), Cintā (thought), Mantā (mantra), Taṇhā (craving), Abhijjhā (greed).

Icchā (desire), Pucchā (question), Jāyā (wife), Māyā (deceit), Mettā (loving-kindness), Mattā (measure), Sikkhā (training), Saṅkhā (calculation).

Jaṅghā (calf of the leg), Bāhā (arm), Gīvā (neck), Jivhā (tongue), Vācā (speech), Chāyā (shadow), Gaṅgā (river), Nāvā (boat).

Niddā (sleep), Kantā (beloved woman), Sālā (hall), Mālā (garland), Velā (time/shore), Vīṇā (lute), Bhikkhā (alms-food), Lākhā (lacquer).

Gāthā (verse), Senā (army), Lekhā (writing), Apekkhā (regard/expectation), Āsā (hope), Pūjā (veneration), Esā (search), Kaṅkhā (doubt).

Aññā (gnosis), Muddā (seal), Khiḍḍā (play), Bhassā (talk), Bhāsā (language), Kīḷā (sport), Sattā (creature), Cetā (maidservant).

Pipāsā (thirst), Vedanā (feeling), Saññā (perception), Cetanā (volition), Tasiṇā (craving), Pajā (progeny/beings).

Devatā (deity), Vaṭṭakā (quail), Godhā (iguana), Balākā (crane), Vasudhā (earth), Sabhā (assembly hall).

Ukkā (torch), Sephālikā (a type of flower), Sikkā (pingo-string), Salākā (voting ticket/peg), Vālikā (sand), Sikhā (crest/summit).

Kāraṇā (cause), Visikhā (street/lane), Sākhā (branch), Vacā (speech), Vañjhā (barren woman), Jaṭā (tangle), Ghaṭā (cluster/multitude).

Pīḷā (oppression), Soṇḍā (elephant's trunk), Vitaṇḍā ca (sophistry), Karuṇā (compassion), Vanitā (woman), Latā (creeper).

Kathā (talk), Nindā (blame), Sudhā (ambrosia), Rādhā (the goddess Radha), Vāsanā (habitual tendency), Siṃsapā (the rosewood tree), Papā (watershed).

Pabhā (radiance), Sīmā (boundary), Khamā (patience), Ejā (craving),

Khattiyā (princess), Sakkharā (gravel), Surā (liquor).

Dolā (palanquin), Tulā (scales), Silā (stone), Līlā (grace/demeanor),

Lālā (saliva), Eḷā (saliva), Mekhalā (girdle), Kalā (part/fraction).

Vaḷavā (mare), Suṇisā (daughter-in-law), Mūsā (crucible), Mañjūsā (casket), Sulasā (the deity Sulasā), Disā (direction).

Nāsā (nose), Juṇhā (moonlight), Guhā (cave), Īhā (exertion), Lasikā (synovial fluid), Parisā (assembly), Nisā (night).

Words such as Mātikā and others are similar to the word Bhāvikā. The words Ammā, Ambā, and Tātā are only slightly similar. However, words such as Mātā, Dhītā, and Panattā are distinct from this (Bhāvikā).

Regarding the word Parisā, in the locative case, it should be declined as 'Parisāya, Parisāyaṃ, Parisati, Parisāsu'. This is because the form 'Parisati' is found in the Pali texts, such as: "O Gotama, on one occasion, in the assembly (parisati) of the Brahmin Todeyya, they were disparaging others." As for the declension of words like Ammā: 'Ammā, Ammā'...
263:
Declining as 'Ammāyo' and so forth according to the method of the word Kaññā, it should be applied at the end as 'Bhoti amma, bhoti ammā, bhotiyo ammā, ammāyo' and so forth.

Mātā, mātā, mātaro. Mātaraṃ, mātaro. Mātarā, mātuyā, matyā, mātūhi, mātūbi. Mātu, mātuyā, matyā, mātarānaṃ, mātānaṃ, mātūnaṃ. Mātarā, mātuyā, matyā, mātūhi, mātūbi. Mātu, mātuyā, matyā, mātarānaṃ, mātānaṃ, mātūnaṃ. Mātari, mātuyā, matyā, mātuyāṃ, matyaṃ, mātūsu. Bhoti mātā, bhotiyo mātā, mātaro.

In this regard, because the feminine forms ending in 'u' are not found in the Pali texts with endings such as 'ehi, ebhi, esu' and 'enaṃ', therefore, although some say 'mātussa, mātarehi' and so forth, they are not mentioned in the Pali texts. This rule applies to other similar words as well. Because it is found in the Pali texts: "Whatever merit has been made, I share it with myself and with your mother (mātuyā). I have been permitted by my mother (matyā)," the forms 'mātuyā' and 'matyā' are used in the places of the instrumental, dative, ablative, genitive, and locative cases. This is because those forms have a common grammatical path in the feminine gender. Thus, in the Ummādantī Jātaka, the word 'matyā' appears in the sense of the ablative and instrumental singular. Just as the word 'khattiyā' becomes 'khatyā' through the elision of the middle vowel, likewise the words 'mātuyā' and 'mātuyāṃ' become 'matyā' and 'matyaṃ'. This method is not obtained in words such as dhītu.

Dhītā, dhītā, dhītaro. Dhītaṃ, dhītaraṃ, dhītaro. Dhītuyā, dhītūhi, dhītūbi. Dhītu, dhītuyā, dhītarānaṃ, dhītānaṃ, dhītūnaṃ. Dhītarā, dhītuyā, dhītūhi, dhītūbi. Dhītu, dhītuyā, dhītarānaṃ, dhītānaṃ, dhītūnaṃ. Dhītari, dhītuyā, dhītuyāṃ, dhītūsu. Bhoti dhītu, bhoti dhītā, bhotiyo dhītā, dhītaro. In this regard...
264:
"Prince Jāli, the daughter Kaṇhājinā, and Queen Maddī, who is devoted to her husband—though I abandoned them for the sake of Enlightenment alone, I did not grieve."

Because the form 'dhītaṃ' is found in the Pali texts, it is said as 'dhītaṃ' in the place of the accusative case; therefore, this meaning should be taken as the essence. Likewise, because the compound word 'asakyadhītarā' is found in the Pali texts, the compound word ending in the nominative singular such as 'seṭṭhidhītarā', which is similar to the word ending in the instrumental singular, must also be accepted. In the Niruttipiṭaka, however, the two words 'mātā' and 'dhītā' are included in the Saddhā method. We have taken them separately because forms such as 'mātāyā' are not found extensively in the Pali texts like the word 'saddhāyā'. Only in compound words do we see such a grammatical path of the word, as in 'rājamātāya, rājadhītāya, seṭṭhidhītāya'. Thus, the Kaññā method is also partially obtained. Likewise, because 'nandamāte' is found in the Pali texts as "Wonderful, O mother of Nanda (Nandamāte)! Marvellous, O mother of Nanda!", the method such as 'bhoti rājamāte, bhoti rājadhīte' is also obtained. There, 'Nandamāte' means: the mother of Nanda is 'Nandamātā'; 'O mother of Nanda' is 'bhoti nandamāte'. In this way, such a grammatical path of the word occurs only in compound words. Therefore, if it is a compound word, the two portions of these original forms 'mātu, dhītu, duhitu' should be taken: the portion of forms shown previously and the portion of forms according to the Kaññā method. Words such as 'nattu' are not only masculine; indeed, they are also feminine. Thus, usages such as "Visākhā's granddaughter (nattā) has passed away" and "Four female mice (mūsikā) have made a deep hole, but they do not dwell there" are seen in the Dispensation.

Nattā, nattā, nattāro. Nattāṃ, nattāraṃ, nattāro. Nattārā, nattuyā, nattūhi, nattūbi. Nattu, nattuyā.
265:
Of the grandchildren (nattārānaṃ, nattānaṃ, nattūnaṃ). By the grandchild, by the grandchildren (nattārā, nattuyā, nattūhi, nattūbhi). Of the grandchild, of the grandchildren (nattu, nattuyā, nattārānaṃ, nattānaṃ, nattūnaṃ). In the grandchild, in the grandchildren (nattari, nattuyā, nattuyaṃ, nattūsu). O grandchild (bhoti natta, bhoti nattā), O grandchildren (bhotiyo nattā, nattāro).

In the same way, for words like 'kattā, vasitā, bhāsitā', etc., when they are compound words, forms such as 'rājanattāyā, rājanatte' occur, similar to 'rājamātāyā, nandamāte'.

This is the analysis of the declension paradigm in the basic form of feminine nouns ending in -ā and -u.

## The feminine nouns ending in -ā,

## having the nature of ending in -ā and -u, are finished.

Now, I shall state the declension paradigm of words like 'bhūmi', etc., placing the view of former teachers at the forefront:

ratti, rattī, rattiyo (the night, the nights). rattiṃ, rattī, rattiyo (the night, the nights [acc.]). rattiyā, rattīhi, rattībhi (by the night, by the nights). rattiyā, rattīnaṃ (of the night, of the nights). rattiyā, rattīhi, rattībhi (from the night, from the nights). rattiyā, rattīnaṃ (of the night, of the nights). rattiyā, rattiyaṃ, rattīsu (in the night, in the nights). O night (bhoti ratti), O nights (bhotiyo rattiyo). This is the view of Yamaka Mahāthera.

One should understand everything as: 'bhūmi, bhūmī, bhūmiyo; bhūmiṃ, bhūmī, bhūmiyo'. In the same way, the declension paradigm should be applied to: bhūti (increase), satti (ability), patti (attainment), vutti (conduct), mutti (liberation), kitti (fame), khanti (patience), titti (contentment), siddhi (success), iddhi (power), vuddhi (prosperity), suddhi (purity), buddhi (wisdom), bodhi (enlightenment), pīti (joy), nandi (delight), mati (intellect), asani (thunderbolt), vasani (clothing), sati (mindfulness), gati (destiny), vuḍḍhi (growth), yuvati (maiden), anguli (finger), bondi (body), diṭṭhi (view), tuṭṭhi (satisfaction), nābi (navel), and so forth.

Furthermore, (there are examples such as): 'The nights pass not in vain. Those who bring oblations by day and by night. There is not even four finger-breadths on the earth. Lying on the earth, he moans. He places the snare that fell on the ground around his neck. These earrings are adorned with hundreds of stripes. They shine like lightning.'
266: Due to seeing such examples, this specific declension paradigm (namikapadamālā) of the words ratti, bhūmi, and nābhi should also be understood. How? ratti, rattī, rattiyo, ratyo. rattiṃ, rattī, rattiyo, ratyo. rattiyā, ratyā, rattīhi, rattībhi. rattiyā, ratyā, rattīnaṃ. rattiyā, ratyā, rattīhi, rattībhi. rattiyā, ratyā, rattīnaṃ. rattiyā, ratyā, rattiyaṃ, ratyaṃ, ratto, rattīsu. O night (bhoti ratti), O nights (bhotiyo rattī, rattiyo, ratyo). In this context, excluding the form 'ratto', all should be understood as: 'bhūmi, bhūmī, bhūmiyo, bhūmyo'. nābhi, nābhī, nābhiyo, nabhyo. nābhiṃ, nābhī, nābhiyo, nabhyo. nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīhi, nābhībhi. nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīnaṃ. nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīhi, nābhībhi. nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīnaṃ. nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhiyaṃ, nabhyaṃ, nābhīsu. O navel (bhoti nābhi), O navels (bhotiyo nābhī, nābhiyo, nabhyo). bodhi, bodhī, bodhiyo, bojjho. bodhiṃ, bodhiyaṃ, bojjhaṃ, bodhī, bodhiyo, bojjho. bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīhi, bodhībhi. bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīnaṃ. bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīhi, bodhībhi. bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīnaṃ. bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhiyaṃ, bojjhaṃ, bodhīsu. O Bodhi (bhoti bodhi), O Bodhis (bhotiyo bodhī, bodhiyo, bojjho). Here, because of seeing the diverse Pali methods such as 'O Victorious Buddha, may you realize [the Dhamma] at the Bodhi tree (bujjhassu jina bodhiyaṃ)' and 'By enlightenment, other than through austerity (aññatra bojjhā tapasā)', the declension paradigm with diverse methods has been stated. All these methods should also be applied in other places as appropriate. This is the analysis of the declension paradigm for the natural forms of feminine nouns ending in -i. ## The Feminine Gender ending in -i with the nature of -i ending is finished.
267:
Now, setting forth the views of the former teachers, I shall describe the declension of the word 'bhūrī' and others:

Itthī, itthī, itthiyo. Itthiṃ, itthī, itthiyo. Itthiyā, itthīhi, itthībi. Itthiyā, itthīnaṃ. Itthiyā, itthīhi, itthībi. Itthiyā, itthīnaṃ. Itthiyā, itthiyaṃ, itthīsu. O woman!, O women!. This is the view of the Great Elder Yamaka.

'Bhūrī, bhūrī, bhūriyo; bhūriṃ, bhūrī, bhūriyo'—this is the same as the word 'itthī'. In this way, the declension of words ending in -ī, such as 'bhūtī', 'bhotī', and 'vibhāvinī' which are derived from the root 'bhū', as well as other words ending in -ī, should be applied. Here, other words ending in -ī are:

'Mātulānī (aunt) and bhaginī (sister), bhikkhunī (nun), sāmugī, ajī (she-goat).
Vāpī (tank), pokkharaṇī (lotus pond), devī (goddess/queen), nāgī (female naga), yakkhinī (ogress), rājinī (queen).
Dāsī (slave woman) and brāhmaṇī (brahmin woman), muṭṭhassatinī (forgetful woman), sīghayāyinī (one who goes fast).
Sākiyānī (Sakyan lady)'—such usages exist.

Among those words, the usage of 'pokkharaṇī', 'dāsī', 'brāhmaṇī', etc., may also exist in other ways as appropriate in verses (gāthā) and prose (cuṇṇiya). Especially in verses, the forms of words such as 'kusāvatī' occur in other ways and are spoken in the singular. Words such as 'kāsī' and 'avantī' are spoken in the plural. Words such as 'candavatī' are spoken according to their usage. This is because of Pali passages such as: 'The lotus ponds were well-created. Those seven hundred wives and seven hundred slave women also exist. And the children, I...'
268:
I shall lead [them] to the servants of the brahmin woman. The rivers flow. On the bank of the Nerañjarā river. May [this] be the abode of fortune.

O Great King, in the city of Vārāṇasī, the King of Crows resides.
Surrounded by eighty thousand [followers], the well-winged King of Crows is attended.
Like King Vessavaṇa at the lotus pond.

Because such Pali passages are found, the declension (nāmikapadamālā) of words such as 'pokkharaṇī' and others should be specifically applied. How? By stating 'pokkharaṇī, pokkharaṇī, pokkharaṇiyo, pokkharañño'. Having stated 'pokkharaṇiṃ' and so on, the singular forms 'pokkharaṇiyā, pokkharaññā' should be used in the places of the Instrumental (karaṇa), Dative (sampadāna), Ablative (nissakka), and Genitive (sāmī) cases. In the place of the Locative (bhumma) case, the singular forms 'pokkharaṇiyā, pokkharaññā, pokkharaṇiyaṃ, pokkharaññaṃ' should be used. In all instances, the words must be made complete.

Similarly, having stated 'dāsī, dāsī, dāsiyo, dāsyo; dāsiṃ, dāsiyaṃ, dāsī, dāsiyo, dāsyo', the singular forms 'dāsiyā, dāsyā' should be used in the places of the Instrumental case and others. In the place of the Locative case, the singular forms 'dāsiyā, dāsyā, dāsiyaṃ, dāsyaṃ' should be used. In all instances, the words must be made complete.

In this context, because of the usage seen in 'yaṭṭhiyā paṭikoṭeti' (he strikes with a staff), 'ghare jātaṃva dāsiyaṃ' (like a female servant born in the house), and 'phusissāmi vimuttiyaṃ' (I shall touch liberation), the word 'dāsiyaṃ' is stated by means of substituting the Accusative (aṃ) case with 'ya'. Among those forms, in the phrase 'ghare jātaṃva dāsiyaṃ', another grammatical method is also obtained due to the substitution of the Accusative case with 'ya'. How? Just as a young woman is called 'dahariyā', so too a female servant is called 'dāsiyā'.

In this context, there are Pali passages such as: 'I see you, a young woman (dahariṃ), a girl (kumāriṃ) of beautiful appearance,' and 'Those who gave to that old man, while such a young woman (dahariyaṃ) existed.'
269: As an illustration, the word 'dāsiyaṃ' is used because the Accusative (upayoga) case is intended. In this sense, the declension (nāmikapadamālā) follows the method of the word 'kaññā' (girl), just like the word 'kumāriyā', as: 'dāsiyā, dāsiyā, dāsiyāyo; dāsiyaṃ, dāsiyā, dāsiyāyo; dāsiyāyā'. This is seen in the Pali: 'kumāriye upasseniye'. Similarly, the declension occurs in the singular method based on the 'kaññā' pattern as: 'pupphavatiyā, pupphavatiyaṃ, pupphavatiyāya, pupphavatiyāyaṃ, bhoti pupphavatiye'. In this matter, the Pali and the Commentary text serve as illustrations: 'In the past, this city of Vārāṇasī was named Pupphavatī. King Ekarāja was one of cruel deeds (luddakamma) in the city of Pupphavatī. Depart from the city of Pupphavatī in the east.'
