Another method: in words such as 'dāsiyā, dahariyā, kumāriyā', the substitution of the letter 'ka' with the letter 'ya' should also be noted. In the word 'brāhmaṇī', having stated 'brāhmaṇī, brāhmaṇī, brāhmaṇiyo, brāhmaṇyo; brāhmaṇiṃ' and so on, the singular forms 'brāhmaṇiyā, brāhmaṇyā' should be used in the places of the Instrumental (karaṇa) case and others; in all instances, the words must be made complete. For the word 'nadī', having stated 'nadī, nadī, nadiyo, nazzo; nadiṃ' and so on, one should say 'nadiyā, nazzā' and 'nadiyaṃ, nazzaṃ'; in all instances, the words must be made complete. In feminine nouns (itthiliṅga), if the Nominative plural (paccattabahuvacana) is seen, the Accusative plural (upayogabahuvacana) is also considered seen, even if not yet encountered. Similarly, if the Accusative plural is seen, the Nominative plural is also considered seen. If any one of the Instrumental, Dative, Ablative, Genitive, or Locative cases is seen, the others are also considered seen. This is shown in the phrase 'dāsā ca dāsyo anujīvino ca', where the Nominative plural 'dāsyo' is seen, and thus the other Accusative plural 'dāsyo' is also considered seen because it is identical to it.
270:
"If Sakka would grant me a boon, and if I were to receive that boon, I would be the protector for one or two nights, delighting with Ummādantī, and then I would be the Sivi King."

In this verse, because the Instrumental (karaṇa) case 'Ummādantyā' is seen, the Dative, Ablative, Genitive, and Locative cases which are identical to it are also considered seen. In the phrase 'brāhmaṇyā paricārake', because the Genitive (sāmī) case 'brāhmaṇyā' is seen, the Instrumental, Dative, Ablative, and Locative cases which are identical to it are also considered seen. In the phrases 'seti bhūmyā anutthunaṃ' and 'pathavyā cārupubbaṅgī', because the Locative singular 'bhūmyā' and 'pathavyā' are seen, the Instrumental, Dative, Ablative, and Genitive cases which are identical to them are also considered seen. In the phrase 'vārāṇasyaṃ mahārājā', because the Locative (bhumma) case 'vārāṇasyaṃ' is seen, other Locative cases such as 'brāhmaṇyaṃ, ekādasyaṃ, pañcamyaṃ' are also considered seen.

The ancient teachers of great virtue also adopted such forms by virtue of composing verses. In the Dispensation (Sāsana) as well, such forms are mostly found in verses.

Kusāvatī. Kusāvatiṃ. Kusāvatiyā, Kusāvatyā. Kusāvatiyaṃ, Kusāvatyaṃ. Bhoti Kusāvati.
Vārāṇasī. Vārāṇasiṃ. Vārāṇasiyā, Vārāṇasyā. Vārāṇasiyaṃ, Vārāṇasyā, and also Vārāṇassaṃ. Bhoti Vārāṇasi.
Naḷinī. Naḷiniṃ. Naḷiniyā, Naḷiññā. Naḷiniyaṃ, Naḷiññaṃ. Bhoti Naḷini. Other words should also be applied in this manner.

When reaching the domain of verses, word forms such as 'Kusāvatimhi, Vārāṇasimhi, Naḷinimhi' should also be applied. Thus, in the Pali, feminine forms ending in the 'mhi' suffix such as 'Kusāvatimhi'...
271:
Such forms are evident only in verses (gāthās), but not in prose (cuṇṇiyapada) compositions. In the science of grammar (akkharasamaya), however, such forms are not prohibited, as seen in rules like "nadimhā ca" etc. The occurrence of feminine forms like "sammādiṭṭhimhi" in the prose sections of the commentaries should be understood as being stated by way of letter-permutation (akkharavipallāsa). This is because in prose sections, forms like "sammādiṭṭhiyaṃ, paṭisandhiyaṃ, sugatiyaṃ, duggatiyaṃ" are found.

The rule here is: In the Dispensation of the Buddha, in both verses and prose, the suffixes nā, sa, smā, smiṃ, mhā, and mhi do not follow the five types of feminine nouns—kaññā, ratti, itthī, yāgu, and vadhū—in their original form. However, the word "mhi" follows feminine nouns ending in i and ī in verses. Regarding this, it is said:

"In verses and in prose, the case endings such as nā, sa, and smā do not occur in their original form. Feminine nouns ending in ā and i/ī follow them. However, the word 'mhi' occurs with feminine nouns ending in i/ī in verses. Indeed, there are usages where this word 'mhi' follows. Just as there is never a male in the womb of a crane (balākayoni), the Great King was the lord of the earth in the city of Kusāvatī."

Thus, words like Kusāvatī occur in other ways. Being names of cities, they are only singular; they are not plural like the names of countries (janapada). The declension (nāmikapadamālā) should be applied in this way: "Kāsī, Kāsiyo. Kāsīhi, Kāsībhi. Kāsīnaṃ. Kāsīsu. O ladies, people of Kāsī." Similarly, "Avantī, Avantiyo," etc. Other words should also be taken. Thus, words like Kāsī, being names of countries, are only plural by convention (rūḷhī), even if the meaning is singular.

Candavatī, Candavatiṃ, Candavatiyā, Candavatiyaṃ, O lady Candavatī—thus in the singular; or Candavatiyo, Candavatiyo, Candavatīhi, Candavatībhi, Candavatīnaṃ, Candavatīsu,
272:
O ladies, Candavatīs; thus the declension (nāmikapadamālā) should be understood in the plural, and other words should also be applied. Since words like "Candavatī" are designations for a single woman or many women, they are applied in the singular or plural according to usage. This method applies elsewhere as well.

## This is the analysis of the declension of the natural form of feminine nouns ending in long Ī.

## The feminine noun ending in long Ī is finished.

Now, since feminine nouns ending in short u derived from the root bhū are rare, we shall complete the declension with other feminine nouns ending in short u:

Yāgu, yāgū, yāguyo. Yāguṃ, yāgū, yāguyo. Yāguyā, yāgūhi, yāgūbhi. Yāguyā, yāgūnaṃ. Yāguyā, yāgūhi, yāgūbhi. Yāguyā, yāgūnaṃ. Yāguyā, yāguyaṃ, yāgūsu. O lady yāgu, O ladies yāgū, yāguyo.

In this manner, words such as "dhātu, dhenu, kāsu, daddu, kaṇḍu, kacchu, rajju" are formed. In this context, the word "dhātu" is masculine when it refers to the elements known as chyle (rasa), blood, flesh, fat, sinew, bone, marrow, and semen. It is feminine when it refers to nature, the bodily relics of the Buddhas, the world-element (lokadhātu), or the elements such as the eye (cakkhu). When it refers to the words (roots) bhū, hū, kara, paca, etc., it is both feminine and masculine. Here, however, the feminine is intended.

## This is the analysis of the declension of feminine nouns ending in short u.

## The feminine noun ending in short u is finished.

Now, we shall state the declension of the word "jambū" and others, placing the opinions of former teachers at the forefront:

Jambū, jambū, jambuyo. Jambūṃ, jambū, jambuyo. Jambuyā, jambūhi, jambūbhi. Jambuyā, jambūnaṃ. Jambuyā, jambūhi, jambūbhi.
273:
Jambuyā, jambūnaṃ. Jambuyā, jambuyaṃ, jambūsu. Madam Jambu, Madams Jambu, jambuyo. This is the view of the Great Elder Yamaka.

Here, the feminine gender of the word 'jambū' is well-known from such passages as "ambā sālā ca jambuyo". However, in the phrase "ime te jambukā rukkha", the masculine form 'jambukā' is used in consideration of the word 'rukkha'. This is because it is called 'jambuka' as it is spoken of as 'jambū'. (The root is 'ke re ge saddeti'). Alternatively, by the power of the feminine gender, 'jambū' itself becomes 'jambukā'; and since those 'jambukā' are trees, it forms 'jambukārukkhā' (as an attributive compound). This is like 'Laṅkādīpo'. Or, on the masculine side, although it should be said as 'jambukaru-kkhā' by the power of the compound, because it is a verse, the sound is lengthened to 'jambukārukkhā' to protect the meter, as in the rule "saraṇāgamane kañcī".

Bhū, bhū, bhuyo. Bhuṃ, bhū, bhuyo. Bhuyā, bhūhi, bhūbhi. Bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. Bhuyā, bhūhi, bhūbhi. Bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. Bhuyā, bhuyaṃ, bhūsu. Madam Bhu, Madams Bhū, bhuyo.

In this manner, "abhū, abhū, abhuyo. abhuṃ, abhū, abhuyo. abhuyā" and so forth should be declined. Here, "abhuṃ me kathaṃ nu bhaṇasi, pāpakaṃ vata bhāsasi" is the illustrative example.

## "Vadhū ca sarabhū ceva, sarabū sutanū camū.
## Vāmūrū nāganāsūrū", etc., are similar to 'jambū'.

This subtle point should be well-borne in mind. "Vadaññū, vadaññū, vadaññuyo. Vadaññuṃ, vadaññū, vadaññuyo. Vadaññuyā" should be declined similarly to the word 'jambū'. In this way, it also applies to "maggannū, dhammannū, katannū", etc.

O friends, in the verse: "When I go from here and obtain a human birth, being generous (vadaññū) and endowed with virtue, I shall perform much merit"...
274:
The masculine gender of words such as *vadaññū* is well-known because such usages are found. If that is so, why is the feminine method shown here? It is because words like *vadaññū* are not exclusively masculine; they possess both genders as they follow the gender of the sense they express (*vāccalinga*). For this very reason:

"I, having gone and attained human life, being generous (*vadaññū*) and free from stinginess, shall repeatedly give gifts to the Saṅgha without negligence."

And also, many Pali passages are found with feminine usage, such as: "An angry and ungrateful (*akataññū*) woman."

Therefore, we have established this *Nīti* treatise.

This is the decision on the classification of the original forms and the declension tables (*nāmika-padamālā*) of feminine nouns ending in *ū* (*ū-kāranta*).

The section on feminine nouns ending in *ū* is finished.

Feminine nouns ending in *o* (*o-kāranta*) formed from the root *bhū* are not well-known, but other feminine nouns ending in *o* are well-known.

It should be understood that the feminine noun ending in *o* is the word *go*.

Some teachers say that the forms of this word in the feminine are the same as its forms in the masculine.

Indeed, some teachers desire the forms of the feminine word *go* to be just like the forms of the masculine word *go* stated in the manner of "*go, gāvo, gavo; gāvuṃ*," etc. In the view of those teachers, because there is no distinction in form—just as there is no distinction in the color of pieces of melted gold—the presentation of the word *go* as feminine is not fit for consideration. Why? Because this statement appears to us like saying the word *mātugāma* has two declension tables in the manner of "*mātugāmo, mātugāmā; mātugāmaṃ*," etc., one for the masculine and one for the feminine; therefore, it is not fit for consideration.

Furthermore, if the forms of the feminine word *go* are identical to the forms of the masculine word *go*, how could the word *go*...
275:
...be established as feminine? (It would not be possible) because there would be no distinction in the paradigm (*rūpamālā*). For example, although the words *ratti*, *aggi*, and *aṭṭhi* are similar in being nouns ending in *i* (*i-kāranta*), a distinction in the paradigm is seen which characterizes the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders. Just as a distinction in the paradigm is seen between two words derived from the same root (*dhātu*) that fall into the masculine and feminine genders, so too should a distinction in the paradigm be seen for the feminine word *go* desired by those teachers, but it is not seen. Just as there is a distinction in the paradigm for two words from the same root falling into masculine and feminine genders, so should there be a distinction in the paradigm for the two *go* words falling into masculine and feminine genders. And just as a distinction in the paradigm is seen for the two *āyu* words falling into masculine and neuter genders, so should there be a distinction in the paradigm for the two *go* words falling into masculine and feminine genders. If there is no distinction, how could there be a classification of them as masculine and feminine? And how could there be usage based on clear and unclear forms?

This point is extremely subtle and fine, exceedingly deep, and a great thicket. It is not possible for anyone who does not well understand the method of the natural linguistics (*sabhāva-nirutti*) of the Māgadha language—the original language of all beings, spoken by the Omniscient Conqueror—and who has not accumulated the necessary store of knowledge, to delve into or untangle it. In our view, however, a distinction in the paradigm of the two *go* words is indeed seen, the classification of masculine and feminine is seen, the usage based on clear and unclear forms is seen, and the usage of the neuter gender as a form distinct from those two is also seen; thus it should be understood.

Now, to make this meaning clear, we shall establish this method (*nīti*) in this place. If this is done, those who practice in the *Pariyatti Sāsana* will not struggle, being free from doubt. Here, to produce expertise for the wise in grasping the meaning, we shall state three declension tables (*nāmika-padamālā*). They are as follows:

*Gāvī, gāvī, gāviyo. Gāviṃ, gāvī, gāviyo. Gāviyā, gāvīhi, gāvībhi. Gāviyā, gāvīnaṃ. Gāviyā, gāvīhi, gāvībhi.*
276:
*Gāviyā, gāvīnaṃ. Gāviyā, gāviyaṃ, gāvīsu. Bhoti gāvi, bhotiyo gāvī, gāviyo.*

This is the declension table (*nāmika-padamālā*) of the feminine word *gāvī*, which ends in *ī* (*ī-kāranta*), expresses the feminine, and is accomplished by the power of the suffix *ī* prescribed after the word *go*.

*Go, gāvo, gavo. Gāvuṃ, gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāvo, gavo. Gāvena, gavena, gohi, gobhi. Gāvassa, gavassa, gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gāvā, gāvasmā, gāvamhā, gavā, gavasmā, gavamhā, gohi, gobhi. Gāvassa, gavassa, gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gāve, gāvasmiṃ, gāvamhi, gave, gavasmiṃ, gavamhi, gāvesu, gavesu, gosu. Bho go, bhavanto gāvo, gavo.*

This is the declension table of the masculine word *go*, which ends in *o* (*o-kāranta*) and expresses the masculine.

*Go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo. Gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāviṃ, gāvo, gāvī, gavo. Gohi, gobhi. Gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gohi, gobhi. Gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gosu. Bhoti go, bhotiyo gāvo, gāvī, gavo.*
This is the declension table of the word *go*, which ends in *o* and expresses both feminine and masculine genders.

In this context, it should be noted that the form "*gāvuṃ*" is not mentioned (in the feminine) because it is exclusively masculine. Its status as exclusively masculine is known through the authoritative Pali (*āhacca-pāḷi*, i.e., the Vinaya): "Here, O monks, a woman invites a monk who has entered the rains-retreat: 'Come, Bhante, I shall give you silver, or I shall give you gold, or I shall give you a field, or I shall give you a site, or I shall give you a bull (*gāvuṃ*), or I shall give you a cow (*gāviṃ*). I shall give you a male servant, or I shall give you a female servant, or I shall give you a daughter to be your wife, or I myself shall be your wife, or I shall bring another woman to be your wife.'" Thus it is known by this authoritative Pali.
277:
In this context, the word 'gāvu' refers to the masculine, and the word 'gāvi' refers to the feminine. In this o-kāranta feminine declension table (padamālā), the word 'gāvī' is stated four times; this word is capable of making known the indistinct usage of the feminine gender, similar to the word 'kaññā'. Among the other genders, there is not even one word that appears four times with the same sound. We shall explain later how these words 'gāvī' and 'gāvi' occur generally for both feminine and masculine in certain places. We have constructed the declension table for the o-kāranta feminine as 'go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo; gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāviṃ', and so on. In that declension table, there is the substitution of the si and yo case-endings with ī from the word 'go', and the substitution of the aṃ case-ending with iṃ. Therefore, the forms 'gāvī, gāvī, gāviṃ' of the o-kāranta feminine are shown. Similarly, in the Mukhamattadīpanī, the grammarian Teacher Vajirabuddha, due to his proficiency in the method of linguistics (nirutti), stated the substitution of the yo case-ending with ī from the word 'go'. Just as there is the substitution of the yo case-ending with ī from the word 'go', so too there is the substitution of the si case-ending with ī and the aṃ case-ending with iṃ. Here are the verses illustrating the adoption of this method:

Even though they are established by the suffix ī, in such words as 'gāvī, gāvī',
at the end of the nominative singular and so on, in the Dispensation of the Conqueror (Jina-sāsana).
The teacher who speaks of the substitution of yo with ī for the word 'go' in the feminine,
in order to declare its indistinctness—we favor the method he has given.

Furthermore, in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā):
Having said 'gāvo', then by the word 'gāviṃ' in the feminine,
in order to declare its indistinctness—we favor the method he has given.

Likewise, in the Commentaries such as the Samantapāsādikā: 'A clever cowherd, taking pebbles in his lap, with a rope and a staff in his hand, goes to the cow-pen early in the morning, and striking the cows on their backs...'
278: '...sitting on top of the gate-post, he counts each cow (gāviṃ) that reaches the gate by throwing a pebble, saying "one, two".' In this passage, having said 'gāvo', the word 'gāviṃ' is used to establish the indistinct usage of the o-kāranta feminine word 'go', which denotes both feminine and masculine. By this word 'gāvo', cows that are both feminine and masculine are taken generally; likewise, by this word 'gāviṃ', cows that are both feminine and masculine are also taken. Thus, the grammarians and commentators, due to their proficiency in the method of linguistics (nirutti), have grouped these words 'gāvo' and 'gāviṃ' together in the same treatise and the same sentence by virtue of their similar gender. If these forms 'gāvī' and 'gāviṃ' were not obtainable in the declension table of the o-kāranta feminine word 'go' which denotes both feminine and masculine, then in the Commentary, after saying 'gāvo', one should only say 'gāvaṃ', and one should not say 'gāviṃ'. Since the commentators used the word 'gāvo' as a comprehensive term for all cows in terms of feminine and masculine, and then, referring to those very cows, again made the grammatical arrangement 'each cow (gāviṃ) that reaches the gate', therefore it should be understood that this word 'gāviṃ' is also a comprehensive term. If it is argued that this 'gāviṃ' is not a comprehensive term because the word 'gāvī' should only be taken as feminine, it is not so; for the alternative meaning is known by virtue of the context (pakarana). In all cow-pens, it cannot be said that 'only females dwell, not males' or 'only males dwell, not females'. Moreover, the Pali text is seen: 'Seeing even a cow (gāviṃ), they flee, thinking "they are monks"'; here too, it should be understood that by the word 'gāviṃ', all cows, both feminine and masculine, are taken. Otherwise, it would imply that 'only a feminine cow should be thought of as a monk'. Thus, by the Pali method, it is known that there is the substitution of the aṃ case-ending with iṃ from the word 'go' which denotes both feminine and masculine in the feminine gender.
279:
Teacher Vajirabuddha also, although the suffix ī could have been applied to the word 'go', did not do so but instead made the substitution of the yo case-ending with ī. His intention might be this: if the suffix ī were applied to the word 'go', the word 'gāvī' produced by the power of this suffix ī would, like 'migī, morī, kukkuṭī', etc., be only feminine-denoting in any context, and would never denote both feminine and masculine. Therefore, by virtue of the usage consistent with the Dispensation, the substitution of the yo case-ending with ī should be made. Thus, in the view of Teacher Vajirabuddha, it is known that the substitution of the yo case-ending with ī occurs from the word 'go'.

Furthermore—since the commentators, in the grammatical arrangement ending with the statement 'striking the cows on their backs... he counts each cow (gāviṃ) that reaches the gate by throwing a pebble, saying "one, two"', must state the method of semantic connection (atthayojanā) as 'eko gāvī, dve gāvī', and the accusative form 'gāviṃ' is also seen. Thus, in the view of the commentators, it is known that from the word 'go', the si and yo case-endings are substituted with ī, and the aṃ case-ending is substituted with iṃ. For that very reason, the declension table we have set forth for the o-kāranta feminine word 'go' as 'go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo, gāvaṃ, gāviṃ', etc., is consistent with the Pali method, consistent with the method of the Commentaries, and consistent with the view of the teachers who, adopting the view of Teacher Kaccāyana, facilitate the formation of words. Moreover, because the word 'gāvī' appears four times, it establishes the indistinct usage of the o-kāranta feminine word 'go'. Thus, when properly investigated with wisdom in the Pali methods and so on, it is extremely logical; there is not even a slight fault in this matter. In this context, the word 'gāviyo' in the plural of the nominative, accusative, and vocative; the word 'gāviyā' in the singular of the instrumental, dative, ablative, and genitive; and the words 'gāvīhi, gāvībhi' in the plural of the instrumental and ablative...
280:
In the place of the dative and genitive plural, the word 'gāvīnaṃ', and in the place of the locative case, the words 'gāviyā, gāviyaṃ, gāvīsu'—these sixteen words in detail should be understood as not being mentioned here because they are established exclusively by the power of the suffix -ī and are exclusively feminine-signifying.

Here, the decision is stated to remove doubt for the listeners: among feminine words, these words 'gāvī' and 'gāvi' are established either by the power of the suffix -ī or by the power of the substitution of -ī and -i. Of these, the latter method (substitution) is intended here; the former method (suffix) is intended elsewhere. Likewise, because these words 'gāvī' and 'gāvi' are also established by the power of the suffix -ī, they are mostly feminine-signifying; and because they are also established by the power of the substitution of -ī and -i, in some instances, they are words that signify both feminine and masculine through a comprehensive sense. Among these also, only the latter method is intended here; the former method is intended elsewhere. However, these words 'gāviyo, gāviyā, gāvīhi, gāvībhi, gāvīnaṃ, gāviyaṃ, gāvīsu' are established only by the power of the suffix -ī, and thus they are words that signify only females in every respect. This is because they occur specifically by the power of worldly convention only in regard to cattle that are female, like the words 'migī' (doe), 'morī' (peahen), 'kukkuṭī' (hen), etc., which occur exclusively in regard to female animals. Furthermore, although words such as 'nadī' (river) and 'mahī' (earth) are feminine and are established by the power of the suffix -ī, it is not appropriate to say that their meanings occur in female beings because they are inanimate things. Indeed, their meanings are devoid of the states of female, male, or neuter. Since the substitution of -e and the vowel -u cannot be obtained in the feminine word 'go', the words 'gāvena, gavena, gāvesu, gavesu' are not mentioned. And since the suffixes -sa, -smā, and -smiṃ do not follow the feminine word 'go' in their original form, the words 'gāvassa, gavassa, gāvasmā, gavasmā, gāvasmiṃ, gavasmiṃ' are not mentioned. And since the vowel -ā and the form -mhā, which are substitutions for the suffix -smā, cannot be obtained there, the words 'gāvā, gavā, gāvamhā, gavamhā' are not mentioned. As for the substitution of the suffix -smiṃ...
281:
The vowel -e and the form -mhi cannot be obtained; therefore, the words 'gāve, gave, gāvamhi, gavamhi' are not spoken of in the feminine. Furthermore, because it is not appropriate to connect them with appositional words such as 'yāya' and 'tāya', the words 'gāvena, gavena', etc., are not spoken of in the place of the feminine. For the words 'gāvena, gavena', etc., should not be connected with 'yāya, tāya', etc., because they are strictly masculine forms.

If some should say: 'The declension table you have set forth for the feminine word 'go' with a base ending in -o, in the manner of 'go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo', etc., is it not similar to what is spoken as 'mātugāmo, itthī, mātugāmā, itthiyo'?' That is not so. For the words 'mātugāma' and 'itthī' have various genders as masculine and feminine, and have various roots as the roots 'gam' and 'isu'. In this context, however, the words 'go' and 'gāvī' have only one gender as feminine, and have only one root as the root 'gam'.

If it be so, since the word 'goṇa' is spoken of by the teacher Kaccāyana as a substitution for the word 'go', and thus arriving at being that substitution and having a single root, should the declension table be spoken of by mixing it with that word 'goṇa'? No, because the word 'goṇa' is extremely masculine and has a base ending in -a. Therefore, that word 'goṇa' is shown separately in the place of the masculine. This declension table 'go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo', etc., should not be regarded as being made by mixing words ending in -o and -ī; rather, it should be understood in essence only as a feminine declension table ending in -o, having words spoken by way of the substitution of -ī and -i for the suffixes -si, -yo, and -aṃ following the word 'go' optionally.

Now we shall state the sutta passages and worldly usages that establish the feminine state of the word 'go': 'Monks, for example, in the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn time, when the crops are thick...'
282:
A cowherd should guard the cows; he should strike those cows from here and there with a stick.

These cows give food (alms), they give strength, they give beauty, and they give happiness.

Knowing this reason, they did not kill the cows.

He gathers all the cows. "Venerable Sir, the cows will go, longing for their calves"—these are the words of the Sutta. "He went while the cows were being milked," etc., are worldly usages. Thus, the feminine nature of the word *go* should be understood in essence, just like its masculine nature.

In that regard, although "go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo," etc., are spoken in the feminine gender, they refer to both females and males according to usage, like the words "pajā" (progeny) and "devatā" (deity). Therefore, when it is said "sā go" or "tā gāvo" by way of the feminine gender, it should be understood that all cattle, both female and male, are included. For in such a place, gender is not always primary; the meaning alone is primary. When it is said, "They milk the cows in the cow-pen," although this word "gāvo" also occurs in the masculine, since the act of milking is impossible in males, the females are understood by the power of the meaning. But when it is said "gāvī duhanti," who among the wise would have a doubt, since it is spoken by the power of both gender and meaning? When it is said "tā gāvo caranti," because it is spoken by way of the feminine gender, someone might occasionally have a doubt, thinking, "Are these not [only] females?" But when it is said by way of the masculine gender, "te gāvo caranti," there is no doubt; both females and males are understood, because in some places the masculine plural is used to include both female and male. As in "atha ettha sīhā vyagghā ca" (then there are lions and tigers), etc. When it is said "gāvī carati" or "gāviṃ passati," only the female (cow) is understood by the word *gāvī*.
283:
...because it [the word *gāvī*] takes [the female cow]. In worldly usages as well as in the Dispensation's usages, the female (cow) is taken by the word *gāvī*. Having intended certain usages in the Dispensation, we have said that the words "gāvī" and "gāviṃ" apply to both feminine and masculine.

This is indeed true: "Monks, just as a skilled butcher or a butcher's apprentice, having slaughtered a cow (*gāviṃ*), would sit at a crossroads having divided it into portions"—thus it is seen in the Pāḷi. And in the Commentaries, having made a word arrangement "gāvo" which applies to both female and male, and again intending that same female and male, the word arrangement "at every door reached, the cow (*gāviṃ*)" is seen.

In this context, both the female and the male belonging to the bovine species come to be designated as "gāvī." Specifically, however, "gāvī" is a designation for the female. This is indeed true; because in various Pāḷi passages, etc., such as: "Not long after the Blessed One had departed, a cow (*gāvī*) with a young calf attacked Bāhiya Dārucīriya and deprived him of life," and "I give you an ox (*gāvuṃ*) or I give you a cow (*gāviṃ*)," and "The grass-lion is like a cow (*gāvī*) the color of a pigeon"—from seeing such usages, it should be said that the female is spoken of by the word *gāvī*. By the word *go*, however, since it is seen in "milking the cow, cow's milk, cow-wealth, and cow-forms," it should be said that both female and male are spoken of.

Now, for the sake of producing skill in the wise, the method of logical meaning based on the Pāḷi method, etc., in the declension (*padamālā*) of the feminine word *go* ending in -o, is stated:

That cow goes, that cow goes, those cows go. He sees that cow, he sees those cows. It is done by those cows. He gives to those cows. He departs from those cows.
284:
The horns of those cows. It is established in those cows. O cow, you stand; O cows, you all stand.

Another method is also stated:

That cow goes crossing the river, that cow goes crossing the river, those cows go crossing the river. He sees that cow crossing the river, he sees those cows crossing the river. It is done by those cows crossing the river. He gives to those cows crossing the river. He departs from those cows crossing the river. The property of those cows crossing the river. It is established in those cows crossing the river.

Among those declensions, the declension of the feminine word *go* ending in -o, set forth as "go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo," etc., has a distinction from the declension of the masculine word *go* ending in -o, spoken as "go, gāvo, gavo," etc. This is because in the positions of the Nominative (*paccatta*), Accusative (*upayoga*), and Vocative (*ālapana*), the *gāvī* words are spoken like the four *kaññā* words. Since there is this distinction, this feminine word *go* ending in -o should be noted as a usage with an indistinct appearance like other feminine [words]; it should not be noted as a usage with a distinct appearance like masculine [words], nor should it be noted as a usage with an appearance free from both like neuter [words].

## Here, a verse for making a decision is stated:

Just as the difference between two *dhātu* words is seen, so too the difference between the two *go* words should be desired.

This is indeed true; the distinction between two *dhātu* words is seen by way of the masculine and feminine genders. How is that so?
285:
dhātu, dhātū, dhātavo. dhātuṃ, dhātū, dhātavo. dhātunā, dhātūhi, dhātūbi. dhātussa, dhātūnaṃ. dhātusmā, dhātumhā, dhātūhi, dhātūbi. dhātussa, dhātūnaṃ. dhātusmiṃ, dhātumhi, dhātūsu. This is the distinction of the masculine gender (pullinga).

dhātu, dhātū, dhātuyo. dhātuṃ, dhātū, dhātuyo. dhātuyā, dhātūhi, dhātūbi. dhātuyā, dhātūnaṃ. dhātuyā, dhātūhi, dhātūbi. dhātuyā, dhātūnaṃ. dhātuyā, dhātuyyaṃ, dhātūsu. This is the distinction of the feminine gender (itthilinga).

Just as the distinction between the two types of the word 'dhātu' is evident, so too is the distinction between the two types of the word 'go' (cow/ox). Just as the distinction between the two types of the word 'āyu' (life), which exist in the masculine and neuter genders, is evident as "āyu, āyū, āyavo" and "āyu, āyū, āyūnī" respectively, so too is the distinction between the two types of the word 'go' evident. This is because usage characterized by a distinct appearance is masculine, usage characterized by an indistinct appearance is feminine, and usage characterized by an appearance free from both is neuter.

Now, to make this meaning even clearer, I shall explain it briefly: 'purisa' (man) is usage with a distinct appearance, 'kaññā' (girl) is usage with an indistinct appearance, and 'rūpa' (form) is usage free from both. Puriso tiṭṭhati (The man stands), kaññā tiṭṭhati (The girl stands), kaññā tiṭṭhanti (The girls stand), kaññā passati (The girl sees), bhotiyo kaññā tiṭṭhatha (O girls, stand!). In this context, one term is different and four are the same. Purisā tiṭṭhanti, purisā nissaṭaṃ, bhavanto purisā gacchatha. Kaññāyo tiṭṭhanti, kaññāyo passati, bhotiyo kaññāyo gacchatha. In each case, three are the same. Purisaṃ passati, kaññaṃ passati. These two are different. Purise passati, purise patiṭṭhitaṃ. These two are the same. Tena purisena kataṃ, tāya kaññāya kataṃ, tāya kaññāya deti, tāya...
286:
...kaññāya apeti, tāya kaññāya santakaṃ, tāya kaññāya patiṭṭhitaṃ. One is different and five are the same. In this way, the usage of the masculine gender with a distinct appearance is seen, and the usage of the feminine gender with an indistinct appearance is seen. In the neuter gender, however, as in "rūpaṃ, rūpāni, rūpā; rūpaṃ, rūpāni, rūpe; bho rūpa, bhavanto rūpāni, rūpā," usage free from both appearances is seen through the power of the distinct paradigm (rūpamālā) in these three positions: Nominative (paṭhamā), Accusative (dutiyā), and Vocative (ālapana). In the masculine and feminine genders, distinct forms are not always present in these three positions. Therefore, it should be understood that usage with a distinct appearance is masculine, usage with an indistinct appearance is feminine, and usage free from both is neuter.

This method is also applicable to words with similar sounds such as "saddhā, sati, hirī," "yā itthī saddhā pasannā," "te manussā saddhā pasannā," "pahūtaṃ saddhaṃ paṭiyattaṃ," and "saddhaṃ kulaṃ," through the power of the paradigm (padamālā). That nature described as the usage of the feminine gender with an indistinct appearance is also found in certain numeral words. This is because words from vīsati (twenty) up to navuti (ninety) are said to be feminine gender ending in the singular. In this context, "vīsatiyā" is used for five different cases. Similarly, it is the same for words from "tiṃsāyā" up to "navutiyā." Thus, it should be understood that in words such as vīsati, usage with an indistinct appearance is found, just like the word kaññā.

If that is so, what about the words 'ti' (three) and 'catu' (four)? Since the words 'ti' and 'catu' follow the gender of the object they denote, as in "tayo, tisso, tīṇi; cattāro, caturo, catasso, cattārī," they associate with words characterized by the absence of distinct, indistinct, or both appearances, such as "purisā, kaññāyo, cittāni," according to their respective genders. Therefore, they should be described as being free from usage characterized by distinct, indistinct, or both appearances, according to each individual gender.
287:
In pronouns (sabbanāma) as well, these three types of appearances are obtained due to their association with distinct forms. How? In the context of masculine and neuter genders, all pronominal forms ending in the Dative (catutthī) and Genitive (chaṭṭhī) cases, such as "tassa, kassa," occur. In the context of the feminine gender, however, all pronominal forms ending in the Instrumental (tatiyā), Dative (catutthī), Ablative (pañcamī), Genitive (chaṭṭhī), and Locative (sattamī) cases, such as "tassā, kassā," occur. Therefore, even in the nature of pronouns, the fact that the feminine gender has usage with an indistinct appearance must be certainly accepted.

In this matter, rather than bringing forward the easily obtainable Dative and Genitive forms, I shall present the Instrumental, Ablative, and Locative forms, which are very difficult to find, from the Dispensation of the Blessed One, so that listeners may attain extremely subtle and profound knowledge with a mind free from doubt regarding the Buddha's teachings. What are they? "The Venerable Udāyī approached where that young girl (kumārikā) was; having approached, he sat together with that young girl (tassā kumārikāya saddhiṃ) alone in a private, secluded, and suitable place." Here, "tassā" is the form of the Instrumental case (tatiyā). Just by seeing the Instrumental form "tassā," the Instrumental forms such as "sabbassā, katarissā," even if they do not directly appear in the Pali texts, are considered as seen, because they follow the same grammatical path as one another, and because it is proper to understand the unseen through what is seen.

In the phrase "kassāhaṃ kena hāyāmi" (By whom and by what do I decline?), "kassā" is the form of the Ablative case (pañcamī). Just by seeing the Ablative form "kassā," the Ablative forms such as "sabbassā, katarissā," even if they do not appear in the Pali texts, are considered as seen.

In the passages "A certain monk, having enticed a female monkey (makkaṭiṃ) with food in the Great Wood at Vesālī, committed sexual misconduct with that female monkey (tassā)" and "A certain monk has a mind attached to another woman (aññatarissā itthiyā)," the terms "tassā" and "aññatarissā" are forms of the Locative case (sattamī). Just by seeing those forms, the Locative forms such as "sabbassā, katarissā," even if they do not appear in the Pali texts, are considered as seen.
288:
O friend, in this instance, “tassā kumārikāya saddhiṃ,” is this word “tassā” spoken by way of case exchange (vibhatti-vipallāsa)? For “tāyā” is indeed its meaning. Likewise, in this instance, “kassāhaṃ kena hāyāmi,” is it also spoken by way of case exchange? For “kāyā” is indeed its meaning. In this instance, “aññatarissā itthiyā paṭibaddhacitto,” is this word “aññatarissā” spoken by way of case exchange? Is “aññatarissaṃ” indeed its meaning? (Thus it is asked).

It is not so, because in such prose passages (cuṇṇiyapada), case exchange is not desired. O friend, even in prose passages, in such places as “Saṅghe Gotami dehi” (Give, O Gotamī, to the Saṅgha), do the teachers not say it is case exchange for the sake of the meaning “Saṅghassa”? True, yet in such places, there are two intentions because the locative (sattamī) and the dative (sampadāna) are both desired in the sense of support (ādhāra) and recipient (paṭiggāhaka).

Therefore, while intending to say, “Give to the Saṅgha (Saṅghassa),” saying, “Give in the Saṅgha (Saṅghe)” is not contradictory; it is indeed appropriate. Likewise, while intending to say, “Give in the Saṅgha,” saying, “Give to the Saṅgha” is also not contradictory; it is indeed appropriate. Just as although the words “alābu” and “lābu” exist separately, in the instance “lābūni sīdanti silā plavanti” (gourds sink, stones float), the elision of the letter ‘a’ is performed by the intellect to preserve the meter of the verse.

Similarly, in places such as “Saṅghe Gotami dehi,” the teachers desire the meaning of case exchange as “Saṅghassa,” having conceived the case exchange through the intellect. Therefore, case exchange is appropriate in places such as “Saṅghe Gotami dehi” and “Vessantare varaṃ datvā” (King Vessantara, having given the boon). However, in places such as “tassā kumārikāya,” it is not appropriate. What is called case exchange is generally to be desired only in verses (gāthā) such as “neva dānaṃ viramissaṃ.”

However, if you say that the Pali you brought forward, “tassā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati,” is not a locative usage.
289:
If it is said that this word “tassā” ending in the genitive case (chabbī-vibhatti) is a genitive because the meaning “he engages in sexual intercourse in the genitals of that female monkey” is possible—it is not so, because it is stated in the Commentary: “Tassā is a locative term (bhumma-vacana).” Furthermore, in the Commentary itself, in the passage “tassā ca sikkhāya sikkhaṃ paripūrento sikkhati, tasmiñca sikkhāpade avītikkamanto sikkhati” (fulfilling the training in that training, he trains; not transgressing in that training rule, he trains), the word “tassā” is pointed out as a locative term.

O friend, if you say that there also, this word “tassā” is a possessive term (sāmivacana) used in the sense of the locative by way of case exchange (vibhatti-vipallāsa)—then it must be said to you: “You are very skilled in the method of case exchange; you are indeed a case-exchanger.” To you, who overstep the Pali spoken by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma and overstep the words of the Commentary, we shall bring forward another Niddesa Pali. If you are of a wise nature, you will understand. If you are of an unwise nature, you will not understand, not letting go of your own view. Listen with respect to the Dispensation (Sāsana).

Explaining the meaning of the Pali, “Tasmā hi sikkhetha idheva jantū” (Therefore, let beings train right here), the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma and Chief Disciple, who reached the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) and was like the Teacher himself, said: “‘Idha’ (here) means in this view (diṭṭhi), in this patience (khanti), in this preference (ruci), in this undertaking (ādāya), in this Dhamma.” In this way, the word “imissā” was spoken as a locative term. Because it expresses the meaning of the word “idha,” it is understood to be a form of the locative. Thus, just as “imissā” is seen as a locative form, locative forms such as “sabbassā” and “katarissā,” though they do not appear directly in the Pali, are indeed considered as seen.

We shall bring forward another Pali spoken directly by the Omniscient One, who has compassion for the whole world; listen with respect: “It is impossible, bhikkhus, it cannot happen, that in one...
290:
...world system (lokadhātu) two Arahant Fully Enlightened Buddhas should arise simultaneously (neither before nor after the other).” In this instance, “ekissā” is a locative form. Just as “ekissā” is seen as a locative form, locative forms such as “sabbassā” and “katarissā,” though they do not appear directly in the Pali, are indeed considered as seen. For not all usages appear in their own forms in the Pali and other texts; some appear, and some do not appear at all. Regarding this, it is said:

“The words such as ‘tassā,’ like ‘tāya’ and others,
Should be known by the wise in five places, starting from the third case (instrumental).
Because they occur as names for the three cases starting with ‘nā’ (instrumental, dative, ablative),
Words like ‘tassā’ and ‘kassā’ occur in the third case and so on.”

In this matter, the explanation of the Pali method and the explanation of the Commentary method are as follows: “tassā kaññāya saddhiṃ gacchati” (he goes with that girl), “tassā kaññāya kataṃ” (done by that girl), “tassā kaññāya deti” (he gives to that girl), “tassā kaññāya apeti” (he departs from that girl), “tassā kaññāya ayaṃ kaññā hīnā” (this girl is inferior to that girl), “tassā kaññāya ayaṃ kaññā adhikā” (this girl is superior to that girl), “tassā kaññāya santakaṃ” (the property of that girl), “tassā kaññāya patiṭṭhitaṃ” (established in that girl). This rare method should be well-noted and mastered for the long-term endurance of the Dispensation. Thus, in every way, according to the methods of the Pali and Commentaries, it should be understood that the feminine gender (itthiliṅga) has usages with indistinct forms.

Knowing this, the wise should reach a conclusion here that “the difference in gender occurs due to the specific declension (rūpamālā) of the two types of the word ‘go’ (cow/ox).” For the word “go” is not a usage with a consistently distinct form like the words “puriso, mātugāmo, orodho, āpo, satthā,” nor is it a usage with a consistently indistinct form like the words “kaññā, ratti, itthī.” This is because when this word “go” is in the masculine gender, it is a usage with a distinct form like the word “dhātu,” but when it is in the feminine gender...
291:
It is a term with an indistinct appearance (avisa-dākāra). In order to enable listeners to understand this meaning and thereby attain extremely subtle and profound knowledge, the unique declension paradigm (namika-padamālā) of the feminine word 'go' ending in 'o' is taught, starting with 'go, gāvī, gāvo; gāviṃ, gavo,' and so on. In this context, the word 'gāviṃ' appears once, words such as 'go, gohi' appear twice, words such as 'gāvo, gāvī, gāvaṃ' appear thrice, and the word 'gāviyā' appears five times. Thus, because an indistinct appearance (avisa-dākāra) is observed by virtue of the words appearing five times in this paradigm, this word 'go' should be understood as feminine. If this method is abandoned, there is no other way by which the word 'go' could be feminine. Therefore, only this view should be accepted as our essence.

As for the view of teachers who say there is no distinction in the declension of both the masculine and feminine words 'go,' it should not be accepted as the essence. This is because, while the declensions of the masculine 'go' and feminine 'go' are identical, their reasoning is like imagining the masculine and feminine states by matching them with the declension paradigms of the word 'mātugāma' (woman).

Ettha pana kiñci liṅgasaṃsandanaṃ kathayāma—Here, let us state a brief comparison of genders—In the declension paradigm of the masculine word 'go' ending in 'o' mentioned below, words such as 'gāvuṃ, gāvaṃ, gāvena' appear once, words such as 'go, gohi' appear twice, and these words 'gāvo, gavo, gavaṃ' appear thrice, similar to 'satthā, rājā,' and so on. Here, there are no words that appear four or five times. Due to that absence, a distinct appearance (visadākāra) is observed. In the declension paradigm of the word 'purisa' as well, words such as 'puriso, purisaṃ' appear once, words such as 'purise' appear twice, and the word 'purisā' appears thrice. Thus, a distinct appearance is observed. In the feminine ending in 'ā,' however, words such as 'kaññaṃ' appear once, 'kaññāhi' appear twice, 'kaññāyo' appear thrice, this word 'kaññā' appears four times, and this word 'kaññāyā' appears five times. Thus, an indistinct appearance is observed. In the masculine ending in 'ā,' words such as 'satthari' appear once.
292:
Words such as 'satthū' appear twice, and words such as 'satthā' appear thrice. Thus, a distinct appearance is observed. By this method, the distinct appearance and indistinct appearance should be understood in all masculine and feminine paradigms. In the declension paradigm of the neuter gender (napuṃsakalinga), however, words similar to the masculine such as 'cittena' appear once, words such as 'cittaṃ' appear twice, and this word 'cittāni' appears thrice. The same method applies to words like 'aṭṭhi' and 'āyu.' Here, an appearance free from both (ubhayāmuttākāra) is observed. Although it might seem that a distinct appearance is found here because there are no words appearing four or five times, nevertheless, because neuter words like 'cittaṃ, aṭṭhi, āyu' do not function according to the method of masculine words like 'gacchaṃ, aggi, bhikkhu,' they do not have a distinct appearance; and because they do not function according to the method of feminine words like 'ratti, yāgū,' they do not have an indistinct appearance. Without approaching either side, they possess forms with their own respective paradigms such as 'cittaṃ, cittāni, cittā; cittaṃ, cittāni, citte,' and so on. Therefore, their appearance should be understood as being free from both.

These three types of appearances are not found in Sanskrit (Sakkaṭa) languages. Therefore, this matter is not mentioned in all grammar treatises. However, it is found in the natural linguistic expression (sabhāva-nirutti) of the Magadhi language, which is the root language of all beings and was spoken by the Buddha. Thus, it is stated in the Nirutti-mañjūsā—What is this that is called gender (liṅga)? Some first say: 'One who has breasts and hair is a woman (itthi); one who has a beard is a man (purisa). One who is between these two is a neuter (itara) and is free from both.' Because of this statement, they say that specific features like breasts and hair are called gender. This statement is not true in every case, because there is no connection with breasts and such in the case of the Ganges river, a rest-house, a tree, and so on.
293:
Other teachers say: 'Ultimately (paramatthato), there is no such thing as gender; gender is merely a term well-known in worldly convention (loka-saṅketa).' In this matter, the conclusion is as follows: A single word can exist in all genders, such as 'taṭaṃ, taṭī, taṭo' (shore). If gender existed in an ultimate sense, how could those genders, which are mutually contradictory, coexist in a single meaning? Therefore, it should be understood that the designation of a certain meaning by an indistinct appearance is the feminine gender, the designation by a distinct appearance is the masculine gender, and the designation by an appearance free from both is the neuter gender.

In this context, indistinct appearance and so on should be taken only by virtue of the sequence of words known as the declension paradigm (namika-padamālā), not by virtue of individual words. For instance, in individual words such as 'kaññā, puriso, cittaṃ' and 'kaññāyo, purisā, cittāni,' the indistinct appearance and so on are not evident. However, since the state of distinct appearance and so on is established by virtue of the sequence, the indistinct appearance and so on are also established in each individual word because of the relationship between the whole (samudāya) and its parts (avayava).

Some teachers, however, without considering the sequence known as the declension paradigm, desire indistinct appearance and so on by virtue of individual words alone. To them, it should be said: 'If indistinct appearance and so on existed only in individual words, then in words such as "kaññā, purisā, satthā, guṇavā, rājā" by virtue of the sound of "ā," in words such as "puriso, satthāro, kaññāyo" by virtue of the sound of "o," and in words such as "cittaṃ, purisaṃ, kaññaṃ" by virtue of the sound of the anusvāra, how could indistinct appearance and so on be possible when there are mutually identical sounds?' They might say: 'It is possible, but it is difficult to penetrate their distinction.' To them, it should be said: 'Do not speak thus; people can know even Nibbāna, which is extremely difficult to know, by relying on a person capable of teaching it. Therefore, speak only after careful reflection.' And thus...
294:
After saying that, they should be asked further: "What genders are the words *bodhi* and *āyu*?" If they know, they will say: "The word *bodhi* is both feminine and masculine; the word *āyu* is both neuter and masculine. These words possess two genders."

They should be told: "If *bodhi* and *āyu* are words with two genders, then how can there be an unclear appearance and a clear appearance in the two *bodhi* words which exist as a single term and have identical sounds? And how can there be an appearance free from both and a clear appearance in the two *āyu* words which exist as a single term and have identical sounds?"

When this is said, they will surely be unable to see anything further and will be without an answer. However, teachers skilled in grammar, taking the method from grammatical treatises, say this:

"In the world, regarding those meanings where '*eso*, *esā*, *etaṃ*' are well-known, the nouns expressing those meanings are called '*itthi*, *puma*, *napuṃsaka*'."

The intention of those teachers is: "This person is a man, this person is a woman, this person is a king, this is a woman, this is a creeper, this is a neuter, this is a mind." Thus, in the world, regarding those meanings among men etc. where '*eso*, *esā*, *etaṃ*' are well-known, those nouns are called "masculine, feminine, and neuter genders"; through that, other nouns are also to be understood. Those teachers who speak thus do not show this distinction: "By such an appearance, the nouns '*eso*, *esā*, *etaṃ*' and other nouns receive names such as masculine gender." However, the Neruttika teachers who know the method of the True Dhamma show it by saying: "The designation of any meaning by way of an unclear appearance is the feminine gender," and so on.
295:
Some teachers say: "The designation that expresses meanings with an unclear appearance is the feminine gender," and so on. This should not be accepted. If the designation that expresses meanings with an unclear appearance were the feminine gender, then words such as *mātugāma*, *kalatta*, *kanta*, *kaṇṭaka*, and *gumba* would also be feminine because their meanings have an unclear appearance. If the designation that expresses meanings with a clear appearance were the masculine gender, then words such as *devatā*, *saddhā*, and *ñāṇa* would also be masculine because their meanings have a clear appearance. Alternatively, if the designation that expresses meanings with an unclear appearance were the feminine gender and the designation that expresses meanings with a clear appearance were the masculine gender, then a single meaning could not be expressed by two genders in the same moment:

"O Yakkha, you are one who desires my welfare. O Devatā, you are one who desires my benefit. I shall do as you say; you are my teacher."

And if the designation that expresses meanings free from both appearances were the neuter gender, then in things like grass and trees which have meanings free from both appearances, gender and number would be contradictory because there is no fixed rule such as "it is this name." Furthermore, by the neuter gender expressions such as "*paññāratanaṃ*" and "*sāriputtamoggallānaṃ sāvakayugaṃ*," it would imply that their meanings are free from both appearances. Furthermore, a single shore could not be expressed by three genders as "*taṭaṃ*, *taṭī*, *taṭo*." A single wisdom could not be expressed by three genders as "*paññāṇaṃ*, *paññā*, *pajānanā*, *amohā*," and so on. Therefore, without taking that method, only the previously mentioned method should be accepted.

In the world, the lower body of women is clear, the upper body is unclear, the breast-flesh is unclear, and movements etc. are...
296:
...unclear. When women walk, they walk with an unclear appearance; when standing, lying, sitting, chewing, or eating, they eat with an unclear appearance. Even if a man is seen as unclear, people say: "He walks, stands, lies, sits, chews, and eats like a *mātugāma*." Thus, just as women mostly have an unclear appearance, so too, whatever designations of meanings—whether sentient or insentient—mostly have an unclear appearance, those alone are called the feminine gender. Examples: *kaññā*, *devatā*, *dhītalikā*, *dubbā*, *saddhā*, *ratti*, *itthī*, *ယာဂု* (*yāgu*), *vadhū*, etc.

For men, the lower body is unclear, the upper body is clear, the breast-flesh is clear, and movements etc. are clear. Men walk with a clear appearance; when standing, lying, sitting, chewing, or eating, they eat with a clear appearance. Even if a woman is seen with clear movements, they say: "She walks like a man," and so on. Thus, just as men mostly have a clear appearance, so too, whatever designations of meanings—whether sentient or insentient—mostly have a clear appearance, those alone are called the masculine gender. Examples: *puriso*, *mātugāmo*, *orodho*, *āpo*, *rukkho*, *moho*, *satthā*, etc.

Just as neuters are free from both appearances, so too, whatever designations of meanings—whether sentient or insentient—are free from both appearances, those alone are called the neuter gender. Examples: *cittaṃ*, *rūpaṃ*, *itthāgāraṃ*, *kalattaṃ*, *နာဋကံ* (*nāṭakaṃ*), *ratanaṃ*, *ñāṇaṃ*, *aṭṭhi*, *āyu*, etc. Thus, of all nominal designations:

*Visadāvisadākārā, ākāro’bhayamuttako.*
*Liṅgassa lakkhaṇaṃ etaṃ, ñeyyaṃ syādippabandhato.*

Clear appearance, unclear appearance, and the appearance free from both—this is the characteristic of gender (*liṅga*) to be known through the connection of suffixes like *si* (*syādi*).
297: This subject (grammatical method), which is difficult to penetrate, has been presented like a great forest cleared of thickets and tangles; it should be well-considered. Thus, based on the connection of meanings of all nouns, because the feminine gender etc. can occur through indistinct usage etc., the feminine gender etc. of both types of the word 'go' (cow/ox) should be understood according to their respective contexts through indistinct usage based on the connection of meanings. This is the analysis of the noun paradigm of the feminine gender ending in -o, together with the decision. The feminine gender ending in -o, having the nature of ending in -o, is finished. Thus, in every way, the six types of feminine genders—by way of ending in -ā, -i, -ī, -u, -ū, and -o—have been completely covered. Among these, the variation seen in some nouns ending in -ā and -ī by way of substituting the nominative singular with -e in certain places will now be stated. Indeed: 'Rādha, you do not know; before midnight has arrived, you weep in vain; the mother born of the Kosiya lineage is disenchanted with our father.' In this Rādha Jātaka, the word which should be said as 'virattā' according to the -ā ending is said as 'viratte' by way of substituting the nominative case with -e. Similarly, the word which should be said as 'Kosiyāyanī' according to the -ī ending is said as 'Kosiyāyane' by way of substituting the nominative case with -e. Therefore, the Commentator explained the meaning: "'Viratte Kosiyāyane' means our mother, the brahmin woman of the Kosiya lineage, has become disenchanted and devoid of love for our father." Venerable Sir, since we see the nominative case as 'viratte' and 'Kosiyāyane' in the Pāḷi, should it not be said that there is also a feminine gender ending in -e? It should not be said so, because those forms are specific variations included within the endings in -ā and -ī.
298: Because it is established by way of substitution, there is no separate feminine gender ending in -e; therefore, only the aforementioned sixfold division of feminine genders should be accepted. Thus, the noun paradigm of feminine genders, adorned with various methods, has been analyzed by me for the benefit of the Dispensation of the Self-Enlightened Buddha. This Sun of Saddanīti possesses a collection of rays which are many good decisions. It dispels the darkness of doubt; whose lotus-like intellect would it not cause to bloom? ## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the expertise of the wise in the linguistic ways of the Three Piṭakas together with the Commentaries and the ninefold division, ## the analysis of the noun paradigm of feminine genders, ## the eighth chapter, is finished. ## 9. Neuter Gender Noun Paradigm. Next, placing the views of former teachers at the forefront, I shall state the noun paradigm of neuter genders ending in niggahīta (ṃ) having the original form such as 'bhūtaṃ': cittaṃ, cittāni. cittaṃ, cittāni. cittena, cittehi, cittebhi. cittassa, cittānaṃ. cittā, cittasmā, cittamhā, cittehi, cittebhi. cittassa, cittānaṃ. citte, cittasmiṃ, cittamhi, cittesu. bho citta, bho cittā, bhavanto cittāni. This is the view of the Great Elder Yamaka. Here, although the nominative plural 'cittā' and the accusative plural 'citte' do not appear [in some texts], because such neuter forms ending in niggahīta are seen in various places, and because they are seen in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi as 'cha cittā abyākatā' (six types of indeterminate consciousness) etc...
299: ...it should certainly be accepted. Therefore, the sequence 'cittaṃ, cittāni, cittā. cittaṃ, cittāni, citte' should be understood. For neuter genders ending in niggahīta, in some places, the nominative and accusative plural forms occur like those of masculine genders ending in -o. These neuter forms occur in the scriptures either in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) with masculine, their own gender, or genderless terms, or they occur alone. In this regard, hundreds of Pāḷi passages should be seen, such as: 'cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. cattāro sammappadhānā. sabbe mālā upenti maṃ. yassa ete dhanā atthi. cattāro mahābhūtā. tīṇindriyā. dve indriyā. dasindriyā. dve mahābhūte nissāya dve mahābhūtā, pañca viññāṇā, caturo aṅge adhiṭṭhāya, semi vammikamatthake, rūပါ saddā rasā gandhā. rūpe ca sadde ca atho rase ca. cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ.' Here, words such as 'satipaṭṭhānā' should not be taken as being stated by way of gender reversal (liṅgavipallāsa), because the word satipaṭṭhāna etc. is not seen to exist as a masculine gender ending in -o in the nominative singular position. However, only words such as 'cattāro' should be taken as being stated by way of gender reversal, because they are seen to be in apposition with neuter words ending in niggahīta such as satipaṭṭhāna. Here, some might say: 'Since we see usages such as satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā'...
300:
The state of being a masculine gender ending in the vowel 'o' for the word 'satipaṭṭhāna' and others is obtainable. If this is so, why do you say, 'Because the state of being a masculine gender ending in 'o' is not seen in the place of the nominative singular for the word satipaṭṭhāna and others'? And why is the neuter gender ending in the niggahīta (nasal -ṃ) for the word satipaṭṭhāna and others always accepted? Is it not to be said that in 'cattāro satipaṭṭhānā' and so on, 'the word satipaṭṭhāna and others are spoken by way of gender transformation (liṅgavipallāsa)' because of seeing phrases like 'satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā'?

It should not be said so. Why? Because even in 'satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā' and so on, the gender transformation of the words satipaṭṭhāna, citta, and others is not desired. In those instances, the Blessed One, the Lord of Dhamma, spoke 'satipaṭṭno, citto, cittā' out of regard for the word 'dhamma', in order to connect them with the masculine word 'dhamma'. Indeed, the words satipaṭṭhāna, citta, and others, when standing alone, are never connected as masculine ending in 'o'; they are only connected as neuter ending in the niggahīta.

Similarly, in the phrase 'citto gahapati,' the name 'citta', which usually occurs for consciousness (viññāṇa), is attributed to a person by way of designation (paññatti) and made to denote a person, being spoken as 'citto' out of regard for the masculine word 'gahapati'. If, however, the mind (citta) known as consciousness (viññāṇa) were intended, it would be spoken only as 'cittaṃ.' Therefore, in 'citto gahapati, cittā itthī' and so on, gender transformation for the word citta and others is not desired because they are dependent on other words. Just as in this case, gender transformation is not desired in 'satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā' and so on. But in 'cattāro satipaṭṭhānā' and so on, there are no words that the word satipaṭṭhāna and others must regard, which would make them masculine. Therefore, changing only the words like 'cattāro' and taking them as neuter like 'cattāri, sabbāni, etāni'...
301:
...they should be connected with words such as 'satipaṭṭhānā, sammappadhānā.' In such instances, some teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) desire the elision of a syllable (nikāralopa), as in the passage: 'yā pubbe bodhisattānaṃ, pallaṅkavaramābhuja, nimittāni padissantī.' Indeed, non-appearance is elision (lopa); therefore, the construction should be made as 'cattāri satipaṭṭhānāni, cattāri sammappadhānāni, sabbāni mālāni,' and so on.

Some, however, regarding the phrase 'sabbe mālā upenti maṃ,' consider the word 'mālā' to be feminine and, changing the masculine word 'sabbe' by way of the feminine gender, explain the meaning as 'sabbā mālā.' Although such an explanation seems somewhat appropriate, it should not be accepted. For it is not that the Blessed One did not know the gender, nor was he unable to speak by making both words feminine as 'sabbā mālā upenti maṃ.' Yet he recited words of different genders in that way. Even though the Blessed One knew and was capable of speaking [otherwise], he recited words of different genders as 'sabbe mālā upenti maṃ.'

Therefore, changing the masculine word 'sabbe' to the neuter 'sabbāni', and connecting it with the neuter word 'mālā' which has an elided syllable—like the word 'tīṇindriyā' in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi—the meaning should be taken as 'sabbāni mālāni.' This is like the instance in some places: 'yassa ete dhanā atthi,' where the meaning is 'yassa etāni dhanāni.' This point should also be noted here. The word 'mālā' has two genders: feminine and neuter. Let its feminine gender remain [aside] as it is easily understood; however, in its neuter form, it exists as 'tīṇi mālāni.' Neuter usages such as 'mālehi ca gandhehi ca bhagavato sarīraṃ pူဇေန္တိ' are also frequently seen.

'O friend, if the word mālā has two genders, feminine and neuter, what fault is there in assuming the word mālā to be feminine in the phrase "sabbe mālā upenti maṃ"?' There is indeed a fault.
302:
Because the feminine gender word does not have a common grammatical relation (samānādhikaraṇa) with a masculine pronoun, whereas the neuter gender is found to have a common grammatical relation with a masculine pronoun (there is a fault). For this very reason, usages such as "ete dhanā" and so forth are frequently seen in the Pāḷi Canon. If it were said here, "Words such as 'dhanā' are only masculine by way of gender reversal (vipallāsa), because they are used in conjunction with common grammatical relation words like 'ete'," it is not so; these are only neuter.

If words such as "dhanā" were masculine, then in some instances of the nominative singular, there would be words like "dhana" ending in the vowel 'o' used in conjunction with common grammatical relation words ending in 'o' such as "eso". Since such forms do not exist, words like "dhanā, indriyā, viññāṇā" are only neuter. This method is available only in the nominative plural. It should be understood as a conclusion here that neuter words, while having distinct characteristics, appear like masculine forms and associate with masculine words, just as eunuchs (napuṃsaka) who wear the guise of men associate with men.

Furthermore, if they were to reverse their previous statement and say: "In 'citto gahapati' and 'cittā itthī', 'citto' means 'citta exists in this man' and 'cittā' means 'citta exists in this woman'. Just as in 'saddhā (masc.)' and 'saddhā (fem.)', the gender reversal must be determined because it is taken by the power of the meaning 'it exists in him/her'; however, in 'satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā' and so forth, since such a meaning cannot be taken, although it should be said as 'satipaṭṭhānaṃ dhammo, cittaṃ dhammo, cittāni dhammā', it is said as 'satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā' by gender reversal, and thus gender reversal should be desired." That is not so, because in "citto gahapati" etc., and in "satipaṭṭhāno dhammo" etc., the words "citta", "satipaṭṭhāna", etc., are desired to be permanently masculine by way of referring to "gahapati", "dhamma", and so forth.
303:
In fact, even the word "puñña", which is strictly neuter, becomes masculine as "puñño abhisaṅkhāro" by way of referring to "abhisaṅkhāra". Similarly, words like "paduma" and "maṅgala", which are strictly neuter, become masculine and feminine by way of referring to other meanings, such as "padumo Bhagavā, padumā Devī, maṅgalo Bhagavā, maṅgalā itthī". Words like "kālāvaka" and "gaṅgeyya", which denote special noble elephants and are strictly masculine, become neuter by way of referring to the clan (kula), as in "kālāvakañca gaṅgeyyaṃ". Indeed, by way of such reference, the masculine usage is seen in the Commentaries as "kālāvako ca gaṅgeyyo". In this way, by way of referring to various meanings, it is seen that the natural gender (pakatiliṅga) is set aside and the word is established in another gender. Not all such genders become other genders by the power of derivative suffixes (taddhita); rather, they become other genders only by way of referring to "gahapati", "dhamma", and so forth. Therefore, gender reversal (liṅgavipallāsa) should be desired only in places such as "petāni bhoti puttāni, khādamānā tuvaṃ pure; siviputtāni cavhaya; evaṃ dhammāni sutvāna, vippasīdanti paṇḍitā", because the words "dhamma" etc. mentioned therein do not refer to anything else. However, in places such as "citto gahapati, cittā itthī, satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā", gender reversal of the words "citta" etc. should not be desired, because those words refer to "gahapati", "dhamma", and so forth; this is the conclusion to be understood here. This point is a place of confusion for some; therefore, for the sake of the endurance of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma), this method should be well-contemplated by sons of good family who are endowed with faith.

However, the teacher Ācariya Dhammapāla, who resided at the Badaratittha Monastery, said, "In some parts of the Pāḷi, 'padā akkharā vyañjanā' should be seen as a case where gender reversal has been made..."
304:
It was said that in some parts of the Pāḷi, "padā akkharā vyañjanā" should be regarded as a gender reversal. Here, we say that this word "padā" is only neuter, like "indriyā, rūpā", because it does not have the status of ending in the nominative singular by way of an 'o' ending. The other two words (akkharā, vyañjanā), however, should be taken as both neuter and masculine, because they are found to have the status of ending in the nominative singular by way of an 'o' ending or a niggahīta ending. Similarly, gender reversal should be desired only in "puttāni, latāni, pabbatāni, dhammāni" and so forth, because they are not found to be in the nominative singular by way of a niggahīta ending; rather, those words are only seen in the nominative singular by way of 'o' or 'ā' endings. In the phrase "jarādhammaṃ mā jīrī", however, it should be understood that it has become neuter by the power of the meaning of another word.

bhūtaṃ, bhūtāni, bhūtā. bhūtaṃ, bhūtāni, bhūte. bhūtena, bhūtehi, bhūtebhi. bhūtassa, bhūtānaṃ. bhūtā, bhūtasmā, bhūtamhā, bhūtehi, bhūtebhi. bhūtassa, bhūtānaṃ. bhūte, bhūtasmiṃ, bhūtamhi, bhūtesu. bho bhūta, bhavanto bhūtāni, bhavanto bhūtā. Thus is the declension table (nāmikapadamālā) according to the method of the word "citta".

By this method, the declension table of words ending in niggahīta formed from the root 'bhū' such as "mahabhūtaṃ, bhavittaṃ, bhūnaṃ, bhavanaṃ", and other words ending in niggahīta such as "vattaṃ", should be known.

vattaṃ (the round of rebirth), rūpaṃ (form), sotaṃ (ear), ghānaṃ (nose), dukkhaṃ (suffering), pupphaṃ (flower), jhānaṃ (meditation), ñāṇaṃ (knowledge).
dānaṃ (giving), sīlaṃ (virtue), puññaṃ (merit), pāpaṃ (evil), vajjaṃ (fault), saccaṃ (truth), yānaṃ (vehicle), chattaṃ (umbrella).
sakaṭaṃ (cart), kanakaṃ (gold), tagaraṃ (shrub/tagara), nagaraṃ (city), taraṇaṃ (crossing), caraṇaṃ (conduct), dharaṇaṃ (bearing), maraṇaṃ (death).

Protection (tāṇa), root (mūla), wealth (dhana), bank (kūla), blessing (maṅgala), lotus (naḷina), fruit (phala), gold (hirañña), water-born lotus (ambuja), grain (dhanya), net (jāla), sign (liṅga), footstep/word (pada), water (jala), limb (aṅga), leaf (paṇṇa), cemetery (susāna), cloth (saṃ), weapon (āvudha), heart (hadaya), forest (vana), stairs (sopāna), robe (cīvara), life (pāṇa), firebrand (alāta), faculty (indriya), family (kula), metal/copper (loha), bran (kaṇa), strength (bala), bench (pīṭha), egg (aṇḍa), object (ārammaṇa), city (pura), forest (arañña), shore (tīra), Bodhi tree (assattha), and such words should be extracted.

These words are similar to the word 'citta' in every aspect. However, the following words are different. They are:

Words such as "camma, vesma" etc., differ in only one way.
Words such as "kamma, thāma, guṇavanta" etc., differ in many ways.

How?
Camme, cammasmiṃ, cammamhi, cammani. Vesme, vesmasmiṃ, vesmamhi, vesmani. Ghamme, ghammasmiṃ, ghammamhi, ghammani. In this way, other words should also be applied.

Kammaṃ, kammāni, kammā. Kammaṃ, kammāni, kamme. Kammena, kammunā, kammanā, kammehi, kammebhi. Kammassa, kammuno, kammānaṃ. Kammasmā, kammamhā, kammunā, kammehi, kammebhi. Kammassa, kammuno, kammānaṃ. Kamme, kammasmiṃ, kammamhi, kammani, kammesu. O kamma, O kammāni, O kammā.

Regarding the word 'thāma', in the third singular case and others, it should be applied as "thāmena, thāmunā, thāmassa, thāmuno" and "thāmā, thāmasmā, thāmamhā, thāmunā".

For words ending in niggahīta that possess the suffixes -vantu, -mantu, and -imantu, by virtue of usages such as "guṇavaṃ cittaṃ (virtuous mind), rucimaṃ pupphaṃ (beautiful flower), pāpimaṃ kulaṃ (evil family)" —
306:
Guṇavaṃ, guṇavantāni, guṇavantā, guṇavanti. Guṇavantaṃ, guṇavantāni, guṇavante, guṇavanti. Guṇavatā, guṇavantena, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Guṇavatā, guṇavantā, guṇavantasmā, guṇavantamhā, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Guṇavati, guṇavante, guṇavantasmiṃ, guṇavantamhi, guṇavantesu. O guṇavanta, O guṇavantāni, guṇavanti.

In this way, it should be applied as "rucimaṃ, rucimantāni, rucimaṃ" etc., and "pāpimaṃ, pāpimantāni, pāpimaṃ" etc. Furthermore, in this context, usages such as "guṇavaṃ, balavaṃ, yasavṃ, satimaṃ, gatimaṃ" etc., should be expanded.

By virtue of the usage of the word 'karonta' as in "karontaṃ cittaṃ (the mind that is doing), karontaṃ kulaṃ (the family that is doing)" —

Karontaṃ, karontāni, karontā, karonti. Karontaṃ, karontāni, karonte, karonti. Karotā, karontena, karontehi, karontebhi. Karoto, karato, karontassa, karontānaṃ, karotaṃ. Karotā, karontā, karontasmā, karontamhā, karontehi, karontebhi. Karoto, karato, karontassa, karontānaṃ, karotaṃ. Karoti, karonte, karontasmiṃ, karontamhi, karontesu. O karonta, O karontāni, O karontā, O karontī—thus it should be applied.

By virtue of the usage of the word 'gacchanta' as in "gacchantaṃ cittaṃ (the mind that is going), gacchantaṃ kulaṃ (the family that is going)" —

Gacchantaṃ, gacchantāni, gacchantā. Gacchantaṃ, gacchantāni, gacchante. Gacchatā, gacchantena, gacchantehi, gacchantebhi. Gacchato, gacchantassa, gacchantānaṃ, gacchataṃ. Gacchatā, gacchantā, gacchantasmā, gacchantamhā ...
307:
...by those who go, because of those who go. Of the one who goes, to the one who goes, of those who go, to those who go. In the one who goes, in those who go, in the one who goes, in the one who goes, in those who go. O one who goes, O those who go, O sirs who go, those who go—thus it should be applied.

In this same manner, the declension (nāmika-padamālā) should be applied to words such as 'carantaṃ' (one who walks), 'dadantaṃ' (one who gives), 'tiṭṭhantaṃ' (one who stands), 'cintayantaṃ' (one who thinks), etc.

However, there is some distinction in the word 'mahanta'. This is because the neuter usage "mahā" is seen in "vārāṇasirajjaṃ nāma mahā" (the kingship of Bārāṇasī is great); thus, the sequence should be understood as "mahantaṃ, mahā, mahantāni, mahantā. Mahantaṃ, mahantāni, mahante. Mahatā". All these are different from the word 'citta'.

This is the analysis of the declension of the natural forms of neuter gender words ending in niggahīta.

## The Neuter Gender Ending in Niggahīta with the Nature of the Vowel 'a'
## is Finished.

Now, placing the views of the former teachers at the forefront, I shall state the declension of the word 'atthivibhāvi' (one who explains the meaning), which has been shortened (to a short 'i')—

Aṭṭhi, aṭṭhī, aṭṭhīni. Aṭṭhiṃ, aṭṭhī, aṭṭhīni. Aṭṭhinā, aṭṭhīhi, aṭṭhībhi. Aṭṭhissa, aṭṭhino, aṭṭhīnaṃ. Aṭṭhinā, aṭṭhīhi, aṭṭhībhi. Aṭṭhissa, aṭṭhino, aṭṭhīnaṃ. Aṭṭhismiṃ, aṭṭhimhi, aṭṭhīsu. O aṭṭhi, O aṭṭhī, O aṭṭhīni. This is the view of Yamaka Mahāthera.

In this regard, although the forms "aṭṭhismā, aṭṭhimhā" do not appear in the ablative case (nissakka-vacana), they should be accepted because similar usages are found in various Pali texts. Just like the word 'aṭṭhi', the forms of words such as "satthi, dadhi, vāri, akkhi, acchi" etc., also occur.
308:
Atthavibhāvi, atthavibhāvī, atthavibhāvīni. Atthavibhāviṃ, atthavibhāvī, atthavibhāvīni. Atthavibhāvinā, atthavibhāvīhi, atthavibhāvībhi. Atthavibhāvissa, atthavibhāvino, atthavibhāvīnaṃ. Atthavibhāvinā, atthavibhāvismā, atthavibhāvimhā, atthavibhāvīhi, atthavibhāvībhi. Atthavibhāvissa, atthavibhāvino, atthavibhāvīnaṃ. Atthavibhāvismiṃ, atthavibhāvimhi, atthavibhāvīsu. O atthavibhāvi, O atthavibhāvī, O atthavibhāvīni.

In the same way, 'dhammavibhāvi', 'cittānuparivatti', 'sukhakāri', etc., are also formed. Among those words, 'aṭṭhi', 'satthi', etc., are primary genders (padhānaliṅga) because they do not depend on others, while 'atthavibhāvi', 'dhammavibhāvi', etc., are secondary genders (appadhānaliṅga) because they depend on others.

This is the analysis of the declension of the natural forms of neuter nouns ending in -i.

## The section on neuter nouns ending in -i is finished.

Now, I shall state the declension of 'gotrabhu' (the word 'āyu'), which has been shortened, following the views of former teachers:

Āyu, āyū, āyūni. Āyuṃ, āyū, āyūni. Āyunā, āyūhi, āyūbi. Āyussa, āyuno, āyūnaṃ. Āyunā, āyūhi, āyūbi. Āyussa, āyuno, āyūnaṃ. Āyusmiṃ, āyumhi, āyūsu. O āyu, O āyū, O āyūni. This is the view of Yamaka Mahāthera.

In this context, although the forms "āyusmā, āyumhā" do not appear in the [paradigm of the] ablative case, they should be accepted because similar usages are seen in various Pali texts. Here, the word 'āyu' should be understood as existing in both masculine and neuter genders. That this is so, in the Pali and Commentaries, of that word 'āyu'...
309:
It is observed that there are two genders. In such places as "punarāyu ca me laddhā, evaṃ jānāhi mārisa. āyu cassa parikkhīṇo ahosi", the word 'āyu' is masculine. By the power of that masculine gender, the declension should be applied as far as possible according to the 'bhikkhu' method, such as "āyu, āyū, āyavo". However, in places such as "aggaṃ āyu ca vaṇṇo ca. kittakaṃ panassa āyū", it is neuter. By the power of that neuter gender, it is declined as "āyu, āyū, āyūnī".

Gotrabhu, gotrabhū, gotrabhūni. Gotrabhuṃ, gotrabhū, gotrabhūni. Gotrabhunā, gotrabhūhi, gotrabhūbhi. Gotrabhussa, gotrabhuno, gotrabhūnaṃ. Gotrabhunā, gotrabhusmā, gotrabhumhā, gotrabhūhi, gotrabhūbhi. Gotrabhussa, gotrabhuno, gotrabhūnaṃ. Gotrabhusmiṃ, gotrabhumhi, gotrabhūsu. O gotrabhu, O gotrabhū, O gotrabhūni. O gotrabhū, O gotrabhūni—thus the plural also occurs. This is our view. In this same way, the declension of other words ending in -u formed with the root 'bhū', such as 'cittasahabhu', and other similar words, should be applied. However, the word 'gotrabhū' ending in -ū which refers to a person, being included in the masculine gender, falls under the 'sabbaññū' method. Other words besides those are "cakkhu, vasu, dhanu, dāru, tipu, madhu, siṅgu, hiṅgu, cittagu", and so forth.

This is the determination of the division of the natural declension of neuter nouns ending in -u.

## The natural state of ending in the vowels u and ū.
## The neuter gender ending in -u is finished.

In this way, the three types of neuter genders—by way of ending in Niggahīta, ending in -i, and ending in -u—have been completely covered. Among those three types—
310:
In some words ending in Niggahīta, a distinction is seen in some nominative singular and plural forms by way of substituting the 'e' vowel. For example: "sukhe dukkhe. ekūnapannāsa ājīvakasate ekūnapannāsa paribbājakasate", and so forth. O Venerable Sir, since such forms are seen in the Pāḷi, should it not be said that "there is also a neuter gender ending in -e"? It should not be said so. Because those forms are merely special forms included within the Niggahīta-ending category. Since they are established by way of substitution (ādesa), there is no separate neuter gender ending in -e. Therefore, only the three types of neuter genders mentioned above should be accepted.

The declension of neuter nouns, which is full of methods, has been analyzed by me for the sake of the Great Sage's Dispensation.
