For whomsoever this Saddanīti text is proficient and well-cultivated, he becomes a refuge and a resort for the sons of good family in the Dispensation.

## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the sake of the proficiency of the wise in the paths of expression in the Tipitaka together with its Commentaries and the ninefold [dispensation],
## the division of the natural declension of neuter nouns
## is the Ninth Chapter.

## 10. Mixed Declension of the Three Genders
Following the words with a single syllable and words with more syllables, I shall declare the declension of the three genders mixed together without confusion—

to the extent of my ability, for the sake of the deep intellectual range of the wise in meanings that have reached various subtle conventions.

Itthī and thī, pabhā and bhā, girā and rā, pavanaṃ and vanaṃ.

Udaka and daka, kaṃ, vitakka, and so forth.
311:
## Bhū, bhūmi, and arañña, araññānī, etc.
## Paññā, paññāṇa, and ñāṇa, etc., may be of three kinds.
## Ko, vi, sā, and bhā, rā, thī, dhī, ku, bhū, as well as kaṃ,
## Khaṃ, go, mo, mā, and saṃ, yaṃ, taṃ, kim, etc., are single-syllabled.

This is the summary of the mixed declension of the three genders. Among those nouns, the declension of the word 'itthī' (woman) is: Itthī, itthī, itthiyo. Itthiṃ. (etc.) O women, bhotiyo itthiyo.

The declension of the word 'thī' (woman) is: Thī, thiyo. Thiṃ, thī, thiyo. Thiyā, thīhi, thībhi. Thiyā, thīnaṃ. Thiyā, thīhi, thībhi. Thiyā, thīnaṃ. Thiyā, thiyaṃ, thīsu. O woman, bhoti thi; O women, bhotiyo thī, bhotiyo thiyo. Here—

"Cocks, gems, staffs, and women of auspicious signs arise for a person who is without sin and has performed merit.
One should not reveal a secret to a woman. The nature of women is difficult to know."
These are the illustrative examples.

The declension of the word 'pabhā' (radiance) is: Pabhā, pabhā, pabhāyo. Pabhaṃ. (etc.) O radiances, bhotiyo pabhāyo.

The declension of the word 'bhā' (radiance) is: Bhā, bhā, bhāyo. Bhaṃ, bhā, bhāyo. Bhāya, bhāhi, bhābhi. Bhāya, bhānaṃ. Bhāya, bhāhi, bhābhi. Bhāya, bhānaṃ. Bhāya, bhāyaṃ, bhāsu. O radiance, bhoti bhe; O radiances, bhotiyo bhā, bhotiyo bhāyo. Here also, "bhākaro (sun)", "bhānu (sun)", etc., are illustrative examples.
312:
The declension of the word girā (speech) is: girā, girā, girāyo. giraṃ. etc. O speeches, bhotiyo girāyo. "Vācā, girā, byappatho (speech)", "O friends, I shall praise you with speeches in due order"—these are the illustrative examples of the feminine gender of the word girā.

The word rā denoting gold is masculine. However, here, the word rā denoting sound is feminine.

The declension of the word rā (sound) is: rā, rā, rāyo. raṃ, rā, rāyo. rāya, rāhi, rābhi. rāya, rānaṃ. rāya, rāhi, rābhi. rāya, rānaṃ. rāya, rāyaṃ, rāsu. O sound, bhoti re, O sounds, bhotiyo rā, bhotiyo rāyo.

It is said that rā means sound. In the Aggañña Sutta Ṭīkā, it is stated: "At this night time, the sound of beings is cut off, therefore it is called ratti (night); it is the time when the sound of beings is calmed." Therefore, since the word rā denotes sound, the word ratti is an illustrative example.

The declension of the word pavana is: pavanaṃ, pavanāni, pavanā. pavanaṃ, pavanāni, pavane.

The declension of the word vana is: vanaṃ, vanāni, vanaā. vanaṃ, vanāni, vane. The rest should be understood as previously explained.

The words pavana and vana sometimes have the same meaning and sometimes different meanings. They are synonymous when denoting a forest, as in: "At that time, fulfilling those dhammas, he entered the pavana (forest). Along with his son, he entered the vana (forest)." However, they have different meanings when denoting wind, craving, and forest respectively, as in: "Where the extremely foul-smelling wind (pavana) blows," and "O monks, having cut down the forest (vana) and the undergrowth (vanatha), be those without a forest (nibbanā)," etc. 

The declension of the word udaka is: udakaṃ, udakāni, udakā. udakaṃ, udakāni, udake.

The declension of the word daka is: dakaṃ, dakāni, dakā. dakaṃ, dakāni, dake. The rest should be understood as previously explained.
313:
"Ambapakkaṃ dakaṃ sītaṃ. Thalajā dakajā pupphā" (Ripe mango, cool water. Flowers born on land and born in water), etc., are the illustrative examples here. In Pali passages such as "Nīlodaṃ vanamajjhato. Mahodadhi. Udabindunipātena, udakumbhopi pūratī" (Blue water from the midst of the forest. Great ocean. By the falling of water drops, even a water-pot is filled), the word "uda" itself expresses the meaning of "udaka" (water) because it stands at the end of a compound. It is like using the word "rittassa" to mean "rittassāda" (empty taste) in a context where "rittassādaṃ" should be said. In the Pali Canon, the word "uda" is never seen alone. If it exists, it should be carefully noted.

kaṃ, kāni, kā. kaṃ, kāni, ke. kena, kehi, kebhi. kassa, kānaṃ. kā, kasmā, kamhā, kehi, kebhi. kassa, kānaṃ. ke, kasmiṃ, kamhi, kesu. O friend (ka), O friends (kā), O friends (kāni). Alternatively, the plural can be joined with the word "bho", as in "bho kāni, bho kā".

Here, "kaṃ" is said to mean water, head, and happiness. Examples such as "kantāro, kandaro, kevaṭṭā, kesā, karuṇā, nāko" should be known. Among those words, "kantāro": "kaṃ" means water, and because it must be crossed or passed over [where there is no] water, it is called "kantāra"; it is a waterless region. However, in terms like "corakantāra" (thief-infested wilderness), it should be noted that by tradition (rūḷhī), the word "kantāra" also applies to a place difficult to travel. In the word "kandaro", "kaṃ" means water, and because it is split or eroded by that water, it is called "kandara" (a grotto/cleft). In words like "kevaṭṭā", they are called "kevaṭṭa" (fishermen) because they move in water (ke) or because the word occurs in the sense of catching (fish). They are called "kesā" (hair) because they depend on and arise on the head (ke). It is called "karuṇā" (compassion) because it obstructs (rundhati) happiness (kaṃ). "Nāko" refers to the celestial realm. "Kaṃ" is happiness, "na kaṃ" is "akaṃ" (suffering); because it is a place where that suffering does not exist, it is called "nāka" (heaven).
314:
...should be taken. Just as the declension of words like "itthī" is applied here, similarly, the declension of "vitakko, vicāro, ābhā, padīpo", etc., should also be applied.

bhū, bhū, bhuyo. bhuṃ, bhū, bhuyo. bhuyā, bhūhi, bhūbhi. bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. bhuyā, bhūhi, bhūbhi. bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. bhuyā, bhuyaṃ, bhūsu. O lady (bhu), O ladies (bhū), O ladies (bhuyo). Examples here are "bhūruho, bhūpālo, bhūbhujo, bhūtalaṃ".

bhūmi, bhūmī, bhūmiyo. The remaining cases should be expanded and understood.

araññaṃ, araññāni, araññā. The remaining cases should be expanded and understood.

Araññānī is said to mean a great forest. Like the word "gahapatānī", it is a word formed by the power of the "inī" suffix and is feminine. The reading "araññānī" is also found in the Commentaries.

araññānī, araññānī, araññāniyo. araññāniṃ, araññānī, araññāniyo. araññāniyā, araññānīhi, araññānībhi. araññāniyā, araññānīnaṃ. araññāniyā, araññānīhi, araññānībhi. araññāniyā, araññānīnaṃ. araññāniyā, araññāniyaṃ, araññānīsu. O lady (araññāni), O ladies (araññānī), O ladies (araññāniyo).

Just as it is applied here according to the aforementioned method, it should also be applied in words like "sabhā, sabhāyaṃ". Sabhāyaṃ is simply sabhā (a hall).
315:
But it is said thus due to the interchange of genders (liṅgavyattaya). The Pali "Sabhāye vā dvāramūle vā vatthabbaṃ" is an example here.

Paññā (meaning): paññā, paññā, paññāyo. paññaṃ, paññā, paññāyo. paññāya.

Paññāṇa (meaning): paññāṇaṃ, paññāṇāni, paññāṇā. paññāṇaṃ, paññāṇāni, paññāṇe. paññāṇena.

"Tathā hi bhante bhagavato sīlapaññāṇaṃ. Sādhu paññāṇavā naro" (For thus, Bhante, is the Blessed One's sign of virtue. Excellent is the man possessed of wisdom), etc., are the illustrative examples here.

Ñāṇa (meaning): ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇāni, ñāṇā. ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇāni, ñāṇe. ñāṇena. All the rest should be understood. In words like "aggi, aggini, gini", the declension should be applied according to the groups that will follow.

In single-syllable (ekakkhara) words like "ko, vī, sā", the word "ko" refers to Brahmā, wind, and the body. Because it denotes these, these usages exist. What are they?

"I worship the lotus-feet of that Victorious Buddha, who brought immeasurable benefit to the world, which are frequented by the bees that are the crowns (of Brahmās)."

kakudharukkho (Kakudha tree), karajakāyo (body), etc., are examples. Among them, in "kamoḷialisevitaṃ", poets intend it to mean (the feet) frequented by the bees which are the crowns of many hundreds of worshipping Brahmās. In the word "kakudharukkho", "ko" refers to wind; teachers say that tree is called "kakudha" because it "angers" (suppresses) that wind, or prevents it by way of removing wind-related diseases. In the word "karajakāyo", "ko" refers to the body; the dust (raja) produced in that body is called "karaja".
316:
What is it? It is semen and blood. Because that (semen and blood) is the effect of the 'dust' (raja) of passion—as it is said, 'Passion is dust, but a speck of dust is not called dust'—it is qualified by the word 'ka', which denotes the body, and is called 'karaja' by way of metonymy (naming the cause by the effect). Teachers say that the body produced by that 'karaja' known as semen and blood is 'karajakāya'. For that very reason, it is said, 'The body is born from the parents.' However, in the Mahā-assapura Sutta Tīkā, it is stated: 'It is called "kara" because it is produced (cast) into the womb; it is the descent of rebirth-linking. Because it is born from that "kara", it is called "karaja", meaning it is born from the semen and blood of the parents. Other teachers say it is born from "kara" because it is produced by the form of the mother and so on. In both cases, "karajakāya" refers to the matter of fourfold origin (catusantati-rūpa).' This latter meaning, however, is not intended here; only the former meaning is intended due to the context of the word "ka".

Ka (Interrogative): Ko, Kā. Kaṃ, Ke. Kena, Kehi, Kebhi. Kassa, Kānaṃ. Kā, Kasmā, Kamhā, Kehi, Kebhi. Kassa, Kānaṃ. Ke, Kasmiṃ, Kamhi, Kesu. Bho Ka, Bhavanto Kā.

In that context (of the letter Vi), 'vī' refers to a bird. For that very reason, the king of the Garudas, who is the lord of birds, is called 'vinda'. Aiming at this meaning, the former teachers also spoke this verse:

'O Lord of Sages (Muninda), I place upon my head, bowed in faith, Your pair of lotus feet which are free from blame. That pair of lotus feet cannot be shaken (divided) even by the hosts of lords of devas, lords of nāgas, and lords of men.'

In that verse, 'vīnaṃ indo' (lord of birds) is 'vindo', meaning the king of the Garudas born in the bird species.

Vī (Bird): Viṃ, Vī, Vayo. Viṃ, Vī, Vayo. Vinā, Vīhi, Vībhi. Vissa, Vino, Vīnaṃ. Vinā, Vismā, Vimhā, Vīhi, Vībhi. Vissa, Vino, Vīnaṃ. Vismiṃ, Vimhi, Vīsu. Bho Vi, Bhavanto Vayo.
317:
Among those (words with various meanings), the word 'sā' is said to mean a female dog. However, in phrases such as 'I have a mother, that mother should be supported by me,' the word 'sā' should be understood as being derived from the word 'ta', which is included in pronouns and refers to a person who is absent (third person). The paradigms (padamālā) of the words 'sā', 'bhā', 'rā', 'thī', 'bhū', and 'ka' have been shown below.

The word 'dhī' is said to mean wisdom. In this context, 'O dear one, know the ministers who are wise and skilled in the welfare' and words such as 'dhīmā, dhīmati, sudhī, sudhinī, dhīyuttaṃ' are illustrative examples.

Paradigm of the word Dhī:
Dhī, Dhī, Dhiyo. (Nominative)
Dhiṃ, Dhī, Dhiyo. (Accusative)
Dhiyā, Dhīhi, Dhībhi. (Instrumental)
Dhiyā, Dhīnaṃ. (Dative)
Dhiyā, Dhīhi, Dhībhi. (Ablative)
Dhiyā, Dhīnaṃ. (Genitive)
Dhiyā, Dhiyaṃ, Dhīsu. (Locative)
Bhoti Dhi, Bhotiyo Dhī, Bhotiyo Dhiyo. (Vocative)

The word 'ku' is said to mean the earth. In this context, 'kudālo' (hoe), 'kumudaṃ' (white water-lily), and 'kuñjaro' (elephant) are illustrative examples. Among these words, it is called 'kudālo' because one digs (dālayati), pierces, or breaks the earth (kuṃ) with this instrument. It is called 'kumudaṃ' because it delights in the earth (kuyāṃ/water). It is called 'kuñjaro' because it makes the earth (kuṃ) tremble. Thus, it is said in the Vimānavatthu Commentary: 'It is called kuñjaro because it makes the earth (kuṃ) tremble by treading on it with its feet.'

Paradigm of the word Ku:
Ku, Kū, Kuyo. (Nominative)
Kuṃ, Kū, Kuyo. (Accusative)
Kuyā, Kūhi, Kūbhi. (Instrumental)
Kuyā, Kūnaṃ. (Dative)
Kuyā, Kūhi, Kūbhi. (Ablative)
Kuyā, Kūnaṃ. (Genitive)
Kuyā, Kuyaṃ, Kūsu. (Locative)
Bhoti Ku, Bhotiyo Kū, Bhotiyo Kuyo. (Vocative)

The word 'khaṃ' is stated to mean a sense faculty (indriya).
The word 'khaṃ' is said to mean the sky (ākāsa).
The celestial realm (heaven) is also called 'khaṃ'.
Emptiness (suññatta) is also known as 'khaṃ'.
318:
Among those (four meanings), it is called 'kha' (faculty) because it is the destination and dwelling place of eye-consciousness and so on. It is called 'kha' (sky) in the sense of being void. Heaven is known as 'kha' because it is the place where those who have performed good deeds must certainly go. Examples in this context include: 'Just as a bird (khago) perched on the top of a tree shakes the branch while alighting,' and 'The Self-Enlightened One, having created one hundred and eight signs in the sky (khe), proceeded forth.'

Paradigm of the word Khaṃ:
Khaṃ, Khāni, Khā. (Nominative)
Khaṃ, Khāni, Khe. (Accusative)
Khena, Khehi, Khebhi. (Instrumental)
Khassa, Khānaṃ. (Dative)
Khā, Khasmā, Khamhā, Khehi, Khebhi. (Ablative)
Khassa, Khānaṃ. (Genitive)
Khe, Khasmiṃ, Khamhā, Khesu. (Locative)
Bho Kha, Bhavanto Khāni, Bhavanto Khā. (Vocative)

## The meanings of the word 'Go' are extracted and stated as follows:
The word 'go' refers to an ox, a sense faculty, the earth, speech, wisdom, the sun, a ray, and water. Among these meanings, in the sense of an ox, it is both feminine and masculine; in the remaining meanings, it is masculine.

Thus, in phrases such as 'He went while the cows (gosu) were being milked' and 'One who has five cows (gopañcamo)', the word 'go' is used in the sense of an ox. In the word 'gocara', it is also used in the sense of a sense faculty; it is called 'gocara' (resort) because the faculties (gāvo) such as the eye range over this object. Thus, the ancient teachers said: 'It is called gocara because cows range there; it is called gocara because it is like a gocara, a place to be frequented repeatedly. "Gāvo" refers to the faculties such as the eye, and the place where those faculties range is called gocara.' In the compositions of ancient poets such as 'I bow to the Gotama who possesses the earth (gomatiṃ)', it is used in the sense of the earth. The meaning is: 'I worship the Gotama Buddha, the Fully Enlightened One, who possesses great wisdom.' Likewise, in the commentary on the Vāseṭṭha Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta: '"Gorakkha" means guarding the fields (khettarakkha) or guarding the cultivation (kasirakkha). The earth is called "go", and a portion of that earth is called a field (khetta).'
319:
In the statement “He is called Gotama by lineage,” the name Gotama also pertains to knowledge (buddhi). Therefore, the ancient teachers said, “It is called gotta because it protects speech (gāṃ).” This name, occurring as “Gotama,” protects both speech and knowledge; it is called gotta because it protects them as its certain objects. Just as knowledge does not occur without an object (ārammaṇa), so a name (abhidhāna) cannot occur without the signified meaning (abhidheyya). Therefore, that meaning called “gotta” is said to protect and guard them (speech and knowledge). What is that meaning? It should be understood as the common characteristic (sāmaññarūpa) that is not shared with other lineages, descends from the first person of that lineage, and is common to all members of that lineage. Indeed, those born in that lineage, such as King Suddhodana and others, are also called “Gotama.” Therefore, the Blessed One said to his father, King Suddhodana, “O Gotama, the Tathāgatas are the most excellent of the excellent.” The Great King Vessavaṇa also addressed the Blessed One, saying, “We pay homage to the Buddha Gotama, who is endowed with knowledge and conduct.” The Venerable Vaṅgīsa also said to the Venerable Ānanda, “O Gotama, out of compassion, please preach well the way to extinguishment (Nirvana).” Thus, this common characteristic is called “gotta” because it protects speech (gāṃ). That lineage is also manifold, such as the Gotama lineage, the Kassapa lineage, and so forth.

Likewise, the word “go” also pertains to the Sun (Ādicca). The composition of the ancient teachers, “I pay homage to Gotama of the Go-lineage,” is the evidence here; it means “I pay homage to the Fully Enlightened One, Gotama, who is of the Sun's lineage.” For the Sun was born in the Gotama lineage, and so was the Blessed One. Thus, because of being of the same lineage as the Sun, praise of the Blessed One is seen in various places with words such as “Kinsman of the Sun” (Ādiccabandhu), as in: “I ask you, O Kinsman of the Sun, Great Sage, about seclusion and the peaceful state,” and “I always pay homage to the Jetavana monastery, the dwelling place of the Kinsman of the Sun,” and “The sole friend of the world, the kinsman of the friend of the lotus (the Sun).” In the word “uṇhagū,” however, the word “go”...
320:
rays. Because he has hot rays (gāvo), he is called 'uṇhagū' (the sun). The former teachers also explained this very meaning in the treatise Chandoviciti.

In the term 'gosītacandana', the word 'go' refers to water. For by the word 'go', water is expressed. It means sandalwood that is cool like water. If that sandalwood is placed into hot oil that has just been removed from the stove and is boiling, that oil becomes very cool at that very moment.

Regarding this, some say: "Sirs, why do you say that the word 'go' occurring in the sense of 'ox/cow' is both feminine and masculine? And why do you say that when it occurs in the senses of 'sense organ, earth, speech, wisdom, sun, ray, and water', it is masculine? Among these, let it be masculine when occurring in the sense of the sun; but should not the word 'go' occurring in the senses of 'sense organ, speech, and water' be neuter? And should it not be feminine when occurring in the senses of 'earth, wisdom, and ray'? This is because we see the designation of gender as neuter for words like 'indriya' (sense organ) and feminine for words like 'pathavī' (earth) when they occur in those respective meanings."

That statement is not correct, because there is no such fixed rule. For even when referring to a female (itthi) meaning, some words are seen to be designated in the masculine gender, such as 'orodha' (harem/consorts). And even when referring to a male (purisa) meaning, some words are seen to be designated in the feminine gender, as in the statement: "O Yakkha, you are one who desires my welfare; O Devatā, you are one who desires my benefit." Furthermore, even for words that do not refer to female or male meanings, some words occurring in a single meaning such as 'wisdom' are seen to be designated according to feminine, masculine, or neuter genders, such as 'paññā' (fem.), 'amoha' (masc.), and 'ñāṇa' (neut.); and 'taṭaṃ' (neut.), 'taṭī' (fem.), 'taṭo' (masc.) for 'shore'. Similarly, although it is not a female, a tree receives the name
321:
'Mātulā' by way of the feminine gender, and based on that tree, a city also receives its name. Therefore, it is said in the Cakkavatti Sutta Ṭīkā: "'Mātulā' is the name of a certain tree obtained by way of the feminine gender; because it was established in a place near that tree, the city was also known as 'Mātulā'." Thus, 'mātulāyaṃ' means in the city of this name.

The declension (nāmika-padamālā) of the word 'go' has been shown below.

'Mo' refers to the moon. In the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), however, the reading 'mā' ending in 'ā' is seen. It should be the reading ending in 'o', because according to the method taken from the Sanskrit Ekakkharakosa, it should be stated as ending in 'o' as in: "Mo refers to Siva and the moon." In this context, the word 'ma' stated as ending in 'o' as a word for the moon has examples such as 'puṇṇamī' and 'puṇṇamā'. Therein, it is called 'puṇṇamī' because the full moon (mo) is in this night; likewise 'puṇṇamā' is a feminine usage in consideration of the night (ratti). In this regard, there is this evidence: "On the night of the Visākha full moon (puṇṇamā), in the first watch, he recollected his past lives." Here it might be asked: If this word 'puṇṇamā' is feminine in consideration of the night, then in verses such as:

"As the moon shines purely in the full moon circle,
So may you, with a full mind, shine in the ten-thousandfold world."
And:
"On the fifteenth day of the half-month, on the full moon (puṇṇamāye) Sabbath,
Having mounted the elephant vehicle, he came to give gifts."

How is the word 'puṇṇamāye' formed? It is formed by the substitution of 'ya' with 'ye'. For the Blessed One, the Lord of the Dhamma, while he should have said 'puṇṇamāyā', said 'puṇṇamāye', reciting 'ye' in place of 'ya'; in the feminine context, in place of the long 'ā'...
322:
...It is like the substitution of the letter 'e', and the substitution of 'ne' in place of 'nī'. This is true; in the Rādhajātaka, it is stated: "abyayataṃ vilapasi viratte kosiyāyane." Although it should be said as "virattā," by saying "viratte," the letter 'e' is read in place of 'ā'. Although it should be said as "kosiyāyanī," by saying "kosiyāyane," 'ne' is read in place of 'nī'. In this way, the Venerable, while saying "puṇṇamāye" when it should be "puṇṇamāyā," reads 'ye' in place of 'yā'. In the teaching of the Mahāsamaya Sutta, it is stated: "dakkhitāye aparājitasanghaṃ." Although it should be said as "dakkhitāyā," by saying "dakkhitāye," 'ye' is read in place of 'yā'; it is the same in this case. However, in the phrase "sabhāye vā dvāramūle vā," the word 'sabhā' is expressed as "sabhāyaṃ" by way of gender transformation (liṅgabyattaya). In this case of "puṇṇamāyaṃ," it is not expressed by gender transformation, but rather by the power of the feminine gender ending in 'ā'. Therefore, the word "puṇṇamāye" should be understood as a locative case (bhūmma) formed by the pronunciation of 'ye' in place of 'yā'.

"Mā" refers to Siri (glory). This is true; in the Vidvamukhamandaṇa-ṭīkā, when explaining the meaning of the word "mālinī," it is said: "Mā vuccati lakkhī, alinī bhamarī—Mā is called Lakkhī (glory); alinī is called a female bee." The word 'Lakkhī' has the same meaning as 'Siri'. Therefore, we agree with the meaning "Mā is called Siri." Similarly, ancient teachers have also shown the meaning: "Maṃ siriṃ dhāreti vidadhāti cāti mandhātā—Because he bears and bestows glory (Siri), he is called Mandhātu." Therefore, the words "mālinī" and "mandhātā" are illustrative examples here. Among them, the declension (nāmikapadamālā) of the masculine word "ma" is as follows:
Mo, mā. Maṃ, me. Mena, mehi, mebhi. Massa, mānaṃ. Mā, masmā, mamhā, mehi, mebhi. Massa, mānaṃ. Me, masmiṃ, mamhi, mesu. Bho ma, bhavanto mā.
323:
This is the declension (nāmikapadamālā) of the feminine word 'mā':
Mā, mā, māyo. Maṃ, mā, māyo. Māya, māhi, mābi. Māya, mānaṃ. Māya, māhi, mābi. Māya, mānaṃ. Māya, māyaṃ, māsu. Bhoti me, bhotiyo māyo.

In this context, the word 'mā' expressing glory and the word 'rā' expressing sound are similar in their grammatical behavior because they are single-syllable words, naturally ending in 'ā', and are of the feminine gender.

Among them, 'saṃ' refers to a man of peaceful mind. In the world, people speak of such a person as a 'virtuous man' (sappurisa), an 'noble one' (ariya), or a 'wise man' (paṇḍita); 'sa' is a designation for him. Thus, regarding the existence of the word 'saṃ' expressing a virtuous man, an noble one, or a wise man in the nominative case (paccattavacana), the sentence "sameti asatā asaṃ" (the virtuous man does not associate with the unvirtuous) is an illustrative usage. In this sentence, when considering the compound "na saṃ asaṃ," it is understood that the meanings of 'virtuous man' and 'unvirtuous man' are expressed by the words 'saṃ' and 'asaṃ'. Therefore, one should not say, "The word 'saṃ' in the nominative case expressing the meaning of a virtuous man does not exist." The words of those who say "it does not exist" should not be accepted. The declension of that word 'saṃ' has been shown below as "saṃ, santaṃ, sante," etc.

When it is of the neuter gender, 'saṃ' refers to wealth (dhana). "Manussassaṃ" (human's wealth), "parassaṃ" (another's wealth), "sabbassaṃ" (all wealth), "sabbassaharaṇaṃ" (stealing all wealth), "parassaharaṇaṃ" (stealing another's wealth), etc., are illustrative words in this context. Among those words, 'manussassa saṃ' becomes 'manussassaṃ'. In this way, 'parassa saṃ' is 'parassaṃ', and 'sabbassa saṃ' is 'sabbassaṃ'. Stealing that wealth is 'parassaharaṇaṃ' or 'sabbassaharaṇaṃ', which are compound words (samāsa). Similarly, 'saṃ' is also said to mean happiness and peace. In ancient poetry, it is stated that it expresses those meanings as follows:
324:
## "Devadevo saṃdehī no, hīno devātidehato.
## Hatopapātasaṃsāro, sāro saṃ detu dehinanti."

Therefore, this verse is an example in this context, as is the word "sankaro" in the phrase "sakalalokasaṅkaro dīpaṅkaro." It should be understood according to the method previously shown: "saṃ, sāni, sā. saṃ, sāni, se. sena," and so on. In this regard, to generate expertise in the excellent teaching of the Buddha for the listeners, I shall fully state the declension of the word 'saṃ' when it occurs at the end of a compound:

Manussassaṃ, manussassāni, manussassā. Manussassaṃ, manussassāni, manussassē. Manussassēna, manussassēhi, manussassēbi. Manussassassa, manussassānaṃ. Manussassā, manussassasmā, manussassamhā, manussassēhi, manussassēbi. Manussassassa, manussassānaṃ. Manussassē, manussassasmiṃ, manussassamhi, manussassēsu. O manussassa, O manussassāni, manussassā.

"Parassaṃ," "sabbassaṃ," etc., follow this same method. All these words should be understood to follow the gender of the object they denote.

As for the declension of the words 'yaṃ', 'taṃ', and 'kiṃ', I shall show them in the section on pronouns (sabbanāmapariccheda) in the three genders.

Thus, the declensions of the words 'ko', 'vi', 'sā', etc., mentioned below, have been analyzed along with illustrative words for other meanings. In that regard, the determination of gender is as follows:

'Ko', 'vi', and 'sā' occur in the masculine gender. 'Bhā', 'rā', 'thī', 'dhī', 'ku', and 'bhū' occur in the feminine gender. 'Kaṃ' and 'khaṃ' occur in the neuter gender. The word 'go' occurs in both masculine and feminine genders. The word 'mo' occurs in the masculine gender. The word 'mā' occurs in the feminine gender. The word 'saṃ' occurs in both masculine and neuter genders. The words 'yaṃ', 'taṃ', and 'kiṃ' occur in all genders.

Other single-syllable words (ekakkhara) besides these should also be examined and noted.
325:
Thus, for the purpose of obtaining extremely pure and extensive wisdom for the wise who are skilled in the arrangement of words, for the purpose of not being confused in the extremely subtle and profound meanings, and for the purpose of displaying intellectual prowess in the Word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) within the Tipitaka—just as a lion king displays its prowess on a golden ground—the declension of nouns (nāmika-padamālā) has been analyzed by mixing the three genders through the power of many additional syllables.

Some are skilled in words, but not in meaning;
Some are skilled in meaning, but not in words.
Therefore, the wise should constantly apply effort,
For supreme mastery in both is the best, so say the wise.

## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the mastery of the wise in the modes of expression of the Tipitaka, the ninefold Dispensation of the Teacher together with the Commentaries,
## the analysis of the declension of nouns mixing the three genders,
## the tenth chapter, is concluded.

## 11. Declension of Nouns Illustrating Predicative and Substantive Genders, etc.

From here onwards, I shall also speak of the declensions in accordance with the spoken word, through the power of the predicative and substantive genders, and so forth.

Therein, 'predicative genders' (vāccaliṅga) are the subordinate genders (adjectives), or the genders known as qualitative nouns (guṇanāma). 'Substantive genders' (abhidheyyaliṅga) are the principal genders (substantives), or the genders known as possessors of qualities (guṇīpada). Since among these, the predicative genders follow the substantive genders, all predicative genders derived from the root 'bhū' should also be applied in accordance with the substantive gender. Although those predicative genders derived from the root 'bhū' are not personally applied in the declension of nouns, according to the method in various places...
326:
Therefore, I shall not show them now. Although vāccalingas not derived from the root 'bhū' are also applied according to the method, I shall speak of them for the purpose of generating skill in usage for the listeners, and I shall show their declension (padamālā) while mentioning some usages.

Dīgho (long), rasso (short), nīlo (blue/dark), pīto (yellow), sukko (white), kaṇho (black), seṭṭho (noble), pāpo (evil), saddhā (faithful), suddhā (pure), ucco (high), nīco (low), kato (done), atīto (past), and so forth.

Long is the night to one who is awake; long is the league (yojana) to one who is weary; long is the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) to the foolish who do not know the True Dhamma.

(Masculine) Dīgho, dīghā. Dīghaṃ, dīghe. Dīghena, dīghehi, dīghebhi. Dīghassa, dīghānaṃ. Dīghā, dīghasmā, dīghamhā, dīghehi, dīghebhi. Dīghassa, dīghānaṃ. Dīghe, dīghasmiṃ, dīghamhi, dīghesu. Bho dīgha, bhavanto dīghā. "You should call me Dīgha"—this statement is the example here.

(Feminine) Dīghā, dīghā, dīghāyo. Dīghaṃ, dīghā, dīghāyo. Dīghāya. The rest is to be understood according to the method of 'kaññā'.

(Neuter) Dīghaṃ, dīghāni, dīghā. Dīghaṃ, dīghāni, dīghe. Dīghena. The rest is to be understood according to the method of 'citta'. Words such as 'rassa' and so forth should also be expanded in this same way. This is the declension of vāccalingas; it is appropriate to call it the "declension of quality-names (guṇanāma)."

Among the abhidheyyalingas, those which have specific distinctions (visesa), I shall now speak of their declension according to the Pāḷi.

Which are those words that have specific distinctions?

Bhavābhava and so forth, Laṅkādīpa and so forth, Bodhi, Sandhi, and so forth are the words that have specific distinctions.
327:
Among those words—

The word 'bhavābhava' is singular in some places and plural in others. Its occurrence is desired whether it is a compound (samāsa) or not a compound. Having stated the analysis (viggaha) and the meaning of the word (padattha), listen to the declension (padamālā) of this word which I shall speak with an undistracted mind.

'Bhavo ca abhavo ca bhavābhavaṃ.' Or, 'bhavo ca abhavo ca bhavābhavāni'—this is the analysis. In that analysis, 'bhava' means a small existence (khuddakabhava). 'Abhava' means a great existence (mahantabhava). Here, the 'a' sound denotes the meaning of greatness. Here, smallness and greatness should be understood by way of happy realms and miserable realms, and by way of the low and the excellent. Alternatively, 'bhava' means growth (vuddhi) and 'abhava' means non-growth (avuddhi). This is the meaning of the word.

This is the declension of the noun (nāmikapadamālā)—

Bhavābhavaṃ, bhavābhavaṃ, bhavābhavena, bhavābhavassa, bhavābhavā, bhavābhavasmā, bhavābhavamhā, bhavābhavassa, bhavābhave, bhavābhavasmiṃ, bhavābhavamhi, bho bhavābhava. Thus, the word 'bhavābhava' is singular. Its singularity is seen in the Pāḷi and the Commentaries—

"Leaving aside the conduct in past aeons, I shall speak of the conduct in various existences (bhavābhave) in this aeon; listen to me."

Or thus,

"Having experienced such manifold suffering and manifold success in various existences (bhavābhave), he attained the supreme self-enlightenment (sambodhi)."

Thus, the singularity of the word 'bhavābhava' is seen in the Pāḷi.
328:
In the Commentary also—

"The world of beings, not fully understanding, goes to various existences (bhavābhavaṃ) frequented by the Buddhas. I pay homage to that excellent Dhamma which destroys the net of defilements such as ignorance (avijjā)."

Thus, its singularity is seen.

Bhavābhavāni, bhavābhavā, bhavābhavāni, bhavābhave, bhavābhavehi, bhavābhavebhi, bhavābhavānaṃ, bhavābhavehi, bhavābhavebhi, bhavābhavānaṃ, bhavābhavesu, bhavanto bhavābhavāni. Thus, the word 'bhavābhava' is also plural. Its plurality is seen in the Pāḷi: "For the one who has shaken off defilements, there is no (attachment) anywhere in the world; speculative views do not exist in various existences (bhavābhavesu)." Mixing both methods, the declension of the noun should be applied. How? "Bhavābhavaṃ, bhavābhavāni. Bhavābhavaṃ, bhavābhavāni. Bhavābhavena, bhavābhavehi, bhavābhavebhi," and so forth, it should be applied according to the diverse method of 'citta'.

These are the singular and plural forms in the neuter gender.

One should explain that this declension is made in the state of being a compound (samāsa). The wise should distinguish the word 'bhavābhava' in two ways: as a compound word and as a non-compound word. It is neuter when it is a compound, and masculine in the other case (non-compound). In the neuter, however, one should mostly speak of it as singular. The wise should state the compound meaning as "existence and non-existence." For the non-compound word, one should speak of the meaning as "from existence to existence" (bhavato bhavaṃ). That word should be understood as masculine through the power of the ablative and accusative cases. Thus, the wise should know the word 'bhavābhava' with distinction.
329:
Just as the declension (nāmika-padamālā) of the term 'bhavābhava' is applied here, so too should the declension of terms such as 'kammākamma' and 'phalāphala' be applied. The meanings of these terms should also be stated as appropriate. These terms are generally in the singular number. In this way, the special characteristics of terms such as 'bhavābhava' should first be understood.

Laṅkādīpo, laṅkādīpaṃ, laṅkādīpena, laṅkādīpassa, laṅkādīpā, laṅkādīpasmā, laṅkādīpamhā, laṅkādīpassa, laṅkādīpe, laṅkādīpasmiṃ, laṅkādīpamhi, bho laṅkādīpa. This is the declension in the form of a compound (samāsa). It should also be applied in the non-compound form.

Laṅkā dīpo, laṅkaṃ dīpaṃ, laṅkāya dīpena, laṅkāya dīpassa, laṅkāya dīpā, laṅkāya dīpasmā, laṅkāya dīpamhā, laṅkāya dīpassa, laṅkāya dīpe, laṅkāya dīpasmiṃ, laṅkāya dīpamhi, bhoti laṅke dīpa. This is the declension in the analytical (byāsa/viggaha) form. This method is not obtainable in the term 'Jambudīpo', because the term 'Jambudīpa' cannot be expressed by the word 'Jambū' alone, whereas 'Laṅkādīpa' can be expressed by the word 'Laṅkā' alone. However, this method of analytical declension is particularly helpful for poets in composing poetry and also for the Sasana. Thus, the compositions of ancient poets are seen through the power of analysis (byāsa):

"I worship that footprint of the Buddha,
On the Samantakūṭa mountain,
Which is like the crest of the island of Laṅkā,
And is the abode of the deity Sumana."

In the Sasana as well, through the power of analysis, such Pali texts are seen as: "A divine chariot appeared for the famous King of Videha," and so forth.
330:
Just as this method is not obtainable in the term 'Jambudīpa', so too in terms such as 'Nāgadīpa', it is not obtainable because 'Nāgadīpa' and others are not expressed by the words 'Nāga' and so forth alone, just as 'Jambudīpa' is not expressed by the word 'Jambū' alone.

O sirs... In the compositions of ancient poets such as, "We, the people of Jambū, worship that tooth-relic of the Buddha which has radiance like the gold from the Jambū river," is it not that 'Jambudīpa' is expressed by the word 'Jambū' because the meaning 'people living in Jambudīpa' is obtainable?

It is true that the meaning 'people living in Jambudīpa' is obtained; however, the word 'Jambū' alone does not express the meaning of 'Jambudīpa'. Rather, when 'Jambudīpanarā' (people of Jambudīpa) should be said, because it is the domain of a verse (gāthā) and to avoid the fault of excessive syllables, the word 'dīpa' is elided and it is said as 'Jambunarā'. Thus, the word 'Jambū' stated through the power of eliding the subsequent word (uttarapada-lopa) is capable of expressing the meaning 'people living in Jambudīpa' by the power of the compound, depending on the word 'nara'. It is not capable independently during the time of analysis (byāsa). Therefore, when 'Jambū' is said, Jambudīpa is not understood, but only the Rose-apple tree (Jambū-rukkha) is understood.

O sirs... Is this method, "Kāko dāso (the slave named Kāka), kākaṃ dāsaṃ, kākena dāsena," obtainable or not? It is obtainable. This is because the slave named Kāka is expressed by the word 'Kāka'. If that is so, in this term 'Jambudīpa' as well, taking the meaning 'the island named Jambū', is this method, "Jambū dīpo, jambuṃ dīpaṃ, jambuyā dīpena," obtainable? It is not obtainable. This is because the word 'Jambū' does not apply to the island by way of designation (paññatti).

The word 'Jambū' applies only to the tree by way of designation, not to the island. Just as the usage 'Citta' applies both to the householder named Citta and to the mind, as in "Citto gahapati, cittaṃ mano mānasaṃ," and so forth; and just as the usage 'Kusa' applies both to King Kusa and to Kusa grass...
331:
"Taking Pabhāvatī and the jewel named Verocana, as well as Kusa grass, the powerful King Kusa went to the city of Kusāvatī. Just as Kusa grass, when wrongly grasped, cuts the hand itself," and so forth; similarly, the word 'Kāka' applies to the crow and also to the slave of that name, as in "The crow cries; the slave named Kāka travels sixty yojanas," and so forth. However, the word 'Jambū' does not apply to the island by way of designation like the words 'Citta', 'Kusa', and 'Kāka' apply to the householder, mind, etc. Therefore, only the aforementioned method should be borne in mind.

Just as the declension of the word 'Laṅkādīpo' is applied here through the power of compound (samāsa) and through the power of analysis (byāsa), so too should the declension of terms such as 'Pubbavidehadīpo', 'Aparagoyānadīpo', 'Uttarakurudīpo', 'Assayujanakkhattaṃ', 'Citramāso', 'Vessantararājā', 'Setavatthaṃ', and 'Dibbaratho' be applied through the power of compound and analysis. The expression of Pubbavideha island and others by the words 'Pubbavideha' and so forth should also be understood. It should also be understood that when there is a use for compound words like 'Dibbaratho', they are to be made separate through the power of analysis. When two words are made to have separate case endings through the power of apposition (samanādhikaraṇa) as in "Dibbo ratho" by the power of analysis, there is the quality of preserving the meter (vutti) and ease of recitation (sukhūccāraṇa) in verses. This method is established because it is in accordance with the Sasana. Therefore, many Pali texts are evident in the scriptures such as, "A divine chariot appeared for the famous King of Videha." In this way, the special characteristics of words like 'Laṅkādīpa' exist.

Now, the special characteristics of 'Bodhi', 'Sandhi', and others will be stated:

Bodhi, Sandhi, Vibhatta, Āyu, Dhātu, Pajāpati,
Dāmā, Dāmaṃ, likewise Saddhā, Saddhaṃ, Taṭaṃ, Taṭī, Taṭo.
332:
Vyañjanaṃ, vyañjano; attho, atthaṃ; akkharaṃ, akkharo;
ajjavaṃ, ajjavō; likewise maddava, gārava;
vaco, vacī, and so forth, while having the same form in their original state (sarūpa),
occur in two or three genders; these should be pointed out as they occur.

Among those words, the word 'Bodhi' first occurs as in "Bodhi Rājakumāro" (Prince Bodhi), and "An Ariyan disciple is called 'Bodhi'; because it is a factor of that Bodhi, it is called Bojjhaṅga." Thus, when referring to a person, the declension (nāmika-padamālā) follows the masculine gender (pullinga) according to the pattern of 'aggi': "Bodhi, bodhī, bodhayo. Bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhayo. Bodhinā," and so on.

However, when referring to the tree, the Path (magga), Nibbāna, or Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), the declension follows the feminine gender (itthilinga) according to the pattern of 'ratti': "Bodhi, bodhī, bodhiyā. Bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhiyā. Bodhiyā," and so on.

Some teachers say, "The word 'Bodhi' referring to the tree is masculine." This statement should be examined as it appears to contradict the scriptures (āgama). In the scriptures, the masculine gender of the word 'Bodhi' is not found when referring to the tree; it is only found when referring to a person. If the word 'Bodhi' referring to a tree were masculine, like the words "sālo, dhavo, khadiro," then the words 'jambū', 'simbalī', and 'pāṭalī' should also be masculine because they refer to trees; however, the masculine gender is not found in those words, nor in this word 'Bodhi', even though they refer to trees. If the word 'Bodhi' referring to the tree were masculine, then the word 'Bodhi' referring to Nibbāna and Omniscient Knowledge would have to be neuter (napumsakalinga), because it expresses meanings like Nibbāna which are designated by the neuter gender as in "Nibbānaṃ."

Those who say, "The word 'Bodhi' referring to the tree is masculine," keep in mind the meaning stated as: "Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four Paths; because the Blessed One attained it here..."
333:
"...the tree is also called Bodhi." Thinking thus, they speak by way of etymological definition (nibbacana), "Because one understands (bujjhati) here, it is Bodhi," and they likely wonder, "Can the word 'Bodhi' referring to the tree not be masculine?" It should not be regarded in this way; rather, it should be regarded thus: The teachers who say, "Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four Paths; because the Blessed One attained that knowledge here, the tree is also called Bodhi," are applying the feminine name and designation of 'Bodhi' (knowledge) to the tree, which is the place of understanding, by way of metaphorical attribution (āropa). Therefore, in such instances, one should not be overly concerned with the etymological definition (nibbacana). The formulation of the etymology "Because one understands here, it is Bodhi" cannot make the word 'Bodhi' referring to the tree masculine, because linguistic usage (vohāra) is established by convention (sanketa). Therefore, although the tree itself is not 'Bodhi' (knowledge), because it is the place where Bodhi-knowledge was attained, those within the Dispensation (sāsanika) refer to it using the feminine conventional term 'Bodhi'. Or, because it is the cause of Bodhi-knowledge, they refer to it by the name of the result (metaphorically). Intending this very meaning, it should be understood that it was said: "Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four Paths; because the Blessed One attained that knowledge here, the tree is also called Bodhi." Thus, the name of the tree proceeds by way of the feminine gender as 'Bodhi'.

Therefore, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), the Follower of the Wheel of Dhamma (Anudhammacakkavattī), who was skilled in linguistic usage, said using the feminine usage: "The manifestation known as 'Buddha' occurred along with the attainment of Omniscient Knowledge at the foot of the Bodhi of the Blessed Buddhas." Furthermore, in various places, it is said: "the branch of the Bodhi tree" (bodhiyā sākhā), and "For what reason is it called Mahābodhi, and to whom does she (sā) belong?", and:

"As soon as she was released from the hand, she rose eighty cubits into the sky, and then emitted beautiful six-colored rays."
334:
In such ways, usages showing the feminine gender of the word 'Bodhi' referring to the tree are seen. 

Alternatively, the word 'Bodhi' referring to the tree has two genders (dvilinga) by way of masculine and feminine. Indeed, in the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya, such word construction is seen by the teacher Buddhaghosa, the great grammarian who knew the method of the Pali: "Dear son, will you be able to go to the city of Pāṭaliputta and bring the Elder Nun Saṅghamittā together with the Mahābodhi (mahabodhinā - masculine)?" and, "That ship carrying the Mahābodhi (sā - feminine), while the Great King was watching, leapt into the midst of the great ocean."

Regarding that word 'Bodhi' referring to the tree, by way of the etymology "Because one understands here, it is Bodhi," the declension should be known as: "Bodhi, bodhī, bodhayo. Bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhayo. Bodhinā," and so on. However, for that same word referring to the tree, by way of the feminine usage occurring in the sense of 'knowledge', established by convention and illuminating the traditional meaning (rūḷhattha), the declension should be known as: "Bodhi, bodhī, bodhiyā. Bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhiyā. Bodhiyā," and so on. Thus:

The word 'Bodhi' referring to a person is masculine.
Referring to knowledge and so forth, it is always feminine.
Referring to the Bodhi tree, it may be masculine or feminine.
Even so, its feminine gender is more desirable (to be accepted),
Because it was spoken by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta).

The declension of words like 'Sandhi' should also be applied according to the established method. For the word 'Sandhi', when referring to vowel junction (sara-sandhi) and so forth, it is masculine; when referring to rebirth (paṭisandhi) and so forth, it is feminine, as seen in "sandhino, sandhiyā," etc. The word 'Vibhatti', when referring to division...
335:
The word *vibhatti* is feminine. However, when it denotes the *syādi* suffixes, it is both masculine and feminine, as seen in "vibhattissa, vibhattiyā," etc.

The word *āyu*, being used only to denote the life faculty (*jīvitindriya*), is both masculine and neuter, as seen in the verse "punarāyu ca me laddhā, evaṃ jānāhi mārisa" and the text "ettakaṃyeva te āyu, cavanakālo bhavissati."

The word *dhātu*, when denoting nature (*sabhāva*) etc., is feminine. When denoting a hand, cooking, etc., it is both masculine and feminine, as seen in "cakkhudhātuyā, karotissa dhātussa, dhātuyo dhātuyā."

The word *pajāpati*, when denoting a specific deity, is masculine. When denoting a wife or a maternal aunt, it is feminine, as seen in "pajāpatissa devarājassa dhajaggaṃ ullokeyyātha" and "attano pajāpatiyā saddhiṃ mahāpajāpatiyā."

The words *dāmā* and *dāmaṃ* denote the same object, such as a jasmine garland, in the feminine and neuter genders respectively. Thus, in worldly usage consistent with the Teaching, both genders are found: "mālatīdāmā lolāḷiṅgalīlā, mālatīdāmaṃ, siṅghitaṃ dāmaṃ bhamerehi, ratanadāmā, ratanadāmaṃ."

The words *saddhā* and *saddhaṃ*, however, denote different objects and are feminine and neuter respectively. The word *saddhā* denotes the characteristic of clarity (faith) and is feminine. The word *saddhaṃ* denotes food dedicated to the deceased (*matakabhatta*) and is neuter. This is seen in "saddhā saddahanā, mayamassubho gotamabrāhmaṇā nāma dānāni dema saddhāni karoma." In this context, "saddhā...
336:
Examples such as "puriso, saddhā itthī, saddhaṃ kulaṃ" should be understood as not being included here because they are *vāccaliṅga* (adjectival gender following the substantive).

The words *taṭaṃ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭော* are all three genders—feminine, masculine, and neuter—in the single sense of a shore.

The word *byañjana* is neuter when it denotes spices, gender, a sentence, or a body part. When it denotes a consonant (letter), it is both masculine and neuter. Among those meanings, for spices, it is referred to in the neuter as "sūpaṃ vā byañjanaṃ vā." Similarly, for gender, "itthibyañjanaṃ purisabyañjanaṃ"; for a sentence, "padabyañjanāni sādhukaṃ uggahetvā"; and for body parts, "asīti anubyañjanāni" are referred to in the neuter. Regarding body parts, it is referred to in the neuter as: "Because they follow and make the defilements manifest, they are called *anubyañjana* (minor marks)." Here, *anubyañjana* refers to various features such as hands, feet, smiling, laughing, speaking, looking, etc. These very features are called "body parts." In the sense of a consonant, however, it is referred to in both masculine and neuter as "byañjano, byañjanaṃ."

The word *attha* is neuter when it denotes Nibbāna. However, when it denotes meaning, wealth, cause, benefit, removal, intention, etc., it is masculine. Thus, in the commentary on the passage "atthatthami" in the *Kathāvatthu*, the word *attha* is used in the neuter as "atthaṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ." Therefore, the word *attha* has two genders.

The word *akkhara* is also masculine and neuter, as seen in "yo pubbo akkharo akkharāni." Alternatively, the word *akkhara* is always neuter when it denotes Nibbāna or a name-concept (*nāmapaññatti*). "padamaccutamakkharaṃ...
337:
... "O Vāseṭṭha, the first syllable 'Mahāsammata' arose," in such passages as "mahājanasammato," and in "He teaches by means of syllables (*akkharāya*); if one syllable is deficient, there is an offense of *pācittiya*," the word *akkhara* should be called masculine or neuter, but not feminine. This word "akkharāya" is a case of an interchange of case endings (*vibhatti-vipallāsa*), like the words "dhanañjayāya" and "vacanāya" in "asakkata casma dhanañjayāya, viramathāyasmanto mamavacanāya," and not due to an interchange of gender.

The words *ajjava* (rectitude), *maddava* (softness), and *gārava* (reverence) are both masculine and neuter. This is seen in "ajjavo ca maddavo ca" (masculine), "ajjavamaddavaṃ" (neuter), "gāravo ca nivāto ca" (masculine), and "At that time, reverence (*gāravaṃ* - neuter) arose in me toward the stupa," etc.

The words *vaco* and *vacī* are masculine and feminine, like the words *ghaṭော* and *ghaṭī*. Among them, the word *vacī* should be declined as "vacī, vacī, vaciyo; vaciṃ, vacī, vaciyo; vaciyā," etc. Some teachers say, "When followed by words such as *duccarita*, *payoga*, *viññatti*, and *sadda*, the ending of the word *vaca* becomes *ī*, and thus forms like *vacīduccaritaṃ* appear." This statement should not be accepted, because the word *vacī* is seen as distinct from the word *vaca*.

In this regard, there are examples from the Pāḷi and the Commentaries. "Speech (*vacī*) is the verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*); the verbal formation is speech; excluding speech and verbal formation, the remaining states are neither speech nor verbal formation," and "The mindful one rejoices, reciting with words (*vacībi*)"—these are examples from the Pāḷi. "Speech itself, known as vocalization, is called vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*) because it is an intimation; the breaking of speech is called *vacībheda*"—these are examples from the Commentaries. In this manner, other words...
338:
The state of having two genders for words with similar forms and words with dissimilar forms should be determined as appropriate. Thus, among the genders that express meaning, the specific denotative genders (abhidheyyaliṅga) should be understood.

Now, in some instances, the declension paradigm (nāmikapadamālā) will be stated according to the nature of dhamma (quality), puggala (person), etc., for denotative genders that are predicative genders (vāccaliṅga), as well as for genders ending in taddhita suffixes that possess those denotative genders. In stating so:

By way of dhamma, puggala, dhamma-puggala, ekanta-dhamma, and ekanta-puggala,
The declension paradigms in those words should occur by way of the nominative case (paccatta), etc.
A word may be similar, dissimilar, or entirely similar; this should be known.

How? The declension paradigm of these words—'micchādiṭṭhi, micchāsaṅkappo, micchāvācā, micchāvāco, micchādiṭṭhiko, micchāsaṅkappī'—should be understood as follows:

'Micchādiṭṭhi, micchādiṭṭhī, micchādiṭṭhiyo. Micchādiṭṭhiṃ, micchādiṭṭhī, micchādiṭṭhiyo. Micchādiṭṭhiyā'—thus it is by way of dhamma (the quality). 'Micchādiṭṭhi, micchādiṭṭhī, micchādiṭṭhino. Micchādiṭṭhiṃ, micchādiṭṭhī, micchādiṭṭhino. Micchādiṭṭhinā'—thus it is by way of puggala (the person). 'Micchāsaṅkappo, micchāsaṅkappā. Micchāsaṅkappaṃ'—thus it is by way of dhamma-puggala. 'Micchāvācā, micchāvācā, micchāvācāyo. Micchāvācaṃ, micchāvācā, micchāvācāyo. Micchāvācāya'—thus it is by way of ekanta-dhamma. 'Micchāvāco, micchāvācā. Micchāvācaṃ, micchāvāce. Micchāvācena'—thus it is by way of ekanta-puggala. 'Micchādiṭṭhiko, micchādiṭṭhikā. Micchādiṭṭhikaṃ'—thus also by way of ekanta-puggala. 'Micchāsaṅkappī, micchāsaṅkappino. Micchāsaṅkappiṃ'—thus also the declension paradigm occurs by way of ekanta-puggala. By way of the nominative (paccatta) and accusative (upayoga) cases, etc., a word may be similar, dissimilar, or entirely similar. This method also applies to 'sammādiṭṭhi, sammāsaṅkappa', and so on.
339:
In this context, the directly spoken usages are as follows: "Monks, for one who has come to ignorance and is unwise, wrong view arises. For one with wrong view, wrong intention arises. For one with wrong intention, wrong speech arises. For one with wrong speech, wrong action arises. For one with wrong action, wrong livelihood arises. For one with wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises. For one with wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises. For one with wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises. Monks, for one who has come to knowledge and is wise, right view arises. For one with right view, right intention arises," and so on in detail. Thus, in some places, the declension paradigms for those that are predicative genders (vāccaliṅga), denotative genders (abhidheyyaliṅga), and genders ending in taddhita suffixes have been taught along with their usage.

Now, I shall state the slight distinctions of these words: the word 'bhavitabba' which has a denotative gender; the words 'sotthi' and 'suvatthi' which have denotative genders; the word 'abbhuta' which has both predicative and denotative genders; and the word 'abhūta' which has a predicative gender. I shall also apply the declension paradigms as appropriate. Among those words, the word 'bhavitabba' is always an abstract noun (bhāvavācaka) expressing a state, and it ends only in the neuter gender, singular number. It should be used with words ending in the instrumental case (tatiyantapada) and with words such as 'evaṃ' and 'na'. A declension paradigm (inflection) is not available for this word 'bhavitabba'. The usages in this context are: "Saddhammagarukena bhavitabbaṃ—one should respect the True Dhamma; no āmisagarukena—one should not respect material things; it must be this thief; it must be these thieves; it must be this female thief; it must be these female thieves; it must be this mind; it must be these minds; it should be thus; it should be otherwise."

In this regard, it is said:

The word 'bhavitabba' is always in the nominative singular, expressing a state (bhāva), and is neuter in the Dispensation of the Omniscient One.
340:
A wise person should understand that the word 'bhavitabba' is to be joined only with instrumental-ended words, the word 'evaṃ', and so on.

This is the distinction of the word 'bhavitabba'.

"Venerable Sir, may there be safety (sotthi) for the king." "The barber goes safely (sotthiṃ)." "He stands in safety (sotthinā)." 'Suvatthi, suvatthiṃ, suvatthinā' are also the same. This is the distinction of the words 'sotthi', 'suvatthi', and so on.

This is the distinction between the two words 'abbhuta' and 'abhūta'. The word 'bhū' always becomes short (rassa) when followed by a double consonant (saṃyoga) or when preceded by the negative particle 'a-' or 'iti'. In what sense? In senses such as 'abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtaṃ' (that which has not happened before, but now happens). In such conditions, if not followed by a double consonant, it does not become short (it remains long). In what sense? In senses such as 'asaccaṃ' (untruth). Therefore, the word 'abbhuta' can mean 'abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtaṃ' (happening for the first time) or 'abbhutakaraṇa' (performing a wonder). The word 'abhūta', however, can mean 'asaccaṃ' (untruth) or 'ajāta' (not yet arisen). Among those senses, "How wonderful, sirs! How unprecedented, sirs! How wonderful in the world! A wonder that makes the hair stand on end!"—these are usages in the sense of 'happening for the first time'.

"You catch me with a cobra, I (will catch you) with a small female frog. Let there be a wonder (abbhuta) for us there, with five thousand strengths"—these are usages in the sense of performing a wonder. Thus, by way of the short vowel and the long vowel, when there is no double consonant, it becomes 'abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ' (untrue, false).
341:
"Atatham" and so forth are common usages in the sense of being untrue. "Abhūtaṃ, ajātaṃ, asañjātaṃ" and so forth are common usages in the sense of not yet having arisen. In this regard, there are these verses:

In this phrase "Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtaṃ," the word "abbhutaṃ" should be understood by the wise in the sense of a marvel; it stands with a short vowel (rassa).

In the sense of performing a marvel, the word "abbhutaṃ" likewise stands with a short vowel; thus the wise should understand.

However, the word spoken with a long vowel (dīgha) as "abhūtaṃ" should be understood as a word expressing what is untrue.

Abbhutaṃ, abbhutāni. Following the method of *citta* (like mind): abbhuto, abbhutā. Abbhutaṃ; following the method of *purisa* (like man): abbhutā, abbhutā, abbhutāyo. Abbhutaṃ should be known following the method of *kaññā* (like maiden). In this way, the declension (padamālā) of the word *bhūta* should also be taken in three genders. Here, the word "abbhutaṃ" is both an attributive gender (adjective) and a substantive gender (noun). The word "abhūtaṃ," however, like the word *sacca*, is in some places an attributive gender or a substantive gender. Thus, this declension (padamālā) along with its appropriate usages has been stated.

Now, for the sake of producing skill in those who recite the texts, the declension (padamālā) by way of combining words is stated: Buddhā Bhagavā, Buddhā Bhagavanto. Buddhaṃ Bhagavantaṃ, Buddhe Bhagavante. Buddhena Bhagavatā; the rest should be expanded. This declension should be understood by way of singular and plural.

Devā Tāvatiṃsā. Deve Tāvatiṃse. Devehi Tāvatiṃsehi. The rest should be expanded. The declension should be understood by way of the plural.
342:
That Blessed One is the one who knows, who sees, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One. To that Blessed One who knows, who sees, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One. By that Blessed One who knows, who sees, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One. For that Blessed One who knows, who sees, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One. The rest should be expanded. The declension (padamālā) should be understood by way of the singular.

King Suddhodana, to King Suddhodana, by King Suddhodana. The rest should be expanded.

King Pasenadi of Kosala, to King Pasenadi of Kosala, by King Pasenadi of Kosala. The rest should be expanded.

King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, by King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha. The rest should be expanded.

King Ajātasattu, the son of Queen Vedehī, of Magadha; to King Ajātasattu, the son of Queen Vedehī, of Magadha; by King Ajātasattu, the son of Queen Vedehī, of Magadha. The rest should be expanded.

Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, by Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī—this should be said five times. In Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, O Lady Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.

Makkhali Gosāla, to Makkhali Gosāla, by Makkhali Gosāla. The rest should be expanded.

The pair of disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna. To the pair of disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna. By the pair of disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
343:
Of the pair of disciples, the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Moggallāna (this is the declension). The remaining words should be understood by expanding them. All these declensions (padamālā) should be understood by way of the singular. Sāriputta-Moggallānā aggasāvakā (The chief disciples Sāriputta and Moggallāna), Sāriputta-Moggallāne aggasāvake (To the chief disciples Sāriputta and Moggallāna), Sāriputta-Moggallānehi aggasāvakehi (By the chief disciples Sāriputta and Moggallāna). The remaining words should be understood by expanding them. They should be understood by way of the plural. This same method applies to other words besides these.

So dāro (That wife), sā dārā (Those wives). Taṃ dāraṃ (That wife), se dāre (Those wives). Sena dārena (By that wife). The remaining words should be understood by expanding them. Sā nārī (That woman), sā nāriyo (Those women). Taṃ nāriṃ (That woman), sā nāriyo (Those women). Sāya nāriyā (By that woman). The remaining words should be understood by expanding them. Taṃ kammaṃ (That action), sāni kammāni (Those actions). Sena kammena (By that action). Taṃ phalaṃ (That fruit), sāni phalāni (Those fruits). Sena phalena (By that fruit). The remaining words should be understood by expanding them.

Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ (The first absorption), paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ (To the first absorption), paṭhamena jhānena (By the first absorption), paṭhamassa jhānassa (Of the first absorption). The remaining words should be understood by expanding them.

Catutthī disā (The fourth direction), catutthiṃ disaṃ (To the fourth direction), catutthiyā disāya (In the fourth direction).

Dhammī kathā (A talk connected with the Dhamma), dhammiṃ kathaṃ (To a talk connected with the Dhamma), dhammiyā kathāya (By a talk connected with the Dhamma), dhammiyaṃ kathāyaṃ (In a talk connected with the Dhamma). In this same way, anupubbī kathā (gradual talk) and evarūpī kathā (such a talk) should also be understood. By this method, in other places as well, one should observe according to the combination of words, according to gender, according to the final consonant, and according to number. Various noun declensions (nāmika-padamālā) should be joined according to the nature of the words.

Now, the differences in words of a single nature according to gender and final consonant should be understood. How? Yādiso, yādisī, yādisaṃ (of what kind). Tādiso, tādisī, tādisaṃ (of that kind). Etādiso, etādisī, etādisaṃ (of this kind). Kīdiso, kīdisī, kīdisaṃ (of what kind?). Īdiso, īdisī, īdisaṃ (of this kind).
344:
Ediso, edisī, edisaṃ (such as this). Sadiso, sadisī, sadisaṃ (similar). Sometimes, feminine forms like "yādisā, tādisā" also occur. The declension (nāmika-padamālā) of these words should be applied according to the patterns of purisa (masculine), itthī (feminine), and citta (neuter).

Now, the declension of words like amama, which are compound (samāsa) or derivative (taddhita) words, will be stated: amamo, amamā, amamaṃ, amame. amamena. The remaining forms should be understood in detail.

Mayhako, mayhakā. mayhakaṃ, mayhake. mayhakena. The remaining forms should be understood in detail.

Āmā, āmā, āmāyo. Āmaṃ, āmā, āmāyo. The remaining forms should be understood in detail.

Regarding the word amama: Amamo means one who has no attachment (mamatta) through craving (taṇhā) or attachment through wrong view (diṭṭhi). Who is that person? It should be said that it is only the Noble Arahat. Alternatively, those who do not make the sense of "this is mine" (mamatta) along with craving and wrong view are also called amama. In this context, the phrase "Manussā tattha jāyanti, amamā apariggahā" (Humans are born there, without attachment and without possessions) is an example taken from the Dispensation (Sāsana). The phrase "Amamo nirahaṅkāro" (Without attachment, without ego) is an example taken from worldly treatises. When used in the feminine gender, the declension is "amamā, amamā, amamāyo". When used in the neuter gender, the declension is "amamaṃ, amamāni".

Regarding the word mayhaka: Mayhako is so called because it laments, "This is mine, this is mine" (idaṃ pi mayhaṃ, idaṃ pi mayhaṃ); it is a specific type of bird. This is taught in the Jātaka: "The bird named Mayhaka, dwelling in mountain slopes and caves, climbs the ripe banyan tree and cries out 'Mine, mine!'" When used in the feminine gender, the declension is "mayhakī, mayhakī, mayhakiyo".

Regarding the word āmā: Āmā is so called because she acknowledges her status as a maidservant, saying, "Lord, I am your maidservant" (āma ahaṃ tumhākaṃ dāsī). She is a household maidservant. This is also taught—
345:
—in the Jātakas: "Where a slave is born in the house (āma-jāta) and, remaining there, speaks harsh words," and "There are also slaves born in the house (āmā dāsā) in the world." Therefore, these are the example words in this context.

Now, the distinction and the appropriate declension (nāmika-padamālā) of the words kati, katipaya, and katimī will be stated. Among these, the declension of the word katimī cannot be found because it only appears in questions such as "Venerable sir, which day [of the month] (katimī) is today?" However, the declension of the words kati and katipaya can be found. That declension exists only in the plural. But in the Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā, it is said that the word katipaya has a singular form.

How many men are standing? (Kati purisā tiṭṭhanti). How many men do you see? (Kati purise passati). How many women? (Kati itthiyo). How many families (kula)? (Kati kulāni). How many faults (chiddāni) are there in the world where the mind does not remain steady? (Kati lokasmiṃ chiddāni yattha cittaṃ na tiṭṭhati). How many are the wholesome states? (Kati kusalā). How many are the elements? (Kati dhātuyo). How many are the bases? (Kati āyatanāni). By how many aggregates, how many bases, and how many elements is it comprised? (Katihi khandhehi kati hāyatanhehi katihi dhātūhi saṅgahitaṃ). By how many people is it illuminated? (Katibhi rajamāne). By how many people is it purified? (Katibhi parisujjhati). Some men (katipayā purisā), some women (katipayā itthiyo), some minds (katipayāni cittāni). These are the declensions.

Kati. Katihi, katibhi. Katinaṃ. Katisu.

Katipayā. Katipayehi, katipayebhi. Katipayānaṃ. Katipayesu. Katipayāyo. Katipayāhi, katipayābhi. Katipayānaṃ. Katipayāsu. Katipayāni. Katipaye. Katipayehi, katipayebhi. Katipayānaṃ. Katipayesu. All these should be understood by the power of the seven cases, and also in the method of compounds (samāsa).
346:
The words kati and katipaya should be applied only in the plural sense. In phrases such as "The monk who has transcended how many fetters (saṅga) is called one who has crossed the flood? (Kati-saṅgātigo bhikkhu)" and "Done by some people (katipaya-janakataṃ)", it should always be understood as a plural compound in the manner of: "Kati (how many), kittakā (how many), saṅgā (fetters), kati-saṅgā (how many fetters)".

Now, the declension of conventional (rūḷhī) words will be stated. Here, conventional words refer to words like yevāpanaka, etc. Yevāpanako, yevāpanakaā. Yevāpanakaṁ. Yevāpano, yevāpanā. Yevāpanaṁ. Yaṁvāpanakaṁ, yaṁvāpanakāni. The remaining cases should be expanded in all instances. Among these, yevāpanako refers to those states not mentioned by their own specific nature (sarūpa) like contact (phassa) and feeling (vedanā), but mentioned by the phrase "yevāpanā" in the sense of "Whatever other immaterial states are also conditionally arisen at that time (ye vā pana tasmiṁ samaye aññepi atthi paṭiccasamuppannā arūpino dhammā)". Thus it is called yevāpanako; the same applies to yevāpano. Similarly, it is called yaṁvāpanakaṁ because it is mentioned by the phrase "yaṁvāpanā" as in "Whatever other matter also exists (yaṁ vā panaññampi atthi rūpaṁ)". This method should be applied appropriately to words like yassakaṁ, yatthakaṁ, etc.

Here, a question might arise: "Sirs, is not the word pana a particle (nipāta)? And since particles are indeclinable (avyaya) because they do not change (vayābhāva) in the three genders, all cases, and all numbers, why does it become an o-ending word as in 'yevāpano'?" It is true that the word pana is a particle. However, it is a particle only in places such as "ye vā pana tasmiṁ samaye", "yaṁ vā panaññampi", or "brāhmaṇā panā", etc. In places like "yevāpanako" or "yevāpano", it is not called a particle. This is merely an imitation (anukaraṇa) of the original phrase. Therefore, in such instances, the usages including the word pana should be taken as conventional words (rūḷhī-sadda). If so, why is the derivation (nibbacana) shown? It is shown for the purpose of making the meaning clear.
347:
There are Tayodhammajātakaṃ, Tayodhammajātakaṃ, Tayodhammajātakena, Tayodhammajātakassa, Tayodhammajātakā, Tayodhammajātakasmā. The remaining cases should be expanded and understood. There are Tayosaṅkhārā, Tayosaṅkhāre, Tayosaṅkhārehi, Tayosaṅkhārebhi, Tayosaṅkhārānaṃ. The remaining cases should be expanded and understood. There are Cattāripurisayugo Saṅgho, Cattāripurisayugaṃ Saṅghaṃ, Cattāripurisayugena Saṅghena, Cattāripurisayugassa Saṅghassa. The remaining cases should be expanded and understood. There are Satokārī, Satokārī, Satokārino; Satokāriṃ, Satokārī, Satokārino; Satokārinā, Satokārīhi, Satokārībhi; Satokārissa. The remaining cases should be expanded and understood. In this context, 'Satokārī' means: because one remembers, one is called 'Sato'; because one acts only while being mindful, one is called 'Satokārī'.

I shall now describe the declension of other conventional terms (rūḷhī-sadda) along with the clarification of their meanings. Aṅgā, Aṅge, Aṅgehi, Aṅgebhi, Aṅgānaṃ, Aṅgehi, Aṅgebhi, Aṅgānaṃ, Aṅgesu, O Angas (Bhontā Aṅgā). There are Aṅgā janapado, Aṅge janapadaṃ, Aṅgehi (or) Aṅgebhi janapadena, Aṅgānaṃ janapadassa, Aṅgehi (or) Aṅgebhi janapadasmā, Aṅgānaṃ janapadassa, Aṅgesu janapade, O Anga country-dwellers (Bhontā Aṅgā janapada). In this same manner, it should be applied to Magadha, Kosala, and so on.

In the feminine gender: Kāsī, Kāsiyo, Kāsī, Kāsiyo, Kāsīhi, Kāsībhi, Kāsīnaṃ, Kāsīhi, Kāsībhi, Kāsīnaṃ, Kāsīsu, O Kasi women (Bhotiyo Kāsiyo). Here, the clarification of meaning is: Kāsī, Kāsiyo janapado (The Kasi country), Kāsī, Kāsiyo...
348:
...the country (accusative), Kāsīhi (or) Kāsībhi janapadena, Kāsīnaṃ janapadassa, Kāsīhi (or) Kāsībhi janapadasmā, Kāsīnaṃ janapadassa, Kāsīsu janapade, O Kasi country-dwellers (Bhotiyo Kāsiyo janapada). In this same manner, the terms Avantī, Cetī, and Vajjī should also be applied. Therefore, the Teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathācariya) said: "Kurūsu janapade". Thus, although terms like Aṅga are singular in meaning, because they are names of countries, they always appear in the plural form by way of convention (rūḷhī). For this reason, in various texts, plural Pali forms are seen, such as "Aṅgesu viharati" (He dwells among the Angas), "Magadhesu cārikaṃ caramāno" (Wandering among the Magadhans), and "Aṅgānaṃ Magadhānaṃ Kāsīnaṃ Kosalānaṃ" (Of the Angas, Magadhans, Kasis, and Kosalans). Such are the declensions of conventional terms.

Now, I shall describe other declensions that are even more specialized than these, which destroy confusion regarding grammatical distinctions and bring about extremely subtle wisdom, for the purpose of accomplishing supreme skill in grasping the meaning and the phrasing for the listeners. These are based on Pali methods such as: "Sambuddhā paṭijānāsi" (Do you claim to be a Buddha?), "Kassako paṭijānāsi" (Do you claim to be a farmer?), "Upāsako paṭijānāsi" (Do you claim to be a lay follower?), and "Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato ime dhammā anabhisambuddhā" (To you who claim to be a Fully Enlightened One, these things are not fully understood). In the phrase "Sambuddhā paṭijānāsi", the meaning should be understood through the elision of the word 'iti', as in: "Do you claim, 'I am a Fully Enlightened One'?" This same method applies to "Kassako paṭijānāsi" and others. However, in the phrase "Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato", because there is a different grammatical construction through the elision of 'iti' as "To you who are claiming, 'I am a Fully Enlightened One'", there is a different penetration of the meaning. This same method applies to "Khīṇāsavassa te paṭijānato" (To you who claim to be one whose taints are exhausted) and so on. In the Commentary, regarding "Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato", it means: "I am a Fully Enlightened One; all things by me..."
349:
"...are fully understood"—the meaning stated for you who thus claim is exactly as shown. Knowing this, a noble son of wise nature should establish this declension along with the verb in this meaning of "Do you claim, 'I am a Fully Enlightened One'?" as spoken by us:

You stand claiming that you are a Fully Enlightened One. He sees you who are claiming to be a Fully Enlightened One. The Dhamma was taught by you who claim to be a Fully Enlightened One. It is given to you who claim to be a Fully Enlightened One. It departs from you who claim to be a Fully Enlightened One. The Dhamma of you who claim to be a Fully Enlightened One. It is established in you who claim to be a Fully Enlightened One. Likewise, it should be expanded as "Do you claim to be a Khīṇāsava (one whose taints are exhausted)?" and so on.

In the sense of "The monk with psychic power, having been one, becomes many; having been many, he becomes one. The monks with psychic power, having been one, become many; having been many, they become one," this declension along with the verb should also be established:

The monk who, having been one, becomes many, and having been many, becomes one, stands. The monks who, having been one, become many, and having been many, become one, stand. He sees the monk who, having been one, becomes many, and having been many, becomes one. He sees the monks who, having been one, become many, and having been many, become one. The Dhamma was taught by the monk who, having been one, becomes many, and having been many, becomes one. The Dhamma was taught by the monks who, having been one, become many, and having been many, become one. It is given to the monk who, having been one, becomes many, and having been many, becomes one.
350:
The remaining meanings should be elaborated. "O monk, who, having been one, becomes many, and having been many, becomes one, preach the Dhamma." "O monks, who, having been one, become many, and having been many, become one, preach the Dhamma." In this context, the Kevaṭṭa Sutta serves as evidence. "Here, Kevaṭṭa, a monk experiences various forms of psychic power (iddhividha). Having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears... A certain person, endowed with faith and confidence, sees that monk experiencing various forms of psychic power, having been one, becoming many, and having been many, becoming one." This is the Kevaṭṭa Sutta.

A single monk, sitting in private with a single woman (mātugāma), speaks thus. Single monks, sitting in private with a single woman, speak thus. One sees a single monk sitting in private with a single woman. One sees single monks sitting in private with a single woman. All should be elaborated.

In this regard, the Pali passage beginning with "A single [monk] should not converse with a single woman" serves as evidence. Here, the term "ekokekāya" (one with one) should be understood as a conventional usage (rūḷhī) similar to an indeclinable (avyaya). It should be known as having attained the status of a single word, like the word "aññamaññaṃ" (each other). In the sense of "himself being alone without a second companion, together with a single woman," this term "ekokekāya" should be regarded as not being a conventional usage (rūḷhī). Even so, the word "eko" is not in grammatical agreement (samānādhikaraṇa) with the word "bhikkhū." If it were in grammatical agreement, one should not say "nisajjaṃ kappen-taṃ" (sitting), etc. The word "ekāya" is also not in grammatical agreement with the word "itthiyā" (with a woman) which is understood by sense. If it were in grammatical agreement...
351:
...one should not say "mātugāmena" (with a woman), because there would be no distinction and it would result in tautology (repetition). Furthermore, because "mātugāmena" is stated, one should have said "ekena." However, in reality, this term "ekokekāya" expects the meaning designated as man and woman; it does not expect a word in grammatical agreement. Therefore, just like the word "aññamaññaṃ" in such phrases as "dve jānipatayo aññamaññaṃ sallapanti" (two spouses converse with each other), the single-word status of "ekokekāya" and its function as an attribute (visesana) of the monk who is sitting should be understood.

Alternatively, in whatever act of sitting where the monk is alone and the woman is also alone, that act is called "ekokekāya" by way of conventional usage (rūḷhī). By such an act of sitting as "ekokekāya," the meaning "together with a woman" is also to be taken. In this manner, the declension of other conventional terms (rūḷhī-sadda) should also be applied according to usage in the singular and plural. Thus, the declension of nouns (nāmikapadamālā) concerning the denotable (vācca), the denotation (abhidheyya), gender (liṅga), etc., has been illustrated in various ways.

This Saddanīti, which has most melodious sounds,
Which is for those of very sharp intellect, well-studied and excellent.
Like the sun, it dispels the darkness of doubt for the wise,
Like the moon, it causes the white lily of wisdom to bloom.
For the sake of the growth of the Dispensation (Sāsana), which is the refuge of wise men,
One should well and truly master this Nīti with wisdom.

## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the sake of the proficiency of the wise
## in the modes of speech of the three Pitakas of the ninefold division together with the Commentaries,
## the section on the declension of nouns (Nāmikapadamālāvibhāga), illustrating the denotable, the denotation, gender, etc.,
## the eleventh chapter, is finished.
352:
By this much, the declension of masculine, feminine, and neuter nouns derived from the root bhū and others has been shown in various ways, as appropriate, along with other genders, other words, and other meanings. Indeed, setting aside the pronouns (sabbanāma), there are no other nouns that have not been included by this method (all have been included).

## 12. The Declension of Pronouns and Nouns Similar to Them

Hereafter, I shall speak of the pronouns and those similar to them, (itoparaṃ pavakkhāmi, sabbanāmañca tassamaṃ.)
And specifically of nouns joined with various other nouns. (nāmañca yojitaṃ nānā-nāmeheva visesato.)
Those words which exist in the three genders, (yāni honti tiliṅgāni,)
And those which are favorable to the three genders, (anukūlāni yāni ca.)
These words I shall specifically declare as nouns. (tiliṅgānaṃ visesena, padānetāni nāmato.)
Because of the meaning "nouns that are common to all," ("sabbasādhāraṇakāni, nāmāni"cceva atthato.)
Twenty-seven words are called pronouns (sabbanāma). (sabbanāmāni vuccanti, sattavīsati saṅkhato.)
Among them, some are joined with forms and with the remaining others. (tesu kānici rūpehi, sesāññehi ca yujjare.)
Some, however, occur only together; this is their characteristic. (kānici pana saheva, etesaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ idaṃ.)
A word that is free from this characteristic is not a pronominal. (etasmā lakkhaṇā muttaṃ, na padaṃ sabbanāmikaṃ.)
