Therefore, words such as "atīta" (past) and so on are called qualitative nouns (guṇanāma). (tasmātītādayo saddā, guṇanāmāni vuccare.)

What are called pronouns are: sabba, katara, katama, ubhaya, itara, añña, aññatara, aññatama, pubba, para, apara, dakkhiṇa, uttara, adhara, ya, ta, eta, ima, amu, kiṃ, eka, ubha, dvi, ti, catu, tumha, amha—these twenty-seven.

Among these, the word "sabba" has the meaning of "all" or "whole"; it should be understood by way of "sabba-sabba" etc. The words "katara" and "katama" have an interrogative sense. The word "ubhaya" denotes a collection of two parts. The word "itara" denotes the opposite of what has been said. The word "añña" denotes another that is obtained. The words "aññatara" and "aññatama" have an indefinite (aniyama) sense. The words beginning with "pubba" and ending with "uttara" denote the determination of direction, time, etc.
353:
The words Pubba, Para, Apara, Dakkhiṇa, and Uttara are masculine when they denote time, place, etc., as appropriate; feminine when they denote directions, etc.; and neuter when they denote locations, etc. The word Adhara also means "lower" and is a word denoting a limit; it exists in all three genders: "Adharo patto (lower bowl), Adharā araṇī (lower fire-stick), Adharaṃ bhajanaṃ (lower vessel/pot)." The word Ya has an indefinite (aniyama) meaning. The word Ta denotes someone absent (parammukha). The word Eta denotes proximity (samīpa). The word Ima denotes extreme proximity (accantasamīpa). The word Amu denotes distance (dūra). The word Kiṃ has an interrogative (pucchana) meaning. The word Eka denotes number (saṅkhyā), etc.

Indeed, the word Eka is found in meanings such as "other" (aññattha), "excellent" (seṭṭha), "solitary/without a companion" (asahāya), and "number" (saṅkhyā). As it is found: in "Sassato attā ca loko ca... ittheke abhivadanti," etc., it is found in the sense of "other." In "Cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ," etc., it is found in the sense of "excellent." In "Eko vūpakaṭṭho," etc., it is found in the sense of "solitary." In "Ekovā kho bhikkhave khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāya," etc., it is found in the sense of "number."

When this word Eka denotes a number, it exists only in the singular. The word Ubha is a synonym of the word Dwi. The words Dwi, Ti, and Catu denote numbers and are always in the plural. The word Tumha is the word to be used for the person spoken to. The word Amha is the word to be used for oneself.

Now, we shall present the declension (nāmikapadamālā) of those words:

Sabbo, sabbe. Sabbaṃ, sabbe. Sabbena, sabbehi, sabbebhi. Sabbassa, sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ. Sabbasmā, sabbamhā, sabbehi, sabbebhi. Sabbassa, sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ. Sabbasmiṃ, sabbamhi, sabbesu. Bho sabba, bhavanto sabbe.
354:
In that regard, all forms of the word Sabba should be joined with masculine nouns in the manner of "Sabbo bhūto, sabbe bhūtā" and "Sabbo puriso, sabbe purisā." The Great Elder Yamaka also taught other forms of words such as Sabba, Katara, and Katama in the context of feminine and neuter genders. What are those forms?

The Elder Yamaka showed the form starting with "Sabbā," and the forms starting with "Sabbe" in the Ablative (nissakka) and Locative (bhummaka) cases.

Let practitioners examine those forms and accept what is appropriate. This is because the forms of the pronoun Sabba are diverse and difficult to understand.

Sabbā, sabbā, sabbāyo. Sabbaṃ, sabbā, sabbāyo. Sabbāya, sabbassā, sabbāhi, sabbābhi. Sabbāya, sabbassā, sabbāsaṃ. Sabbāya, sabbassā, sabbāhi, sabbābhi. Sabbāya, sabbassā, sabbāsaṃ. Sabbāyaṃ, sabbassā, sabbassaṃ, sabbāsu. Bhoti sabbe, bhotiyo sabbā, sabbāyo. This is the declension (nāmikapadamālā) in the feminine gender.

In this context, feminine pronouns should be joined with all feminine nouns, such as "Sabbā bhāvikā, sabbā bhāvikāyo" and "Sabbā kaññā, sabbā kaññāyo." Also, here the word "Sabbassā" exists in five cases by virtue of the Instrumental, Dative, Ablative, Genitive, and Locative cases. This is because of the usage of the Instrumental case (karaṇappayoga), etc., as seen in "Tassā kumārikāya saddhiṃ."

Sabbassā kaññāya kataṃ. Sabbassā kaññāya deti. Ayaṃ kaññā sabbassā kaññāya hīnā virūpā. Ayaṃ kaññā sabbassā kaññāya uttamā abhirūpā. Sabbassā kaññāya apeti, sabbassā kaññāya dhanaṃ. Sabbassā kaññāya patiṭṭhitaṃ.

Sabbaṃ, sabbāni. Sabbaṃ, sabbāni. Sabbena, sabbehi, sabbebhi. Sabbassa, sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ. Sabbasmā, sabbamhā, sabbehi...
355:
...sabbebhi. Sabbassa, sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ. Sabbasmiṃ, sabbamhi, sabbesu. Bho sabba, bhavanto sabbāni. This is the declension (nāmikapadamālā) in the neuter gender.

In this context, neuter pronouns should be joined with all neuter nouns, starting from "Sabbaṃ bhūtaṃ, sabbāni bhūtāni. Sabbaṃ cittaṃ, sabbāni cittāni." Thus is the declension of the word Sabba by virtue of the three genders.

Now, the formation of compounds (samāsa) of this word Sabba with other words should be known as "Sabbasādhāraṇo" and "Sabbaverī." In those compounds, the analysis (samāsaviggaha) is: Sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇo = Sabbasādhāraṇo (one who is common to all). Sabbesaṃ verī (enemy of all), or Sabbe vā verino yassa so'yaṃ sabbaverī (he for whom all people are enemies). Just as the declension of the word Sabba is applied according to the three genders, so should the words starting from Katara and ending with Adhara be applied.

Among those, the masculine abridgment (peyyāla) excluding the word Ubhaya is:
Kataro, katare. Kataraṃ... etc. Bho katara, bhavanto katare. Katamo, katame. Itaro, itare. Añño, aññe. Aññataro, aññatare. Aññatamo, aññatame. Pubbo, pubbe. Paro, pare. Aparo, apare. Dakkhiṇo, dakkhiṇe. Uttaro, uttare. Adharo, adhere... etc. Bho adhara, bhavanto adhere.

The neuter abridgment (peyyāla) including the word Ubhaya is:
Kataraṃ, katarāni. Kataraṃ... etc. Bho katara, bhavanto katarāni. Katamaṃ. Ubhayaṃ. Itaraṃ. Aññaṃ. Aññataraṃ. Aññatamaṃ. Pubbaṃ. Paraṃ. Aparaṃ. Dakkhiṇaṃ. Uttaraṃ. Adharaṃ, adharāni. Adharaṃ... etc. Bho adhara, bhavanto adharāni.
356:
Now, I shall describe the alternative word formations (rūpasiddhi) of words such as *para* in the masculine and neuter genders. In the *Kaccāyana* grammar, just as there is "*purisā*", the nominative plural form "*parā*" is found. Although this method is not common (rarely used) among the nine words ending with *aññatama*, such as *apara*, *sabba*, and *katara*, it may be found in the four words: *pubba*, *dakkhiṇa*, *uttara*, and *adhara*. Similarly, just as there is "*purise*", the locative singular is found as "*pubbe*" in the Pāḷi texts, "*itare*" in the *Saccasaṅkhepa* treatise, and "*pare*" in the *Kaccāyana* grammar. Although this method is not common in the words *sabba* and *añña*, it may be found in the remaining twelve words ending with *adhara*, such as *katara* and *katama*. Likewise, the ablative singular method such as "*sabbā*" and "*katarā*", similar to "*purisā*", is not common in the Pāḷi texts. Nevertheless, one should examine this method repeatedly and adopt it if it is appropriate.

The feminine ellipsis (peyāla) including the word *ubhaya* is as follows:
*Katarā*, *katarā*, *katarāyo*. *Kataraṃ*... *Bhoti katare*, *bhotiyo katarā*, *katarāyo*. *Katamā*. *Ubhayā*. *Itarā*. *Aññatarā*. *Aññatamā*. *Pubbā*. *Parā*. *Aparā*. *Dakkhiṇā*. *Uttarā*. *Adharā*, *adharā*, *adharāyo*. *Adharaṃ*... *Bhoti adhere*, *bhotiyo adharā*, *adharāyo*.

In fact, among these words, because forms like "*itarissā*" are found in the Pāḷi texts for the words *itara*, *añña*, *aññatara*, and *aññatama*, some distinctions...
357:
Therefore, in the places of the dative and genitive singular, they should be joined as: "itarissā, itarāya, aññissā, aññāya; aññatarissā, aññatarāya, aññatamissā, aññatamāya." Similarly, in the places of the instrumental and ablative singular, as seen in the usage of the instrumental and the connective (nissakkappayoga): "tassā kumārikāya saddhiṃ (together with that young girl); kassāhaṃ kena hāyāmi (because of whom and by what do I decline?)"; and in the place of the locative singular, they should be joined as: "itarissā, itarissāṃ, itarāya, itarāyaṃ, aññissā, aññissāṃ, aññāya, aññāyaṃ, aññatarissā, aññatarissāṃ, aññatarāya, aññatarāyaṃ, aññatamissā, aññatamissāṃ, aññatamāya, aññatamāyaṃ." This is because it is seen in the Pāḷi texts: "aññataro bhikkhu aññatarissā itthiyā paṭibaddhacitto hoti (a certain monk has a mind attached to a certain woman)."

Among those, the word sabba is seen used in four scopes (visaya): sabbasabba (the all-inclusive all), padesasabba (the partial all), āyatanasabba (the all of the sense bases), and sakkāyasabba (the all of the personality). Thus, in passages such as "sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthamagacchanti (all phenomena in every aspect come into the range of the Blessed Buddha's knowledge)," it appears in the sense of sabbasabba. In "sabbesaṃ vo sāriputtā subhāsitaṃ pariyāyena (Sāriputta, the speech of all of you is well-spoken in its own way)," it appears in the sense of padesasabba. In "bhikkhave, I will teach you the all (sabbaṃ); listen to that well, pay attention, I will speak... and what, bhikkhus, is the all? The eye and forms... the mind and mental objects," it appears here in the sense of āyatanasabba. In "sabbaṃ sabbato sañjānāti (he perceives the all as the all)," it appears in the sense of sakkāyasabba. Among these four, the word sabba appearing in the sense of sabbasabba is without remainder (nippadesa), while in the other three, it should be understood as having a remainder (sappadesa). Thus:
358:
The word sabba occurs in the four senses of sabbasabba, padesa, āyatana, and sakkāya.

Between the words katara and katama, the word katara occurs in reference to a few things—one, two, three, or slightly more than a few. The word katama occurs in reference to many things—one, two, three, or many. Indeed, katara has a narrow scope, while katama has a broad scope. In those cases, these are the usages: "By which path should one go? (katarena maggena). Which ocean is this? (samuddo kataro ayaṃ). What is the contact at that time? (katamo phasso). Which are the wholesome states? (katame dhammā kusalā). There are four cardinal directions, four intermediate directions, and above and below, making ten directions; in which direction (katamaṃ disaṃ) does the Naga king stay?" These and others are the examples.

Ubhayo, ubhayaṃ, ubhayo, ubhayena. In the remaining cases in the masculine, it is the same as the word sabba. "Two people stand (ubhayo janā tiṭṭhanti). He sees two people (ubhayo jane passati)." It is used like "ubho puttā (two sons), ubho putte (two sons [acc.])." The word "ubhayo" is well-known only as having a plural ending, like the word "ubho," and not as having a singular ending. In this context:

"In a single night, both (ubhayo) you and Dhanusekha, greatly delight only in food; both (ubhayo) gods and humans."
"Both (ubhayo) your father and brothers"—these should be understood as the illustrative examples that establish that meaning. Venerable Sirs, if you should see the word "ubhayo" with a singular ending, then pay close attention to it. For who is able to [know] the method without remainder in the Jina's Dispensation, the Tipitaka together with the Commentaries, which is adorned with infinite methods?
359:
It is difficult for anyone other than one who has attained analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā) and is accomplished in the scriptures (āgama) and realizations (adhigama) to see and to show this. In this matter, this noteworthy point should be understood:

The words añña, pubba, dakkhiṇa, uttara, and para are included among both pronouns (sabbanāma) and non-pronouns (asabbanāma).

The inclusion of these words among pronouns has already been clarified. Now, their inclusion among non-pronouns will be stated—among those words, first, when the word 'añña' denotes a fool (bāla), it is not a pronoun. Because it is a non-pronoun, it should be declined in all ways according to the paradigms of purisa, kaññā, and citta. This is because: 'añño' (a foolish man) is one who does not know; 'aññā' (a foolish woman) is one who does not know; 'aññaṃ' (a foolish clan/family) is that which does not know—such is the word-meaning (vacanattha). Knowing this, in the masculine gender, the declension (nāmika-padamālā) should be applied according to the purisa method as 'añño, aññā; aññaṃ, aññe', and so on. In the feminine gender, it should be applied according to the kaññā method as 'aññā, aññā, aññāyo', and so on. In the neuter gender, it should be applied according to the citta method as 'aññaṃ, aññāni', and so on.

In this specific sense of 'foolish person', if one who wishes to speak says 'aññe janā' instead of 'aññā janā', that person's speech does not accomplish the intended meaning, because the meaning would be understood differently. Likewise, if one says 'aññesaṃ janānaṃ' or 'aññesānaṃ janānaṃ' instead of 'aññānaṃ janānaṃ', that person's speech does not accomplish the intended meaning. Similarly, if one says 'aññāsaṃ itthīnaṃ' instead of 'aññānaṃ itthīnaṃ', or if one says 'aññesaṃ kulānaṃ' or 'aññesānaṃ kulānaṃ' instead of 'aññānaṃ kulānaṃ', it is the same. However, if one wishes to speak of 'other people' as understood by the power of pronouns, one should say 'aññe janā', etc., and not 'aññā janā', etc. This is because the speech 'aññā janā', etc., does not accomplish the intended meaning, as the meaning would be taken differently.
360:
Because the meaning would be taken differently. Thus, in cases where the expression 'aññā janā', etc., is appropriate, the expression 'aññe janā', etc., is inappropriate; whereas in cases where the expression 'aññe janā', etc., is appropriate, the expression 'aññā janā', etc., is inappropriate. The wisdom that repeatedly reflects on this specific meaning is the path of Nīti (method/logic), as it is the cause for investigating what is appropriate and what is inappropriate. In the world, the investigation of what is appropriate and inappropriate is called Nīti. And that Nīti cannot be accomplished without wisdom. In this way, the word 'añña' also becomes a non-pronoun.

Among the words pubba, dakkhiṇa, uttara, and para: the word 'pubba' is a non-pronoun in instances where it denotes a chief/leader, and in instances such as 'semhaṃ pubbo' (pus from blood), where it denotes pus. In the first meaning, it has three genders; in the second meaning, it has only one gender. The words 'uttara' and 'para' when denoting the highest/supreme meaning are also non-pronouns and have three genders. Likewise, the word 'dakkhiṇa' is a non-pronoun when it denotes 'well-trained' or 'dexterous', as in 'dakkhiṇassā vahantimaṃ'. However, in instances such as 'petānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ dajjā', the word 'dakkhiṇā' which denotes a gift to be given (deyyadhamma) is necessarily feminine and is only a non-pronoun. Thus, since the words añña, pubba, dakkhiṇa, uttara, and para can also be non-pronouns, their inclusion in both pronouns and non-pronouns should be understood.

Now, the formation of compounds (samāsa) of the word 'katara', etc., with a subsequent word will be presented: 'kataragāmavāsī' (dweller of which village?), 'katamagāmavāsī', 'ubhayagāmavāsino', 'itaragāmavāsī', 'aññataragāmavāsī', 'pubbadisā', 'parajano', 'dakkhiṇadisā', 'uttaradisā', 'adharapatto'. In these cases, the analysis of the compound (samāsa-viggaha) should be made accordingly, such as: 'kataro gāmo kataragāmo', 'katamo gāmo katamagāmo', 'ubhayo gāmā ubhayagāmā'. The compounding of the word 'katara' together with the word 'katama' is also desired; the two forms 'katarakatame' and 'katarakatamā' are evident.
361:
Because it is shown by the word 'vā' (or). Therefore, the declension (nāmika-padamālā) of the words 'katara' and 'katama' should be applied according to the pronominal method and, among pure nouns, according to the purisa method. Due to such application, in the places of the dative (sampadāna) and genitive (sāmī) cases, three forms would occur: 'katarakatamesaṃ', 'katarakatamesānaṃ', and 'katarakatamānaṃ'. When forming a compound in the feminine gender as 'katarā ca katamā ca katarakatamā', it should be applied according to the pronominal method and, among pure nouns, according to the kaññā method. When forming a compound in the neuter gender as 'katarañca katamañca katarakatamāni', it should be applied according to the pronominal method and, among pure nouns, according to the citta method.

In this context, this distinction should also be understood: words such as pubba and apara, having reached the rules of dvanda compounds, etc., do not retain their pronominal forms. How is that? 'pubbāparā', 'adharuttarā', 'māsapubbā purisā', 'diṭṭhapubbā purisā', 'tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbā sāvakā'—these are nominative plural forms in the masculine gender. Here, the substitute (ādesa) 'ekāra' (the 'e' ending) is not seen. 'pubbāparānaṃ', 'adharuttarānaṃ', 'māsapubbānaṃ purisānaṃ'—these are dative and genitive plural forms in the masculine gender. Here, the substitutes 'saṃ' and 'sānaṃ' are not seen. Likewise, 'tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbānaṃ sāvakānaṃ', 'tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbānaṃ sāvikānaṃ', or 'kulānaṃ'—these are dative and genitive plural forms in the three genders. Here too, the substitutes 'saṃ' and 'sānaṃ' are not seen. 'māsapubbāyaṃ', 'māsapubbāya', 'piyapubbāyaṃ', 'piyapubbāya'—these are locative, dative, and genitive singular forms in the feminine gender. Here, the substitutes 'saṃ' and 'sā' are not seen. 'māsapubbānaṃ itthīnaṃ', 'piyapubbānaṃ itthīnaṃ'—these are dative and genitive plural forms in the feminine gender. Here, the substitute 'saṃ' is not seen. Other forms should also be applied as they occur. We shall explain the compound analysis (samāsa-viggaha) of pubba, apara, etc., in the section on compounds (samāsa-pariccheda).
362:
Now, the declension table (nāmika-padamālā) of the word 'ya' will be presented:

Yo, ye. Yaṃ, ye. Yena, yehi, yebhi. Yassa, yesaṃ, yesānaṃ. Yasmā, yamhā, yehi, yebhi. Yassa, yesaṃ, yesānaṃ. Yasmiṃ, yamhi, yesu. This is the masculine gender (pullinga).

Yaṃ, yāni. Yaṃ, yāni. Yena. The remaining cases are the same as the masculine. Alternatively: Yaṃ, yāni, yā. Yaṃ, yāni, ye. Yena. The remaining cases are the same as the masculine. In some instances, the elision of 'ni-kāra' occurs. Or, in verses, the substitution (ādesa) of 'ā-kāra' and 'e-kāra' in place of 'ni-kāra' also occurs.

"Yā pubbe bodhisattānaṃ, pallaṅkavaramābuje. Nimittāni padissanti, tāni ajja padissare," and "Kiṃ māṇavassa ratanāni atthi, ye taṃ jinanto hare akkhadhutto"—these are the Pali examples in this context. This is the neuter gender (napuṃsakalinga).

Yā, yā, yāyo. Yaṃ, yā, yāyo. Yāya, yāhi, yābhi. Yāya, yassā, yāsaṃ. Yāya, yāhi, yābhi. Yāya, yassā, yāsaṃ. Yassaṃ, yāyaṃ, yāsu. This is the feminine gender (itthilinga).

Thus, the declension table of the word 'ya' is formed according to the three genders. In this context, vocative (ālapana) forms are not found. Similarly, they are not found in the declension tables of the word 'ta' and others.

Now, the extraction of meanings (atthuddhāra) for the word 'yaṃ' will be presented: The word 'yaṃ' is seen in the nominative case (paccatta-vacana) in such passages as: "Bhante, I have heard that word in the presence of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, I have received it in their presence; Bhante, I report that to the Blessed One."

It is seen in the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) in such passages as: "We have asked about that which was asked; he has explained it to us. We shall ask about that other matter; speak it quickly."

It is seen in the instrumental case (karaṇa-vacana) in such passages as: "Monks, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that in a single world-system (two Buddhas should arise simultaneously)..."

"That Blessed Vipassī, the Worthy One..."
363:
"...the Perfectly Enlightened One arose in the world"—in such passages, it is seen in the sense of the locative case (bhamma-vacana). In this regard, it is said:

"The word 'yaṃ' occurs in these four instances: the nominative (paccatta), the accusative (upayoga), the locative (bhamma), and the instrumental (karaṇa)."

The formation of compounds (samāsa) of the word 'ya' with a subsequent word should also be understood, such as: "yaṃkhandhādi, yaṃguṇā, yagguṇā." In those instances, the resolution of the compound (samāsa-viggaha) is: "yo khandhādi = yaṃkhandhādi" (that which is the aggregates, etc.) and "ye guṇā = yaṃguṇā" (those which are the qualities).

Accordingly, in the Visuddhimagga, it is stated: "This name is 'yaṃguṇanemittika' (derived from qualities); they speak this verse to manifest those qualities." In this word, the etymological derivation (nibbacana) should be understood as: "ye guṇā = yaṃguṇā; the yaṃguṇā themselves are the cause (nimitta), thus yaṃguṇanimitta; this name 'Bhagavā' arising from that is yaṃguṇanemittika."

In the word "yagguṇā," however, the derivation is: "yassa guṇā = yagguṇā" (whose qualities). Accordingly:

"Even the Omniscient Wisdom might not know the qualities of that person;
If so, who else could know them?
I pay homage to that Buddha, whose qualities are like the earth (bhūguṇa)."

In this ancient poetic composition, the derivation "yassa guṇā = yagguṇā" is intended.

When the word 'ya' forms a compound with subsequent words, there may be either the augment of a nasal (niggahīta-āgama) or the doubling of the consonant (dvibhāva). Thus, the compounding of the word 'ya' should be noted.

Now, the declension table of the word 'ta' will be presented:

So, te. Naṃ, taṃ, ne, te. Nena, tena, nehi, tehi, nebhi, tebhi. Assa, nassa, tassa, nesaṃ, tesaṃ (āsaṃ). Asmā, nasmā, tasmā, namhā, tamhā, nehi, tehi, nebhi, tebhi. Assa, nassa, tassa, nesaṃ, tesaṃ (āsaṃ). Asmiṃ, nasmiṃ, tasmiṃ, amhi, namhi, tamhi, tyamhi, nesu, tesu. This is the masculine gender.
364:
In this context, the verse "Nevāsaṃ kesā dissanti, hatthapādā ca jālino" serves as evidence for the existence of the word "āsaṃ"; that word should be understood to exist in all three genders. As evidence for the existence of the word "tyamhi":

"When that person attains virtue, wisdom, and purity,
Then one may place trust in him (tyamhi), and his secrets need no longer be guarded."

This verse is the evidence. In this regard, the distinct form should be noted as in "ariyavinaye" or "sappurisavinaye." In Pali passages such as "ese se eke ekaṭṭhe," the indication of these 'ta' words in the nominative singular ending in 'e' (ekāranta) is also seen.

Now, the extraction of meanings for the word 'te' will be presented: The word 'te' appears in the sense of the nominative plural (paccatta-bahuvacana) by virtue of the word 'ta' in passages such as: "Na te sukhaṃ pajānanti, ye na passanti nandanaṃ." It appears in the sense of the accusative plural (upayoga-bahuvacana) in passages such as: "Te na passāmi dārake."

In passages such as "Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama, namo te buddha vīratthu," it appears in the sense of the dative (sampadāna) by virtue of the word 'tumha'; they say it means "tuyhaṃ" (to you). In passages such as "Kinte diṭṭhaṃ, kinti te diṭṭhaṃ, upadhī te samatikkantā, āsavā te padālitā," it appears in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa). In passages such as "Kinte vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ," it appears in the sense of the genitive (sāmi); they say it means "tava" (your). In this regard, it is said:

"The word 'te' is seen in five senses: the nominative (paccatta), the accusative (upayoga), the instrumental (karaṇa), the dative (sampadāniya), and the genitive (sāmi)."

Taṃ, tāni. Taṃ, tāni. Nena, tena, and so forth. The remaining cases are the same as the masculine. This is the neuter gender.
365: Sā, tā, tāyo. Naṃ, taṃ, nā, tā, nāyo, tāyo. Nāya, tāya, nāhi, tāhi, nābi, tābi. Assā, nassā, (tissā,) tassā, nāya, tāya, nāsaṃ, tāsaṃ, sānaṃ, āsaṃ. Assā, nassā, tassā, nāya, tāya, nāhi, tāhi, nābi, tābi. Assā, nassā, (tissā,) tassā, nāya, tāya, nāsaṃ, tāsaṃ, sānaṃ, āsaṃ. Nāya, tāya, assaṃ, nassaṃ, tissaṃ, tassaṃ, nāyaṃ, tāyaṃ, nāsu, tāsu, tyāsu. This is the feminine gender (itthiliṅga). In this context, however, because the usages "Abhikkamo sānaṃ paññāyati, nāsaṃ kujjhanti paṇḍitā. Khiḍḍā paṇihitā tyāsu, rati tyāsu patiṭṭhitā. Bījāni tyāsu ruhanti" are found, these terms "sānaṃ, āsaṃ, tyāsu" are said to be places where the intellectual eye of grammarians (akkharacintaka) becomes confused. Thus is the declension (nāmika-padamālā) of the word 'taṃ' used in reference to someone not present. In this regard, it is said: "Taṃ tvaṃ gantvāna yācassu" etc., (the word 'taṃ') is seen. Although 'taṃ', 'te', etc., are seen at the beginning, 'naṃ', etc., are not found in that way. 'Naṃ', 'ne', 'nena', etc., like 'vo', 'no', etc., are found in the Buddha's Dispensation (jinasāsana) only when they follow another word. The wise should point out usages such as "Atha naṃ atha ne āha, na ca naṃ paṭinandati". Who would say in this matter: "Just as a river, a path, a tavern, a rest-house, and a water-stand are for everyone, so too are the women in the world; the wise do not get angry with those women"?
366: In this matter: Since the word "nāsaṃ" is seen even after a word, "naṃ", "ne", etc., should also be desired at the beginning. To that person, it should be said: "In your doctrine, (that usage) is not obtained. Only the words nāsaṃ, na, and āsaṃ are obtained. Therefore, the meaning is simply: 'The wise do not get angry with women (āsaṃ)'; O wise ones, remember this well." Alternatively, since in the Niruttipiṭaka text, words like "naṃ", "ne", etc., are mentioned as in "naṃ purisaṃ passati, ne purise passati" even when following another word, therefore, by that method also, those (naṃ, ne) following a word might occasionally occur. We, however, shall state the occurrence of those words according to the method of the Pali Canon; this point should be carefully considered. In this regard, the compound formation (samāsa) of the word 'taṃ' with other words should also be known as: "taṃputto, taṃsadiso, tanninno, tappoṇo, tappabbhāro, tabbhūto, tagguṇo, tassadiso". When the word 'taṃ' forms a compound with other words, there is the arrival of Niggahīta in the preceding word and the doubling of the consonant in the following word. Thus, the compound formation of the word 'taṃ' should be noted. Now, the declension (nāmika-padamālā) of the word 'eta' is stated: Eso, ete. Etaṃ, ete. Etena, etehi, etebhi. Etassa, etesaṃ, etesānaṃ. Etasmā, etamhā, etehi, etebhi. Etassa, etesaṃ, etesānaṃ. Etasmiṃ, etamhi, etesu. This is the masculine gender (pulliṅga). Etaṃ, etāni. Etaṃ, etāni. The remaining cases are the same as the masculine; this is the neuter gender (napuṃsakaliṅga).
367:
*Esā*, *etā*, *etāyo* (Nominative). *Etaṃ*, *etā*, *etāyo* (Accusative). *Etāya*, *etāhi*, *etābhi* (Instrumental/Ablative). *Etāya*, *etissā*, *etissāya*, *etāsaṃ* (Dative/Genitive). *Etāya*, *etāhi*, *etābhi* (Ablative). *Etāya*, *etissā*, *etissāya*, *etāsaṃ* (Dative/Genitive). *Etāya*, *etissaṃ*, *etāsu* (Locative). This is the feminine gender. Thus is the declension (nāmikapadamālā) of the word *eta*.

In this context, the formation of compounds with a subsequent word should also be understood in such instances as: "*Etadatthāya lokasmiṃ, nidhi nāma nidhiyyati. Etapparamāyeva devatā sannipatitā ahesuṃ*," etc.

In a compound, when the word *eta* is joined with subsequent words, the appearance of the *niggahīta* (nasal sound) in the preceding word sometimes occurs and sometimes does not.

## Now, the declension (nāmikapadamālā) of the word idaṃ is described:

*Ayaṃ*, *ime* (Nominative). *Imaṃ*, *ime* (Accusative). *Anena*, *iminā*, *ehi*, *ebhi*, *imehi*, *imebhi* (Instrumental). *Assa*, *imassa*, *esaṃ*, *esānaṃ*, *imesaṃ*, *imesānaṃ* (Dative). *Asmā*, *imasmā*, *imahmā*, *ehi*, *ebhi*, *imehi*, *imebhi* (Ablative). *Assa*, *imassa*, *esaṃ*, *esānaṃ*, *imesaṃ*, *imesānaṃ* (Genitive). *Asmiṃ*, *imasmiṃ*, *amhi*, *imahmi*, *esu*, *imesu* (Locative). This is the masculine gender.

*Idaṃ*, *imāni* (Nominative/Accusative). The remaining case endings are the same as the masculine. This is the neuter gender.

*Ayaṃ*, *imā*, *imāyo* (Nominative). *Imaṃ*, *imā*, *imāyo* (Accusative). *Imāya*, *imāhi*, *imābhi* (Instrumental). *Assā*, *assāya*, *imissā*, *imissāya*, *imāya*, *imāsaṃ* (Dative). *Assā*, *imissā*, *imāya*, *imāhi*, *imābhi* (Ablative). *Assā*, *assāya*, *imissā*, *imissāya*, *imāya*, *imāsaṃ* (Genitive). *Assaṃ*, *imissaṃ*, *imāya*, *imāyaṃ*, *imāsu* (Locative). This is the feminine gender. Thus is the declension (nāmikapadamālā) of the word *idaṃ*.

In the *Kaccāyana* grammar, however, only the word *ima* is stated as the base form (pakati) in the rule "*imassidamaṃsisu napuṃsake*". But in this work, since the base form is seen as "*idaṃ*" in the context of "*idappaccayatā*", only the word *idaṃ* is presented as the base form.
368:
In fact, it is said: "Because of these causes, they are *idappaccaya* (phenomena having these causes); *idappaccaya* themselves are *idappaccayatā* (the state of having these causes); or the collection of *idappaccaya* is *idappaccayatā*." In this context, although the word is expanded with the suffix *-tā* in "*idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā*," there is no difference in meaning, just as in "*devo eva devatā*." However, in the statement "*idappaccayānaṃ samūho idappaccayatā*," the suffix *-tā* is used in the sense of a collection, just as in "*janānaṃ samūho janatā*." In the *Cūḷanirutti* and the *Niruttipiṭaka*, the word *idaṃ* is also mentioned in its natural state.

In a compound (*samāsa*), when the word *idaṃ* is joined with a following word, the form becomes only "*idappaccayatā*," and the following letter (*pa*) must be doubled (*dvitta*).

## Idāni amusaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate -

Asu, amu, amū (Nominative). Amuṃ, amū (Accusative). Amunā, amūhi, amūbhi (Instrumental). Amussa, dussa, amūsaṃ, amūsānaṃ (Dative). Amusmā, amumhā, amūhi, amūbhi (Ablative). Amussa, dussa, amūsaṃ, amūsānaṃ (Genitive). Amusmiṃ, amumhi, amūsu (Locative). This is the masculine gender (*pullinga*).

Aduṃ, amūni (Nominative/Accusative). The remaining cases are the same as the masculine. This is the neuter gender (*napuṃsakalinga*).

Asu, amu, amū, amuyo (Nominative). Amūṃ, amū, amuyo (Accusative). Amuyā, amūhi, amūbhi (Instrumental). Amussā, amuyā, amūsaṃ, amūsānaṃ (Dative). Amuyā, amūhi, amūbhi (Ablative). Amussā, amuyā, amūsaṃ, amūsānaṃ (Genitive). Amuyā, amuyaṃ, amussaṃ, amūsu (Locative). This is the feminine gender (*itthilinga*). Thus is the declension table (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *amu*; however, its use in compounds is rare.

In that context, because the usage "*dussa me khettapālassa, rattibhattaṃ apābhataṃ*" (this night-meal of mine, the field-guard, has been brought) is found, the form "*dussa*" is established by us. By the arrival of the letter *ka* (the suffix *-ka*), other non-pronominal forms also occur.
369:
By virtue of those [suffixes], the declension table of these three genders will be stated—the masculine method (*purisanaya*) is obtained as in "*asuko, asukā; asukaṃ, asuke*," etc., and "*amuko, amukā; amukaṃ, amuke*," etc. The feminine method (*kaññānaya*) is obtained as in "*asukā, asukāyo*," etc., and "*amukā, amukāyo*," etc. The neuter method (*cittanaya*) is obtained as in "*asukaṃ, asukāni*," etc., and "*amukaṃ, amukāni*," etc. In this context, although these words are not pronouns, they are mentioned to show the distinction by virtue of the arrival of the letter *ka*.

Now, the declension table of the word *kiṃ* will be stated: Ko, ke (Nominative). Kaṃ, ke (Accusative). Kena, kehi, kebhi (Instrumental). Kassa, kissa, kesaṃ (Dative). Kasmā, kamhā, kehi, kebhi (Ablative). Kassa, kissa, kesaṃ (Genitive). Kasmiṃ, kismiṃ, kamhi, kimhi, kesu (Locative). This is the masculine gender.

In this context, a special form should also be known. It should be understood according to the Pali perspective: "*Ke gandhabbe ca rakkhase nāge, ke kimpurise ca mānuse, ke paṇḍite sabbakāmadade, dīghaṃ rattaṃ bhattā me bhavissati, ke ca chave pāthikaputte, kā ca tathāgatānaṃ arahantānaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ āsādanā*." Since in such Pali passages as "*ke gandhabbe ca rakkhase nāge*," the nominative case (*paccattavacana*) "*ke*" is also seen as ending in the letter *e*, therefore, the special form "*ke*" should be known in this context. Likewise, the following should be known as illustrative examples: "*Kissassa ekadhammassa, vadhaṃ rocesi gotama. Kasmiṃ me sivayo kuddhā. Kamhi kāle tayā vīra, patthitā bodhimuttamā*," etc. Moreover—

In Pali passages such as "*Ko te balaṃ mahārāja*," it should be known that this sound "*ko*" occurs in the sense of the word "*kva*" (where).
370:
"*Petaṃ taṃ sāmamaddakkhiṃ, ko nu tvaṃ sāma jīvasi*." In this text, it is said that [the word *ko*] occurs in the sense of the word "*kathaṃ*" (how); in these two senses, this sound "*ko*" is found. It should be taken as an indeclinable (*nipāta*) merely because of the similarity in sound.

In the neuter gender: Kaṃ, kāni (Nominative). Kaṃ, kāni (Accusative). The remaining cases should be joined similarly to the masculine. Alternatively, because of seeing usages such as "*Kiṃ cittaṃ? Kiṃ rūpaṃ? Kiṃ parābhavato mukhaṃ? Kiṃ icchasi?*", one may say "*Kiṃ, kāni; kiṃ, kāni*" and join the rest similarly to the masculine. This method is more appropriate; this is the neuter gender.

Kā, kā, kāyo (Nominative). Kaṃ, kā, kāyo (Accusative). Kāya, kāhi, kābhi (Instrumental). Kāya, kassā, kāsaṃ, kāsānaṃ (Dative). Kāya, kassā, kāhi, kābhi (Ablative). Kāya, kassā, kāsaṃ, kāsānaṃ (Genitive). Kāya, kassā, kāyaṃ, kassaṃ, kāsu (Locative). In this context, regarding the existence of the word "*kāyo*," the example "*kāyo amoghā gacchanti*" should be observed. This is the feminine gender. Thus is the declension table of the word *kiṃ*.

In this context, the extraction of the meanings (*atthuddhāra*) of this word *kiṃ* will be stated: The word *kiṃ* appears in the sense of reproach (*garaha*) in such passages as "*Kiṃ rājā yo lokaṃ na rakkhati? Kiṃ nu kho nāma tumhe maṃ vattabbaṃ manyathā?*" It appears in the sense of the indefinite (*aniyama*) in such passages as "*Yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ*," etc. It appears in the sense of uselessness (*nippayojana*) in such passages as "*Kinte vakkali iminā pūtikāyena diṭṭhena, yo kho vakkali dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passati*," etc. It appears in the sense of acceptance (*sampaṭicchana*) in such passages as "*Kiṃ na kāhāmi te vaco*," etc. It appears in the sense of inquiry (*pucchā*) in such passages as "*Kiṃsūdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭhaṃ*," etc. And as for inquiry—
371:
The word 'kiṃ' has many varieties by way of asking for a reason and so forth. Therefore, the occurrence of the word 'kiṃ' should be understood in detail by way of asking for a reason and so forth. Indeed, this word 'kiṃ' occurs in the sense of asking for a reason in such sentences as: "O charioteer, why (kiṃ) do you dig a pit so hurriedly? Why do you not delight in rebirth? Why is your appearance like this?" It occurs in the sense of asking for a purpose in sentences such as: "What (kiṃ) will you do with a pit?" It occurs in the sense of asking for the nature (sarūpa) in sentences such as: "What (kiṃ) is virtue? What is concentration?" It occurs in the sense of asking for an object in sentences such as: "What (kiṃ) do you eat? What do you drink?" It occurs in the sense of asking about an action in sentences such as: "Do you eat? Do you drink?" It should be understood that the five types of questions, such as the question to clarify what is not yet seen (adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā), are not included here because they are not to be brought in for the extraction of the meaning of the word 'kiṃ'. In this regard, it is said:

The word 'kiṃ' occurs in censure, uncertainty (aniyama), pointlessness, acceptance, and questioning.

Its compounding with other words should also be known, as in "kiṃsamudayo, kiṃvedano, kiṃsaññojano." Here, the words associated with 'kiṃ' which are declined according to the three genders as "ko, ke; kā, kā, kāyo; kiṃ, kāni," remain in their original form as 'kiṃ' when in a compound. However, when compounded with the word 'nāma', two ways are seen: "kinnāmo" and "konāmo." All these should be applied according to the feminine gender, neuter gender, and plural number.

When the word 'kiṃ' is compounded with the word 'nāma', there are two ways: "kinnāmo" and "konāmo."
372:
"What is the name of your preceptor?" and so forth are examples here.

When compounded with other words, it is heard only as "kiṃ kiṃ."

Indeed, in sentences such as "Bhikkhu, what kind of mind (kiṃcitto) do you have? What kind of work do you acknowledge?" the word 'kiṃ' remains without abandoning its own form. There, he who has such a mind is called "kiṃcitto." The act of doing or uttering the sound 'kiṃ' as in "Master, what (kiṃ) shall I do?" is called "kiṃkāra"; because of acknowledging that sound, the definition "kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī" should be desired. However, in words like "kinnaro" (kinnara) and "like what fruit (kiṃpakka) is it eaten?", the derivation is not obvious; the word 'kiṃ' is heard only as a part of the word. Indeed, that word 'kiṃ' is heard in some places as a part of a word, and in some places in association with words such as nu, su, nukho, and kāraṇa. Here are the usages: What is this woman to you? What are these people to you? Frequented by kinnaras (kimpurisānucinṇo). Why (kiṃ nu) do you stand as if afraid? Having cut what (kiṃsu) does one sleep happily? What (kiṃ nukho) is the reason? Mother, for what reason (kiṃ kāraṇā) do you neglect? What (kiñhi) is it for one who gives up, not giving even a little by speech? and so forth. In this regard, it is said:

The word 'kiṃ' is seen in the teaching of the Sugata either as a separate part of a word or joined with words like 'nu' and so on.

Other varieties according to the method of Pali should also be understood in detail by the wise who know the method of the True Dhamma.
373:
Now, the distinction in the declension of other words 'ko' and 'kaṃ' which have the same sound as the words 'ko' and 'kaṃ' existing as pronouns should be stated; that distinction was mentioned below in the section mixing the three genders. Because they are not pronouns, they are declined only according to the method of 'purisa' and 'citta'. To be sure, when the word 'ko' expresses the meanings of body, Brahmā, and wind, and the word 'kaṃ' expresses the meanings of head, water, and happiness, then those words are not pronouns. Why? Because they are not made of the word 'kiṃ', they are devoid of the uncommon forms known as pronominal forms, and they express meanings other than the sense of questioning. Here, however, for the sake of making known the different meanings by way of similar sounds, they are called the word 'ko' and the word 'kaṃ'; but in reality, it should be understood that in the sense of a pronoun, it is only the word 'kiṃ', and in the sense of a pure noun, it is only the word 'ka'. Thus:

The word 'ka' occurs in the three genders in the sense of body, Brahmā, wind, head, water, and happiness. It is masculine in the first three and neuter in the last three.

In this way, the occurrence of the words 'kiṃ' and 'ka' which have become pronouns should be understood.

Now, a summary of the meanings mentioned here, which causes the increase of wisdom, will be stated in part.

What is similar to the kimpakka fruit? What is the origin of the body? Speak. Sensual pleasure is similar to the kimpakka fruit; the body has its origin in craving (taṇhā) and so forth.

In the hot season, what (water) do they desire? What (water) do those who are thirsty desire? What (happiness) do enemies desire? What (happiness) do those oppressed by suffering desire?

What is the benefit of which body? Who is the protector of whom on the face of the earth? Who has the pleasure born of jhāna? What is noble among the limbs of whom?
374:
Below, we have analyzed the paradigm of nominal declension for the word 'kiṃ', which is designated as a pronoun, according to the three genders. Among those declensions, in the masculine and neuter positions, excluding the forms 'kebhi, kissa, kasmā, kamhā, kamhī', and in the feminine position, excluding the forms 'kāyo, kābhi, kāsānaṃ, kāyaṃ, kassa', one should take forms of this nature by applying the particles 'ci', 'cana', and 'canaṃ' to the remaining words as appropriate. For example:

Koci, keci, kecana. Kiñci, kiñcanaṃ, keci, kecana. Kenaci, kehici. Kassaci, kesañci. The singular of the ablative case is missing because it does not appear in the Pali texts. Kehici. Kassaci, kesañci. Kasmiñci, kismici, kesuci. These should be viewed according to the masculine and neuter genders. Here, 'kismici' is stated by way of the elision of the anusvāra.

According to the feminine gender: kāci itthī, kāci itthiyo. Kāci, kāci. Kiñci, kāci. Kāyaci, kāhici. Kāyaci, kassāci, kāsañci. Kāyaci, kāhici. Kāyaci, kassāci, kāsañci. Kāyaci, kāsuci—these are the forms.

In this context, usages such as 'iti bhāsanti kecana' (thus some people say), 'na naṃ hiṃsāmi kiñcana' (I do not harm him even a little) and so on should be understood. It should be understood that these terms 'koci, kāci, kiñci', etc., stated according to the three genders, are expressions that encompass small or limited things.

Again, I shall demonstrate those same words by joining them with the word 'yaṃ' as appropriate:

Yo koci, ye keci. Yaṃ kiñci, ye keci. Yena kenaci, yehi kehici. Yassa kassaci, yesaṃ kesañci. Yasmā kasmāci, yehi kehici. Yassa kassaci, yesaṃ kesañci. Yasmiṃ kasmiñci, yesu kesuci.
375:
In this context, usages such as 'Whoever listens to me with respect. Of the flavors that exist on earth, truth is the most excellent flavor' and so on should be understood. These are masculine forms. Yaṃ kiñci, yāni kānici. Yaṃ kiñci, yāni kānici. The remaining forms are similar to the masculine. In this context, usages such as 'Whatever treasure exists in the mansion of King Dhataraṭṭha. Whatever wealth exists here or elsewhere. Whatever forms exist' and so on should be understood. These are neuter forms. Yā kāci itthī, yā kāci itthiyo. Yaṃ kiñci, yā kāci. Yāya kāyaci, yāhi kāhici. Yāya kāyaci, yāsaṃ kāsañci. Yāya kāyaci, yāhi kāhici. Yāya kāyaci, yāsaṃ kāsañci. Yāya kāyaci, yāsu kāsuci. In this context, usages such as 'Whatever feeling (vedanā) past, future, or present' and so on should be understood. These are feminine forms. It should be understood that these terms 'yo koci, yā kāci, yaṃ kiñci', etc., stated according to the three genders, are expressions that encompass everything without exception. It should also be understood that all these are not indeclinable words (nipāta), but are linguistic occurrences that resemble indeclinables. If they were indeclinable words, they would remain in a single form across the three genders and seven cases; however, they do not remain so. Therefore, they are not indeclinable words, but are merely linguistic occurrences that resemble indeclinables.

Furthermore, when there is a desire to express meanings using the pronouns 'ya, ta, kiṃ, eta' by applying the suffixes '-ttaka' and '-ttika' according to the gender, the words that are formed are expressions of determination (pariccheda) and are not pronouns. Their paradigm of nominal declension should be joined according to the methods of 'purisa', 'citta', and 'kaññā'. What is that method?
376:
Yattako jano, yattakaṃ cittaṃ, yattikā itthī. Tattako, tattakaṃ, tattikā. Kittako, kittakaṃ, kittikā. Ettako, ettakaṃ, ettikā. These words, although not pronouns, are stated for the sake of the proficiency of the wise in other meanings that arise through the power of suffixes.

Now, the paradigm of nominal declension for the word 'eka', which expresses number and so on, will be stated. Indeed, the word 'eka' is used to express number, uniqueness (peerlessness), solitude (being without a companion), some, and being mixed. When it expresses number, uniqueness, or solitude, it is only in the singular.

Eko, ekaṃ, ekena, ekassa, ekasmā, ekamhā, ekassa, ekasmiṃ, ekamhī. Thus, the word 'eka' expressing number and so on is singular. This is true; in the context of number, such as 'eko, dve, tayo', the word 'eka' is only singular. Also, in expressing uniqueness or solitude, such as 'I am the unique (peerless) Perfectly Enlightened One. I, the King, sleep alone', it is only singular. This is the pronominal paradigm of nominal declension in the singular.

However, when those who are without companions or those in the sense of number are to be spoken of in the plural, the augment 'ka' is added after the word 'eka', resulting in 'ekakā, ekake, ekakehi, ekakebhi'. The paradigm of nominal declension should be joined by way of the plural according to the 'purisa' method. This is true; meanings of number can also be plural. For is it not said, 'cattāro ekakā siy uṃ' (there may be four ones)? Those without companions can also be plural. This is true; in a situation where one would say, 'This householder also came alone, this householder also came alone', the expression 'These householders came individually (one by one)' is seen. This method does not fall into the category of pronouns because it lacks non-common (unique pronominal) forms, but it is stated for the purpose of making other meanings known.
377:
When there is a word expressing the meaning 'some', it is stated as: "Eke, eke, ekehi, ekebhi, ekesaṃ, ekehi, ekebhi, ekesaṃ, ekesu." This is also a pronominal declension (sabbanāma padamālā) in the plural. Here, 'eke' means 'ekacce' (some). This same method applies to the remaining cases. However, when there is a word that has reached a state of mixing, it is stated by the power of the plural in the masculine method as: "Ekā, eke, ekehi, ekebhi, ekānaṃ." The Pali text is seen as: "May both the King of Pañcāla and the King of Videha become one (ekā)." Although this method does not follow the pronominal side because of the absence of an uncommon form (asādhāraṇarūpa), it is stated for the purpose of making another meaning known. In that context, 'ekā bhavantu' means let them become one, let them be mixed; it means let them converge and agree without being otherwise, like the water of the Ganges and the water of the Yamunā.

Teachers, however, without showing this distinction, take only the pronominal nature of the word 'eka' and apply the nominal declension like the word 'sabba'. How?

Eko, eke. Ekaṃ, eke. Ekena, ekehi, ekebhi. Ekassa, ekesaṃ, ekesānaṃ. Ekasmā, ekamhā, ekehi, ekebhi. Ekassa, ekesaṃ, ekesānaṃ. Ekasmiṃ, ekamhi, ekesu. This should be known as the pronominal declension (sabbanāma padamālā).

Some teachers say: "The word 'eka' expresses the meanings of number, equality, being without a companion, and 'other'. When it expresses number, it always ends in the singular in all meanings; in other meanings, it also ends in the plural. In all meanings such as 'eko, ekā, ekaṃ', it is similar to the word 'sabba'. There is a distinction only in numbers." Thus they state the method of application in the three genders. Those teachers who speak thus do so without showing the distinction. We, however, shall speak by showing the distinction for the purpose of producing skill in applications for the listeners.
378:
Furthermore, this distinction should also be noted here: in the Pali passage "Eke ekaṭṭhe same samabhāge," the reference to the word 'eka' as a nominative singular ending in 'e' is also seen. These are the masculine forms.

Ekaṃ, ekāni. Ekaṃ, ekāni. The remaining cases are similar to the masculine. In that context, 'ekāni' means 'ekaccāni' (some things). This same method applies to the remaining plural cases. These are the neuter forms.

Ekā, ekā, ekāyo. Ekaṃ, ekā, ekāyo. Ekāya, ekāhi, ekābhi. Ekāya, ekissā, ekāsaṃ. Ekāya, ekāhi, ekābhi. Ekāya, ekissā, ekāsaṃ. Ekāya, ekāyaṃ, ekissaṃ, ekāsu. Here, in the plural positions, 'ekā' means 'ekaccā' (some women), 'ekāhi' means 'ekaccāhi', 'ekāsaṃ' means 'ekaccānaṃ', and 'ekāsu' means 'ekaccāsu'. These are the feminine forms. All these pronouns have been stated by way of the singular and plural.

Furthermore, when the word 'eka' is stated by way of repetition (vīcchā), there are only singular forms in all three genders. How?

Ekeko, ekekaṃ, ekekena, ekekassa, ekekasmā, ekekamhā, ekekassa, ekekasmiṃ, ekekamhi. These are the masculine forms.

Ekekaṃ, ekekaṃ. The remaining cases are similar to the masculine. These are the neuter forms. Ekekā, ekekaṃ, ekekāya, ekekissā, ekekāya, ekekissā, ekekāyaṃ, ekekissaṃ. These are the feminine forms.

All these words should be called distributive pronouns (vīcchā-sabbanāma). Plural forms do not exist here because of the absence of usage. Thus, in these forms of the three genders stated by way of repetition, one should not consider them as compounds (samāsa), because words of repetition are indefinable (anibbacaniya). Indeed, it is so: "Pabbaṃ..."
379:
"Becoming joint by joint, connection by connection, limit by limit, making a 'tata-tata' sound like sesame seeds thrown into a hot frying pan, the conditioned things (saṅkhāra) perish." In such words, the ancient teachers did not show the derivation (nibbacana) by means of forming a compound for words like 'pabbapabba'. Since the reduplication (dvirutti) occurring in repetition (vīcchā) is established only by worldly usage and not by grammatical rules (lakkhaṇa), therefore, one should not consider a compound in that context.

Now, the nominal declensions of the words 'ekacca', 'ekatiya', and 'ekacciya' are stated—firstly, in the masculine: Ekacco, ekacce. Ekaccaṃ, ekacce. The remaining cases are similar to the word 'purisa'. Here, only the nominative plural 'ekacce' is similar to the pronominal form because it is an uncommon form (asādhāraṇarūpa). "Here, some son of a good family (idhekacco kulaputto). Here, some foolish men (idhekacce moghapurisā)" are the illustrative examples.

Ekatiyo, ekatiye. Ekatiyaṃ, ekatiye. The remaining cases are similar to the word 'purisa'. Here too, only the nominative plural 'ekatiye' is similar to the pronominal form because it is an uncommon form. 'Ekatiye manussā'—some people.

"One should not trust only some people, whether householders or those who have gone forth. Having been good, they become not good; having been not good, they become good again." These are the illustrative examples. When the word 'ekacciya' exists:

"It is true that some men in this world have said so. A floating log is better; but some man is not." "Ekacciyaṃ āhāraṃ"—some food. These are the illustrative examples. Ekacciyo, ekacciyā. Ekacciyaṃ, ekacciye. In every way, it follows the method of the word 'purisa'. These are the masculine forms.
380:
Ekaccaṃ, ekaccāni. Ekaccaṃ, ekaccāni. The remaining forms are similar to the masculine gender. Ekatiyaṃ, ekatiyāni. Ekatiyaṃ, ekatiyāni. The remaining forms are similar to the masculine gender. Ekacciyaṃ, ekacciyāni. Ekacciyaṃ, ekacciyāni. The remaining forms are similar to the masculine gender. These are the neuter gender forms.

"Ekaccā, ekaccā, ekaccāyo" should be declined according to the method of kaññā; likewise, "ekatiyā, ekatiyā, ekatiyāyo. Ekatiyaṃ" and "ekacciyā, ekacciyā, ekacciyāyo. Ekacciyaṃ" should also be declined according to the method of kaññā. These are the feminine gender forms.

Now, the paradigms of nouns (nāmikapadamālā) will be stated by virtue of the words ekākī and ekākiya:
Ekākī, ekākī, ekākino. Ekākiṃ, ekākī, ekākino. These should be known according to the method of daṇḍī. Ekākiyo, ekākiyā. Ekākiyaṃ, ekākiye. Ekākiyena. These should be known according to the method of purisa. These are the masculine gender forms.

Ekāki kulaṃ, ekākī, ekākīni. Ekākiṃ, ekākī, ekākīni. The remaining forms are similar to the masculine gender. Ekākiyaṃ, ekākiyāni. Ekākiyaṃ, ekākiyāni. The remaining forms are similar to the masculine gender. These are the neuter gender forms.

Ekākinī, ekākinī, ekākiniyo. Ekākiniṃ, ekākinī, ekākiniyo. With ekākiniyā, it is similar to the word itthī. Ekākiyā, ekākiyā, ekākiyāyo. Ekākiyaṃ, ekākiyā, ekākiyāyo. With ekākiyāyā, it is similar to the word kaññā. These are the feminine gender forms. It should be understood that all these forms are stated as non-pronoun forms (asabbanāmika) for the purpose of conveying a different meaning.

Now, the paradigm of nouns for the word ubha, which is a synonym of the word dvi, always ending in the plural, and being a pronoun, is stated:
381:
“Ubho, ubho, ubhohi, ubhobhi, ubhinnāṃ, ubhohi, ubhobhi, ubhinnāṃ, ubhosu” — this is the paradigm of words stated in accordance with the Pali method. Herein, the examples are: Ubho kumārā nikkītā (Two boys have been bought). Ubho itthiyo tiṭṭhanti (Two women stand), ubho cittāni tiṭṭhanti (Two minds stand), ubho putte adāsi (He gave two sons). Ubho kaññāyo passati (He sees two maidens). Ubho pādāni bhinditvā, saññamissāmi vo ahaṃ (Having broken both feet, I shall restrain you). Ubhohi hatthehi (With both hands). Ubhohi bāhāhi (With both arms), ubhohi cittehi (With both minds), ubhinnāṃ janānaṃ (Of two people), ubhinnāṃ itthīnaṃ (Of two women), ubhinnāṃ cittānaṃ (Of two minds), ubhosu purisesu (Among two men), ubhosu itthīsu (Among two women), ubhosu passesu (On both sides) — such is our preference (view). However, the teachers also desire “ubhehi, ubhebhi, ubhesu.” In the Kaccāyana text as well, it is stated as “ubhe tappurisā.” All these should indeed be borne in mind. The compound (samāsa) of the word ubha is rare. These forms are common to the three genders.

Now, the paradigms of nouns for the numerals dvi and catu, which always end in the plural and are pronouns, are stated:

Dve, dve, dvīhi, dvībhi, dvinnāṃ, duvinnāṃ, dvīhi, dvībhi, dvinnāṃ, duvinnāṃ, dvīsu. In the Cūḷanirutti text, however, the paradigm “dvinnannaṃ” appears. These (forms of dvi), like the word ahaṃ etc., although free from being exclusively feminine etc., are employed in all three genders as in “dve purisā, dve itthiyo, dve cittāni,” and so forth. These forms are also common to the three genders.

The form “dve” is a form of the word dvi; that form may occur in a compound.
The word dvi exists only with the roots dvi and ti; it may occur in various contexts (meanings).
Dvibhāvo and dvebhāvo, dvirattañca duvassako.
Dohalinī and dupattañca; in the state of taddhita, dvayaṃ dvayaṃ (two by two).
382:
Tayo, tayo, tīhi, tībhi, tiṇṇāṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, tīhi, tībhi, tiṇṇāṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, tīsu. These are the masculine gender forms.

Tisso, tisso, tīhi, tībhi, tissannaṃ, tīhi, tībhi, tissannaṃ, tīsu. These are the feminine gender forms. In the Cūḷanirutti text, the dative and genitive plural appear as “tissannannaṃ,” while in the Niruttipiṭaka text, it is “tiṇṇannaṃ.” If those forms are found upon repeated investigation and contemplation in the Tipiṭaka Buddha-vacana along with the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), they should be accepted.

Tīṇi, tīṇi, tīhi, tībhi, tiṇṇāṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, tīhi, tībhi, tiṇṇāṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, tīsu. These are the neuter gender forms. In some Pali contexts, the elision of the syllable 'ṇi' of the word tīṇi also occurs, as in “dve vā ti vā udakaphusitāni.” The passage “Tiṇṇannaṃ kho bhikkhave indriyānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā piṇḍolabhāradvājena bhikkhunā aññā vyākatā” is an illustration of the existence of the word “tiṇṇannaṃ.”

Those forms which are stated as “tisso, tīṇi, tayo”;
In the scope of a compound, they should have the root “ti.”
Because when the word “ti” in a compound occurs with a subsequent word—
It should be indicated as “tivedanaṃ, ticittaṃ” and “tilokaṃ.”
In this regard, the neuter gender is specifically praised due to its frequent occurrence.
In this context, the masculine gender is also desired as in “tibhavo khāyate.”

Cattāro, caturo, cattāro, caturo, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnāṃ, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnāṃ, catūsu. These are the masculine gender forms.
383:
catasso, catasso, catūhi, catūbi, catubbhi, catassannaṃ, catunnaṃ, catūhi, catūbi, catubbhi, catassannaṃ, catunnaṃ, catūsu. These are the feminine forms. In the feminine gender, the term "catunnaṃ" is mentioned because it is found in the Cūḷanirutti, Niruttipiṭaka, the Pāḷi Canon, and the Commentaries. Thus, in the Cūḷanirutti, "catunnaṃ" appears in the feminine; in the Niruttipiṭaka, "catunnaṃ kaññānaṃ" appears. In the Pāḷi Canon, such as in the Soṇadanda Sutta, it appears as "samaṇo gotamo catunnaṃ parisānaṃ piyo manāpo". In the Commentaries, specifically in the Suttanta Commentary, it appears as "catūhi acchariyabbhutadhammehi samannāgato catunnaṃ parisānaṃ piyo manāpo". In the Sattilaṅgha Jātaka Commentary, it appears as "ācariyo panassa catunnaṃ sattīnaṃ laṅghanaṃ sippaṃ jānāti".

cattāri, cattāri, catūhi, catūbi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūhi, catūbi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūsu. These are the neuter forms.

They are pronounced as "cattāro", "catasso", and "cattāri".

Rūpaṃ samāsabhāvamhi, catuppakatikaṃ bhave.
Nidassanapadānettha, kamato kamakovido.

In the state of a compound, the form has four natures. Here, one who knows the sequence should show the illustrative terms in order. One should point out: "catubbidhaṃ, catussālaṃ, catussaccaṃ".

These pronouns starting from "two" are only plural; they do not have singular forms. However, in the Cūḷanirutti, it says "catassannaṃ" for all three genders; that statement seems untenable upon reflection.

Now, the noun paradigms (nāmikapadamālā) of the words tumha and amha will be stated. Among those words, for the person speaking, the tumha words occur in the vocative (ālapana).

tvaṃ, tuvaṃ, tumhe. taṃ, tuvaṃ, tvaṃ, tavaṃ, tumhe. tayā, tvayā, tumhehi, tumhebi. tuyhaṃ, tava, tumhaṃ, tumhākaṃ. tayā, tvayā, tumhehi, tumhebi. tuyhaṃ, tava, tumhaṃ, tumhākaṃ. tayi, tvayi,
384:
tumhesu. There, they should be applied as: "tvaṃ puriso (you are a man), tvaṃ itthī (you are a woman), tvaṃ cittaṃ (you are the mind)," etc.

In connection with oneself, the amha words occur.

ahaṃ, ahakaṃ, mayaṃ, amhe. maṃ, mamaṃ, amhe. mayā, amhehi, amhebi. mayhaṃ, mama, amhaṃ, amhākaṃ, asmākaṃ. mayā, amhehi, amhebi. mayhaṃ, mama, amhaṃ, amhākaṃ, asmākaṃ. mayi, amhesu, asmesu.

Here, because the Pāḷi text "kathaṃ amhe karomase" is found, it should be known that there is a nominative form (paccattavacana) "amhe", just like the nominative form "tumhe". The variant form "ahakaṃ" is also desired. As evidence for the existence of that form, this Pāḷi text is an example: "ahakañca cittavasānugā bhāsissaṃ". Here, "ahakaṃ" has the same meaning as "ahaṃ". There, they should be applied as: "ahaṃ puriso, ahaṃ kaññā, ahaṃ cittaṃ," etc. These are also forms common to all three genders.

In the Kaccāyana, Cūḷanirutti, and Niruttipiṭaka, however, "tumhākaṃ" and "amhākaṃ" are called accusative plural (dutiyā bahuvacana). In the Kaccāyana, "tumhānaṃ" and "amhānaṃ" are called nominative and accusative plural; and "tumhaṃ" and "amhaṃ" are called dative and genitive singular, as well as nominative and accusative plural. In the Cūḷanirutti and Niruttipiṭaka, however, "tumhaṃ" and "amhaṃ" are called accusative singular, and "tumhe" and "amhe" are called dative and genitive plural. These should be examined, and if they are found in the Suttas along with the Commentaries, they should be accepted.

When the words tumha and amha form compounds with other words, usages such as "maṃdīpā" arise from the mouth of the Buddha and others. From the mouth of the Buddha, it comes as: "ete gāmaṇi maṃdīpā maṃleṇā maṃsaraṇā". From the mouth of those skilled in linguistics (niruttaññu), it comes as: "tayyogo, mayyogo". In the Kāvyādāsa text, it comes as: "tvaṃmukhaṃ kamaleneva, tulyaṃ".
385:
## nānyena kenacīti ca candena tvaṃmukhaṃ tulyanti ca kavimukhato.

In that (Pāḷi), because of the meaning "I am the island for these people," it becomes maṃdīpā (those who have me as their island); because of the meaning "I am the resting place (refuge) for these people," it becomes maṃleṇā; thus maṃsaraṇā (those who have me as their refuge). Connection with the word tumha is tayyogo, which means exactly this: connection with the word tumha. Connection with the word amha is mayyogo, which means exactly this: connection with the word amha. Your face is tvaṃmukhaṃ. Even by way of the plural, the analysis (viggoha) is made as: "The face of you all is tvaṃmukhaṃ."

In this (grammar text), because of the showing of maṃdīpā etc. in the Pāḷi Canon, tvaṃdīpā etc. should also be accepted; and because of the showing of tvaṃmukhaṃ in the Kāvyādāsa text, tvaṃvaṇṇo, tvaṃsaro, maṃmukhaṃ, maṃvaṇṇo, maṃsaro, etc., should be accepted. Among those (terms), because of the meaning "You are the island for these people," it is tvaṃdīpā; or because of the meaning "You all are the island for these people," it is tvaṃdīpā. Your appearance is tvaṃvaṇṇo. My face is maṃmukhaṃ, or our face is maṃmukhaṃ—these are the analyses. This method should be understood in other such places as well.

In a compound, the words tumha and amha become (tvaṃ, maṃ) when connected with subsequent words.

"tvaṃmukhaṃ" as well as "maṃdīpā, tayyogo, mayyogo" (are examples).

Here, if one asks, "Are these the only forms of the words tumha and amha, or are there others?" There are te, me, etc. If that is so, why is the paradigm not taught separately? There is a reason for not teaching it. This is the reason:

"te, me, vo, no" rūpāni, parāni padato yato.
tato nāmikapantīsu, na tu vuttāni tāni me.

Because the forms "te, me, vo, no" occur only after a word, I have not taught them in the noun sequences.

In this (text), I will state the extraction of the meanings (atthuddhāra) of the words mayaṃ, me, vo, and no—the meaning of the word te has already been stated. Because the teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathācariya) say the word mayaṃ even in the place of the word mayā, and the word mayā even in the place of the word mayaṃ, we shall also say the same. The word mayaṃ in such passages as "anuññātapatiññātā, tevijjāmayamasmubho"...
386:
... It occurs in the sense of the word 'amha'. In this (verse), "Mayam nissāya hemāya, jātā mandosīsūpagā," it occurs in the sense of designation (paññatti). In such passages as "Manomayā pītibhakkhā sayampabhā," it occurs in the sense of arising (nibbattiattha). They are called 'manomayā' (mind-made) because they arise by the mind alone without external conditions (paccaya). In such passages as "Yaṃ nūnāhaṃ sabbamatttikāmayaṃ kuṭikaṃ kareyyaṃ" (What if I were to make a small hut made of clay), it occurs in the sense of modification (vikāra). In such passages as "Dānamayaṃ sīlamayaṃ," it occurs in the sense of a mere verse-filler (padapūraṇa). In this (Pali), "Pīṭhaṃ te sovaṇṇamayaṃ uḷāraṃ" (Your couch is a noble one made of gold), it should be understood either in the sense of modification or as a mere verse-filler. When the meaning is that 'suvaṇṇa' (gold) itself is 'sovaṇṇa', then the word 'maya' in 'sovaṇṇamaya' should be understood in the sense of modification, as a modification of gold. It is also appropriate to say it is in the sense of arising (nibbattiattha). However, when the meaning is that 'sovaṇṇa' is that which has arisen from gold, then the word 'maya' in 'sovaṇṇamaya' should be understood as a mere verse-filler, meaning 'sovaṇṇa' itself.

The word 'me' occurs in the sense of the instrumental case (karaṇa) in such passages as "Kicchena me adhigataṃ, halaṃ dāni pakāsituṃ" (With difficulty has it been attained by me; enough now with preaching it). It means 'mayā' (by me). In such passages as "Tassa me bhante bhagavā saṅkhittena dhammaṃ desetu" (Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One preach the Dhamma in brief to me), it is said to be in the sense of the dative case (sampadāna), meaning 'mayhaṃ' (to/for me). In such passages as "Pubbeva me bhikkhave sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato" (Before my enlightenment, monks, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta), it is also said to be in the sense of the genitive case (sāmi), meaning 'mama' (my). In this regard, it is said:

The word 'me' should be known by the wise who see the method as occurring in the instrumental sense, the dative sense, and the genitive sense.
387:
Standing at this point, I shall state the analysis (vinicchaya) regarding the explanation of the meanings of the words 'te' and 'me' made by the Commentators (Atthakathācariya). This is for the purpose of uprooting the doubts of the listeners by clarifying their intention. Indeed, the Commentators explained the words 'te' and 'me' by way of the dative sense as "to you, to me," and by way of the genitive sense as "your, my." Thus, where can this rule of meaning, shown by those teachers without confusion, be found in the Tipitaka, the Word of the Buddha, together with the Commentaries? For the words 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ', and the words 'tava' and 'mama', which express the meanings of the words 'te' and 'me', occur in the dative and genitive senses without a fixed rule.

In this regard, there are these examples: "Idaṃ tuyhaṃ dadāmi" (I give this to you). "Tuyhaṃ vika़ppemi" (I assign to you). "Brahmin, I shall perform the offering with your (tuyhaṃ) flesh, fat, and head." "This is your (tuyhaṃ) father, the lion of men." "Where is your (tuyhaṃ) mother?" "The gift should be given to me (mayhaṃ) alone, not to others." "The gift should be given to my (mayhaṃ) disciples alone, not to others." "She is not my (mayhaṃ) wife." "The hermitage is well-made for me (mayhaṃ)." "Omniscience is dear to me (mayhaṃ)." "Dear son, my (mayhaṃ) mother's face is of one kind, your (tumhākaṃ) mother's face is of another." "My (mayhaṃ) husband will die now." "It is given to you (tava)." "It is praised to you (tava)." "It is praised to me (mama)." "Going forth is pleasing to me (mama)." "Your (tava) son." "Both mother and father are mine (mama)." Thus, they occur without a fixed rule.

For in the Cūḷanirutti text, the Great Elder Yamaka stated the lack of distinction between the dative and genitive cases: "The dative and genitive are indistinct in all places; the instrumental and ablative cases..."
388:
"...and the plural form as well," (he says). If this is so, when the Commentators say in such passages as "Namo te purisājañña" and "Namo te buddha vīratthu" that there is the dative sense of "to you" by the power of the word 'tuyhaṃ', and in such passages as "Kiṃ te vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ" that there is the genitive sense of "your" by the power of the word 'tava', would they not arrive at the point of saying, "They have given an improper explanation," or "They did not see what should be seen"? They indeed explained properly, and they saw what should be seen. For those teachers, thinking "The science of grammar (saddasattha) is also partially conducive to the Dispensation (sāsana)," took the method from the science of grammar out of compassion for others and explained the meanings of the words 'te' and 'me' as "to you, to me" by way of the dative sense, and as "your, my" by way of the genitive sense. Indeed, in the science of grammar, the forms of the dative and genitive are entirely different, but in the Dispensation, they are similar. Therefore, by making the dative and genitive forms that occur generally in the Dispensation consistent with the dative and genitive forms that occur specifically in the science of grammar, they showed the fixed rule of the occurrence of the words 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ' in the dative sense, and the fixed rule of the occurrence of the words 'tava' and 'mama' in the genitive sense, out of compassion for others. Since this rule exists because of compassion for others, this is only a 'fault' of compassion, not a fault of the Commentators. It was because of that very compassion that they made such an explanation.

In this matter, some might say: "Sirs, is it not possible to say that the Commentators, relying on the method of grammar, showed the method of the interchange of cases (vibhattivipallāsa) in genitive contexts such as 'tuyhaṃ maṃsena medena' and 'na mayhaṃ bhariyā esā' by stating the meaning as 'your, my' when the words 'te' and 'me' occur in the genitive sense? Likewise, relying on that same grammatical method, when the words 'te' and 'me' are in the dative sense..."
389:
Can it be asserted that the method of case substitution (vibhaktivipallāsa) is demonstrated in dative contexts (sampadāna), such as in the phrases 'Food is not pleasing to you (tuyhaṃ)' and 'Going forth is pleasing to me (mayhaṃ)', using the words 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ' in the sense of 'yours' and 'mine'? It cannot be so asserted. Because, just as in verses (gāthā), in prose (cuṇṇiya) as well, the words 'tuyhaṃ', 'mayhaṃ', 'tava', and 'mama' occur in both senses without a fixed rule. In such instances, whether in verse or prose, case substitution is not to be accepted. It is only in such contexts as 'I am afraid of that kingship (tassa rajjassa)' or 'Why do I fear that happiness?' that case substitution is to be accepted.

If, based on grammatical methods, case substitution were desired in 'tuyhaṃ maṃsena medena' (with your flesh and fat), etc., then in phrases like 'He gives a beloved son to the brahmin' or 'The father of the brahmin gives', one would have to state the sense of case substitution as 'brāhmaṇāya', etc., based on grammatical methods. This is because dative (catutthī) and genitive (chaṭṭhī) forms are treated separately in the treatises. If it is asked, 'What is the fault in this?', there is indeed a fault. The reason is that dative-genitive forms ending in the substitute '-āya' (āya-ādesa), whether associated with giving (dāna) or salutation (namo), are not found in the Buddha’s word of the Tipiṭaka along with the Commentaries. Therefore, in stating the sense of case substitution as 'brāhmaṇāya', etc., there is the fault of apprehending what is non-existent as existent. Since performing case substitution in such places is faulty, case substitution is not to be accepted in 'tuyhaṃ maṃsena medena', etc., either.

Dative and genitive forms are seen to be identical, as in 'He gives to the man (purisassa)', 'The man’s wealth (purisassa)', 'He gives to the brahmins (brāhmaṇānaṃ)', and 'The brahmins’ property (brāhmaṇānaṃ)'. Thus, in the Pali scriptures, that word 'naṃ' [suffix] occurs in both the dative and genitive senses...
390:
...generally occur. This occurrence should be demonstrated by such usages as 'The wise one is a giver of the best (aggassa dātā medhāvī)'. In this context of 'aggassa dātā medhāvī', when the word 'aggassa' occurs in the dative sense depending on the recipient of the action, it occurs with the meaning 'a giver to the supreme Triple Gem'. When it occurs in the genitive sense as the object depending on the action, it occurs with the meaning 'a giver of the supreme gift-object'. Thus, in every respect, case substitution is not your refuge.

Similarly, since the word 'mayhaṃ', which you firmly hold to be a 'dative expression' based on grammatical methods, is found in the sense of possession (sāmi) in the context of a designation (paṇṇatti), case substitution is certainly not your refuge. That is true: 'There is a bird named Mayhaka that wanders in the mountain clefts. Having climbed a ripe pipphalī tree, it cries out, "Mine, mine!" (mayhaṃ, mayhaṃ)'. In this context, 'Mayhaka' is the name of a certain species of bird. Because it wanders with great greed, crying 'This too is mine, this too is mine', it is called 'Mayhaka'. It is formed by the power of the root 'ke, re, ge' [meaning 'to sound'] with the word 'mayhaṃ' as a prefix.

The examination of the term in this regard is as follows: If the words 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ' were fixed only in the dative sense, and the words 'tava' and 'mama' were fixed only in the genitive sense, then the All-Knowing One, who is skilled in worldly parlance, would not have given the designation 'Mayhaka' to that bird, as it would be subsumed under the dative sense. Instead, because it is subsumed under the genitive sense, the designation should have been 'Mamaka'. If it is argued here that 'Mayhaka' is stated by way of case substitution, it is not so; for in the sphere of designation, there is no ground or opportunity for the transformation of cases. Furthermore, in this instance, the word 'mayhaṃ' remains in its original form as a case-ending word because it has become a single term with the word 'ka'. Even so...
391:
...this word 'Mayhaka', which denotes this particular bird, while standing in the nominative case (paccatta), also indicates a slight sense of possession (sāmi), just like the words 'Sujampati' and 'Rājapurisa'. For this reason as well, case substitution (vibhaktivipallāsa) is not your refuge. Thus, it is established that because the word 'mayhaṃ', which is a component of the designation 'Mayhaka', is stated without case substitution, case substitution is not to be accepted in the words 'tuyhaṃ', 'tava', and 'mama' either. Therefore, it should be understood that the Commentarial teachers, out of compassion for others and based only on grammatical methods, demonstrated the aforementioned rule (niyama) for the words 'tuyhaṃ', 'mayhaṃ', 'tava', and 'mama', which are otherwise identical and generally occur in both dative and genitive senses.

"Teachers spoke of 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ' in the dative sense.
They spoke of 'tava' and 'mama' in the genitive sense, taking the method from the scriptures.
Even so, there is no [strict] rule for these in the Pali.
We have seen some distinction among them; listen to that.
Where both genitive and dative senses are possible—
Usages of 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ' are not difficult to find.
The words 'tava' and 'mama' mostly occur in the genitive.
But usages of those words in the dative are few.
In the Dispensation, rather than 'tava' and 'mama', it is 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ'—
That occur in the genitive sense in many thousands of Pali passages."

All these methods are extremely subtle and difficult to see; they should be carefully reflected upon by one of energetic nature.

Among the words 'vo' and 'no', the word 'vo' is found in the nominative (paccatta), accusative (upayoga), instrumental (karaṇa), dative (sampadāna), and genitive (sāmi) cases, as well as in the sense of an expletive (padapūraṇa). "Kacci vo...
392:
The word 'vo' is found in the sense of the nominative (paccatta) in such passages as 'Anuruddhā samaggā sammodamānā' (Anuruddhas, being in harmony and rejoicing). It is found in the sense of the accusative (upayoga) in such passages as 'Gacchatha bhikkhave paṇāmemi vo' (Go, monks, I dismiss you). It is found in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa) in such passages as 'Na vo mama santike vatthabbaṃ' (You should not live in my presence). It is found in the sense of the dative (sampadāna) in such passages as 'Vanapatthapariyāyaṃ vo bhikkhave desessāmi' (Monks, I shall preach the Discourse on the Forest Thicket to you). It is found in the sense of the genitive (sāmi) in such passages as 'Sabbesaṃ vo Sāriputta subhāsitaṃ' (Sāriputta, the speech of all of you is well-spoken). It is found in the sense of a mere expletive (padapūraṇa) in such passages as 'Ye hi vo ariyā parisuddhā kāyakammantā' (Those noble ones who have pure bodily actions...).

In the nominative, the accusative, the instrumental, the dative,
In the genitive, and likewise in the expletive—
In these six instances, the word 'vo' occurs.

The word 'no' occurs in the sense of the nominative, accusative, instrumental, dative, genitive, emphasis (avadhāraṇa), the meaning of the word 'nu' (interrogative), negation (paṭisedha), and as a mere particle (nipātamatta). This word 'no' is found in the nominative sense in this instance: 'Gāmaṃ no gaccheyyāma' (We shall go to the village). It is found in the accusative sense in such passages as 'Mā no ajja vikantiṃsu, rañño sūdā mahānase' (Let the king's cooks not cut us up today in the kitchen). It is found in the instrumental sense in such passages as 'Na no vivāho nāgehi, katapubbo kudācanaṃ' (Marriage with the Nāgas was never performed by us at any time). It is found in the dative sense in such passages as 'Saṃvibhajetha no rajjena' (Divide the kingdom for us). It is found in the genitive sense in such passages as 'Satthā no bhagavā anuppatto' (The Blessed One, our teacher, has arrived). It is found in the sense of emphasis in this instance: 'Na no samaṃ atthi tathāgatena' (There is indeed no one equal to the Tathāgata). It may also be said to be in the sense of an inquiry (pucchā), which is the meaning of the word 'nu', in such passages as 'Abhijānāsi no tvaṃ mahārāja' (Do you know, O Great King?). It is found in the sense of negation (paṭisedha) in such passages as 'Subhāsitaññeva bhāseyya, no ca dubbhāsitaṃ bhaṇe' (One should speak only what is well-spoken, and should not speak what is ill-spoken). It is found as a mere particle in such passages as 'Na no sabhāyaṃ na karonti kiñci' (They do not do anything in our assembly).
393:
The word 'no' occurs in the nominative (paccatta), the accusative (upayoga),
The instrumental (karaṇa), the dative (sampadāna),
The genitive (sāmi), the emphasis (avadhāraṇa/ablative),
In the sense of the word 'nu', in prohibition,
And likewise as a mere particle.

Now, the mixed paradigm (missaka-padamālā) of all pronouns will be stated briefly as appropriate:

Yo so (He who), ye te (They who). Yaṃ taṃ (That which [acc.]), ye te (Those which [acc.]). Yena tena (By him who). The rest should be expanded. Yā sā, yā tā. Yaṃ taṃ, yā tā. Yāya tāya. The rest should be expanded. Yaṃ taṃ, yāni tāni. The rest should be expanded. In this manner, the application in the three genders should be made.

One should apply the paradigm according to usage as: 'Eso so, ete te. Ayaṃ so, ime te. So ayaṃ, te ime,' and so forth. For instance, various usages are seen such as: 'Yo so bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako' (He who is the Blessed One, self-become, without a teacher); 'Ete te bhikkhave ubho ante anupagamma majjhimā paṭipadā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā' (Monks, there is this Middle Way, realized by the Tathāgata without approaching these two extremes); 'Ayaṃ so sārathi eti' (This charioteer comes). Thus, the mixed paradigm of pronominal terms should be applied.

In the Dispensation of the All-Seeing One who has accomplished all goals,
For the sake of the listeners' proficiency in the Dispensation,
Together with non-pronominal nouns and pronominal terms,
I have spoken all pronouns in their proper order.

For those who apply themselves to these pronouns, the understanding of the subtle meaning
Will be achieved through penetration without difficulty; of this there is no doubt.

## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise composed for the sake of the proficiency of the wise
## in the linguistic paths of the Three Pitakas together with their commentaries,
## the twelfth chapter, called the Analysis of the Declension of Nouns Similar to Pronouns,
## is completed.
394:
## 13. The Declension of Numerals with Analysis

Henceforth, I shall speak of the series of numeral nouns,
To be joined with forms derived from the root bhū and with others.

Previously, we have stated the declension of the pronominal numerals 'eka' (one), 'dvi' (two), 'ti' (three), and 'catu' (four). Setting those pronouns aside, the declension of non-pronominal numeral nouns such as 'pañca' (five), 'cha' (six), 'satta' (seven), etc., is stated here for the purpose of joining them with forms derived from the root bhū and others:

Pañca (five), pañcahi, pañcabhi, pañcannaṃ, pañcasu. It should be understood by means of the seven cases. It should be applied in all instances such as: 'pañca bhūtā' (five elements), 'pañca abhibhavitāro' (five conquerors), 'pañca purisā' (five men), 'pañca bhūmiyo' (five grounds), 'pañca kaññāyo' (five maidens), 'pañca bhūtāni' (five beings), 'pañca cittāni' (five consciousnesses). Cha (six), chahi, chabhi, channaṃ, chasu; also 'chassu'.
