For there is the Pali: 'Chassu loko samuppanno' (The world arises in the six [bases]), 'Chassu kubbati santhavaṃ' (He makes acquaintance with the six [bases]). Satta (seven), sattahi, sattabhi, sattannaṃ, sattasu. Aṭṭha (eight), aṭṭhahi, aṭṭhabhi, aṭṭhannaṃ, aṭṭhasu. Nava (nine), navahi, navabhi, navannaṃ, navasu. Dasa (ten), dasahi, dasabhi, dasannaṃ, dasasu. Similarly, ekādasa (eleven). Dvādasa, bārasa (twelve). Terasa, tedasa, teḷasa (thirteen). Catuddasa, cuddasa (fourteen). Pañcadasa, pannarasa (fifteen). Soḷasa (sixteen). Sattarasa (seventeen). Aṭṭhārasa (eighteen), aṭṭhārasahi, aṭṭhārasabhi, aṭṭhārasannaṃ, aṭṭhārasasu. All these should be taken in the plural sense.

Ekūnavīsati, ekūnavīsaṃ (nineteen), and so forth also exist. Ekūnavīsāya, ekūnavīsāyaṃ. 'Ekūnavīsa bhikkhū tiṭṭhanti' (Nineteen monks stand), 'Ekūnavīsaṃ bhikkhū passati' (He sees nineteen monks). Thus it should be applied with 'kaññāyo', 'cittāni', and so forth. 'Ekūnavīsāya bhikkhūhi dhammo desito' (The Dhamma was preached by nineteen monks), 'Ekūnavīsāya kaññāhi kataṃ' (It was done by nineteen maidens), 'Ekūnavīsāya cittehi kataṃ' (It was done by nineteen consciousnesses), 'Ekūnavīsāya bhikkhūnaṃ cīvaraṃ deti' (He gives a robe to nineteen monks), 'Ekūnavīsāya kaññānaṃ dhanaṃ deti' (He gives wealth to nineteen maidens), 'Ekūnavīsāya cittānaṃ ruccati' (It is pleasing to nineteen consciousnesses), 'Ekūnavīsāya bhikkhūhi'...
395:
There is the word 'apeti'. In this way, it is expressed with various inflections like the word 'kaññā'. Because it belongs to nineteen monks, it becomes 'ekūnavīsāya bhikkhūnaṃ santakaṃ'. In this way, it is expressed with various inflections like the word 'kaññā'. Because it is established in nineteen monks, it becomes 'ekūnavīsāyaṃ bhikkhūsu patiṭṭhitaṃ'. In this way, it should be applied as 'kaññāsu cittesu'. (The declensions are) ekūnavīsati, ekūnavīsatiṃ, ekūnavīsatiyā, ekūnavīsatiyaṃ.

Vīsati, vīsatiṃ, vīsatiyā, vīsatiyaṃ. Vīsa, vīsaṃ, vīsāya, vīsāyaṃ. Similarly, in ekavīsa, dvāvīsa, bāvīsa, tevīsa, catuvīsa, etc., (the declensions are the same). Tiṃsa, tiṃsaṃ, tiṃsāya, tiṃsāyaṃ. Cattālīsa, cattālīsaṃ, cattālīsāya, cattālīsāyaṃ. There are also forms like cattārīsa, etc. Paññāsa, paññāsaṃ, paññāsāya, paññāsāyaṃ. Paṇṇāsa, paṇṇāsaṃ, paṇṇāsāya, paṇṇāsāyaṃ. Saṭṭhi, saṭṭhiṃ, saṭṭhiyā, saṭṭhiyaṃ. Sattati, sattatiṃ, sattatiyā, sattatiyaṃ. There are also forms like sattari, etc. Asīti, asītiṃ, asītiyā, asītiyaṃ. Navuti, navutiṃ, navutiyā, navutiyaṃ.

In this manner, or by other methods, numerical forms should be taken. There are also forms like ekūnavīsehi, ekūnavīsānaṃ, ekūnavīsesu. Because numerical forms like 'channavutīnaṃ' are found in some places, some grammarians always use the word 'ūnavīsati' only as a feminine gender ending in the singular. Some teachers say, 'Numbers starting from vīsati up to ninety-nine (ānavuti) are feminine genders ending in the singular.' However, some teachers say:

'The words vīsati and so on stand in the singular in the sense of the thing to be numbered (saṅkhyeyya) and the number (saṅkhyā). But in the sense of number, those feminine words up to ninety-nine also stand in the dual and plural.'

In this regard, the dual number (dvivacana) should be discarded because it does not exist in the Buddha's words (Pali). The statements of all those teachers are appropriate when applied to certain Pali passages, but inappropriate when applied to others. Because words like vīsati, vīsaṃ, tiṃsaṃ, etc., which have the sense of number, are found in the Pali Canon even with plural usage...
396:
...because it is seen, and because in the Kaccāyana treatise, forms arising from the 'yo' inflection are seen (it is inappropriate). Therefore, as far as possible and in accordance with the Pali Canon, the singular ending of those numbers in the feminine gender should be understood, just like the words 'atthi' and 'natthi'.

Because the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' are indeclinables (nipāta), they occur in both singular and plural, such as in 'puttā matthi dhanammatthi' (sons are to me, wealth is to me), 'natthi attasamaṃ pemaṃ' (there is no love equal to oneself), 'natthi samaṇabrāhmaṇā' (there are no recluses and brahmins), etc. Although they have no gender, the feminine gender of these words is seen in some places. In the Abhidhamma, the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), the Follower of the Wheel of Dhamma (Anudhammacakkavatti), who is skilled in usage and who accomplishes skill in usage (Venerable Sāriputta), showed the feminine form ending in the singular as 'atthiyā nava, natthiyā navā' (nine in atthi, nine in natthi). Therefore, in vīsati, vīsatiṃ, etc., as far as possible and in accordance with the Pali Canon, the singular ending in the feminine gender should be understood.

In that regard, some teachers think that the usage 'hetuyā adhipatiyā' should be taken as a gender variation (liṅgavipallāsa). According to the view of those teachers, the masculine gender should be shown as 'hetumhi adhipatimhi', which has the same meaning as 'hetupaccaye adhipatipaccaye'. Alternatively, these two, 'hetuyā adhipatiyā', should be taken as masculine forms that resemble feminine forms. This is because there exist masculine forms that resemble feminine forms, such as 'hetuyo jantuyo', etc. However, the usage 'atthiyā natthiyā' should not be taken as being said by way of gender variation, because the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' have no gender distinction. Indeed, the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' are not included in any one of the three genders. Among those words, the word 'atthi' differs by way of being a verb (ākhyāta) and an indeclinable (nipāta). 'Atthi santi saṃvijjati' (it is, they are, it clearly exists), 'atthikhīrā' (there are milks)...
397:
...in words such as 'brāhmaṇī', the word 'natthi' is purely an indeclinable (nipāta). Thus, the explanation of the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' and other indeclinables by way of gender and number is appropriate, because they do not function by way of feminine gender, etc., or by way of singular number, etc. 

And it has been said:
'That which is the same in the three genders, in all case inflections, and in all numbers, and which does not change, is called an indeclinable (avyaya).'

In this matter, there might be a question: 'According to the statement that the words atthi, sakkā, labbhā are in the nominative (pathamā), is the word atthi not associated with the nominative case? If so, why is it said to be the same in the three genders, etc.?'

It is true; the word 'atthi' is associated with the nominative case. Similarly, the word 'natthi' is also associated with the nominative case because it should be taken as the remainder of the word 'atthi' and because they are a pair of words. However, this statement 'the same in the three genders', etc., is said with reference to the group of non-inflected words (asaṅkhyāsadda) known as prefixes (upasagga) and particles (nipāta), and not with reference to each individual non-inflected word.

Indeed, among the prefixes and particles that have received the designation 'asaṅkhyā' and 'avyaya', all prefixes possess all case inflections and numbers. Among the particles, however, some are associated with case inflections like the nominative as appropriate, while some are not associated with case inflections. Among those particles, to whatever extent they are associated with case inflections, to that extent they possess those numbers.

Although it is not possible to identify each individual prefix and particle as 'having this specific number', the former teachers spoke in a collective sense, saying 'the same in the three genders', etc. The teacher Kaccāyana also said, 'sabbāsamāvusopasagganipātādīhi ca', with reference to this very meaning. All case inflections are not obtained from the word 'āvuso'; rather, because it expresses the sense of address (ālapana), only the nominative cases in the singular and plural are obtained. This is our conviction (khanti).
398:
Some teachers assert that all case endings should be elided from all indeclinables (nipātas); this view should not be accepted. This is because of such statements as, "The words 'atthi', 'sakkā', and 'labbhā' exist in the nominative case (paṭhamā). The words 'divā', 'bhiyyo', and 'namo' exist in both the nominative and the accusative (dutiyā) cases," and because of the mention of indeclinables like "atha, khalu, vata, vatha" which merely fulfill the verse (pādapūraṇa) and are not associated with case endings.

In this regard, one might ask: "Venerable Sir, while there can be indeclinables not associated with case endings, why are the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' presented with case endings as 'atthiyā nava, natthiyā navā' instead of being presented without them?" It is because the meaning cannot be indicated in every respect without case endings.

If that is so, according to the statement, "The words 'atthi', 'sakkā', and 'labbhā' exist in the nominative case," the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' should be presented only as nominatives by virtue of the elided nominative case ending. Why then, instead of doing so, are they presented as locatives (sattami) as 'atthiyā' and 'natthiyā'?

It is true that the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' should be presented only in association with the nominative case. However, in explaining the meaning, "nine in the presence condition (atthi-paccaya), nine in the absence condition (natthi-paccaya)," there is no scope for the nominative, but there is scope only for the locative. Therefore, it is said, "atthiyā nava, natthiyā navā."

Thus, when the status of the words 'atthiyā' and 'natthiyā' as ending in the locative case is established, their status as ending in the instrumental (tatiyā), dative (catutthī), ablative (pañcamī), and genitive (chaṭṭhī) cases is also established. Therefore, in words such as 'atthibhāvo' and 'atthitā', the analysis of compounds (samāsa) and derivatives (taddhita) must necessarily be desired as 'atthiyā bhāvo atthibhāvo' (the state of being present), 'natthiyā bhāvo natthibhāvo' (the state of being absent), and 'atthiyā bhāvo atthitā'.

This statement of ours should not be said to "contradict the Pali Canon," because it is spoken in accordance with the methods of the Pali Canon.

Let it be so. Why, then, are 'atthiyā' and 'natthiyā' presented in the feminine gender? Are not indeclinables (nipātas) and prefixes (upasaggas) devoid of gender distinctions? It is true, but this point is extremely subtle. Nevertheless...
399:
Relying only on the authority of the former teachers, I shall state the decision. Just as the scholars of grammar (saddasattha) allow the feminine gender for numerals such as 'vīsati' (twenty), even though they do not inherently denote a substance (adabbavācaka), in the same way as words that do denote substances like 'latā', 'mati', 'ratti', 'itthī', 'yāgu', and 'vadhū'; so too, the scholars who know the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) allow the feminine gender for the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' in certain places. Therefore, the Venerable General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati Sāriputta) said: "atthiyā nava, natthiyā navā" (nine in the presence-section, nine in the absence-section).

Alternatively, these words 'atthiyā' and 'natthiyā' should be understood as indeclinable terms ending in the locative case that are free from the nature of gender. In this matter, one should not object, saying, "Such indeclinable terms were not spoken by the former teachers; therefore, this statement should be discarded."

For in the Dispensation (pāvacana), many various indeclinable terms are seen even if they were not specifically pointed out by the teachers. Nor should an objection be raised in cases such as "hetuyā, adhipatiyā, atthiyā, natthiyā" that "these are incorrect words (apasadda)." This is because in the words of the Buddha—who, with unimpeded knowledge produced by the merit of perfections (pāramitā) of inconceivable power, sees the entire range of knowable things as clearly as an emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) fruit on the palm of his hand—the linguistic lapses of others can certainly not be found.

Friends, one might ask: "These words 'hetuyā, adhipatiyā, atthiyā, natthiyā' are the words of the Elder Sāriputta, having been laid down by him. These terms did not exist when the Tathāgata preached in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. This being so, why do you call them 'the Word of the Buddha' (Buddhavacana)?" They are indeed the Word of the Buddha. For the method (naya) was given to the Venerable Sāriputta by the Tathāgata. He, the Chief Disciple, who had attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) and was like the Teacher himself, having received the method from the Teacher, properly formulated the phrasing (byañjana). Indeed, all the Noble Ones (ariyas) who have attained the analytical insights do not speak incorrectly (dunnirutti) because they are highly skilled in the science of language (nirutti-pabheda). Therefore, it should be understood that this is the usage of the Noble Ones, which is not the domain of others.
400:
## Now, the declension of the word 'sata' (one hundred) and others is stated:

Sataṃ, satāni, satā. Sataṃ, satāni, sate. Satena, satehi, satebhi. Satassa, satānaṃ. Satā, satasmā, satamhā, satehi, satebhi. Satassa, satānaṃ. Sate, satasmiṃ, satamhi, satesu. In this manner, 'sahassaṃ' (one thousand) and 'sahassāni' should be declined. The same method applies to 'dasasahassaṃ' (ten thousand), 'satasahassaṃ' (one hundred thousand), and 'dasasatasahassaṃ' (one million). The usage here is: "sataṃ bhikkhū" (one hundred monks), "sataṃ itthiyo" (one hundred women), "sataṃ cittāni" (one hundred consciousnesses). "Bhikkhūnaṃ sataṃ" (a hundred of monks), "itthīnaṃ sataṃ" (a hundred of women), "cittānaṃ sataṃ" (a hundred of consciousnesses). In the case of 'sahassa' and other words, the method is the same. In this way and in other ways, the word-forms occur. The words 'koṭi', 'koṭī', and 'koṭiyo' (crore) should be understood according to the method of the word 'ratti'.

The teachers said that numerals from one up to ten primarily denote the object numbered (saṅkhyeyya).

They explained that numerals from twenty up to one hundred primarily denote both the number (saṅkhyā) and the object numbered (saṅkhyeyya).

Furthermore:
It should be indicated that numerals from twenty up to a crore (koṭi) primarily denote both the number (saṅkhyā) and the object numbered (saṅkhyeyya).

Therefore, the Pali is seen as: "asīti koṭiyo hitvā, hiraññassāpi pabbaji" (Having abandoned eighty crores of gold and silver, he went forth), and "khīṇāsavā vītamalā, samiṃsu satakoṭiyo" (One hundred crores of stainless Arahants assembled).

In this place, for the purpose of clarifying all numeral word-forms so that the wise may obtain subtle knowledge, I shall bring forth and show the Udāna Pali passage along with its commentary, as well as other Pali passages and commentary statements.
401:
“Visākhā, those who have a hundred dear ones have a hundred sufferings. Those who have ninety... eighty... seventy... sixty... fifty... forty... thirty dear ones. Visākhā, those who have twenty dear ones have twenty sufferings. Those who have ten... nine... eight... seven... six... five... four... three... two dear ones. Those who have one dear one have one suffering.” (said the Buddha).

In this passage, 'sataṃ piyāni' means a hundred objects that are loved and cherished. Some also read it as 'sataṃ piyaṃ'. Here, from one to ten, because the counted object (saṅkhyeyya) is primary, the Pāḷi appears as 'yesaṃ dasa piyāni, dasa tesaṃ dukkhāni' and so on. However, some read it as 'yesaṃ dasa piyānaṃ, dasa tesaṃ dukkhānaṃ', but such a reading is not good. From twenty to a hundred, both the counted object (saṅkhyeyya) and the number (saṅkhyā) can be primary; therefore, even there, taking only the counted object as primary, the Pāḷi appears as 'yesaṃ kho visākhe sataṃ piyāni, sataṃ tesaṃ dukkhāni' and so on. In all versions, it should only be 'yesaṃ ekaṃ piyaṃ, ekaṃ tesaṃ dukkhaṃ' and not 'dukkhassa'. This is because in a single sequence of words, the Buddha's teaching has a single flavor. Therefore, the Pāḷi should be understood according to the method mentioned. This is a portion of the Udāna Pāḷi along with its Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).

Now, another portion of the Pāḷi and the portion on the method of reading the Commentary will be presented:
402:
“A hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred chariots drawn by mules, a hundred thousand maidens wearing gem-earrings—these are not worth even a sixteenth part of a single step (of one who perceives the Dhamma).” Thus it appears in the Pāḷi.

In this context, 'sataṃ hatthī' and so on are the terms to be qualified, and 'sahassāni' is the qualifier. Therefore, the word 'sata' should be combined with the word 'sahassa', and 'hatthī' and so on should be treated as prefix-words (upapada) to understand the meaning. (That is to say) a hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses, a hundred thousand chariots drawn by mules, and a hundred thousand maidens wearing gem-earrings. This is the interpretation according to the counted object (saṅkhyeyya) being primary. According to the number (saṅkhyā) being primary, the meaning can also be taken as: 'a hundred thousand of elephants, a hundred thousand of horses, a hundred thousand of chariots drawn by mules, and a hundred thousand of maidens wearing gem-earrings.' This method should be applied in other similar instances.

'The Himavā, a hundred yojanas high, having five mountains'—this is the reading of the Commentary. Here, the word 'pañca' should be combined with the word 'sata', and as in the phrase 'sippikānaṃ sataṃ natthi', the meaning should be taken according to the number being primary as 'the Himavā mountain is five hundred yojanas high.' The term 'pañca satāni' is also in the accusative case (upayogavacana) by way of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga) of distance. This method should be applied in other similar instances.

The word 'sataṃ' is singular in such phrases as 'sataṃ homi, sahassaṃ homi'. It is plural in such phrases as 'atthetthekasataṃ khatyā, anuyantā yasassino'. Thus, the singular and plural nature of words like 'sahassa' can also be found. That this is so should be understood from the fact that in 'bhiyyo naṃ satasahassaṃ, yakkhānaṃ payirupāsati', 'satasahassaṃ' is singular, and in 'parosahassaṃ kho panassa puttā bhavissanti', 'sahassaṃ' is plural.
403:
“A hundred thousand eons and four incalculables ago, there was a city named Amara, beautiful and delightful to the heart.” Thus it appears in the Pāḷi. Here, in “kappe ca satasahasse caturo ca asankhiye,” the plural accusative (upayoga) case is used in the sense of the genitive (sāmī). Therefore, the meaning should be taken as “at the end of a hundred thousand great eons and four incalculables.” The word “matthake (at the end)” is an elliptical term remaining in this sentence. “At the end of four incalculables plus a hundred thousand eons” is also this same meaning. This method should be understood in other such instances.

“A hundred thousand eons and four incalculables—whatever conduct was practiced during this interval, all of it was for the maturing of enlightenment (bodhipācana).” Thus it appears in the Pāḷi. Here, “kappe” is the plural accusative case in the sense of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga) expressing time. Because it is connected with the word 'kappa', “satasahasse kappe” is a masculine usage and an accusative usage. This term is in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) with the word 'kappa'. “Caturo ca asankhiye” are also plural accusative cases in the sense of continuous connection. If one asks, “incalculables of what?”—since nothing else is mentioned and eons (kappa) are mentioned, the meaning is understood by context as “incalculables of eons.” For it is not proper to set aside what has been mentioned and take something else that has not been mentioned. The word 'ca' expresses the sense of collection (saṃpiṇḍana) as in “in four incalculables of great eons and a hundred thousand great eons.” This method should be understood in other such instances.

“Many thousands of pots and many hundreds of water-jars (exist).” Thus it appears in the Pāḷi. Here, “ghaṭā” means “ghaṭānaṃ (of pots).” This nominative (paccatta) case is used in the sense of the genitive (sāmī). It means “many thousands of pots.” “Kumbhīnañca satā bahū” means many hundreds of water-jars. Here, it should be understood that the case ending (nikāra) has been elided. This method should be understood in other such instances.
404:
“The realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) occurred for ten thousand and twenty thousand beings. The realization of the Dhamma for one or two, however, is incalculable (asaṅkheyya) by count,” so it is stated in the Pāḷi. Here, ‘dasa-vīsa-sahassānaṃ’ means for ten thousand and twenty thousand. ‘Dhammābhisamaya’ means the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. ‘Eka-dvinnāṃ’ is a mention of only the peak; by such a mention, it means an incalculable number in sequence, such as ‘one, two, three, four... ten,’ and so on. This method should also be understood in other such instances.

“Four hundred thousand Arahants of great power, possessing the six supernormal knowledges, always surround Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World,” so it is stated in the Pāḷi. Here, although the word ‘cattāri satasahassāni’ differs in gender, it is in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) with these two words, ‘chaḷabhiññā mahiddhikā.’ For in such instances, even a word expressing an incalculable number tends to be only in the neuter gender; therefore, these three words—‘cattāri satasahassāni,’ ‘chaḷabhiññā,’ and ‘mahiddhikā’—are in coordinate relation (samānādhikaraṇa). Alternatively, ‘chaḷabhiññā mahiddhikā’ should be regarded as the nominative case (paccatta) used in the sense of the possessive genitive (sāmī), meaning ‘of the powerful Arahants possessing the six supernormal knowledges.’ In this sense, ‘cattāri satasahassāni’ becomes the word expressing the number. This same method should be applied in instances such as ‘three hundred thousand well-adorned women.’

“And those seven hundred wives, and seven hundred female slaves,” so it is stated in the Pāḷi. Here, ‘satā’ should be taken as ‘satāni’ in the neuter gender; it should not be taken as feminine. ‘Satā’ is merely a neuter form like ‘pañca cittā vipākā,’ etc. Just as there is no word ‘sata’ that is feminine, there is also no word ‘sata’ that is masculine. If the word ‘sata’ had two genders...
405: If it were so, then like the words ‘puriso’ (man) and ‘kaññā’ (maiden), there should also be masculine forms ending in ‘o’ and feminine forms ending in ‘ā’ for the word ‘sata.’ Neither of these two forms exists for the word ‘sata’; therefore, it is known that ‘the word sata is strictly neuter.’ O friend, in this passage ‘tā devatā sattasatā uḷārā,’ is the word ‘sata’ not seen as feminine? No, it is only neuter. O friend, is it not in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) with the word ‘devatā’? True, it is in apposition, yet it is still only neuter. In such numerical contexts, being in apposition is not a reason (for gender agreement). For instance, in the passage ‘pañca paccekabuddhasatāni imasmiṃ isigilismiṃ pabbate ciravāsino ahesuṃ,’ one sees the neuter gender in apposition with the masculine. Therefore, in this passage ‘tā devatā sattasatā uḷārā,’ it should be understood as only the neuter gender, as in ‘sattasatāni.’ In instances such as ‘satta hatthisate datvā,’ the word ‘sata’ is also only neuter. This method should be applied in other such instances as well. In the Pāḷi ‘navutikoṭisahassehi, parivāresi mahāmunī,’ the meaning should be taken according to whether the numbered or the number is primary, as in ‘by ninety thousand crores of monks’ (navutikoṭisahassehi bhikkhūhi) or ‘by ninety thousand crores of monks’ (bhikkhūnaṃ navutikoṭisahassehi). This method should be applied in other such instances as well. In the Pāḷi ‘satasahassavassāni, āyu tassa mahesino,’ the word ‘satasahassavassāni’ is in the accusative case (upayogavacana) by way of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga). Likewise, it is so in the Pāḷi ‘dasa vassasahassāni, agāramajjhe so vasī.’ This method should be applied in other such instances as well.
406:
In the Pāḷi ‘ito satasahassami, kappe uppajji nāyako’ and ‘ekanavute ito kappe,’ the phrase ‘satasahassami kappe’ means at the end (completion) of a hundred thousand aeons. ‘Ekanavute kappe’ means at the end of ninety-one aeons; thus the locative case (bhumma) should be understood in the sense of the genitive-locative (sāmibhumma). This is just as in the passage ‘bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati,’ where the locative case is understood in the sense of the genitive-locative as ‘in the presence of the Blessed One.’ This method should be applied in other such instances as well.

“If there be thousands, hundreds, and millions there; no fear at all for us exists in the forest among wild beasts.” The meaning of this Pāḷi is: if there be thousands, hundreds, and millions of fierce wild beasts in that forest. Alternatively, ‘sahassāni satāni’ means the number one hundred thousand; if there be a hundred thousand and millions of wild beasts. Even if such wild beasts exist, ‘koci’ means ‘kvaci’ (in any place). For the word ‘koci’ functions in the sense of ‘kva,’ just as the word ‘ko’ does in ‘ko te balaṃ mahārājā,’ and this expression is in the causal sense (nimitta). Therefore, the meaning should be taken as: ‘In any place, regarding any wild beast, or because of even a single wild beast, no fear exists for us.’ Alternatively, ‘koci’ means even a little. Here, ‘vāḷesu’ is the locative case in the causal sense (nimitta). It means that because of wild beasts, not even a little fear exists for us. This method should be applied in other such instances as well. “All a hundred thousand, thirty-six in circumference, and ten thousand, and three and a half hundred...”
407:
The Commentary passage: In this context, words that are identical in terms of sound (grammar)—such as case-ending (vibhatti), gender (liṅga), and number (vacana)—or words that are different in case-ending, gender, and number but identical in meaning, may have a single connection (sambandha) even if they are positioned far apart. Other words, however, may not have a connection even if they are positioned close together. Therefore, the word 'sabbaṃ' should be connected with 'parimaṇḍalaṃ'. The word 'chattiṃsā', however, should be connected with 'satasahassāni'. This method should also be applied in other similar instances.

"Two hundred thousand and forty thousand; this earth is said to have this much thickness."
This is the Commentary passage. Here, 'duve' is the qualifier (visesana), and 'satasahassāni' is the qualified (visesitabba). Similarly, 'cattāri' is the qualifier, and 'nahutāni' is the qualified. This is because, as the words 'satasahassāni' and 'nahutāni' are qualified by 'duve' and 'cattāri', they express the meaning of 'two hundred and forty thousand'. Even so, the ancient teachers did not state that numerical terms like 'duve' etc., are in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) with numerical terms like 'satasahassāni' etc. This is because in instances such as 'duve puthujjanā vuttā' (two worldlings are mentioned) or 'satasahassaṃ bhikkhū' (one hundred thousand monks), the qualified words denote substances (dabba), and thus apposition is obtained. However, in instances such as 'duve satasahassāni', the qualified words do not denote substances, and thus they are not in apposition. Therefore, in such instances, apposition is not desired as there is no logical basis (yutti) for it. If it were so, one might ask if these words are devoid of mutual connection like 'kusalā', 'rūpaṃ', 'cakkhumā', etc.? No, they are not, because they are taken in the relationship of qualifier and qualified. If that is the case, one might ask if the state of apposition is obtained? No, it is not obtained, because it is not an absolute rule. In fact...
408:
...because the state of apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) exists only between the quality (guṇa) and the possessor of quality (guṇī) which are qualifier and qualified; it does not exist in other words even if they are in a qualifier-qualified relationship.

In that context, 'ettakaṃ' is a term expressing magnitude (pamāṇa). 'Bahalattena' is the third case-ending (instrumental) used in the sense of qualification. By both terms, this meaning is shown: "This earth is said to be this much, namely two hundred thousand and forty thousand yojanas, in thickness." The state of apposition of the word 'ettakaṃ' with the words 'duve satasahassāni cattāri nahutāni ca' or with the word 'vasundharā' is not desired. For 'ettakaṃ' is an adverbial neuter (bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ), which is called an adverb (kriyāvisesana) in grammatical treatises. Its meaning is simply 'by this much magnitude'. Furthermore, the apposition of the words 'duve satasahassāni cattāri nahutāni ca' with the word 'vasundharā' is also not desired, because they are merely expressions of number, like the word 'sata' in 'bhikkhūnaṃ sataṃ' (a hundred of monks). For that very reason, it is said 'ettakaṃ'. However, the state of apposition of the words 'saṅkhātā' and 'ayaṃ' with the word 'vasundharā' is obtained. This entire method should be applied in other similar instances.

"In this place, there are ten white, beautiful, and delightful stripes. There are six and fifteen reddish-yellow stripes. There are fourteen yellow stripes."
This is the Pali text. Here, 'cha piṅgalā pannarasā' should be understood to mean twenty-one reddish-yellow stripes, by adding six and fifteen.

Likewise:
"To him, there were also many sons; 'they have a single name,' so I have heard. There were eighty, ten, and one sons of great power named Inda."
Such is the passage.
409:
In this context, where it should be said "ninety-one", it is said "eighty, ten, and one". Indeed, the Pali Canon taught by the Buddha has varied word arrangements (vicittasaddaracana). This method should also be applied in other similar instances.

"Thirty thousand and nine hundred men were assembled one by one. I have never seen anyone equal to them while wandering throughout this entire earth." Thus is the Pali.

In this context, it means "thirty thousand and nine hundred men are called 'tiṃsa nāvutyo'". In this instance, it should not be understood that 'tiṃsa nāvutyo' is said by eliding the word 'sahassa' from the word 'tiṃsa' and the word 'sata' from the word 'navuti'. If it were understood in this way, such a word arrangement would have to be made anywhere, and the meaning of such a word arrangement would not be known by those who hear it without a teacher's instruction (upadesa). Therefore, it should not be understood in that way. It should be understood only in this way: the expression 'tiṃsa nāvutyo' is a term of conventional worldly usage (saṅketa-rūḷha). Since the meaning of a conventional term is known by hearing it through previously established signs and not merely from formal instruction, it should be understood that all people knew the meaning of the word without instruction, both at the time it was spoken by King Brahmadatta and at the time the Teacher (the Buddha) brought forth that account and taught it.

Thirty thousand and nine hundred are called "tiṃsa nāvutiyo" in the Ummaṅga Jātaka.

In the Pali Canon taught by the Buddha, there are methods that are inconceivable and terms with very profound meanings, which were taught by the Buddha out of compassion for beings.

Therefore, a wise person should always receive the instruction (upadesa) in the profound Pali Canon of the Buddha along with its Commentary, while properly serving the teacher.

One who is devoid of the teacher's instruction cannot attain the essence of the meaning. Devoid of the essence of the meaning, that person falls away from the True Dhamma (Saddhamma).
410:
One who receives the teacher's instruction is endowed with the essence of meaning; while protecting the True Dhamma, such a person does not fall away from the True Dhamma.

Therefore, for the sake of the True Dhamma, I have also spoken the Saṅkhyāmālā (Garland of Numbers) according to the appropriate arrangement of words, together with the determination of meanings.

## Thus, for the sake of the proficiency of the wise in the matters of speech of the three Pitakas together with the Commentaries and the ninefold Dispensation,

## in the Saddanīti treatise which has been composed,

## the section named Nāmikapadamālā-vibhāga of the nouns of number together with their determination,

## the thirteenth chapter is finished.

## 14. Atthatthika-vibhāga

We have elaborated all these matters, taking as primary these two: the root bhū and the forms derived from that root bhū.

Now, I shall state the excellent classification of the three meanings (atthatthika) by virtue of the verb bhavati. In this work, there are three groups: the extraction of meanings (atthuddhāra), the tumanta words, and the tvādiyanta words.

Therefore, first, I shall demonstrate the extraction of the meanings of the word "bhūta" derived from the root bhū:

The word bhūta occurs in the sense of the aggregates, beings, humans, existence, elements, Arahants, trees, and so forth.

The wise should also understand the word bhūta in the sense of arising (uppāda). When this word bhūta occurs with a prefix (upasagga), it also occurs in the senses of abundance, contempt, destruction, defeat, experience, name, and manifestation.

Thus it is also said: The word bhūta is found in the sense of the five aggregates, humans, elements, existence, Arahants, beings, trees, and so forth. For in such passages as "Monks, see these five aggregates as what has come to be (bhūta)," this word bhūta is found in the sense of the five aggregates.
411:
In this Pali passage, "Yānīdha bhūtāni samāgatāni," (the word bhūta) refers to non-humans—spirits and ghosts. In this Pali passage, "Monks, the four great bhūtas are causes," it refers to the elements (dhātu). In such Pali passages as "There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) regarding a being that exists (bhūta)," it refers to existence (vijjamāna). In this Pali passage, "There is an Arahant (bhūta) who consumes time," it refers to an Arahant (khīṇāsava). In this Pali passage, "All beings (bhūta) in the world will lay down their bodies," it refers to beings (satta). In this Pali passage, "Because of the destruction of the plant community (bhūtagāma)," it refers to trees and so forth. This is the statement of the Mūlapariyāya Sutta Commentary. In the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā), however, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), arising (uppāda) and so forth should be taken.

Indeed—in such Pali passages as "born (jāta), become (bhūta), conditioned (saṅkhata)," the word bhūta is found in the sense of arising (uppāda). When it occurs with a prefix (upasagga), however—in such Pali passages as "The noble one performs much (pabhūta) merit," it is found in the sense of abundance (vipula). In such Pali passages as "Mostly, he has an appearance that is despised (paribhūta) by the monks," it is found in the sense of contempt (hīḷana). In such Pali passages as "Sāṇavāsī became manifest (sambhūta)," it is found in the sense of designation (paññatti). In such Pali passages as "Māra has been vanquished (abhibhūta), the battle has been won," it is found in the sense of crushing (vidhamana). In such Pali passages as "This naked ascetic Pāthikaputta has the appearance of one who is defeated (parābhūta)," it is found in the sense of defeat (parājaya). In such Pali passages as "Pleasure and pain have been experienced (anubhūta)," it is found in the sense of experiencing (vediyana). In such Pali passages as "It has been made clear (vibhūta) by wisdom," it is found in the sense of making manifest (pākaṭīkaraṇa). It should be understood that all those meanings are included by the word "and so forth" (ādi) in the phrase "in trees and so forth."

Now, the tumanta words shall be stated:
bhavituṃ, ubbhavituṃ, samubbhavituṃ, pabhavituṃ, parābhavituṃ, atibhavituṃ, sambhavituṃ, vibhavituṃ, bhotuṃ, sambhotuṃ, vibhotuṃ, pātubhavituṃ, pātubbhavituṃ or pātubhotuṃ. These are intransitive (akammaka) tumanta words.
412:
paribhotuṃ, paribhavituṃ, abhibhotuṃ, abhibhavituṃ, adhibhotuṃ, adhibhavituṃ, atibhotuṃ, atibhavituṃ, anubhotuṃ, anubhavituṃ, samanubhotuṃ, samanubhavituṃ, abhisambhotuṃ, abhisambhavituṃ. These are transitive (sakammaka) tumanta words. All these words occur in the sense of the simple agent (suddhakattu).

"bhāvetuṃ, pabhāvetuṃ, sambhāvetuṃ, vibhāvetuṃ, paribhāvetuṃ"—such words as these are tumanta words expressing the causal agent (hetukattu). All tumanta words expressing the causal agent are transitive (sakammaka) only. This is the brief exposition (uddesa).

Among those words, for those with the same meaning, only the first word should be taken to provide the detailed explanation (niddesa): bhavituṃ means to be (hotuṃ), to exist (vijjituṃ), to be known (paññāyituṃ), or to obtain its own nature (sarūpaṃ labhituṃ). According to the method stated here, the detailed explanation of the remaining tumanta words should also be expanded. All tumanta words occur in the sense of the dative case (catutthī), as in this Pali passage: "Having known my mind, you have come to ask (yācituṃ) for my eye." For yācituṃ means for the purpose of asking (yācanatthāya). Therefore, the meaning of such words as bhavituṃ should also be taken as "for the purpose of being" (bhavanatthāya), or "for the purpose of being" (bhavanatthaṃ), or "for being" (bhavanāya), and so forth.

Alternatively, since in the Pali passage "to see (daṭṭhu) renunciation (nekkhamma) as safety," the word daṭṭhu is seen to be interpreted as "having seen" (disvā), the tumanta words should also be taken according to the sense of words ending in the suffix -tvā as appropriate. These tumanta words are included among the indeclinables (nipāta). Indeed, in the Niruttipiṭaka, in the chapter on indeclinables, it is said: "The suffix -tuṃ occurs in the sense of the dative case." The meaning there is: "This indeclinable ending in -tuṃ occurs in the sense of the dative case."

## The Discussion on Tumanta is Finished.
413: Now, the words ending with the suffix -tvā and its variants will be discussed: bhavitvā, bhavitvāna, bhavituna, bhaviya, bhaviyāna. ubbhavitvā, ubbhavitvāna, ubbhavituna, ubbhaviya, ubbhaviyāna. The same method applies to these words: "samubbhavitvā, parābhavitvā, sambhavitvā, vibhavitvā, pātubbhavitvā." These are words ending in the suffix -tvā that are intransitive (akammaka) and carry the sense of endeavor (ussukkanattha). bhutvā, bhutvāna, paribhavitvā, paribhavitvāna, paribhavituna, paribhiya, paribhiyāna, paribhuyya. abhibhavitvā, abhibhavitvāna, abhibhavituna, abhibhaviya, abhibhaviyāna, abhibhuyya. The same method applies to these words: "adhibhavitvā, atibhavitvā, anubhavitvā." An example in this context is: "The king said to him, 'Having also experienced (anubhiyāna) that benefit, come back quickly; to whom shall I also perform an offering?'" anubhutvā, anubhutvāna. adhibhotvā, adhibhotvāna. "For sixty thousand aeons, he will delight in the celestial realm. Having surpassed (adhibhotvā) other devas, he will exercise sovereignty." This verse is the Pali evidence here. These are words ending in the suffix -tvā that are transitive (sakammaka) and carry the sense of endeavor. These four types occur only in the active agent (suddhakattar). "bhāvetvā, bhāvetvāna. pabhāvetvā, pabhāvetvāna. sambhāvetvā, sambhāvetvāna. vibhāvetvā, vibhāvetvāna. paribhāvetvā, paribhāvetvāna," and so on; these are transitive words ending in the suffix -tvā with the sense of endeavor, and they occur only in the causative agent (hetukattar). This is just a brief exposition. Among those words with the same meaning, taking only the first word to explain in detail: bhavitvā means having become, having appeared, or having obtained a form. According to the method already stated, the detailed explanation of the remaining words ending in the suffix -tvā should also be expanded and understood.
414: The distinction is as follows: the word bhutvā should be understood in the transitive (sakammaka) sense as "having enjoyed prosperity." The wise who know the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) desire the identity of meaning between the words bhutvā and anubhutvā. In this regard, it is said: "The words 'bhutvā' and 'bhutvāna' indicate only the meaning of 'anubhutvā.' They do not at all indicate the meaning of the word 'hutvā.'" Some teachers desire that word to be a long vowel (dīgha) as "bhūtvā" in the Dispensation (Sāsana). Both the long vowel and the short vowel (rassa) forms are found. In the science of grammar (saddasattha), however, the word associated with the long vowel as "bhūtvā" indicates the meaning of the word "bhavitvā," but not in the Dispensation. In the Dispensation of the Conqueror (Jinasāsana), it indicates only the word "hutvā." The meaning of the word "bhavitvā" does not exist in that word elsewhere. Thus, the wise who see the essence should examine the speech along with its distinctions in both the Dispensation and the science of grammar. In this way, the words ending in the suffix -tvā that occur in the sense of endeavor have also been explained. All these should be understood as indeclinable (avibhattika) words. Indeed, in the section on particles (nipātapariucheda) of the Niruttipiṭaka, words ending in the suffix -tvā are stated as being indeclinable. However, in the view of teachers who know the meaning of grammar, they are declinable (savibhattika) by way of the nominative case (paṭhamā-vibhatti) and so on. Furthermore, in this context of the suffix -tvā, this point should also be noted: bhutvā gacchati (having eaten, he goes), bhutvā gato (having eaten, he went), bhutvā gamissati (having eaten, he will go), kasitvā vapati (having plowed, he sows). umangā nikkhamitvāna, vedeho nāvamarūhi (having emerged from the tunnel, King Videha boarded the boat). bhutvāna bhikkhu bhikkhassu (O monk, having eaten, seek alms), and so forth, are usages of the suffix -tvā etc., in the prior time (pubbakāla) of roots having the same subject (samānakattuka). In the phrase "bhutvā gacchati," the word "bhutvā" is a word indicating the prior action. The word "gacchati" is a word indicating the subsequent action. These words have the same subject because they express actions of a single agent. Likewise, in this case, whichever...
415: ...is the agent of the action of going, that same one should be seen as the agent of the action of eating. This method should be applied in other such instances as well. "Having dispelled (nihantvāna) the darkness, this sun has risen. Having illuminated (obhāsetvā) the appearance with the light of wisdom, it has ascended." Such passages are also usages of the suffix -tvā etc., in the simultaneous time (samānakāla) of actions having the same subject. Here, the word "nihantvāna" is a word indicating a simultaneous action. The word "udito," however, should not be called a word indicating a subsequent action, because here only the simultaneous action is intended. Therefore, it should be taken only as a word indicating a simultaneous action. This method should be applied in other such instances as well. Some teachers, however, give examples such as: "mukhaṃ byādāya sayati" (opening the mouth, he sleeps), "akkhiṃ parivattetvā passati" (turning the eye, he looks). Others give: "nisajja adhīte" (sitting, he recites), "ṭhatvā katheti" (standing, he speaks). In those examples, the time following the opening of the mouth or the turning of the eye is marked by the action of looking, which is characterized by the subsiding of the opening. In the sentences "sitting, he recites" and "standing, he speaks," the state of prior and subsequent time can be conceived because of simultaneity, and also because sitting and standing can exist before the reciting and speaking. Therefore, only the previously mentioned examples are appropriate. This is because the dispelling of the darkness, which is to be dispelled by the rising of the sun, occurs exactly at the same time as the rising of the sun. "dvāramāvaritvā pavisati" (having closed the door, he enters) and so forth are usages of the suffix -tvā etc., in the subsequent time (aparakāla) of actions having the same subject. Since the action of entering is prior here, and the action of closing is subsequent, the word "āvaritvā" should be understood as a word indicating a subsequent action. The word "pavisati" is a word indicating a prior action. This...
416:
This method should also be applied in other such instances. Other teachers give the example: "The stick falls, making the sound 'dha'." Since the simultaneity of the sound produced by impact is obtained here, it should be noted that the previous examples are also appropriate in this case.

"Seeing the demon, fear arises in him. Seeing with wisdom, his taints are exhausted." These and similar instances are usages with different subjects. Here, seeing the demon, fear arises in the man; seeing with wisdom, the taints are exhausted in that person. Thus, it should be understood that the identity of the subject of the roots is not obtained, because the action of seeing occurs in the men, while the action of being, etc., occurs in fear, etc. This method should also be applied in other such instances.

This point should also be noted here: "Before reaching the river, there is a mountain; having crossed the mountain, the river flows." These and similar instances are usages of spatial and temporal sequence. "Seeing a lion, fear arises; drinking ghee, strength is produced; making the sound 'dha', the stick falls." These and similar instances are usages showing signs, causes, and so forth. "Going after bathing, sleeping after eating, depending on form (upādāya rūpaṃ)." These and similar instances are also linguistic accomplishments through grammatical variation.

Thus, in every way, there is the usage of the word 'tvā', etc., in the prior time of roots with the same subject, in the simultaneous time of roots with the same subject, in the subsequent time of roots with the same subject, and in the case of roots with different subjects.
417:
The usage of words ending in the suffix -tvā, etc., should be known in seven ways: spatial and temporal sequence, connection with signs and causes, etc., and linguistic accomplishment through variation.

If so, why in the Kaccāyana grammar is it taken as "in the prior time with a single subject" (pubbakālekakattukānaṃ tuna tvāna tvā ဝါ)? It is because, for the most part, words ending in the suffix -tvā, etc., indicate an action in the prior time. In the Kaccāyana treatise, "pubbakālekakattukānaṃ" is stated with reference to the most frequent occurrence. Since the meaning of words such as "iti katvā" is also explained by former teachers in the sense of cause (hetu-attha), therefore, in words ending in the suffix -tvā formed from the root bhū such as "bhavitvā", and others such as "pacitvā", the causal meaning should also be taken according to usage, such as "because of being," "because of cooking," and so forth. In this regard, it is said:

Since words having the sense of effort also occur in the causal sense,
Therefore, a wise person should also state the meaning by way of cause.
In the explanations of the meaning of the word "iti katvā",
The wise take the meaning as "because of doing so."
"I go now to Nibbāna, where because of going one does not sorrow."
In this text also, the causal sense is taken by the wise of old.
For it is said: "because of the going into that Nibbāna."
Thus, this method should be understood in other places as well, according to the causal sense.

In this way, the extraction of the meaning of the word bhū, the word ending in the suffix -tum, and the word ending in the suffix -tvā—this threefold collection of meanings—has been analyzed.
418:
Whoever bears in mind this well-analyzed collection of three meanings, which is like ear-drops for the ears of scholars, shall become one who is free from doubt regarding the Buddha's teachings that possess profound meanings.

## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the purpose of the wise becoming proficient in the linguistic usage of the Three Piṭakas together with the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) which have nine factors,
## the fourteenth chapter,
## named Atthattikavibhāga (The Analysis of the Three Meanings), is concluded.
## Thus, the various forms of the root bhū have been shown in various ways.
## The paradigm (padamālā) is finished.
